# TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS AND MOST POWERFUL STATES OF THE PROVINCE OF UTRECHT, FATHERS OF THE FATHERLAND.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'Q' containing floral and leaf patterns within the counter of the letter.</image-desc>

With your permission, **ILLUSTRIOUS NOBLES**, I come to interrupt your most weighty preoccupations. Indeed, no matter could have granted me such confidence, were I not approaching to plead the cause of God and Religion before you; than which no cause is more serious, none more worthy of your investigation and defense. I intend to speak in such a way that I do not seek my own interests, but rather make manifest those things which belong to God and Christ. Nor do I think I should fear that this will be less pleasing to you than if I were to attempt to force upon you some deception or flattery with far-fetched verbal allurements: a skill I have never learned, nor one which you, in your wisdom, would deem tolerable in a man of my station <note>The author refers to his role as a member of the clergy or a theologian</note>. He alone deserves the name of a Theologian <term>Theologian: literally "one who speaks of God"</term> who, on every given—indeed, even sought—occasion, speaks of God, from God, and for the glory of God, whether before the common people or before the Magistrates. Let me be permitted to do this now before you for a little while, **ILLUSTRIOUS NOBLES**. Just as nothing is more ancient or more sacred to a Christian heart than those volumes which were dictated by the inspiration of the Divine Spirit, by the wis—

# D E D I C A T I O N

<note>original: "Dedicatio"</note>

Just as these writings, composed long ago by the most learned and upright of men, have reached us through the long passage of centuries; so too has the most bitter enemy of the human race—and of the Divine glory—judged that they must be attacked, leveled, and overthrown with every kind of weapon, were he only able to do so. Indeed, pious men, upon whose minds the rays of a more sublime doctrine have shone, receive this incomparable heavenly deposit <note>The "deposit" refers to the Sacred Scriptures entrusted to the Church</note> not without a certain sacred awe. And just as they gratefully kiss the incredible goodness of the Divinity who deigns to instruct them with His own discourse, so it cannot be expressed with what great pleasure they gather the inestimable treasures of wisdom from that rich vein of secret volumes. From this source, it is a joy to learn—as if from a painted panel—the beginnings of things; the origins of nations; the start of the arts; the births of Kingdoms and Empires; the migrations and spread of peoples by which the world was gradually filled; the rudiments of laws, inscribed not on tablets or bronze, but in minds, or revealed by familiar oracles; and, what is the head of the matter, the most ancient institutions of religion by which the mortals of old piously worshipped the Divinity present among them; and finally, whatever exotic wisdom confesses is unknown to itself or suppressed by the dark night of fables. From here, it is a joy to perceive the singular benevolence of God toward Abraham, Isaac, and the latter's grandsons through Jacob; whom He set apart from the rest of the nations of the whole world and, with a strong hand and fearful portents, claimed for Himself after delivering them from Egyptian slavery; whom He fed, led, and ruled in a truly unusual manner as they wandered through the vast solitudes of the Arabs for forty whole years; to whom He promulgated His laws from the midst of thunders and lightnings, from the trembling, smoking, seething peak of Mount Sinai which could not bear the presence of God; to whom, through Moses, His necessary minister of intimate admission...

<summary>This dedication page extols the historical and spiritual value of the Holy Scriptures, describing them as a divine treasure that reveals the origins of civilization and the miraculous history of the Israelites.</summary>
<keywords>Divine glory, sacred history, origins of nations, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Exodus, Mount Sinai, Moses, providence</keywords>

# DEDICATION

...our [God], prefigured the entire appearance of His worship—a system indeed laborious and wonderful, yet utterly wise. It was not only tempered to the character of the people, but also pregnant with secret meanings. For this reason, they were bound to look up to it as a kind of school <note>Latin: gymnasium</note> for the greatest matters which were to be known, believed, and hoped for concerning the promised Messiah. It is also pleasing to be carried higher, namely to the meditation of that eternal counsel by which God, the Best and Greatest, disposed the fates of the human race according to the judgment of His own power. By this counsel, He decreed to make the riches of His glorious grace visible in the unending life and salvation of His people; by this, He appointed His Only-begotten Son as the Savior <note>Latin: Sospitatorem</note> for otherwise lost mortals—He who, having to be clothed in human flesh, was to fulfill every requirement of the law on behalf of those whose person and cause He had undertaken. It is pleasing to learn from the same master-page by what verbal obscurities and wrappings of types and figures at first, and then by more eloquent and clear speech (in which you may find the key to the ancient enigmas), He explained that counsel of His to the chosen people at many times and in many ways. By this variety of dispensations <note>The different stages of God's revelation throughout history</note>, He finally accomplished that great work He was laboring toward by sending His Son to earth. This Son satisfied Divine justice both by the most exact holiness of His life and by the death He underwent for sins. Through stupendous wonders performed by Himself and His followers—and, what is most important, by the raising of His body from the dead, His elevation above all the heavens, the miraculous pouring out of the Spirit upon the Apostles, the most just cutting off of the rebellious Jews, and finally the gracious and effective calling of the Gentiles into their place—He openly demonstrated Himself to be the Savior of the human race. It is also pleasing [to learn] the principles of all duties, and of the purest virtue so...

It frames the Old Testament rituals as a preparatory school designed to lead the faithful toward the Messiah's ultimate sacrifice and the calling of the Gentiles.</summary>

to contemplate precepts rather than examples, as they are depicted in the sacred tablets, without deceit and without trappings, they present themselves to the eyes of the readers; such purity, holiness, and efficacy you will find nowhere else. While pious men read, learn, and meditate upon these things from the sacred instruments of both covenants <note>The Old and New Testaments</note>, they seem to themselves to be dwelling among mountains dripping with new wine, and hills flowing with milk, or swimming in rushing rivers of honey and butter; and they are nearly moved to cry out what we have heard one of the Bohemian Martyrs <note>Refers to the followers of Jan Hus or the Moravian Brethren who faced persecution for their faith</note> inscribed upon a volume of the Gospels: **BEHOLD OUR PARADISE**. For they judge the matter as it truly is: that they cannot lack for wisdom, or holiness, or the joy of a soul exulting in God, nor indeed salvation itself, if they hold those Divine books not only in their hands and eyes, but in the deepest recesses of their hearts. However, it is entirely impossible that he <note>The Devil/Satan</note> who envies God His glory and mortals their salvation, should not snarl in a driven fury against these same books, which he knows were prepared for the destruction of his own kingdom. Therefore, he leaves nothing undone by which he might, whether by force or by craft, shake them from the hands of mortals. In former times, he incited tyrants to seek them out from every quarter to burn them in the flames: and there was a time when he congratulated himself—though falsely and foolishly—on a victory won and the religion of Christ deleted. He has also used heretics, men of cast-off boldness and prostituted shame, to lay wicked hands upon the most sacred tablets: either by corrupting the writing itself—

# DEDICATION

<sig>* *</sig>

...or, where they were unable to do that, they corrupted its genuine meaning with their venomous interpretations <note>original: "glossis"</note>. But in this century, this madness rages most fiercely, yet with greater cunning than ever before. Since the rebirth of fine literature within our fathers' memory, many people everywhere have devoted themselves to learning the learned languages, crawling through all the hidden recesses of antiquity, and finally cultivating all those arts by which minds are thought to be formed and polished toward refinement <note>original: "humanitatem"</note>. Some, indeed, with pious zeal, have contributed whatever they gathered to the elucidation of the Divine Instruments <note>The "Divine Instruments" refers to the books of the Bible</note>, whose memory will always be sacred and venerable to the Church <note>original: "Ecclesiæ"</note>. Others, however, have nefariously abused all their talent to overturn the faith and authority of the Divine books, though secretly and through tunnels <note>meaning through underhanded or subversive methods</note>. It is in the interest of the Christian cause that their sacrilegious arts be uncovered to their eternal confusion. It is also your concern, **ILLUSTRIOUS NOBLES**, that with the wisdom and power you possess, you restrain these plagues of the soul.

Doubtless, after Christianity <note>original: "Christianismo"</note> was publicly received and the Divine authority of the Sacred Scriptures was openly acknowledged everywhere, anyone who professed to come and attack it without any detour would make himself detestable at the first opening of his impious mouth. Therefore, a different pretext had to be sought by these crafty men. Since the darkness of the schools <note>referring to medieval Scholasticism</note> has been driven out and the light of a better Philosophy and a more learned Criticism <note>term: Criticism (Critices) — here referring to the academic study and textual analysis of historical documents</note> has recently dawned, they say it is to be lamented if the torches that are lit from there for other sciences and arts are not also carried into the inner sanctuaries <note>original: "adyta"</note> of the Scriptures. For why should that remarkable good fortune be envied for the Divine writings, which has happened to the other monuments of the most excellent men, which have been greatly cleansed, adorned, and illustrated by this new art? This foundation having been laid, minds must be released from empty fear,

-># DEDICATION<-

...they act as if the same thing could not have happened to our Sacred Books—through the injury of time and the neglect or even malice of men—as has happened to all other writings: that they stand in need of a healing hand. Minds must also be stripped of those prejudices by which a crude and credulous antiquity attributed certain sacred books to authors who did not write them, or to ages far too ancient. "We do not object," they say, "to your believing that the origin of the Mosaic Pentateuch <note>The first five books of the Bible: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy.</note> is owed to God as its Author; but do you know in what manner?" Prepare a fee for instruction <note>original: "Minerval"</note>, all you who wish to be initiated into a more secret wisdom; prepare a fee, I say, for the Queen of Sciences, the Divine Critic <note>original: "Diva Critica"; a personification of the field of Biblical Criticism</note>, who has deigned to look upon this our century and these our lands with a more favorable countenance than ever before. 

She will teach that from ancient times almost all peoples—certainly those who were more civilized than the rest—had their own public registrars. These men recorded with great diligence and the highest good faith those memorable events that occurred in each period, to be placed and preserved in the Archives of the Kingdom. The Egyptians especially, a most wise nation, appointed their Priests and Hierophants <note>term: Hierophants (interpreters of sacred mysteries)</note> to this task. Moses learned this from them, being well-educated in the discipline of the Egyptians; and therefore, from the very first beginnings of the Israelite Commonwealth, he selected certain prudent men, endowed with a great measure of the Divine Spirit, to whom the care of writing Sacred History was entrusted. 

When these men had performed that duty faithfully and at great length, and had left behind books of almost "elephantine" size <note>note: "elephantinos libros" refers to massive, voluminous scrolls or records</note>, it happened as time passed—I know not when, perhaps after the release from the Babylonian captivity—that others (I know not who, yet, lest you be angry, they were not without a share of Divine inspiration) compiled from those records this work which we now possess, and which we kiss as the venerable Pentateuch of Moses. Furthermore, these compilers...

--- Page 21 ---
<meta>This page continues a dedication discussing the historical transmission and structural challenges of ancient sacred texts, specifically focusing on the role of "Sacred Criticism" in restoring them.</meta>

# ->DEDICATION<-

Since there have been various authors, and each had his own particular purpose, it is not surprising if the histories are sometimes poorly joined, and frequent repetitions occur—sometimes idle and even annoying—which are not likely to have come from a single, and that a wise, hand. But another disadvantage has also been added, for which you would seek a remedy in vain from any source other than <term>Sacred Criticism</term><note>original: "Sacra Critice"; the scholarly study and restoration of biblical texts</note>. Namely, since the ancients wrote their titles upon scrolls, the parts of which were joined by no glue or binding, but were wound around cylinders and unwound when in use; from this it could easily happen, and indeed has happened, that when the parts of the scrolls were disturbed and not put back in their proper place, the order of the <term>pericopes</term><note>original: "pericoparum"; specific passages or sections of scripture</note> was also sometimes wonderfully and miserably disordered. These must be restored to their original brilliance by a certain sharp ingenuity of mind wherever the situation demands.

Certain most learned men, seized by the inspiration of "Divine Criticism," to whom this has been granted by special favor, are said to have approached this task under favorable omens and to have completed it more successfully than can be described. Where they seemed to themselves to detect disjointed and gaping members of the sacred discourse, which did not sufficiently correspond to the laws of Grammar, Rhetoric, or Logic <note>original: "Grammatices aut Rhetorices, aut Dialectices"</note> which they had learned as boys, they considered it a matter of their own piety to first dislocate those parts—however much they might ache, resist, or protest—and then reposition them where the Art (which it is right to acknowledge as being above all exception) dictates they would be more conveniently placed. 

And they have done this with such great skill that they could not have done better if they had seen the <term>autographs</term><note>original: "autographa"; the original manuscripts written by the authors' own hands</note> themselves, and had all the columns, lines, and letters ready at hand. They acted with such confidence in their art that they attempted no less regarding the sacred volumes of Moses or Job than the boldest of the secular critics might attempt regarding some Aristophanes or Plautus. These things, which are said merely for the sake of example, and many others of that kind...

# DEDICATION

The first things, which I am both ashamed and loath to recount, are boasted of with great display; thus they are heard by the unwary not without a certain admiration for what seems like a more profound erudition. These listeners, suspecting no such thing at the start, find themselves gradually sliding into an opinion which they soon discover can scarcely—or perhaps not even scarcely—be reconciled with the Divine authority of the Holy Books. These are the arts of our age, but they are nefarious, wicked, and utterly Diabolical; it is impossible to say how many are deceived by them—those who strive for the reputation of possessing some rare, free, and noble wisdom.

Nor does it seem at all suitable for fostering and strengthening the opinion which we have imbibed from our earliest years concerning the Divine origin and secret meanings of the Mosaic Institutes <note>original: "Institutorum Mosaicorum"; referring to the laws and religious systems established by Moses</note>, if that entire matter is transformed into a Political scheme, where the cunning of ruling holds the primary place.

And this is what I must now especially explain to you, **ILLUSTRIOUS NOBLES** <note>original: "ILLUSTRES PROCERES"; a formal address to the patrons or magistrates to whom the book is dedicated</note>: for this is what gave rise to the work soon to be laid at your feet. Nor, I think, will it be unwelcome to you, or useless to the public interest, to learn by what windings of reasoning certain most Learned Men have finally arrived at this point. They posit that, from the most ancient times following the Universal Deluge <note>The Great Flood of Noah</note>, a religion prevailed that was forged from certain laborious and mystical ceremonies, and rites pertaining only to the fingers <note>likely referring to manual gestures or superficial, external rituals</note>; this religion first obscured, and finally utterly eliminated, the simple, easy, and heart-felt worship of the ancient Patriarchs. In inventing, forming, and so greatly multiplying rites of this kind—to the point that they almost exhaust Arithmetic itself—Egypt easily held the first rank, that famous school of superstition. There, the nation of the Hebrews, made of such thick and vile clay that it differed perhaps by only a small interval from the nature and disposition of brutes, [remained] for many years

# DEDICATION

** 3

<note>The author is discussing the difficulty of reforming a people deeply influenced by their environment.</note> It could hardly have happened otherwise: those who first drew breath in Egypt, joined by such close ties to the Egyptians and further broken and harassed by so many misfortunes in that land, gradually consigned to oblivion the remnants of their ancestral religion—which had been received and preserved only through the help of the <term>Kabbalah</term> <note>The Jewish mystical tradition, here suggested as the oral vehicle for preserving ancient truths.</note>. In their place, touched by the fatal plague of Egyptian superstition, they became enamored with the gloomy nonsense of their masters. This foolish common folk, born among bricks and idols, did not know how to suddenly cast off customs that, through many years of use, had been woven into the very fabric of their souls. Therefore, anyone who attempted to immediately wean the Hebrew people in their infancy from those Egyptian and worldly rites would have undertaken a task full of dangerous risk. For if we look back at past times, we will easily observe that any sudden changes regarding rituals—to which long duration and religious opinion have granted the highest favor and reverence among the common people—have stirred up the most ruinous movements and disturbances.

Therefore, skill was needed so that the intractable Israelite people might be called to a better fruit, and so that the demon of stupid obstinacy, which held the nation from its earliest infancy, might be cast out by a charming but effective song of exorcism. A truly new form of worship had to be introduced; but, to avoid disturbances, it had to be done under an old appearance. For all new things, unless they put on some appearance of the old, are endured with a more hostile mind. And so, those who truly strive for new things in any kingdom, who unfix old laws and turn everything upside down, are nevertheless accustomed to leave the old names of offices and other minor things formerly in use untouched, in order to win over the people. Hence that saying of <term>Tacitus</term> <note>A Roman historian known for his analysis of power and political strategy.</note>: THE SECRET OF A NEW STATE IS THE IMAGE OF THE OLD. <note>original: "ARCANUM NOVI STATUS, IMAGO ANTIQUI"</note> It was therefore done by a most prudent counsel, so that the object of the old worship and some of its circumstances were changed rather than abolished entirely...

<summary>The author argues that the Israelites were so corrupted by Egyptian idolatry that God or their leaders had to use "political" prudence, introducing new religious laws under the guise of familiar Egyptian customs to avoid rebellion.</summary>

*Since I have already explained the occasion and subject matter of this work in the first chapter, and its importance in the Dedication to the Illustrious Orders, there seem to be only a few small matters remaining that I should further advise you of, Kind Reader. Among these, the following claims the primary place: two years after the first edition of this book—specifically in the year 1685 <note>original: "anno... LXXXV"</note> of the current century—there appeared in the light of day at Cambridge John Spencer’s, Doctor of Divinity, **Three Books on the Ritual Laws of the Hebrews and their Origins**. This is a massive work, completed with much care and adorned with a great deal of erudition; in it, the most learned author has pursued at great length that which he formerly attempted in his **Dissertation on the Urim and Thummim** <note>The Urim and Thummim were ancient Hebrew oracular devices used by high priests to determine the divine will</note>. I do not know, however, whether by such a vast heap of varied materials he has rendered that opinion—which we have taken it upon ourselves to examine—more probable than is right to a reader who is not unskilled in Hebrew Antiquities. For the more topics he took upon himself to explain, the more he was almost necessarily forced to labor under a great scarcity of firm arguments. And I am mistaken if, upon the inspection of almost any chapter, a skilled judge of these matters does not easily perceive that, in place of convincing reasons, things are thrust forward which do not have even the appearance of a demonstration. Certainly, I claim nothing for myself, nor do I wish to detract anything from the judgment of that most ingenious man. But—may I say it without offense <note>original: "præfiscine"</note>—it would be easy for me to provide proof for what I affirm with many evident examples, if I were inclined to wander out into that field now. But such a dispute would exceed the limits of a Preface, and I have long been weary of prolixity. Those things which I have thoughtfully discussed in my **Miscellanies** concerning the Tabernacle, the Ark, and the Cherubim may serve as a specimen. And many other things have other most learned men subjected to their own examination. Therefore, regarding the new observations from the great volume of the most renowned Spencer...*

# GREETINGS TO THE READER.

If I have not expanded upon these Egyptian matters of mine, it was not because the task would have been difficult to accomplish. Rather, it was partly because others have now taken up that particular subject, and partly so that the symmetry of my work would not be disturbed by the addition of too many parts or by the unhealthy <note>original: "vasano," likely a typo for "vesano" meaning insane or excessive</note> growth of other sections. This second edition, therefore, does not differ much from the first, except that in some places it has been somewhat improved. I repeat what I had indicated once before: that I have cited the page numbers of Marsham <note>Sir John Marsham (1602–1685), an English writer known for his work on ancient chronology</note> not according to the London edition in "Folio" <term>Folio: a large book format where sheets are folded only once</term> (of which I had no copy while I was writing this), but according to the German edition in "Quarto" <term>Quarto: a medium book format where sheets are folded twice to create four leaves</term>, published at Leipzig in the year 1676. The typographical errors that have crept in are mostly so small that it would hardly be worth the effort to list them. I offer this one warning: I cannot everywhere guarantee the numbers of the Books, Chapters, or Pages from which something is cited, even though I have attended to them with as much accuracy as I could. In preparing the indexes, a certain friend of mine—a learned and skillful man—provided me with excellent assistance. Farewell, Kind Reader, and commend my studies to God in your prayers.

# BOOK I. CHAPTER I.

[Page 3]

He had to enter upon a specific path: He forbade the worship of Idols to His people under penalty of death, and any ancient rite that stood as an example or occasion for sin, He cut away with the sword of His law from the body of ancient worship, like a most corrupt limb. Others, however, not a few, **WHICH HE KNEW TO BE MORE TOLERABLE FOLLIES**, and more suitable for foreshadowing some mystery, He transcribed into the register of sacred things, **HAVING AMENDED THEM A LITTLE**. And from this arose the fact that He transferred to the worship and the household of His sacred rites so many empty rituals of washings <note>original: "baptismorum ritus"</note>, the festivals of the new moons formerly celebrated in honor of the moon's rebirth (unless we place vain faith in Maimonides), *the custom of leading dances during sacrifice, the solemnities of feasts, the white garment, and the use of instrumental music* while they performed divine service, and other things of the same condition.
<margin>Maimonides, Guide for the Perplexed, Part III, chapter 46.</margin>

V. And indeed, in this matter, God the Best and Greatest displayed illustrious examples of His *Wisdom* and *Goodness*. Of *Wisdom*: for by no art could that people of "duller nose" <note>A Latin idiom for those lacking discernment or being slow-witted.</note> have been so easily enticed to a *truly new* worship as through some shadowy remnants of the old. For the more foolish common people are accustomed to bear all new things with an unfair mind, unless they put on some appearance of the old. Whence that saying of *Tacitus*: *The secret of a new state is the image of the old.* But the Supreme Lawgiver provided no less evidence of His *Kindness*: for when it seemed good to Him to attempt a reformation, He did not immediately go about removing whatever could be removed from ancient use (after the manner of men of a fiery temperament); but whatever could be conveniently tolerated, He tolerated until the <term>time of reformation <note>original Greek: kairon diorthoseos; a reference to Hebrews 9:10 regarding the transition from old rituals to the new covenant.</note></term>. In this way, He tempered Himself to the measures of weak men, and through *those old rites, slightly amended, as if through the first and lighter rudiments of obedience*, He gradually and gently educated the infancy of the people toward a *manly and severe piety*.

VI. Many things have been gathered by most learned men by which they give credit to this assertion of theirs. Moreover, since these things contain much recondite erudition, it seems that these most illustrious authors should not be cheated of their praise, nor should studious readers be deprived of the pleasure and utility that can be perceived therefrom. It is also in our interest that all things be reported candidly, so that a more accurate examination may be instituted over them, and a more prudent and sincere judgment may be formed. I demand this one liberty for myself from most fair-minded men: that those things which they themselves have written here and there in their commentaries, scattered as the reasoning of their argument required...

# ON MATTERS EGYPTIAN

left behind; these I have collected into one body and arranged in an order that is, I believe, not inelegant. I present them to the reader for meditation as if in a single glance, occasionally interspersed with other findings my own reading has supplied; each point shall be attributed to its respective author.

VII. I believe I shall proceed most conveniently if I first demonstrate, through a long induction of examples drawn from the minds—and largely the words—of the most learned men, that *there exists a clearly great and admirable agreement in matters of religion between the ancient Egyptians and the Hebrews.* Since this cannot be accidental, it must be that either the *Egyptians* derived their customs from the *Hebrews*, or conversely, the *Hebrews* derived theirs from the *Egyptians*. Next, I shall set forth those reasons by which most erudite men testify they were led to believe that many of the *Hebrew* streams were derived from *Egyptian* fountains. Finally, I shall subjoin my own judgment <note>original: "ἐπίκρισιν" (epikrisin) - a formal decision or critical judgment</note> on all these matters, to be strengthened by the force of arguments as the nature of the undertaking allows. This is by no means intended to detract from the labors of most learned men, but to exercise myself and my readers in investigating the truth—if perhaps it be granted to me to straighten what is crooked and to wipe away the blemishes scattered upon an otherwise excellent body of work.

# BOOK I. CHAPTER II.

<margin>Propyl. Agonif. ch. II.</margin>
If we look with watchful eyes through the veil of obscure antiquity at the rites of all nations, we shall find that the *Egyptians* and the *Hebrews*, above all others, were most similar in their customs. Nor did this escape the notice of *Kircher* <note>Athanasius Kircher (1602–1680), a famous Jesuit scholar who studied Egyptian hieroglyphs.</note>, whose words are these: *The Egyptians have such an affinity to the rites, sacrifices, ceremonies, and sacred disciplines of the Hebrews, that I am plainly persuaded that either the Egyptians were Hebraizing, or the Hebrews were Egyptianizing.* Nor is it unlike the truth that this affinity was the reason why, among the Romans, it was <margin>Annals book 12.</margin> <margin>chapter XXVI.</margin> *decided at the same time to expel the Egyptian and Jewish mysteries:* as reported by *Tacitus*. *Suetonius* similarly says in his life of *Tiberius*: *He suppressed foreign ceremonies, specifically the Egyptian and Jewish rites.*

II. But what need is there for words? Let us come to the matter at hand. Most Religion is comprised of three principal parts. I. DOCTRINES OF THINGS TO BE BELIEVED. II. PRECEPTS OF THINGS TO BE DONE. III. CERTAIN RITES AND SACRED CEREMONIES. In each of these, a wonderful agreement of minds between the *Egyptians* and *Hebrews* is proved as follows.

<margin>Marsham p. 155.</margin>
<margin>Preparation for the Gospel book IX. ch. X.</margin>
III. Regarding the DOCTRINES OF THINGS TO BE BELIEVED, it is certainly established that the goal of all Religion is to lead man to a happiness worthy of a rational creature. *For what else is Religion, but a certain Divine Philosophy, demonstrating the way to blessedness?* And that philosophy came forth from the school of the *Egyptians*, at least if faith is to be placed in the oracle of *Apollo*. For thus he speaks in the writings of *Eusebius* <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, a 4th-century historian and bishop.</note>:
> Steep is the path of the blessed, and very rugged,
> Opening at first with gates bound in bronze;
> There are paths born within, beyond description,
> Which the first of mortal men revealed for boundless success,
> Those who drink the beautiful water of the land of the Nile.
<note>The author provides both the original Greek and a Latin verse translation; both are rendered here into English. The "land of the Nile" refers to Egypt.</note>

Perhaps he will set aside a significant portion of his indignation who allows himself to be persuaded that the Divine Nature, along with its operations and effects, was not inaptly represented by the emblem of such a serpent. For it must be known (as *Athanasius Kircher* <note>A famous 17th-century Jesuit scholar and polymath who studied Egyptian hieroglyphs.</note> established) that the Egyptians were curious investigators of the nature of almost all animals native to Egypt, and especially of the serpent. For when they saw that the serpent moves without the aid of hands or feet, using only the long stretch of its body; that it consists of no limb besides a mouth; and that it is an animal full of fiery spirit, lively, and capable of restoring its youth every year by shedding its old skin, they believed it impossible that something great, excellent, and utterly Divine did not lie hidden beneath these traits. Added to this was the fact that, by the wavy motion of its flexible body, it could express nearly all shapes—now moving its tail toward its head in a twisted circle to represent Eternity, now coiled in spirals to display the revolutions of the celestial spheres. Compare *Vossius, On Idolatry, Book IX, chapter XI.*

VIII. And lest anyone think these are merely the idle inventions of modern writers, let him know that *Sanchuniathon* <note>An ancient Phoenician author whose works are mostly lost but quoted by others.</note> left behind the same accounts, written in almost the same words from the records of *Taautus* <note>The Phoenician equivalent of the god Thoth or Hermes.</note>, which can be seen in the works of *Eusebius*. There it is added from the writings of *Epeës*, who was called the <margin>Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book I, chapter X, near the end.</note> greatest Hierophant <note>original: μέγιστος & ἱεροφάντης — a high priest or interpreter of sacred mysteries.</note> and Sacred Scribe <note>original: ἱερογραμματεὺς</note> of the Egyptians: *That one serpent was held to be the most Divine of all, which bore the form of a Hawk, and was most pleasant to behold. For indeed, whenever it opened its eyes, it immediately filled all the primordial places of its region with light; but if it closed them, darkness followed at once.*

IX. Let us add another point. These same Egyptians represented God under the <margin>Kircher, *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*, Hieroglyphic Gymnasium, class XII, chapter IX.</margin> emblem of Sigalion Harpocrates <note>The Greek name for the Egyptian god Horus the Child.</note>, whom they depicted as a naked boy, urging silence with a finger pressed to his lips; holding a horn of plenty in his left hand; and having under his feet a staff marked with the head of a Hoopoe <note>A bird considered sacred in ancient Egypt.</note>, along with a curved wand and a sundial pointer. This is the explanation of these things: *He is painted as a naked boy because God, being far removed from all contagion of matter, remains unchangeable in a perpetual flower of youth. He is shown with the sign of silence because he is to be honored with silence rather than described with many swelling words. The horn of plenty denotes the abundance of all good things which he contains within himself. The staff with the other insignia teaches that he is the author of all worldly variety, harmony, and order.* From

# EGYPTIAN STUDIES

The Word of God <note>original Greek: ὁ τοῦ Θεοῦ Λόγος / Latin: Dei VERBUM</note> leaped forth at once from the downward-tending elements into the pure creation of Nature; and it was united with the Creator Mind, for it was of one substance <note>original Greek: ὁμοούσιος / Latin: CONSUBSTANTIALIS. This is the same technical term used in the Nicene Creed to describe the relationship between Father and Son.</note> with Him.

V. Finally, this is especially noteworthy: The Father-Creator made the entire world, not with hands, but by the Word <note>original Greek: λόγῳ</note>. After Kircher <note>Athanasius Kircher (1602–1680), a Jesuit polymath and celebrated scholar of Egyptian antiquities.</note> had recounted these and several other points, he concluded with these words: *And these are the most ancient sacred dogmas of all Theology, revealed to the primeval world by Zoroaster and Hermes; accordingly, Proclus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who lived in the 5th century AD.</note> asserts not without merit that this doctrine is "God-handed-down" and "God-given" <note>original Greek: Θεοπαράδοτον, καὶ Θεόδοτον</note>.*

VI. Regarding what he said about the Hieroglyphic Symbol of the Trinity, the matter stands as follows. Hermes depicted a winged circle, pregnant with a serpent; as is evident from the Pamphylian Obelisk <note>The Agonalis Obelisk currently in the Piazza Navona, Rome, which Kircher famously attempted to decipher.</note> and from the Isiac Tablet <note>A bronze tablet with Egyptianizing motifs, also known as the Bembine Tablet.</note>, where it is seen placed above every single image. By the circle—the pure form of Divinity—he signified the Eternal Deity, Immense and abstracted from all the filth of matter. By the serpent, he aptly noted the second form of Divinity (for the serpent is a most lively animal, and according to Horus <note>Horapollo, the supposed author of a treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs.</note>, consists of no limb except the mouth), or the Word of God and the second mind. By the wings attached to the globe, he fitly signified the Third form of Divinity, the Spirit pervading all things. And in this way, through the whole composed of three parts, considered as a single entity, he expressed the Divine nature consisting of three distinct powers. Our Kircher offers a more abundant exposition of all these things, established by countless 
<margin>Book III, page 400.</margin>
authorities in the *Pamphylian Obelisk*, for the curious reader to weigh.

VII. It might rightly seem a wonder to anyone how those first "Theosophists" <note>Literally "those wise in the things of God."</note> were advanced to such enlightenment of the mind. But the most learned Kircher does not allow his readers to be held by that difficulty. He supposes that Hermes was of Canaanite stock and a contemporary <note>original Greek: σύγχρονον</note> of Abraham; he testifies that he has demonstrated this in various places. From this, it must be inferred that a curious and all-knowing mind could not help but fish out many things from them concerning true and right Theology—which they held by word of mouth, originating from the first-formed man <note>Adam</note> and derived in continuous succession down to Noah (among which mysteries of Divine revelation the mystery of the Trinity was not the least). These things he then handed down to posterity, clothed in various coverings of symbols.

### CHAPTER IV.

->The agreement of the Egyptians with the Hebrews in their faith regarding the creation of the World, the creation of the First Man, the immortality of the Soul, and the state after this life.<-

*I. The Egyptians represent the creative Reason of the World under the emblem of Cneph pouring an egg from his mouth. II. Nor do they seem to have been entirely ignorant of the sequence of creation. III. Eurysus, from the school of Pythagoras, hand down that Man was formed according to the Pattern of God. IV. The Hebrews were less concerned about the immortality of the soul and the state after death. V. The Egyptians are said to have been the first to hand down both doctrines. VI. They were also the authors of the transmigration of souls <term>metempsychosis: the belief that the soul moves into a new body after death</term>. VII. They call "Amenthes" what the Greeks call "Hades." VIII. The Egyptian rites of burial testify to their faith regarding the different states of souls after this life. IX. The Hebrew "Sheol" corresponds to the "Amenthes" of the Egyptians. X. The Hebrews trifle with similar ideas to the Egyptians regarding the transmigration of souls. XI. ## II.

But neither were they ignorant of that ORDER which Moses records as having been observed by God in the creation of the world. For Diodorus Siculus <note>A Greek historian of the 1st century BCE</note> explains their 

<margin>
Book I, at the beginning.
</margin>

opinion in this way:

> When all things first began to exist, the heavens and the earth had a single appearance, their natures being mixed together. After these bodies had separated from one another, the World attained that order which we now see; the air became possessed of perpetual motion. That part of it which was most fiery was carried up to the high places, since such a nature tends upward due to its lightness; and for the same reason, the sun and the rest of the multitude of stars remained in a perennial whirl. But that which was muddy and turbid, along with the moist condensation, settled in one place by the force of gravity. As it was continually tossed and turned, the sea was produced from the moist parts, and the earth from the more solid parts, though it was very clay-like and soft. This earth, as soon as the fire of the sun began to shine upon it, grew firm; then, as the surface began to ferment, the moisture swelled in many places, and in those spots putrefactions arose, surrounded by thin membranes. This is seen to happen even now in marshes and swampy places, where after the ground has cooled, the air suddenly grows hot and is not changed gradually. When the moist parts had been made pregnant and filled by the heat in this manner, nourishment was supplied to the fetuses at night from the surrounding mist, while by day they were solidified by the heat. ...when these embryos had reached full size, and the coverings of their membranes had been scorched and thus ruptured, all kinds of living forms appeared. Some of these, having obtained a great deal of heat, departed to the higher regions and became winged creatures. But those which were endowed with an earthy thickness were placed in the class of reptiles and other creatures living on the ground. Those which drew most from a moist nature were brought to a place kindred to themselves and are called swimming things. Thus far Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian of the 1st century BCE</note>: whose words, though somewhat lengthy, I have not been reluctant to add, so that it might be established how greatly the philosophical systems of the Egyptians agree with the traditions of the Hebrews. <margin>On the Truth of Religion, in the notes to Book I, Section 15.</margin> Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius, a famous 17th-century Dutch legal scholar and theologian</note> brings forward similar points about the Egyptians from Diogenes Laertius and Macrobius.

### III. REGARDING THE CREATION OF THE FIRST MAN, what the wiser Egyptians thought is gathered with some probability from Eurysus, a disciple of Pythagoras.

Since it is credible that the disciple drew these things from his master, and all agree that Pythagoras learned his own doctrines from the Egyptians, that which is excellent in the writings of the Pythagoreans will be rightly credited to them. <margin>Grotius, in the same place.</margin> This Eurysus, therefore, in his *Book on Fortune*, speaks in these words: <note>original Greek: "τὸ σκῆνος τοῖς λοιποῖς ὅμοιον..."</note> *Man is similar in body to the rest, since he is composed of the same matter; but he was fashioned by the best artisan, who in making him used himself as the archetype.* Who does not see how similar these things are to the Mosaic accounts of man being created in the image of God?

### IV. REGARDING THE IMMORTALITY OF THE SOUL, the Egyptians seem to have known more than many of the Hebrews.

<margin>Marsham, page 225.</margin> The wisdom of the ancient Hebrews was placed in the knowledge of their own law. Regarding the state after death, they were less concerned. <margin>On the Truth of the Christian Religion, Book II, Section 9.</margin> On that matter, let me use the words of the illustrious Hugo Grotius: *Moses, in the institution of the Jewish religion, if we look at the express covenants of the law, promised nothing beyond the goods of this life: a fertile land, a plentiful storehouse, victory over enemies, a long and healthy old age, and surviving descendants with good hope. For if there is anything beyond, it is covered in shadow, or must be gathered by wise and difficult reasoning; which was the reason why many who professed to follow the law of Moses, such as the Sadducees <note>A Jewish sect that famously denied the resurrection and the immortality of the soul</note>, cast away all hope of obtaining goods after this life.*

VII. Furthermore, *Amenthes*, which we just mentioned, is what the Egyptians call that which the Greeks call *Hades*. <margin>Book 1, p. 58.</margin>
VIII. How common and pervasive this opinion on the immortality of the soul was among the Egyptians is shown by their accepted custom of burial, which Diodorus Siculus has accurately recorded. When a body is to be buried, the relatives announce the day of the funeral to the judges, kinsmen, and friends of the deceased, and specifically proclaim that he is about to cross the Lake. Then more than forty judges sit together in a certain semicircle prepared next to the Lake; and a boat, previously readied, is drawn up, which a pilot steers whom the Egyptians call *Charon* in their own language. Once the vessel is brought into the lake, before the coffin of the dead is placed upon it, anyone is permitted to bring an accusation. If anyone proves that he lived a bad life, the judges pass sentence;

When there is either no accuser or the accusation is false, the relatives lay aside their mourning and praise the deceased: regarding their *Lineage*, as the Greeks are accustomed to do, they mention nothing, because they believe all in Egypt to be equally noble; but they recount the education of his childhood, the piety and justice of his manhood, as well as his self-control and his other virtues; and they call upon the gods below to receive him as a companion to the godly <note>original Greek: καὶ παρακαλοῦσι τοὺς κάτω Θεοὺς σύνοικον δέξασθαι τοῖς εὐσεϐέσι</note>, and they ask the infernal Gods that he be received into the company of the pious. The multitude applauds and joins in proclaiming the praises of the deceased, as one who is to spend eternity in the underworld with the godly <note>original Greek: ὡς τὸν αἰῶνα διατρίϐειν μέλλοντι καθ᾽ ᾅδου μετὰ τῶν εὐσεϐῶν</note>, *as one who is to spend everlasting time with the pious in the Underworld.*

IX. This entire Theology of the Egyptians concerning the immortality of the soul and the state after this life—whatever it contains of both truth and falsehood—seems to have passed over to the Hebrews. For many of them, whom the *Pharisees* <note>A Jewish sect known for strict adherence to traditional and written law</note> followed later, <margin>Josephus, Antiquities, Book XVIII, Chapter II</margin> *believe that souls are immortal, and that judgments of them take place beneath the earth: then rewards fall to each according to the merit of virtue or malice, and the latter are condemned to perpetual prisons, while for the former there is an easy return to life.* The *Amenthi* <note>The Egyptian underworld</note> of the Egyptians corresponds to the *Sheol* <note>The Hebrew place of the dead</note> of the Hebrews, which, just as *Amenthes* is named from receiving and giving, so *Sheol* is named from seeking and demanding.

X. Nor were they strangers to the migration <note>original Greek: μεταϐάσει</note> or reincarnation <note>original Greek: μετενσωματώσει</note> of souls, which they call in their own language the *revolution of souls* <insert>Gilgul Neshamot</insert>: for which Herodotus used the term "circling" <note>original Greek: περιήληξιν</note>. The *Pharisees* believed, <margin>Josephus, The Jewish War, Book II, Chapter VII</margin> that every soul is indeed imperishable, but only those of the good pass into another body, while those of the wicked are punished with eternal suffering <note>original Greek: ψυχὴν πᾶσαν μὲν ἄφθαρτον, μεταϐαίνειν δ᾽ εἰς ἕτερον σῶμα, τὴν τῶν ἀγαθῶν μόνην· τὴν δὲ τῶν φαύλων ἀϊδίῳ τιμωρίᾳ κολάζεσθαι</note>. *That every soul is indeed incorruptible, but only those of the good pass into other bodies, while the wicked are tortured with eternal punishment.*

XI. It is believed by some that from this opinion flowed the reports in the Gospel history that Jesus Christ was by some thought to be John the Baptist, by others Elijah, and by others Jeremiah, or one of the Prophets. <margin>Matthew 16:14</margin> Certainly, it is the opinion of the *Kabbalists* <note>Followers of Jewish mysticism</note> that the soul <margin>Elijah Tishbi under the word "Gilgul"</margin> of the first man, through revolving, arrived into the body of King *David*, and from *David* it is to revolve into the body of the *Messiah*: and they say this is signified by the letters found in the name *Adam* <note>Hebrew: אדם</note>, each of which constitutes a whole word: **A** for *Adam*, **D** for *David*, **M** for *Messiah*.

XIV. And from this perpetual fire of the Valley of Hinnom, he thinks it came about that hell is called Gehenna, in which there is a perpetual fire. And from this he explains the saying of Christ in Matthew 5:22: *He shall be liable to the Gehenna of fire* <note>original Greek: Ἔνοχός ἔσται εἰς τὴν γέενναν τοῦ πυρὸς</note>. He ought to be cast unburied into Gehenna, or the Valley of Hinnom, which is by far the most serious and shameful fate of all.

II. Such was the funeral Apology <note>A formal defense or justification of one's life.</note> of the Egyptians; which indeed is not at all dissonant from those things which Moses commanded in the second table of the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments</note>; or from those which are called the precepts of the *Noachides* <note>The Seven Laws of Noah, considered universal moral laws for all humanity</note> by the Talmudic Masters; and according to their tradition, they belong to this age. For in the Babylonian *Gemara* <note>A component of the Talmud comprising rabbinical analysis</note> it is read: *The Israelites received ten precepts in Marah: seven which belonged to the Noachides; and now were added Judgments, the Sabbath, and the Honor of Parents.* That stay in Marah was within a month of the Exodus: and about 40 days before the proclamation of the Decalogue. The Masters call all Nations except the Hebrews "Noachides"; who prefer to be called *Abrahamides*, or rather *Israelites*. Moreover, they maintain that the seven precepts of the Noachides have always been in force; and they take them for *Natural Law*, common to all men. In the mentioned passage of the *Gemara*, they are enumerated thus: *Concerning judgments, concerning the Cursing of the Deity, concerning Foreign Worship <note>Idolatry</note>, concerning the Revelation of turpitudes <note>Sexual immorality</note>, concerning the shedding of Blood, concerning Robbery or Theft, and concerning the limb of a living animal.* Although other Masters list them slightly differently. Out of these precepts, there are two which pertain to Divine worship; four which pertain to the mutual duties of men; and one is added regarding *Food*. Let us inquire individually into what the Egyptians feel in all these matters in common with the Hebrews, beginning from those which pertain to Divine worship.

III. Just as the *Hebrews* believe that all foreign worship is forbidden to them, so too did the *Egyptians* detest whatever was not demonstrated by their ancestors, as we have observed above. For the rest, it must be admitted that there is a monstrous discrepancy between their institutions here, which Tacitus also noted. <note>Tacitus (c. 56–120 AD) was a Roman historian who wrote extensively—and often critically—about Jewish customs in his *Histories*.</note> The *Egyptians* venerate many animals and composite images; the *Jews* acknowledge only one deity with the mind alone. They regard those who fashion God out of mortal materials into human likenesses as profane; they believe that supreme being to be eternal, neither changeable nor subject to perishing. Indeed, the precepts of the Hebrews are so arranged that they are diametrically opposed <note>original: "ἐκ διαμέτρου" (ek diametrou)</note> to the institutions of the Egyptians; and they expressly rebuke those monstrous gods of every kind that were worshipped by the latter.

<margin>Marsham, page 165.</margin>
IV. V. From the precepts pertaining to the mutual duties of men, let us first weigh that concerning Homicide: regarding which it was said to the *Noachide* <note>A descendant of Noah; referring here to the "Noahide Laws" believed to be binding on all humanity.</note>, *I will require your blood from your souls*. That the prohibition of Homicide was also in the moral discipline of the *Egyptians* is manifest from the confession of the *Libitinarius* <note>An official in charge of funeral rites or a mortician.</note> praised by us above: *I have killed no other man*. But let us hear *Diodorus Siculus* speaking on the laws of the *Egyptians* regarding this matter. *If any of the Egyptians had intentionally killed either a free man or a slave, the Laws commanded him to be condemned to death; which, weighing not the condition of fortune but the intent of the deed, deterred men from crimes; and at the same time, by avenging the death of a slave, the free were rendered more secure. If anyone making a journey found a man being killed by robbers, or suffering any violence, and did not bring help if he were able, he was guilty of death. If he were unable to bring help, he was bound to report the robbers and prosecute the injury by accusation; he who neglected these things was punished with a certain number of lashes and went without food for three days.* How closely related these are to the Laws of the *Hebrews*, the matter speaks for itself.

## CHAPTER VI.

### The Agreement of the Egyptians with the Hebrews regarding Sacred Times, Places, and Persons.

*I. Matters pertaining to the understanding of sacred rites. II. The Thebans are said to have been the first to discover the system of the Year and Months. III. Whose intercalation, however, the Egyptian Priests did not admit. IV. Hence a twofold measure of the year. V. Almost as among the Hebrews, there is a Sacred and a Civil year. VI. The festival days of the Egyptians are older than those of the Hebrews. VII. The seven-day cycle, and the very religion of the Sabbath, was drawn from the innermost storehouse of Egyptian antiquity. VIII. The oldest shrines of the Egyptians, and those without a statue, at least a human one. IX. Their structure corresponds to the Sanctuary of Moses and Solomon.*

I. Let us now proceed to the Sacred RITES. For a fuller understanding of these, we may distinctly consider the Sacred TIMES, PLACES, PERSONS, ACTIONS, and certain INSTRUMENTS of Divine worship.

<margin>Book II. ch. IV.</margin>
<margin>Book I.</margin>
II. Let us begin with TIMES. *Herodotus* <note>A Greek historian from the 5th century BCE, often called the "Father of History."</note> said that the *Egyptians* were the first of all men to discover the YEAR, and to distribute twelve seasons into it, having learned these from the stars. The *Thebans*, however, claim this memorable invention for themselves. *They*, says *Diodorus* <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian known for his monumental universal history, the Bibliotheca historica.</note>, say that they are the most ancient of all men; and that *Philosophy* and *more exact astrology* <note>In this context, "astrology" refers to the scientific study of stars, which we now call astronomy.</note> were discovered by them, the location of their land assisting them in more clearly recognizing the rising and setting of the stars. They claim that Months and Years were arranged among them in a peculiar way. For, measuring their days not by the motion of the Moon, but by the motion of the Sun, they assign thirty days to the Months, but after every twelfth month they intercalate <note>term: Intercalate (to insert extra days into a calendar to keep it aligned with the solar year)</note> five days with a Quarter-day; and in that manner, they complete the annual circle.

<margin>Marsham p. 247.</margin>
<margin>Gemini's Introduction, Petavius Edition p. 33.</margin>
III. Nevertheless, the Priests, although they knew the Quarter-day agreed with the calculations of the Sun, did not intercalate it, nor did they add a festival day every four years. Religion was the cause, because they detested intercalation as something ominous. For they were eager not to represent the sacred rites of the Gods at the same times; rather, they wanted them to pass through all the seasons of the year; so that the same festival might be in summer, winter, autumn, and finally spring. For that reason, they do not introduce the Quarter-day, so that the solemnities may recede <note>This refers to the "vague year" where festivals slowly rotated through the seasons over a 1,461-year cycle.</note>.

IV. Thus there was a twofold method of the year among the Egyptians. One was Sacred, consisting of 365 days without any addition of hours, which is called *Egyptian*, and can be called *Sethiac* or *Canicular*, because it is established according to the course of the Dog-star <note>original: "Canicula"; the star Sirius, whose rising signaled the flooding of the Nile.</note>. The other is Natural, and adds a fourth part of a day to the 365 days: this can be called *Theban* and *Heliac*, because it is formed according to the course of the Sun.

# EGYPTIAN STUDIES

<margin>Marsham, page 390.</margin>
V. Similarly, among the Hebrews, from the time of the Exodus, there was a twofold year; one was *Civil*, the other *Sacred*. The *Civil* year, which they used in contracts, agreements, marriages, and other matters of that kind, was uniform and had full months of thirty days; the Moon had no place in it. Its beginning was from *Tishri* <note>The first month of the Hebrew civil year, occurring in autumn</note>, which for the Egyptians is *Thot*, that is, from the *Autumn*. The *Sacred* year, which they used for festivals and sacred solemnities, began from the month *Nisan* <note>The first month of the ecclesiastical year, occurring in spring</note>, which is closest to the Vernal Equinox; it owes its origin to Divine institution in Exodus 12:2. This year was *Lunar*, and quite unequal. And since both of these years differ greatly from the solar period, the calendar was so wandering and uncertain that, unless an intercalation <term>intercalation: the insertion of leap days or months to align a calendar with the solar year</term> had been applied, Passover—which must always be in the spring—would have eventually occurred in summer, then autumn, then winter. However, it is not necessary for us to discuss the method of that intercalation at length now.

<margin>
On the Syrian Goddess. At the beginning.
Marsham, page 193.
Herodotus, Book II, chapter 49.
Book II, chapter 58.
</margin>
VI. From the *Year*, let us pass to the sacred DAYS. It escapes no one's notice that, by the Mosaic Law, three anniversary <term>panegyrias: general assemblies or festive religious gatherings</term> were established: namely, *Passover*, *Pentecost*, and *Tabernacles* <note>original: Scenopegias</note>. But the festivals of the Egyptians seem to have been more ancient. *Lucian*, a researcher of Assyrian antiquity, says: <note>original Greek: πρῶτοι ἀνθρώπων Αἰγύπτιοι λέγονται Θεῶν τε ἔννοιαν λαβεῖν, καὶ ἱερὰ εἴσασθαι, καὶ τεμένια καὶ πανηγυρίας ἀποδεῖξαι</note> *The Egyptians are said to be the first of men both to have perceived the notion of the Gods, and to have established temples, and to have designated sacred precincts and solemn assemblies.* They were therefore the first who celebrated <term>heortasimos: festival days</term>. *Melampus*, who transferred these customs from Egypt to the Greeks, was indeed a little younger than Moses; for Moses died while *Pandion* was reigning in Athens, whereas Melampus flourished under *Erichthonius*, the son of Pandion. Nevertheless, since the Egyptian solemnities are called "ancient" by *Herodotus*, while the Greek ones are called "recent," the festivals of the Egyptians may rightly seem to have been older than the Mosaic times.

<margin>
Marsham, page 196.
Book II, chapter 82.
</margin>
VII. Furthermore, there is the most celebrated Seven-day Cycle, or the seventh day perpetually recurring in weekly periods of days, which is highly relevant to the matter we are treating: such as the Hebrew SABBATH. The Egyptians, the most ancient architects of time, are said to have derived the weekly circle of days from the number of the Planets, and to have spread that system of time along with their Astrological discipline. *Herodotus*, concerning the inventions of the Egyptians, says: *Other things were also invented by the Egyptians. <note>original Greek: μείς τε καὶ ἡμέρη ἑκάστη Θεῶν ὅτευ ἐστί</note> Which month, and which day, belongs to which of the Gods.* Moreover, the days of the Gods...

...are the days of the week, named after the seven planets. For those planets hold the name of Gods in the <term>Genethliacal</term> <note>The art of casting birth charts or horoscopes</note> art of the Egyptians; and to each planet its own day of the week is assigned. <margin>Book 36, page 37.</margin> Indeed, Dio Cassius says that the practice of assigning days to the seven stars called planets was certainly an invention of the Egyptians. Furthermore, the star of Saturn is considered gloomy and malevolent among Astrologers: therefore, according to their discipline, the seventh day is held to be dark and inauspicious, and unsuitable for conducting business. Even the Egyptian priests observed "Weeks" in their purifications. <margin>On Abstinence, Book IV, Chapter VII.</margin> Chæremon, as quoted in Porphyry, writes: *When the time approached in which they were to celebrate some sacred rite, for a number of preceding days—some for forty-two (that is, six weeks), others for more, others for fewer, but never less than seven days (or one week)—they abstained from all animal products.* Since these things are so, it is very likely that the weekly cycle of days was drawn from Mathematical discipline and from the inner storehouse of Egyptian antiquity: but the sacred worship of every seventh day, and the feast of the weekly Sabbath established by the Mosaic Law, was only then first publicly received into the Hebrew Religion.

VIII. After Sacred Times, let us speak of Sacred PLACES: such as TEMPLES and Shrines. Their first invention is attributed to the Egyptians. <margin>Marsham, page 34.</margin> Herodotus confirms what we just cited from Lucian: *They say the Egyptians were the first to establish altars, and images, and shrines for the Gods.* Yet the most ancient temples of the Egyptians, according to Lucian's testimony, were without statues. <margin>Strabo, Book 17.</margin> And in the most magnificent Temples of subsequent times, <note>original Greek: ξόανον δ’ οὐδὲν, ἢ οὐκ ἀνθρωπόμορφον, ἀλλὰ τῶν ἀλόγων ζώων τινός</note> *there was either no statue at all, or one not in human form, but fashioned in the likeness of some irrational beast.*

IX. <margin>Marsham, page 210.</margin> But the structure of the Temples is especially to be noted; which Strabo describes in roughly this manner. At the entrance of the sanctuary is a Pavement, in width an acre or a little less; in length triple or quadruple. By Callimachus it is called the <term>Dromos</term> <note>A paved processional way or "Course"</note>. Afterward is a great <term>Propylon</term> <note>A monumental gateway or Vestibule</note>, and when you have proceeded, another Vestibule, and again another. After the vestibules is the Temple, having a large and excellent Court, but a modest Shrine. From this you may gather that there were four parts of the Egyptian Temple: the Pavement, the Gateway, the Fore-temple, and the Inner Sanctuary. <note>original Greek: Λιθόστροτον, προπύλαιον, πρόναον, καὶ τὸν Ναόν</note> The Sanctuary constructed by Moses at God's command was not unlike this, and the Temple of Solomon was later built according to the same form...

XI. Now let us look at the PERSONS who performed the ministry in sacred places during festive times. Here, however, the greatest agreement between the Hebrews and the Egyptians reveals itself. The Priests of both groups held nothing more ancient or more religious than cleanliness. Hence, for both, there was applied: I. CIRCUMCISION. Concerning the Egyptians, *Herodotus* says: *They circumcise the male organs for the sake of cleanliness, making it of more account to be clean than to be handsome.* Moreover, *Philo the Jew* offers this other reason for *Jewish Circumcision*: *the cleansing of the whole body, so as to be fitting for the priestly order.* II. SHAVING <note>original: Tonsura</note>. Egyptian Priests shave their entire body every third day, lest a louse or other filth be bred upon those worshiping God. XV. It is also credible that the *small bells* of the High Priest sought their origins from the received <margin>Spencer, chapter 4, section 12.</margin> pomp of Egyptian worship, as if from a primary model. For among the Egyptians and others, it was arranged by a very ancient institution that everything should resound far and wide with sistrums <note>A sistrum is an ancient percussion instrument, a metal rattle associated with the goddess Isis.</note> and rattles while the sacred rites were performed. Hence, in the works of Martial, the *priests of Isis are called the sistrum-bearing crowd*. And Egypt itself is called the *land of the צלצל כנפים <note>Hebrew: tsiltsal kenaphayim</note> cymbal of wings* <note>The author translates this as "the land of the cymbal of borders/fringes."</note>. Truly, the *sistrum* is a species of cymbal. And it is deservedly called צלצל <note>tsiltsal</note>, that is, a *tinkling instrument*. For צלצל means to tinkle. And the sistrum was no less tinkling than the common cymbal. Hence Ovid: <margin>Metamorphoses, book 11.</margin>
> *Tossing the tinkling sistrums with an Egyptian hand.*
Therefore, by the "land of the cymbal of borders," Egypt is signified enigmatically <note>original: "αἰνιγματωδῶς" (ainigmatōdōs)</note> in the Prophetic manner.

# BOOK I. CHAPTER VII.

II. A consequence of *Circumcision* was the SHUNNING of others who were not circumcised: this was true not only among the *Hebrews*, which is known to everyone, but also among the *Egyptians*. <margin>Book II, chapter 41.</margin> Regarding them, *Herodotus* writes: *No Egyptian man or woman will kiss the mouth of a Greek man, nor use his knife, his roasting spit, or his kettle; nor will they eat the meat of a clean ox if it has been cut with a Greek knife.* <margin>Clement, Miscellanies, Book I, page 302.</margin> For this reason, *Pythagoras*, in order to associate with the Prophets of the *Egyptians*, underwent circumcision by them. *Chaeremon*, as cited in *Porphyry*, confirms *Herodotus*: <margin>On Abstinence, Book IV, § 6; ibid. § 8.</margin> *They would not live with anyone of a foreign religion.* <note>Original Greek: Τῶν ἐξωτικῶν θρησκείας οὐδενὶ συνεβίουν.</note> *Indeed, they even considered it a most impious thing to sail away from Egypt, guarding themselves against the luxury and customs of foreigners.* Truly, that "peculiarity of life" <note>Original Greek: περὶ τὸν βίον ἰδιότης</note>—that specific way of living and abstaining from foreign nations which *Josephus* attributes to the *Jews*—was also a custom among the *Egyptians*.

III. A certain BAPTISM also served for initiation, both for the *Israelites* and for *Proselytes* <term>Proselyte: a convert to Judaism</term>. When the *Israelites* were to be initiated into the *Mosaic* teachings, *Moses* went down to the people and sanctified them, and *they washed their clothes*. Exodus 19:14. It is the constant tradition of the Teachers <note>The Rabbis</note> that the washing of the body of the person wearing the clothes was included in this washing of garments: according to that passage in Leviticus 15:10-11: *He shall wash his clothes and wash his body with water.* From this, the *Jews* derive the origin of their Baptism. Likewise, the Baptism of *Proselytes*. No one with even a common education is now ignorant of the fact that these converts were formerly initiated into the *Israelite* Church through *Circumcision*, *Baptism*, and *Offering*. <margin>Marsham, page 200.</margin> And a most noble man <note>Likely referring to Sir John Marsham</note> conjectures that this *Baptism of the Hebrews* was perhaps modeled after the example of the *Egyptians*. <margin>Metamorphoses, Book IX.</margin> *Apuleius*, who was himself to be initiated into the rites of *Isis*, teaches that a ritual washing was indeed solemn in sacred initiations. *The Priest,* he says, *escorted by a religious retinue, led me to the nearest baths; and after I was first handed over to the customary washing, having prayed for the God's forgiveness, he washed me by sprinkling water all around most purely.* <margin>On Baptism, chapter 5.</margin> Nor is there any doubt that this was done according to ancient custom. Regarding these and other matters, *Tertullian* writes: *The nations are initiated into certain sacred rites through a washing, such as those of a certain Isis or Mithras. The former is the name of an Egyptian Goddess, the latter of the highest deity among the Persians.*

V. After initiation, there was no worship in antiquity more frequent than that of **SACRIFICES**, which could be taken either from **HUMANS** or from **LIVESTOCK**.

VI. It is very well known from sacred history that Abraham, as a test of his Faith and Obedience, was commanded by God to slaughter his only son Isaac—who was dearer to him than his own eyes—and offer him as a burnt offering to the deity. <margin>Marsham, p. 77</margin> However, this kind of sacrifice was not something new or unheard of to Abraham. *Philo the Jew*, in his *Book on Abraham*, recording the opinion of others, asks: "What is the point of praising him <note>Abraham</note> as the author of a novel deed, <note>original: "ὡς ἐγχειρητὴν κεκαινοργημένης πράξεως"</note> which both private individuals, and kings, and entire nations perform as the occasion arises?" That deadly rite of sacrificing was older than the times of Abraham. *Philo of Byblos*, drawing from *Sanchuniathon* <note>An ancient Phoenician author</note>, attributes it to *Saturn* <note>The Roman name for the god Cronus</note> himself, who, during a raging famine and pestilence, offered his only son as a burnt offering to his father, Heaven. By the example of *Saturn*, this religious practice gained strength. *Philo the Jew*, in the place cited, acknowledges that this was an ancient superstition of the Barbarian nations. It appears from the first book of *Philo's History of the Phoenicians*, found in *Eusebius*, that the *Phoenicians* had already been performing that unspeakable sacrifice for a long time.

<margin>Preparation for the Gospel, Book IV, chapter 16</margin> "Among the ancients, it was the custom in times of great danger for the rulers of cities or nations to give their most beloved son to be slaughtered for the public calamity, in order to appease the wrath of the Gods. Those thus devoted are had their throats cut in a mystical ceremony. Indeed, Saturn," whom the Phoenicians call *Il* <note>original: "ὃν οἱ Φοίνικες Ἰλ προσαγορεύουσι"</note> (thus *Marsham* corrects the copies of *Eusebius*, in which *Israel* is constantly read instead of *Il*), "who was also consecrated as the star of Saturn after death, while he was reigning in that region, had a son by a local Nymph named Anobret. This son he called **JEUD** (a word which even now among the Phoenicians signifies 'only-begotten'). When a very great danger from war was imminent, he dressed his son in royal attire and sacrificed him at an altar he had built himself." From these things you may gather that this trial of Abraham was not some new deed, nor recently devised,

<margin>Marsham, page 79.</margin>
VII. The customs of the Egyptians are now the subject of our consideration: it is not easy to say when this rite first took root among them. <margin>Book 1.</margin> It was certainly most ancient. *Diodorus Siculus* <note>A Greek historian of the 1st century BCE.</note> says: *They say that men of the same color as Typhon (who was red-haired) were sacrificed by the ancient Kings at the tomb of Osiris. Since, however, few Egyptians are found to be red-haired, but many foreigners are; from this there arose among the Greeks the myth <note>original: "$\pi\epsilon\rho\grave{\iota}$ $\tau\tilde{\eta}\varsigma$ $B\alpha\sigma\acute{\iota}\rho\iota\delta o\varsigma$ $\xi\epsilon\nu o\kappa\tau o\nu\acute{\iota}\alpha\varsigma$"</note> concerning the cruelty of Busiris in slaughtering strangers. It was not that any king was actually named Busiris, but the tomb of Osiris had that name in the native tongue.* <margin>Found in Plutarch, On Isis.</margin> *Manetho* <note>An Egyptian priest and historian.</note> relates similar things: *They burned Typhonian men alive, and scattered and destroyed their ashes by winnowing: this was done openly, and at a fixed time, during the dog-days.*

<margin>Marsham, page 201.</margin>
VIII. Sacrifices of livestock are as ancient as they are common. Moses was not the first to institute sacrifices, but he prescribed the manner of sacrificing. The distinction of livestock and gender was received into the Hebrew religion after the exodus from Egypt. The victims of the Hebrews consisted for the most part of cattle, sheep, or goats. Moreover, even if those of Memphis worshiped the Ox, those of Mendes the Goat, and those of Thebes the Ram; nevertheless, these three species of victims were also sacrificed by the Egyptians in various places. <margin>Herodotus, Book II, Chapter 42.</margin> The Thebans, abstaining from sheep, sacrifice goats. The Mendesians, while sparing goats, sacrifice sheep: but all Egyptians sacrifice male cattle, provided they are pure, and calves.

IX. Among the Hebrews, it was a sin to bring polluted animals, or those marred by some defect, to the altar. Deuteronomy 17:1. Leviticus 22:21, 22, 23, <margin>On the beginning of victims.</margin> 24. And indeed, according to the testimony of Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish philosopher.</note>, there was such great caution regarding both those offering the victims and the sacrifices themselves, that the most skilled of the priests were accustomed to examine them from the tips of the feet, searching all visible parts as well as those hidden by the belly and thighs, lest even the smallest blemish lie concealed. <margin>Herodotus, Book II, Chapter 38.</margin> The same care preoccupied the Egyptians: *who consider male cattle to belong to Epaphus (for Apis is "Epaphus" in the Greek tongue) and therefore they examine the ox: and if they see even one black hair on it, they do not consider it pure. A priest appointed for this purpose searches while the beast is standing,*

The word *Azazel* is unknown to the Jews themselves. Some wish it to be the name of a *Mountain*, others of the *Goat* itself, others of a *Demon*. <margin>Bochart; Marsham, p. 205.</margin> Bochart contends the word is *Arabic*. But since it is *unexplained* <note>original: *ἀπεμήνυτον*</note>, what prevents us from divining that it is *Egyptian*? The Septuagint <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> in verse 8 translates it as *to the Sender-away* <note>original: *τῷ Ἀπομπαίῳ*</note>. According to Suidas, *certain Gods were called by this name, and "sending away" was used for "averting evil."* These Gods, according to Pollux, are *deliverers* and *protectors*—in a word, *averters of evil* <note>original: *averrunci*</note>. They attempted to appease these beings so they would not cause harm. For the Ancients believed there were two kinds of Gods: some the authors of good, others the authors of evil. Whatever *Zoroaster the Magician* and the *Persians* said regarding *Oromazes* the God of Light and *Areimanios* the God of Darkness; whatever the *Chaldeans* said regarding the *Planets, as Beneficent and Maleficent deities*; whatever the *Greeks* said regarding the good fortune of *Olympian Jove*,

I. NOW, finally, it remains for us to speak concerning certain INSTRUMENTS of Divine worship. By far the most majestic and celebrated of them all is the **URIM** <note>A ritual device used by the High Priest to determine God's will</note>, through which God revealed His will to Israel concerning secret matters in such an illustrious manner. What this was, and in what way it was taken over from the customs of the Egyptians, must now be explained by us according to the mind of the most learned Spencer <note>John Spencer (1630–1693), a scholar who argued that many Jewish rites had Egyptian origins</note>. So that this may be done conveniently, the matter must be traced back more deeply, and something must be said beforehand regarding the condition of the ancient **TERAPHIM**, of which there is such frequent mention in the sacred speech.

<margin>Chapter 4, section 2.</margin>
II. The Teraphim, therefore, were certain small images, in frequent use in the most ancient ages, first set apart in sacred shrines; which, *animated by the presence of a certain spirit (often an impure one), were accustomed to pour forth oracles: like household gods or protectors of the home.* This description can be gathered from *Genesis 31:19 and following; Ezekiel 21:21; Zechariah 10:2; 2 Kings 23:24.*
