VIII. The remaining points may be passed over as less relevant to the present case; however, what is said regarding the **Ephod** and the **Teraphim** <note>original: *Theraphim*; these were ancient figurines or cult objects</note> is worthy of its own consideration. It must be understood that two types of **Ephods** are mentioned in the sacred records. One is the **Common** type, by which is meant a garment made of linen alone, ordinary for priests and to be worn only when they were occupied with the ministries of the temple. The other is the **Pontifical** <note>High Priestly</note> type, which was a garment of great art and skill, distinguished and variegated with gold, gems, and colors, which the High Priest alone was permitted to wear when celebrating sacred rites. Now, there were two parts to this **Ephod**: the **shoulder-piece** <note>original: *superhumerale*</note>, which extended from the shoulders down to the belt, covering the entire chest; and the **Breastplate** <note>original: *Pectorale*</note>, joined to the shoulder-piece by such firm and religious bonds that they could not be pulled apart from one another without great difficulty. From this necessary connection which existed between the **Breastplate** and the **Ephod**, it happened that more than once in the sacred codex, the **Breastplate** (its inseparable companion) is understood by the name of the **Ephod**. See 1 Samuel 30:7 and elsewhere. Now, the text of **Hosea** which we have at hand is not to be interpreted as referring to the common **Ephod** (since, as **Moncæus** <note>François de Monceau, a 16th-century scholar</note> observes, the Jews were permitted to have and carry that at all times, however bad, even in the midst of captivity), but rather the **Pontifical** one, into which the **Urim** <note>A ritual device used for seeking divine oracles</note> was inserted.

IX. By **Teraphim** in this passage, we should not understand the idols of the gentiles, but rather those sacred little images <note>original: *icuncula*</note> which, animated by an Angel, were messengers of Divine counsel, to be included in the Ephod or the attached **Breastplate** according to Divine prescription: that is, the **Urim** itself. For it is not at all consistent with reason that the Prophet, whose task was to predict the mournful fate of the Israelite people, should count among their future evils the fact that they would lack idols. The thing which God threatens through the Prophet to take away from the Israelites, in order to take vengeance for their sins, must be something good and lawful; otherwise, to take it away would have been a benefit rather than a punishment. Of what good and lawful thing, then, can we interpret the **Teraphim** in that place with any appearance of truth, if not of the **Urim** of God, which coheres to the Ephod by such a holy bond? This is also why the **Ephod** and **Teraphim** are presented joined together, to be read as if in one continuous breath; whereas all other things mentioned in the text, being things of a plainly different family, are separated from one another by the repeated disjunctive word **without** <note>original Hebrew: אֵין (*ein*)</note>.

XI. Let this first argument be supported by a second from *Judges 17:4-5*. <margin>Section 1. chapter 4.</margin>
Regarding this history, the most learned *Spencer* <note>John Spencer (1630–1693), a scholar who argued that many Jewish rituals originated from Egyptian customs.</note> proceeds by explaining first *what* *Micah* made, and then *with what intention* he made them.

XII. Among *the things he made*, Spencer observes *three* instruments of dissimilar nature, yet all prepared for religious use. I. *Two images, a carved one and a cast one*, in which it is likely that he expressed the forms and number of the *Cherubim* with perfect likeness. It is reasonable to believe that one of these was fashioned from carved wood (like the *Cherubim* of the Temple) and covered with silver plates; the other was made of *solid silver*. These were placed in *Micah's* sacred chapel, adorned according to the form of the *Tabernacle* and the *Mosaic* worship. II. An *Ephod*, that is, an elaborate and splendid garment, so that his priest, clothed in it, might perform Divine matters with decorum. For *Spencer* easily believes that this garment did not deviate at all from the form of the *High Priest's Ephod*; except perhaps that the stones inscribed with the names of the tribes were missing, since that Levite was not performing the priesthood publicly nor in the name of all Israel. III. *Teraphim*; which, as in *Hosea*, so also in this whole history of *Micah*, are joined together as the inseparable companions of the *Ephod*, with no word ever placed between them, as if by a sacred bond. This serves as an argument that *Micah's Teraphim* held the place of the <unclear>Urim</unclear> in his rites, which was bound to the *Ephod* by a covenant and perpetual law.

XIII. A most learned man explains the *purpose* of Micah in this manner. He says that Micah did not furnish his small shrine with these instruments destined for sacred use with the intention of meditating on a withdrawal from the faith and worship of the True Deity. For just as his mother had consecrated her silver pieces to *Jehovah* <note>original: "Jehovæ"</note>, namely for His worship and honor; so too he himself gave excellent proofs of his zeal for God and the Divine law. This is seen in the fact that he considered it better to hire a Priest originating from the *Levitical* tribe at any price, as soon as the opportunity was presented to him, in order to satisfy the *new Divine Law* <note>The author likely refers to the Mosaic code as "new" in the context of the early Judges period</note>; rather than to retain his firstborn son in that office, though he had been consecrated *holily and religiously according to the custom of the ancestors*. Therefore, it is credible that Micah, led by a perhaps poorly concealed zeal for the *Mosaic* worship, decided to fashion the rites of his own religion after that model.

XIV. To be sure, at that time no King—that is, no Judge—presided over the people; therefore, as often happens, the roads were infested with robbers and assassins; the Priests were perhaps also lacking in their duties; public exercises of religion could not be attended except at the greatest risk to one's life; in short, all things were turned upside down. Since, therefore, the face of the Church was so deformed, Micah set his own example against that age which was rushing into every evil; he was, as it were, a *supporter* of religion, and decreed to worship God—if not exactly as he wished, then certainly as he was able. And so, he expressed by imitation at least a faint image of the Mosaic worship in that little shrine which he had dedicated to Jehovah.

XV. It seems one should be more inclined to agree with this opinion because the Most Holy Deity showed such an illustrious testimony to both Micah and his sacred objects *by an oracle given from the Teraphim* <note>Teraphim: household idols or cult objects used for divination in ancient Israel</note>. For the Danites, whom the doubtful outcome of their journey held anxious, approached Micah’s Levite, who was equipped with his Teraphim, asking that he consult God in his place (Judges 18:5). From him, they received this response: *Go in peace; the way you are about to enter is before the Lord.* What room is left for doubting the heavenly origin of this response? For it is established that the Danites, taking heart from that joyful omen, gave it the most certain credit; nor does the religion of the Levite allow us to believe that he, hired for no small price, would have simulated a Divine oracle with such a brazen forehead <note>A Latin idiom meaning "shamelessness"</note>. But also, the very outcome of events seems to have sufficiently fulfilled the faith of that oracle sent from heaven. But who is so void of heart as to think that the Danites [expected] Divine responses from Micah’s Teraphim...

XVII. Just as he does another argument nearly equal to it: that the *Hebrews*, the good and the bad alike in every age, were led by a supreme affection and admiration for the *Teraphim*. This is confirmed not only by the example of *Micah*, whom we read was greatly tormented in mind and driven by certain religious excesses when the Danites had stolen his *Teraphim* with an armed hand, but also by the example of *Rachel*, who stole her father *Laban's* *Teraphim*. She certainly did not do this to call her father's interests away from idolatry, nor to prevent him from learning of *Jacob's* journey by inspecting them. For if *Rachel* had intended that, she could have buried them in the road or thrown them into the flowing Euphrates with much less trouble and danger. But having followed those little images <note>original: "icunculas"</note> with a religious—or if you prefer, *superstitious*—affection, she took primary care that she might possess those *Teraphim* above all things that were most dear to her family. Nor did *Jacob* himself consider the *Teraphim* to be of no value, as is proven by his speech to *Laban* in Genesis 31:32: *With whomever you find them, let him suffer the penalty of death.* It is as if he believed the stain of such great sacrilege could only be expiated by the sacred head of the thief. Since, therefore, it is established that *Rachel*, and perhaps even *Jacob* (from whom the *Israelites* derive their race), held the *Teraphim* in the highest price and honor, who can deny that their sons drank in the use and love of the *Teraphim* with their very milk and their parents' first instructions? In this they were wonderfully confirmed when they saw that the *Chaldeans*, *Syrians*, and *Egyptians* had their own *Teraphim* from the deepest memory of antiquity. XVIII. Other points, which the most Illustrious Author himself would not deny are of lesser importance, I pass over without reluctance; yet I cannot remain silent on this one thing which he, with his exceptional erudition, acutely observed: that the words *Urim* and *Teraphim*, however much they differ in sound, are nevertheless *in reality* almost synonymous, and maintain a great similarity of meaning under a mask of great discrepancy. For *Urim*, in the genuine notion of the name, does not properly and primarily signify *lights*, but *fires*. And not just any *fires*: certainly not those lying inert in ashes or some coal and close to death; but *flaming* fires, casting forth a more joyful splendor. This is what <term>Mercer</term> and <term>Schindler</term> <note>Sixteenth-century Hebraists and lexicographers</note> also noted. Hence it differs from the word *Esh* <note>original: אשׁ</note>, which denotes *fire* simply considered: the very words of God confirm this distinction in *Isaiah 50:11*: <note>original: באור אשׁכם</note> *Walk in the flame of your fire*. Thus <term>Arias Montanus</term> <note>A famous Spanish Orientalist</note> says best: *We can render "Ha-Urim" as inflammations and illuminations*. The word *Teraphim*, however, is either Hebrew or Chaldean, and was formerly used among some of the Easterners for *Seraphim* (by the very slight and frequently used change of the letter *Shin* [ש] into *Tav* [ת]). That *Seraphim* sounds like *Burning ones* or *Inflaming ones* is a fact that escapes neither the Masters nor the Masters' pupils. Whence also the most ancient Egyptians worshipped *fires* under the name of *Seraphim*, according to <term>Stuckius</term> <note>Johann Wilhelm Stucki, a scholar of ancient rituals</note>. Therefore, both words—*Urim* as well as *Teraphim* or *Seraphim*—are of the same significance; and for that reason, it is not

# BOOK I. CHAPTER VIII.

...adopted: since we read that at the very beginnings of the world, flaming fire was divinely instituted as a symbol of the Angelic presence. <note>See Genesis 3, last verse: "He placed at the east of the garden of Eden Cherubims, and a flaming sword."</note> But it is also probable that men, following a most ancient custom, placed statues or small columns as symbols to celebrate the memory of Angels, or to signify their presence, especially in places dedicated to religion. Indeed, it is not inconsistent with the truth that Angels gave testimonies of their presence around the <term>Teraphim</term><note>Household idols or cult objects mentioned in the Old Testament, the nature of which is debated by scholars.</note>, and from there sometimes addressed the worshippers of the true Deity in the most ancient ages. You may gather this with some probability from the devotion of Rachel, Micah, and the Danites toward the Teraphim; but especially from the oracle delivered to the Danites through the Teraphim. For we all hold it as certain that God frequently used some Angel in making His counsels known. Finally, it should also be placed in the class of probabilities that these images eventually succeeded to the titles of the Angels—of whom they were symbols and, as it were, <term>tripods</term><note>A reference to the Delphic tripod, signifying a seat of prophecy or oracular communication.</note>—and were commonly called *Teraphim* instead of *Seraphim* by the Syrians and others steeped in Chaldean culture. The most illustrious Spencer confirms these observations of his by the authority of *Cornelius a Lapide* and *Louis de Dieu* among the more recent scholars, and *Jerome* and *Cedrenus* among the ancients.

XX. The sum of all these points comes back to this: that we may be persuaded that the love of the Teraphim, handed down from the ancestors, flourished again in the minds of the Israelites through their living among the Egyptians. Therefore, when God, in His immense wisdom, noticed that a stubborn people would be torn away from them only with difficulty, He gave to Israel the *Urim* <note>A ritual device used by the High Priest to determine the will of God.</note> in their likeness. Because of the agreement in both *form* and *use*, and by a right of *succession*, as it were, it is marked with that same name of *Teraphim*, since it is also of the same significance. We have been somewhat more wordy in explaining this matter because it is more noble than the others and worthy of a more diligent examination.

Kircher, *Sphinx Mystagoga* on Mummies. Part II. chapter IV.

I. IT COULD also be considered whether the CHERUBIM, which were the ornaments of the ARK, were formed in the likeness of certain sacred emblems among the Egyptians. To the Supreme Deity *Hempta*—for whom *Plutarch* says *Emet*—they attribute various attendants for administering the worldly Economy; and from these, they identify these four principal ones as counselors, whom the Greeks call *Genii* <note>guardian spirits</note>, and the Egyptians call the attendants of the deity *Hemptheus*, and most prompt Messengers for executing his commands. The first of these, *Horus*, in the form of a *Boy*, denotes the *Generative Deity of the sensible world*. The second is marked as *Dog-faced* <note>original Greek: "Κυνοπρόσωπος"</note>, conspicuous by a canine face, and represents the most vigilant guardian of the *Anubic or Hermetic Economy*. The third, under a *Hawk-like* countenance, whom they call *Thaustum*, likewise distinguished by the horn of *Ammon*, denoted *Solar heat* and fertility in the lower world. The fourth, formidable with a *Lion's face*, was *Momphta*, that is, the Guardian of the *Material world* <note>original: "Hylai mundi"</note>, or of the entire moist nature. Is it not in almost the same manner that to the supreme Deity—who is the *God of Truth* <note>original Hebrew: "אלהי אמת", transliterated as "Elohei Emet"</note>, having His Throne upon the propitiatory lid of the Ark of the Covenant—there are joined standing Angels and faithful ministers of His commands in the Universal world, under the *Emblem of the Cherubim*? For what else were these but the figures of monstrous living creatures, representing four different faces: of a *Man, a Lion, an Ox, and an Eagle*? As may be gathered from *Ezekiel* 1:10. In place of the *Dog-face*, God chose the *Ox-face*; in place of the *Hawk-face*, the *Eagle-face*, as being more honorable. The rest are almost the same. But I do not remember these things being observed by anyone else. Yet because they are not unlike the rest, I have been pleased to add them here, perhaps to provide an occasion for not unprofitable meditations.

Chapter V. section IV.

III. The word *Totaphot* itself seems to lead us to the same conclusion, which the illustrious Scaliger <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609), a famous Renaissance scholar</note> thinks is an Egyptian word signifying an amulet. Regarding this, it is worth mentioning how Samuel Petit <note>A French scholar known for studying ancient laws</note> philosophizes, since it pertains greatly to this matter. *It is certain,* he says, *and undisputed among the ancients, that amulets primarily featured "ridiculous things" <note>Greek: *γελοῖα* (geloia)</note>, and among them especially shameful parts, which, formed from various materials, they wore hanging [from themselves] to turn away envy <note>Greek: *ἐπὶ φθόνου ἀποτροπῇ*; to ward off the "evil eye"</note>: from which it happened that the word "fascinum" <note>A Latin term for both an amulet and the male organ</note> is used for shameful parts. God did not want his Israelites to use these kinds of pagan safeguards <note>Greek: *φυλακτηρίοις* (phylakteriois)</note>; which they had become accustomed to doing, it seems, while they served as inhabitants in Egypt, protecting their foreheads with the superstitious amulets of the Egyptians: but rather He wills that they carry the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments</note> described on small parchments on their foreheads; and let it be for them in place of the Egyptian amulets, "for frontlets" <note>Hebrew: *לטוטפות* (le-totaphot)</note>, "for safeguards" <note>Greek: *εἰς φυλακτήρια* (eis phylakteria)</note>. Totaphot, in my judgment, is a word composed of "Tet" <note>Hebrew: *טט*</note>, from which comes "Tit" <note>Hebrew: *טט*</note>, which signifies mud or slime; and "Phot" <note>Hebrew: *פות*</note>, that is, baseness or a shameful thing. Therefore, *Totaphot* are shameful things formed out of mud: because those things were most common in amulets, it happened that *Totaphot* generally signifies any amulet or safeguard.*

IV. This is further supported by the etymology of the name *Tefillin* <note>Hebrew: *תפילין*</note>, by which the Jews interpret *Totaphot*, and which the Syrian [translator] in Matthew interprets as "safeguards" <note>Greek: *τὰ φυλακτήρια*</note>: namely, it is derived from "Taphal" <note>Hebrew: *טפל*</note>, and *Tefillin* are "the ridiculous things." This, not so observed by others, was taught by Johann Christoph Wagenseil <note>A prominent 17th-century Hebraist</note>, a man most skilled in these letters, in his Notes to the *Codex Sotah* page 497, where he proves that the word *Tephillim* is used for sexual matters, contrary to the stumblings of Buxtorf. (Let it be allowed to add this to Petit's observations along the way.) To the same thing he refers the term "unshaken" <note>Greek: *τὰ ἀσάλευτα* (ta asaleuta)</note>, as it is commonly written in the version of the Seventy Interpreters <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note>. Which he thinks should be emended to *azaleuta* <note>Greek: *ἀζάλευτα*</note>, a composite word derived from *aza* and *aleuo*. Moreover, *aza* signifies "dust," as is clear from Hesychius <note>An ancient Greek lexicographer</note>. "Dust" seems to signify the shameful parts. *Aleuo*, by the testimony of the same Hesychius, is the same as "to guard"—

### V. The LIGHTING OF LAMPS in sacred rites also formed a certain part of the Hebrew religion. The use of the Candelabrum <note>The Menorah</note> seems necessary for illuminating the tabernacle, for we do not read of any windows there. Among the Jews there was an ancient custom that every father of a family, on the eve of the Sabbath, would light lamps for the following night. Indeed, even if due to poverty he lacked something to eat, he was expected to beg from door to door to obtain oil for himself for this purpose; because this was a part of the Sabbath joy. Josephus certainly counts the "lighting of lamps" <note>original: "λύχνων ἀνακαύσεις"</note> among those things which the nations learned from the Hebrews. However, Clement of *Alexandria* says, "The Egyptians were the first to show how to burn lamps" <note>original: "Αιγύπτιοι... πρῶτοι κατέδειξαν"</note>. Concerning them, *Herodotus* writes in these words: *When they have gathered in the city of Sais for the sacrifice, they all light many lamps at night all around their houses in the open air. The lamps are vessels full of salt and oil, upon which the wick floats, burning all night. The name of the festival is* Lychnokaie <note>original: "Λυχνοκαΐη"</note>, *the Lighting of Lamps. Those who do not go to the assembly, observing the night of the sacrifice, light lamps; thus lamps are lit not only in Sais, but throughout all of Egypt.* There is a very ancient story of *Mencheres*, or, as *Herodotus* calls him, *Mycerinus* (he was the 12th King of the Memphites), who buried his deceased daughter, his only child, in the belly of a wooden and gilded cow, and placed it in an adorned chamber, so that all kinds of incense might be burned to her daily, and a lamp lit every night. One may compare the things which *Kircher* laboriously collected regarding the lamps of the Egyptians in *Egyptian Oedipus, Volume III, Treatise XX.*

The *Egyptians* in particular are celebrated for a certain local magic <note>original Greek: μαγείᾳ τινὶ ἐπιχωρίῳ</note> regarding the charming of serpents. # OF THE EGYPTIANS

We have not been able to report these matters from the minds of the most learned men without many points arising simultaneously which are fit—as those men indeed suppose—to create the belief that the *Hebrews* drew those things which they have in common with the *Egyptians* from the *Egyptians*, and not, on the contrary, the *Egyptians* from the *Hebrews*. For we have already heard it confirmed by frequent testimonies of the most ancient and authoritative authors that the *Egyptians* were the very first of all to discover those things which pertain to religion; and that the other neighboring nations, and in the course of time even more remote ones, borrowed these things from them. It is to them that an ancient oracle of Apollo attributed the first discovery of *the way of the blessed, the path to the seats of the happy* <note>original: "τὴν μακάρων ὁδὸν, viam ad beatorum ſedes"</note>. It is for them that *Herodotus, Diodorus Siculus, Strabo, Plutarch, Lucian*, and others—citing testimonies in their proper place—claim the very first recognition and assertion of the *immortality of the soul, the discovery of the system of astrology adapted for sacred uses, the distinctions of months, weeks, and days, the construction of Temples, the practice of circumcision*, and many other things of that kind. And indeed, the authority of these most serious writers becomes the *first argument* with which it has pleased these most accomplished men to fight for the support of their opinion.

<margin>
Spencer, chapter IV, section XII. <note>Refers to John Spencer’s "De Legibus Hebraeorum," a famous 17th-century work on Hebrew rituals.</note>
</margin>
<margin>
Book II, chapter XCIII.
</margin>
II. There is added a *second argument*, sought from the *character* and customs of the *Egyptian Nation*. To be sure, the *Egyptians* were so swollen with pride in their reputation for antiquity, wisdom, and religion, that they looked down upon other nations with immense disdain, as if they were mere names and shadows of men. *Herodotus* says: *They refuse to use Greek customs, and (to speak once for all) they are unwilling to use the customs of any other men whatsoever.* <note>original: "Ἑλληνικοῖσι δὲ νομαίοισι φεύγουσι χρᾶσθαι· τὸ δὲ σύμπαν εἰπεῖν, μηδ᾿ ἄλλων μηδαμᾶ μηδαμῶν ἀνθρώπων νομαίοισι"</note> Nay, indeed, that absurd loathing of all others had finally driven that nation so far astray that they considered it unworthy of their name and birth to receive any foreigner at a common table with them, or to be joined to the human race by any fellowship of manners and rituals.

<margin>
On the Situation of the World, Book I, chapter IX.
</margin>
*Pomponius Mela* <note>A Roman geographer of the 1st century AD.</note> once noted that fanatic character of the *Egyptians*: *They use their letters perversely,* he says. *They knead mud with their hands, but flour with their heels. Women attend to the marketplace and business, while men care for the spinning-work and the homes; the former carry burdens on their shoulders, the latter on their heads. It is a necessity for daughters to support parents when they are in need, but for sons it is optional. They take their meals openly and outside their houses; they retreat to the innermost parts of the buildings for shameful acts.* <note>Mela is describing the "topsy-turvy" nature of Egyptian customs compared to Greco-Roman norms.</note>

<margin>
The Learned Banqueters, book VII, chapter XIII.

Is it credible that those who loved to have customs so diverse from other nations, and institutions so contrary to them, would have brought themselves to borrow such a great part of their religion from the Hebrews?

<margin>Against Apion, Book 1.</margin>
IV. From the *Hebrews*, I say. Against whom all the Egyptians, above all other inhabitants of the world, burned with a deadly and hereditary hatred: whom they detested as their former slaves and as the sole cause of all the evils by which they were nearly destroyed. *Josephus* himself testifies to this: *For all the Egyptians in common appear to have been most hostilely disposed toward us.* <note>original: "Φαίνονται γὰρ..."</note> Indeed, he wisely explains the causes of that hatred and envy, *of which*, he says, *they had many. First, because our ancestors became powerful in their region; from whence, having returned to their own lands, they were successful again. Then, the diversity of their sacred rites created many enmities between them; our piety being as much more excellent than their ceremonies as the nature of God is undoubtedly superior to irrational animals.* From this he concludes that they could by no means have imitated the *Hebrews'* integrity regarding Divine reason. For all we mortals are so born that we depart far from the customs of those whom we either hold in contempt or with whom we engage in the most serious enmities.

# CONCERNING EGYPTIAN MATTERS

V. A *third* argument is added, drawn from the condition and character of the Hebrew people: just as they were prone to adopting the institutions of other nations, it is unlikely that they wished—or even if they had wished, that they were able—to communicate their own dogmas to other nations.

<margin>Spencer, chapter 4, section 12 <note>John Spencer (1630–1693), an English theologian who argued that many Jewish rituals originated in Egypt.</note></margin>
VI. There are infinite examples teaching us that this was the nature of the Israelite race: *that they easily clothed themselves in the customs of others*. They rejected their ancestral customs with the same loathing that the Egyptians felt for foreign ones. Furthermore, they were almost always carried away by a brutal and impatient impulse toward the more splendid customs and all forms of worship—whether of the body or the mind—prevalent among foreign nations, especially the Egyptians. For this reason, an unbridled desire for a *King* took hold of them: not because they had need of one, but so that they might enjoy the presence of men distinguished by the glorious name of King, after the fashion of neighboring nations (1 Samuel 8:5). This vanity of the race seems to have occupied Solomon himself, who is read to have acquired seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines so that he might imitate or exceed the customs and pomp of neighboring Kings (1 Kings 11:3). From that itch for emulating all things foreign, it arose that foreign garments—that is, those fashioned according to the style and character of ethnic <note>original: "ethnici," referring here to non-Jewish or pagan peoples</note> luxury—were so highly prized and delightful to the Jews; and that they always loved foreign women so desperately and insanely that, in comparison to them, they erased all other beauties from their hearts.

VII. Nor did the minds of the Hebrews rush into foreign sacred rites with any less sluggish an impulse; the many imitations of idolatrous worship, so often grazed by the sharp-pointed sermons of the Prophets, abundantly prove this. But they were especially dazzled by the pomp of Egyptian rituals, enticed into a stupid love for them like little birds by the glitter of glass. Hence it has been observed by most learned men that almost all their idols, and the forbidden rites mentioned in Scripture, first flowed from Egypt as if from a perennial fountain of superstition. Since, therefore, the Israelites perpetually rushed into the idols and customs of Egypt with such mental force, we easily conclude that they formerly had a great deal of commerce with them, and loved those things in their innermost senses: just as we conclude, not without reason, that torches which catch fire most quickly were extinguished only a short time before.

<margin>Oedipus <note>referring to the work "Oedipus Aegyptiacus"</note> volume 1, Treatise 3, chapter 1.</margin>
VIII. # BOOK I. CHAPTER X.

...matters, by whose wicked customs and meager teachings the Egyptians were instructed. In the course of time, they gained followers of their institutions not only among other neighboring nations but especially among the Hebrews, who dwelt with them for nearly two hundred years. Of the second kind were the *concubines of Solomon*, foreign women, mostly Egyptians, by whose charms and deceitful love the Sacred Scriptures say Solomon was ensnared; he built shrines, altars, and groves, and erected idols to which they might offer incense. Seduced by his wicked example, the rest of his successors, the Kings of Israel—if you except a few—all adhered to this shameful worship.

IX. Nor did a plausible cause for this wicked emulation seem to be lacking, at least as a pretext. For it was probable that a carnal people, immersed in the pleasures of the senses, would embrace those dogmas by whose help they hoped to reach the pinnacle of all happiness. To instill this persuasion, that tranquil, peaceful, and ultimately most fortunate life of the Egyptians—which they attributed to the tireless worship of idols, sacrifices, and other impious arts as the sole cause—carried great weight in the minds of those prone to idleness. This can be made manifest from this single fact: that excited by this *Egyptian* prosperity and the fame of their memorable deeds, not *only the Hebrews*, but also the *Persians, Arabs, Phoenicians, Syrians, Babylonians, and Greeks* betook themselves to *Egypt* with the intent that, imbued with that wonderful knowledge of the Priestly disciplines and made participants in the *Isiac* <note>Refers to the mysteries of the goddess Isis</note> secrets by their help, they too might attain the same happiness as the *Egyptians*. All these things provide proof that the Israelites, with inclined minds, embraced many of the sacred rites of the Egyptians.

<margin>Marsham, page 153.</margin>
X. But they [the Jews] did not have the same willingness to communicate their own sacred rites to others. They boasted that the Law was the inheritance and private possession of the Church of Jacob (Deuteronomy 33:4), and thus peculiar to themselves, not to be shared with other nations through any translation into a profane language. <margin>Josephus, Antiquities, Book XII, Chapter II, at the end.</margin> When Ptolemy Philadelphus wondered why none of the historians or poets had mentioned the Mosaic laws, Demetrius responded that *certain people who had meddled with them had been punished by divine power: Theopompus was deprived of his mind, and Theodectes of his sight.* <note>Theopompus was a Greek historian and Theodectes a dramatist; legend claimed they were struck down for trying to incorporate scripture into secular works.</note> Added to this was the fact that the Jews had almost no social intercourse with foreigners; they neither visited them, nor were they visited by them. <margin>Against Apion, Book I.</margin> *We*, says Josephus, *do not inhabit a maritime land, nor do we delight in trade, nor do we have dealings with others for that reason; but our cities are far from the sea...*

...to be; *but we, inhabiting a fertile land, labor in its cultivation. This is a citation from Josephus, Against Apion, explaining Jewish isolation.</note> Indeed, the Jews, by the decree of their wise men, regarded all Gentiles as unclean, so much so that uncleanness was contracted from contact with them. Certainly, those who lived by such customs did not make it their business to propagate their institutions among other nations.

XI. But even granting as much as possible that they had wished to do so, it is nonetheless impossible that they could have carried it out. They were so dejected and contemptible in the judgment of other peoples. Although they were God's "special possession," they were nevertheless held to be the *filth and refuse of the nations.* <margin>Spencer, chapter 4, section 12.</margin> <note>John Spencer (1630–1693) was a pioneer in the comparative study of religion.</note> These nations held the Jewish people and their sacred rites in such low esteem that the credibility of Pagan annals is hard-pressed even to believe the Israelites existed. The persons of the Jews and their "anomalous loves" <note>A reference to perceived Jewish social exclusivity or specific cultural practices.</note> provided an occasion for jokes and laughter among the Gentiles, as if they held that people only as a whetstone *for the public wit.* From this, the most learned **Spencer** concludes that it is altogether unlike the truth that the Egyptians—those creatures of glory—would have wished to conform themselves to the customs of the Jews, whom the nations believed were, *like apes, born only to provoke laughter.*

XII. In the fourth place, these most erudite men fight with the *authority of the Sacred Scriptures* themselves, as if with decisive weapons. Nowhere, indeed, does Scripture assert in express words that many of the rites of the Israelites flowed from the customs of the age, changed only slightly—<margin>Spencer, chapter 4, section 7.</margin> (*for why,* they say, *would it speak in such a way about a matter that was hidden from no one at that time?*). Nevertheless, they argue that this is not poorly inferred from the twentieth chapter of Ezekiel, roughly in this manner: There, they say, God recalls to the people's memory that idolatry with which they once polluted themselves while dragging out their lives in Egypt (verses 4, 7, 8). Then, He records at length those moral laws which He gave to the Israelites having recently departed from Egypt (verses 10, 11, 12), and that in the meantime they held His statutes in contempt and returned to the rites of the Gentiles (being unable to strip off their nature and habit) (verses 13, 14). Therefore, He says, since they had cast behind their backs my statutes—those eternal righteous laws <note>original: "αἰώνια illa δίκαια" (aionia illa dikaia)</note> which give life to those observing them—had polluted my Sabbaths, and had too often cast their eyes upon the idols of their Fathers, at last, as if broken and wearied by the character of a froward people, I myself gave them *statutes that were not good, and judgments by which they should not live.* <note>A reference to Ezekiel 20:25, a controversial verse often used by scholars to explain the origin of burdensome ritual laws.</note> Here, let the learned consider whether "statutes that were not good" should not be understood as the ritual laws; for that title fits them especially well.

# BOOK I. CHAPTER X.

...by *reason of the material* <note>original: "ratione materiæ"</note>, insofar as they command nothing that is desirable in itself or capable of perfecting human nature; by *reason of the effect*, for they brought death to those who violated them, but not life to those who obeyed; but especially by *reason of their origin*. This is because those statutes owed their beginning to the customs of the age, being enacted so that some people, marked by a particular vice, might be removed from the midst, while others might be tolerated with the greatest caution. For it was necessary that God place a bridle upon a brutish people who would otherwise rush headlong into the crooked paths of the earth. He left certain rituals—manifestly free from crime—to be observed so that through those lighter exercises of religion, performed in God's honor and according to His command, they might emerge skilled and initiated for more severe examples of obedience that are pleasing in themselves. And certainly, unless God, through those *statutes that were not good* <note>A reference to Ezekiel 20:25, often debated by theologians regarding the "imperfect" ceremonial laws.</note>, had yielded to that people who were so stubbornly devoted to all ancient things, it was to be feared that they would utterly shrink from His sacred rites, in which they could detect no character of antiquity or received custom.

XIII. But also called to support this are *those words of Paul* found in Acts 13:18. Where, discussing the Israelites acting in the desert, he says: God, *for forty years, bore with their manners* <note>original Greek: "ἐτροποφόρησε" (etropophorēsen). The author argues God endured or adapted to their character.</note>. That by *those old manners* we should understand customs placed beyond fault and adopted into the number of their rituals is proved by this: it must be far from us to think that the Best Deity wished to dismiss with impunity any custom that sinned against the laws of eternal justice. Indeed, He was so far from tolerating with a mild spirit any idolatry, unbridled lust, or manners of this kind branded with the blackest marks, that every single person who went out from Egypt, infamous for these behaviors, paid the penalty for their crimes with a premature death.

XIV. Fifth follows the *reasoning suggested by a just and holy estimation of Divine wisdom*; which regards partly the *Jews* and partly the *Gentiles*. As for the *Jews*, it is not at all probable that God wished to burden His worship and almost overshadow the precepts of the Moral Law with so many weak and fleshly rituals—neither pleasing to Himself nor known to His true worshippers for two thousand years—except for the fact that the Israelite people, seized by a zeal for ancient vanities, would have wished to offer worship to a Demon through them, if it had not been permitted to do so for God.

...let us bring this forward into the open. Because, he says, when animals are born they are very tender and cannot be nourished by dry food, therefore God adapted breasts for them to produce milk: so that they might be nourished by moist food of this kind, which is suitable for the temperament of their own limbs, until they are dried and strengthened by degrees and in order. And one may observe a plainly similar method of the governance of God, the Best and Greatest, in many things in *our Law* <note>original: "Lege nostra," referring to the Torah</note>, because it is not possible to pass suddenly and in a moment, as it were, from one contrary to another; and consequently, according to the nature of man, it cannot happen that he leaves in a moment that to which he has been accustomed for a long span of time. Therefore, when God sent *Moses*, our Teacher of pious memory, to make us a royal Priesthood and a holy nation—first in the knowledge of God, and then in His worship—the usual custom then in the world to which everyone was accustomed, and the universal worship in which everyone had been educated, was that various species of animals were offered in those temples in which they placed images, and people would prostrate themselves before them and burn incense. Moreover, there were certain sequestered worshippers, as it were, destined for that worship which was practiced in temples built in honor of the *Sun, Moon*, and the rest of the stars. Therefore, the Wisdom and Providence of God, which shines in all His creatures, did not wish to command that all those forms of worship be abandoned or abolished. For the human heart, which perpetually inclines toward that to which it is accustomed, would not naturally have been capable of such a thing. --- For this reason, God still retained these forms of worship, but transferred them from created things and phantasms, which have no truth, to His own name; and He commanded that we ourselves should build Temples, that an altar be consecrated to His name, that sacrifices be offered to Him, and that we should bow down and offer incense before Him. Thus He separated priests for the worship of the sanctuary, etc.

XVI. Furthermore, it seems that the lack of sophistication not only of the *Israelite* people, but also of the *Gentiles* (for Divine mercy took care for them as well), demanded that some ancient customs be transcribed into the worship and Law of God. For since no hope of salvation shone upon them except from the *Jewish Church*; this certain agreement of rituals was naturally suited to foster the inclined interests of the Gentiles toward the Jews and their religion; and that communion of sacred rites, however great, joined their minds more easily and more charmingly to the worship and communion of the Jews, and kept them bound to it. From these people they might perhaps have shrunk away entirely, as if from those eager for a hated novelty and despisers of the human race, if [they had introduced] *strange* <note>original Greek: "ξενίζοντα" (xenizonta), meaning foreign or strange things</note>...

XVII. Finally, to confirm this opinion of theirs, they call upon a complete and well-equipped phalanx <note>A military metaphor for a strong line of supporting arguments</note> of witnesses, both ancient and modern: who not only proclaim that the Hebrews borrowed their customs from the Egyptians; but also confidently assert that God Himself, for the reasons often praised now, adopted many rites from the customs of the age into the number of His own sacred ceremonies. Among the ancients, Cyril of Alexandria <note>A 5th-century Church Father and Patriarch of Alexandria</note> defends those views thus: *The most insane nation of the Gentiles, following their own customs and living in the manner of mute cattle, used to promise their hair, professing to grow it for Demons. And indeed one person would offer it to the Nymphs, whom they called Oreads <note>Mountain nymphs in Greek mythology</note>, another to a river, as it seemed fit, and that matter was held in place of religion. Therefore the most wise Moses, or rather God through Moses, understanding that the Hebrews could not easily lay aside the customs they had soaked up in Egypt, decided to institute similar rites, gradually separating them from their ancient errors: by which rites they would no longer worship demons, but God Almighty, as if under a shadow and a figure.* For that reason, He brought forth the law concerning sacrifices, and accepted those bloody victims with very little pleasure. # BOOK II. CHAPTER I.

And so, let it be our right and divine law to candidly set forth, strengthen, and defend this honor, for the vindication of the Israelite people, for the elucidation of many passages in the sacred texts, and finally, for the protection of sacrosanct truth.

II. It is my pleasure to encompass our opinion in certain Theses, which we shall presently undertake to clarify and confirm. We establish them in this manner:

III. I. From the *depraved customs, superstition, and idolatry of the Egyptians*, the *Israelites* did indeed adopt many things; but they also borrowed similar things from other neighboring peoples; nor did they take from the Egyptians all those things which some writers have ascribed to them as the original inventors.

IV. II. In the *Dogmas, Institutions, and Rites approved by God*, there is *not* so great a similarity between the *Egyptians* and the *Hebrews* as learned men proclaim—who do so not always cautiously, and sometimes neither purely nor holily enough. <note>The author is likely critiquing scholars like John Spencer or Pierre Daniel Huet who argued for "Egyptian borrowing."</note>

V. III. Where they do agree, the *Egyptians* and *Hebrews* held those things in common with other more civilized peoples, drawn from the common fountain of either *Reason* or *Tradition*: both of which were purer and more incorrupt among the *Hebrews*.

VI. IV. Regarding those things further removed from the law of *Nature* which were nevertheless common to both *Egyptians* and *Hebrews*, it cannot be proven that they were more ancient among the Egyptians than among the Hebrews; since all those praised writers <note>referring to Greek historians like Herodotus or Diodorus Siculus</note> are not a little more recent than *Moses*.

VII. V. On the contrary, it is probable that the *Egyptians* received many things from *Abraham, Joseph, Moses, and Solomon*.

VIII. VI. From the same source the *Greeks* drew, whether directly <note>original: ἀμέσως (amesos)</note> or indirectly <note>original: ἐμμέσως (emmesos)</note>.

IX. VII. It was by no means the intent of God in the *ceremonial institutions* as learned men imagine; namely, that He tempered Himself to the stubborn character of the people by adopting into His own worship those things—though slightly purged—to which they had become wickedly accustomed by emulating foreign superstitions. But rather: I. *That by these laborious exercises, as if by a most difficult yoke, He might subdue the untamable ferocity of the people.* II. *That, as if by a partition wall, He might separate them from other nations, and especially from the Egyptians, from whom they came, and the Canaanites, to whom they were going.* III. *And most of all, that they might be figures and shadows of spiritual things.*

# CHAPTER II.

### That the Hebrews derived their idolatry and shameful superstitions from the Egyptians and neighboring peoples.

I. *The Israelites emulated the idolatry of the Egyptians both while in Egypt and after their departure.* II. *From this came the Golden Calf of Aaron.* III. *Regarding its origin, some have handed down false accounts,* IV. *Others have handed down uncertain ones.* V. *It is more true that it was made in the likeness of Apis <note>The sacred bull of Memphis, worshipped by the Egyptians as a god.</note>.* VI. *Arguments proving this.* VII. *The Egyptians worshipped Oxen before the departure of the Israelites.* VIII. *And images of oxen.* IX. *And these were golden, during the mourning for Osiris.* X. *Which Osiris is the same deity as Apis.* XI. *Stephen <note>Referring to Saint Stephen’s speech in Acts 7.</note> reproaches the Israelites for their emulation of the Egyptians in this regard.* XII. *The very similarity of the superstitions proves it.* XIII. *The calves of Jeroboam are of the same origin.* XIV. *In Tammuz, the Jews worshipped Adonis;* XV. *A Phoenician deity, but one from Egypt, and the same as Osiris.* XVI. *Which signified the sun in hieroglyphics.* XVII. XVIII. *When and how his cult came from Egypt to the Jews.* XIX. *But the Israelites also imitated the shameful things of other nations, first in the desert,* XX. *And then in their own land.*

# BOOK II. CHAPTER II.

...she multiplied her prostitutions, remembering the days of her youth in which she had played the harlot in the land of the Egyptians. <note>A reference to Ezekiel 23:19, suggesting Israel's recurring attraction to foreign gods.</note>

II. Of this matter—to pass over other points—the evident proofs are those **GOLDEN CALVES**, first cast by *Aaron* at the command of the common people who were <term>mad for idols</term> <note>original Greek: ειδωλομανεῖν</note>, and later by *Jeroboam*. Concerning the former, *Philo the Jew* writes: *When Moses had ascended the mountain, certain men turned his absence into an occasion for impiety, and forgetting the holiness due to the* BEING <note>original Greek: τὸ ὌΝ, referring to the true God</note>, *they became emulators of Egyptian fictions; having forgotten piety toward the first* BEING, *they became imitators of Egyptian fabrications: then, having prepared a golden bull, to appear to be an imitation of the animal considered most sacred in that region [Egypt], they made a golden bullock, as they thought, in imitation of that region's most sacred animal.* *Lactantius, Jerome, Augustine, Basil of Seleucia*, and countless more recent authors hold similar views.

III. And they are indeed correct: for what some argue—that *Aaron* wished to represent God to the people under such a ridiculous form so that he might turn them away from idolatry—is not likely. For all the circumstances of the text show that *Aaron* acted in earnest. Nor is the opinion of *Moncaeus* <note>François de Moncaeius, a 16th-century jurist who argued the calf was a cherub</note> closer to the truth, who suggested that *Aaron* fashioned this ox after the example of a Cherub, upon which he had seen God sitting when He appeared to the elders. *Exodus 24:10.* For there we read indeed that God was seen, *having under his feet as it were a work of sapphire stone, or like the sky when it is clear*; but we do not read that He was carried by a Cherub, much less one in the form of a calf. Indeed, God expressly denies that any form of animal appeared to Israel at that time. *Deuteronomy 4:15.*

<margin>Book I, chapter xv.</margin>
IV. It is not so clearly false what the *Author of the Wonders of Scripture* (under the name of *Augustine*) relates concerning *Joseph*; he asserts that a likeness of an ox was established by the Egyptians near Joseph's tomb, because the ox cooperates with man in agriculture. *For this reason also,* he continues, *the children of Israel, when they wished to worship an idol in the desert, made no other statue than a calf, that is, an ox: for this reason above all, because he [Joseph] was worshipped in Egypt near his tomb in the form of an ox.* However, even this rests only upon uncertain conjectures.

<margin>Book XVII.</margin>
V. It is more certain that Apis and Mnevis, sacred bulls of the *Memphites* and *Heliopolitans*, were worshipped as Gods. *Strabo* writes: *A sacred female cow is nourished there, just as Apis is in Memphis, and in the City of the Sun [Heliopolis] is Mnevis. These indeed are considered Gods.* *They nourish a sacred cow there: just as Apis is indeed at Memphis,*

# EGYPTIAN MATTERS

In Heliopolis, however, the *Mnevis* <note>A sacred bull of ancient Heliopolis, considered an incarnation of the sun god Ra</note> is nourished. And indeed, these are considered Gods.
<margin>On the Nature of the Gods, Book 1.</margin> Cicero, speaking in the persona of Cotta to the *Epicurean*, says: *What do you think? Does not that Apis, the Holy bull of the Egyptians, seem a God to the Egyptians?*
<margin>Book 8, Chapter 46.</margin> Pliny says: *In Egypt, a bull is even worshipped in place of a deity; they call him Apis.*
<margin>Book 1, Chapter 9.</margin> Mela: *Apis is the deity of all those peoples; a black bull, distinguished by certain spots, and unlike others in its tail and tongue. It is rarely born, and not by the mating of cattle, as they say, but divinely conceived by celestial fire; the day on which it is born is the greatest festival for the nation.* Nothing is simpler than for us to think that this golden Calf was cast by Aaron in imitation of this superstition. Let it be permitted to explain this in the words of Pererius <note>Benedict Pereira (1535–1610), a Jesuit theologian</note>: *The superstitious Hebrew nation,* he says, *had seen the solemnities of the Egyptians in the worship of the Bull while staying in Egypt and still mingling with them; they saw also the cause of such great worship, namely the abundance of earthly goods resulting from it. Therefore, while they underwent harder times in the desert, they suddenly adopted for themselves those Gods who could remedy their want—such as they, along with the Egyptians, judged the Apis bulls to be.*

VI. Which will be seen to be most true, unless I am mistaken, if we demonstrate these three things: I. That the worship of brutes, and specifically of Bulls, was so ancient among the Egyptians that it preceded the departure of the Israelites from Egypt. II. That the Egyptians worshipped not only living animals, but also their images. III. That the Israelites are even reproached for their <term>bad imitation</term> <note>original: κακοζηλίαν (kakozēlian) - a perverse or misguided zeal/imitation</note> of the Egyptians in this very matter.

VII. That which we asserted in the first place is gathered from that response which Moses and Aaron gave back to Pharaoh when he said, *Go, sacrifice to your God in this land.* They said, *It is not fitting to do so, because we would be sacrificing the abomination of the Egyptians to the Lord our God. Behold, if we were to sacrifice the abomination of the Egyptians before their eyes, would they not stone us?* (Exodus 8:25-26). The animals sacrificed by the Israelites were *Sheep and Bulls*. Concerning these, see Exodus 24:5. These are called the *abomination of the Egyptians*; either because the Egyptians abused those animals for horrific idolatry (for the idols of the Gentiles are everywhere called *abominations* by the Sacred Writers), or because such sacrifices were an abomination to the Egyptians, who would not suffer those things which they themselves adored to be slaughtered. To this effect, the Chaldean <note>Referring to the Targum, an Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible</note> says: *Since the animal which the Egyptians fear (worship), we are going to take to sacrifice.* And the Syrian <note>The Peshitta, the Syriac version of the Bible</note>: *If we sacrifice the Gods of the Egypti—*

# BOOK II. CHAPTER II.

*In the eyes of the Egyptians.* To this same point belongs the joke of *Anaxandrides* <note>A Greek comic poet of the 4th century BCE</note>, mentioned by us above:

> *You worship the Ox; I sacrifice him to the Gods.*

Whichever way you take it, what could be said more clearly than that testimony of *Moses*, by which it is established that the deification of Oxen existed in that age and near the time of the Exodus? Many also refer to this the fact that the Egyptians detested shepherds (Genesis 46:34), who are accustomed not only to pasture cattle but also to slaughter them; <gloss>because they are as gods to them</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: לפי שהן להן אלוהות</note>, says *Rabbi Solomon* <note>Referring to Rashi, the medieval French rabbi and commentator</note>.

VIII. Regarding what we said in the second place concerning the sacred images of consecrated animals, which the Egyptians held in high value and veneration, this can be taught not only from profane histories but also from the Sacred Scriptures. For I shall not now repeat what we previously produced from *Strabo*—that in the ancient temples of the Egyptians there was no image fashioned in the likeness of man, yet there were others fashioned in the likeness of beasts—*Mela* states in express words: <margin>Book 1, chapter IX.</margin> *They worship the effigies of many animals, and the animals themselves even more.* That *Moses* was looking back at the idolatry of the Egyptians in Deuteronomy 4:16, 17, 18 is proved by the enumeration of those animals which everyone knows were religiously worshipped by the Egyptians. Since he wishes that not even images of them be made by the Israelites, *because Jehovah led them out of the iron furnace from Egypt* (verse 20), nothing is more likely than for us to gather that the Egyptians fashioned sculptures of that kind. And indeed, that which he forbade concerning the making of the form of *male or female*, is drawn by most learned men to refer primarily to the sexes of Oxen. For they worshipped male oxen dedicated to *Osiris*, and females dedicated to *Isis*.

IX. Certainly, in the mourning for *Osiris*, or his "Disappearance" and "Finding" <note>original Greek: Ἀφανισμῷ & Εὑρέσει</note>, there was a **Gilded Ox**, clothed in a dark garment of fine linen, which was accustomed to be shown openly and solemnly by the Priests for four continuous days as an image of the Deity. Lest anyone doubt it, we will give the very words of *Plutarch*: <margin>On Isis.</margin> <gloss>The priests perform other gloomy rites, and covering a gilded ox with a black linen cloth, they display it in the mourning of the Goddess. For they consider the Ox to be the image of Osiris.</gloss> <note>original Greek: Οἱ ἱερεῖς ἄλλά τε δρῶσι σκυθρωπὰ, καὶ βοῦν διάχρυσον ἱματίῳ μέλανι βυσσίνῳ περιβάλλοντες, ἐπὶ πένθει τῆς Θεοῦ δεικνύουσι. Βοῦν γὰρ ᾿Οσίριδος εἰκόνα νομίζουσι.</note> At that time the priests, while they perform other somber rites, display the **Gilded Ox** in a black linen shroud during the mourning of the Goddess. For they consider the Ox the image of Osiris.

<margin>Book XVII.</margin>
*It also has temples, specifically that of Apis, who is the same as Osiris, where the bull Apis is nourished in a certain shrine.* Since, therefore, not only a living bull but also an image of one—and indeed a gilded one—was sacred to *Osiris*, and since *Osiris* and *Apis* are the same deity, it follows that we should believe *Apis* was also worshipped in the form of a Bull's image. However, we would not want this to be interpreted as if the entire fable of *Isis, Osiris,* and *Typhon*, as *Plutarch* relates it, were older than the times of *Moses*. For now, it is enough to have observed that from ancient times, a gilded Bull was held in veneration by the Egyptians. Just as the most noble *Marsham* <note>Sir John Marsham, an English chronicler</note> will not grudge that this be proved from the rites of *Apis*, so I would not wish it to be held against me that I now believe, along with most learned men, that *Apis* or *Osiris* was more ancient than *Moses*.

XI. Finally, that the *Hebrews* were reproached for having worshipped a cast calf in the desert after the example of the *Egyptians* is proved by those words of *Stephen* the first martyr in *Acts* 7:39, 40, 41:
> They turned back in their hearts to Egypt, saying to Aaron, "Make us gods to go before us," and they made a calf in those days, and offered sacrifice to the idol.

But it is a wonder that this most learned man <note>Likely referring to a previous commentator on the Book of Exodus</note> did not consider what *Selden* <note>John Selden (1584–1654), a famous English jurist and scholar of Oriental antiquities</note> had already observed before: that with that writing tool, the marks of *Apis* <note>The sacred bull of Memphis, worshipped as a god</note> or something similar could have been engraved. <margin>On the Syrian Gods, Syntagma 1, chapter IV.</margin> For the Egyptians are said to have fashioned and painted *Apis*—who bore the image of the moon, and whom they therefore foolishly imagined was conceived by lunar rays—with a black color, a square white spot on the forehead, a natural mark on the right side, and an image resembling the crescent moon. For when *Apis* was found, while he was being led by the priests in a solemn procession to Memphis, the royal city of the Egyptians, boys in that sacred retinue sang a song in honor of the deity in groups. And because of the birth and discovery of the God, a "Pandaesia" <note>original: πανδαισία; a general feast or public banquet</note> or a most joyful banquet was celebrated with great public joy, as Suidas writes. <margin>Under the entry "Apis."</margin> Hence Philo says of the Israelites: <margin>On the Life of Moses, Book III.</margin> *Having fashioned a golden bull in imitation of the Egyptian Typhon, they set up dances.* <note>original Greek: τεκησάμενοι ταῦρον χρυσῶν Ἀιγυπτιακῶ μίμημα τύφω, χοροὺς ἴσασαν</note> This is correct, provided that instead of *Typhus* or *Typhon*, he had said *Osiris*. For this is a persistent error of Philo’s, which *Bochart* <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a French Protestant biblical scholar</note> learnedly corrected: that he attributes to Typhon what properly belonged to *Osiris*. *Typhon* was not regarded by the Egyptians so much as a God, but as an Evil Spirit <note>original: Cacodæmone</note>. And they do not attribute the Ox to him, but the most stupid of tame animals, namely the Ass; and the most savage of wild ones, the Crocodile and the <margin>Plutarch, On Isis.</margin> Hippopotamus.

XIII. Of the same origin are the Calves erected by Jeroboam in Dan and Bethel. For since he had spent many years in Egypt as a familiar and close associate of King Shishak <note>original: Sesaco</note>, (1 Kings 11:40), having become accustomed to the Egyptian calves, he was induced to transfer them into the sacred rites of the Israelites. And he seems to have obtained this more easily from them because their ancestors had once been mad with the same madness. Certainly, Jeroboam spoke of his calves in the same words (1 Kings 12:28) with which the Israelites spoke of Aaron's calf (Exodus 32:4): *These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt.* And this is the reason why God finds fault with *Aholah* (that is, Israel), because she did not abandon her prostitutions brought from Egypt (Ezekiel 23:8). But we have dealt with this matter more extensively elsewhere.

MUZ, and the frantic wailing of the little women over him, which God showed to Ezekiel in the spirit. Ezekiel 8:14. *The author of the Alexandrian Chronicle rightly observed that Thammuz is Adonis.* And

> *Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), known for translating the Bible into Latin.</note>: The one whom we have interpreted as Adonis, both the Hebrew and Syrian languages call Thammuz <note>original: תמוז</note>. Whence, because according to the pagan fable, in the month of June, the lover of Venus and a most beautiful youth is said to have been killed and subsequently to have lived again: they call that same month of June by the same name, and they celebrate an annual solemnity for him, in which he is mourned by women as if dead, and afterwards, coming to life again, he is sung of and praised.*

The ceremonies common to both *Thammuz* and *Adonis* in the solemnities of each confirm this observation: a month common and sacred to both, and finally, the same mourning for both.

XV. Moreover, Adonis was a Phoenician deity. The name itself is from the dialect of the Syrians, for whom *Adon* signifies *Lord*. *Hesychius <note>A 5th-century Greek grammarian.</note>:* "Adonis <note>original: Ἅδωνις</note>, lord among the Phoenicians." The Phoenicians had him from the Egyptians. For Adonis is the same as *Osiris*. And this entire scene of mourning in the disappearance <note>original: ἀφανισμῷ (aphanismo) — the ritual disappearance or death of a god</note> of *Osiris* was first established by the Egyptians. The Egyptians shared it with their neighbors. The *Alexandrians*, on the very day that the festival of mourning or the Adoniasm <note>original: Ἀδωνιασμῷ — the ritual lamentation for Adonis</note> was celebrated among the people of *Byblos* in *Phoenicia*, used to send a letter every year enclosed in a jar or a vessel made of rushes or papyrus, after the ceremonies had been duly performed, into the sea; this was carried of its own accord to *Byblos*

<margin>Concerning the Syrian Goddess.</margin> and announced that *Adonis* had been found. *Lucian <note>Lucian of Samosata, a satirist who wrote "De Dea Syria" (On the Syrian Goddess).</note>* calls that vessel or jar a "papyrus head" <note>original: βυβλίνην κεφαλήν</note>, and says it was carried from Egypt to *Byblos* in seven days, the sea and wind having been divinely prepared. As soon as the women of *Byblos* received this message—waiting for it with the greatest eagerness—they changed their wailing and lamentations into applause and sacred joys, and with wonderful gladness they spent what remained of the festival because of the finding of the once-lost *Adonis*. From this Egyptian custom of letters enclosed in rushes and transmitted across the sea to *Byblos*, *Procopius* interprets that passage of *Isaiah 18:1-2*: *Sending ambassadors by the sea, even in vessels of bulrushes upon the waters.* Where the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> have "papyrus letters" <note>original: ἐπιϛολὰς βυβλίνας</note>. But we shall show the true origin of this superstition in its proper place from our own sacred writings. Whatever the case may be, that which to the Phoenicians and Syrians is *Adonis*, killed by a *Boar*, deplored by *Venus* and *Proserpina*, and recalled from the underworld, is to the Egyptians *Osiris*, slain by *Typhon* (whom they called a *Boar* on account of his monstrosity and ferocity) and deplored by *Isis* and her companions; the same was to the *Jews*

# BOOK II. CHAPTER II.

*Thammuz*, regarding whose name it is unclear whether it was transferred from the month to the deity, or from the deity to the month.

XVI. This much is clear: the ancients took *Adonis* to represent the Sun. They imagined him struck down by a *Boar*—a shaggy and rough beast—because winter is rough and shaggy, and during that season the powers of the sun gradually fail. Hence, those who first established these dirges celebrated the festival of *Adonis* in the month of *Thammuz* (which is *June*), specifically around the summer solstice. At this time, the sun leaves the Northern regions and travels toward the South. They intended nothing else than to denote the approach and departure of the sun, mourning him as if lost, and then welcoming him back with joyful omens as if reborn. See Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, book 1, chapter 21. <note>Macrobius was a 5th-century Roman writer; his Saturnalia is a primary source for ancient solar myths.</note>

XVII. It is not surprising that the Jews—a people very prone to idolatry and even the most absurd superstitions—drew this from their neighbors and changed the name to *Thammuz*. This is especially likely since the same solemn rite existed in Egypt, and many Egyptians were in Judea at that time. Here, I prefer to stand with *Selden* <note>John Selden (1584–1654), an English polymath and author of 'De Diis Syris' (On the Syrian Gods).</note> rather than ascend with *Kircher* <note>Athanasius Kircher (1602–1680), a Jesuit scholar known for his vast, though often speculative, works on Egyptology.</note> into the most ancient of antiquities. However, it is worth hearing what Kircher brings forward from *Abenephius*. He was a Jew by religion who left behind a book written in the Arabic language *On Egyptian Servitude*. In that book, among other memorable things, he relates the following:

> *At the time,* he says, *when the Israelites were dwelling in the land of Egypt, there was a certain King among those then ruling in Egypt named Thammuz. He was the first to institute the rites and ceremonies usually practiced in that mournful festival of Osiris, to be repeated annually. The Hebrews, mixed among the Egyptians, learned their practices. Once set free and returned to the land promised to their fathers, they celebrated the profane sacrifices into which they had been initiated with the same wailing and mourning they were accustomed to in Egypt. Furthermore, they named the month in which these were usually celebrated 'Thammuz,' after their first author, Thammuz.*

Thus far *Abenephius*. To me, however, to tell the truth, it does not seem probable that this idolatrous superstition among the Hebrews is of such great antiquity, since it has not been reproached by any of the Prophets until now. <note>The author suggests that if the practice were that old, earlier biblical prophets would have condemned it sooner.</note>

XVIII. Nevertheless, it must not be concealed that Philastrius <note>A 4th-century bishop and writer on heresies.</note> discussed things consistent with Abenephius.

> *Thammuz,* he says, *was the son of a King of the gentiles, whose image the Judean women adored with weeping. For the Pharaoh who presided over the Egyptians under the blessed Moses was called Thamus.*

# EGYPTIAN MATTERS

<margin>Biblical Questions, Book II, chapter 15.</margin>
This provided *Johann Heinrich Ursinus* <note>A 17th-century German scholar and theologian</note> with the opportunity to offer commentaries that are considerably wiser than those of the *Abenephians* <note>Followers of the Arab writer Abenephius, whose works were often cited by Athanasius Kircher</note>. He believes he possesses probable arguments to assert that the first superstition arose from that public mourning and wailing of the Egyptians, of which Holy Scripture testifies there was none like it before or after, *Exodus 11:6 and 12:3*. Later, because this annual mourning tended toward the glory of the God of Israel, the matter was obscured by the cunning of the Devil through newly devised fables, and finally attributed to natural causes. It is agreed that at the time the Israelites departed from Egypt, there reigned <margin>Against Apion, Book I; Miscellanies, Book I, page 370.</margin> *Themosis*, as *Josephus* holds, or *Amosis*, according to *Ptolemy of Mendes* cited in *Clement of Alexandria*. Nor does he think *Thamus* was anyone other than the king of all Egypt, to whom *Theut*, or *Mercury*, came bringing the arts he had invented, along with numbers and letters. For as to the objection *Selden* <note>John Selden, a prominent English jurist and polymath</note> raises—that chronologists calculating more accurately claim *Themosis* lived several centuries before *Moses*—*Ursinus* says this is of no consequence. *For no chronologist,* he says, *has ever been found, nor will one be found hereafter, who has reduced the monstrous lies of the Egyptians—mere sand without lime <note>A metaphor for a weak foundation or incoherent argument</note>—to a rational system of time and calculation.* It shall suffice for us to have reported these things and to commit them to the fair judgment of the reader. If anyone desires more concerning *Thammuz*, let him consult *Vossius on Idolatry, Book II, chapter 4, and Book IX, chapter 10; Selden on the Syrian Gods, Treatise II, chapter 10; and Kircher’s Oedipus, Volume I, Treatise IV, chapter 9,* where he will find enough to quench his thirst for knowledge.

# ON EGYPTIAN MATTERS

That superstitious and idolatrous use of the **THERAPHIM** <note>Hebrew: *teraphim*; small household idols or figurines used for divination</note>, which we have recently seen Kircher derive—with how much effort!—from the Egyptians to Abraham’s servants, and from them (upon returning with Abraham to his homeland) to the Chaldeans and Syrians, and from those again to Jacob’s family and later descendants; but, unless my mind deceives me, this is entirely contrary to all reason.

II. I suppose now that the Theraphim were certain domestic idols whose use displeased God. Many testimonies of Scripture provide proof of this matter, in which you may see them relegated to the category of wicked abominations. For thus Samuel spoke to Saul in 1 Samuel 15:23: *“Because rebellion is as the sin of divination,* <note>original Hebrew: *ve-aven u-teraphim haph-tsar*</note> *and stubbornness is as iniquity and* **THERAPHIM**.” And in 2 Kings 23:24, *King Josiah is narrated to have removed the* **THERAPHIM** *along with the mediums, the soothsayers, the dung-gods, and the rest of the abominations.* Zechariah does not indeed strip them of all use of speech, but convicts them of *lying* in Zechariah 10:2: *“The Theraphim speak vanity.”* I am not investigating now whether God wished to apply little images of that kind, purged of superstition, to His own worship. There will be a place for speaking of that later. For now, I consider them in no other way than as they served superstition and idolatry, which is how Kircher considers them along with me. And I say that they were brought into the family of the Hebrews not first from the Egyptians, but from the Syrians or Chaldeans.

III. It is certain that *Laban the Syrian* held them as his gods in the time of *Jacob* (Genesis 31:30), and he complains that they were stolen from him by *Jacob’s* household. However, the idea that Laban or his parents learned that superstition from *Abraham’s* servants returning from Egypt is extremely remote from all likelihood. For what arguments and evidence does Kircher have for that return of Abraham into Mesopotamia after he had departed from there, called out by God’s command? Especially since we have the Apostle as our authority that *time to return* was indeed not lacking to him, *but he was not mindful of that country from which he had gone out*; and thus he lacked the will to return (Hebrews 11:15). Evidence of this is that oath by which he bound his servant, that he should not, for any cause whatsoever, lead his son back into *Syria*: so much so that, if it were necessary, he preferred him to lack a wife of his own kindred than to undergo the danger of a journey to his idolatrous relatives (Genesis 24:5-6). But suppose Abraham had returned to Syria—and not just once, if you wish, but several times—is it credible that Abraham’s dome- <note>The text cuts off mid-word; "domestic" or "domestics" is intended.</note>

## V.
To suggest that the household servants of *Abraham* were so imbued with the religion of Egyptian little images <note>Latin: imaguncularum; likely referring to small votive statues or amulets</note> during the very short time they spent in Egypt, that upon returning with him to their fatherland, they filled all of Chaldea and the neighboring regions with that same superstition in a short time, is so monstrous to say that the very sound of it strikes horror into the listener. For it is proved by no argument that the name of the *Teraphim* <note>Hebrew: household gods or idols</note> was known to the Egyptians at that time. Nor is it credible that *Abraham's* domestics, who saw the piety of the Lord increased by such immense wealth, embraced the superstitions of the Egyptians on account of their prosperity. And it is assumed without evidence that *Abraham* ever returned to the Chaldeans. But that the *Teraphim* were held in veneration by *Abraham's* countrymen and kinsmen, from whose midst he departed—that indeed the Scripture explains. The piety of so distinguished a man bids us believe that *Abraham* himself abominated those petty gods <note>Latin: Deastros</note> and did not tolerate them among the furniture of his servants. Yet he could not achieve so much as to drive them out from the soul and house of his brother *Nahor*; whence *Laban*, the grandson of *Nahor*, opposes the *gods of his grandfather to the God of Abraham*.
<margin>Genesis 31:53</margin>
And this is that *Laban* who greets the *Teraphim* stolen from him by the *name of his gods*; and from whose house they were transferred into the family of *Jacob* by *Rachel his daughter*. But this was against the will of a man of ancient piety: who, being about to perform sacred rites at *Bethel* to God his Savior, first ordered the foreign gods to be removed, and hid them under the oak which is near *Shechem*.
<margin>Genesis 35:2, 4</margin>
What part, then, is left for the Egyptians in this whole business?

## VI.
*Kircher* <note>Athanasius Kircher (1602–1680), a Jesuit scholar famous for his attempts to decipher hieroglyphs and his theories on Egyptian influence</note> indeed presses the origin of the word *Teraphim*, which he contends with great effort is Egyptian and the same as *Serapis*; since it is familiar to the Chaldeans to change the letters Shin (ש), Tsade (צ), or Zayin (ז) into Tav (ת) or Tet (ט). From this he draws this conclusion: *Since therefore the Hebrew-Chaldeans, imbued with the worship of Serapis in Egypt, heard the name of Serapis frequently repeated, and they themselves bringing his idols along with the name into Chaldea, made it their own; those images which the Egyptians called Serapes, they called* תרפיס *Theraphis; which word afterwards having become entirely a matter of Hebrew law, the final 's' (ס) being changed into 'm' (ם) due to similarity, it was called Theraphim instead of Theraphis, and finally was numbered among the remaining words of the Hebrews. So says he.*

For first, how many verbal twists are required so that from *Serapis* (for so the *Egyptians* used to pronounce it) *Serapis* is formed, then from the Chaldean-Hebrews *Theraphis*, and finally *Theraphim* is forged? Even if it were common for the Chaldeans to change the letters *Shin*, *Tsade*, or *Samech* into *Tav* <note>The author is discussing phonetic shifts between Semitic languages, specifically the "S" sounds becoming "T" sounds</note>; this was not the case for the *Hebrews*, whose speech flourished in the family of *Abraham*.
