Especially when they were transforming a final *Samech*, the pronunciation of which was by no means harsh or heavy to them, into a *Mem* without any necessity.

<margin>Treatise III. chapter v.</margin>
VIII. Furthermore, if you set aside some similarity of sound, what is there truly in common between the *Theraphim* and *Serapis*? *Sorapis*, according to *Nymphodorus* and supported by *Kircher* <note>Athanasius Kircher (1602–1680), a Jesuit scholar and polymath known for his attempts to decipher hieroglyphs</note>, signifies a "bull-chest." *Sor* denotes a chest and *Ap* a bull to the *Egyptians*. Hence he is not displeased by the opinion of *Varro*, *Plutarch*, *Lucian*, and others, who wish *Serapis* to be so named from the *Bovine Ark* (bearing that appearance) into which *Osiris* was cast after death and worshipped by *Isis*. What has this to do with the *Theraphim*, such as *Laban* and the *Israelites* possessed? Moreover, whatever the figure of *Serapis* was among the *Egyptians*, can *Kircher* prove by any appearance of reason that the *Theraphim* were worshipped by the *Chaldeans* and *Hebrews* in honor of *Serapis*?

IX. But whatever weight this argument has, it plainly collapses if the antiquity of *Serapis* is not certain or established even among the *Egyptians* themselves. Indeed, *Herodotus*, to whom we owe so much concerning the gods of the *Egyptians*, does not even mention the name of *Serapis*; nor does anyone else before the times of *Alexander*. *Clement of Alexandria* <margin>Exhortation p. 31.</margin> relates on the credit of others that his image was sent as a gift by the people of *Sinope* to *Ptolemy Philadelphus*, who had earned their gratitude by sending grain from *Egypt* when they were suffering from famine. If these things are true, *Serapis* was unknown to the *Egyptians* before those times. *Tacitus* refers this to an earlier ruler than *Philadelphus*, namely *Ptolemy Lagus*. <margin>Histories book IV.</margin> The words of that most judicious of historians are worthy of being presented here. *The origin of this God*, he says, *has not yet been made famous by our authors. The priests of the Egyptians record it thus: To King Ptolemy, the first of the Macedonians to consolidate the power of Egypt, when at Alexandria, recently...*

# EGYPTIAN MATTERS

Once the city walls were built and temples and religious rites were established, a young man of extraordinary beauty and of a stature greater than human appeared [to King Ptolemy] in a dream. He warned the King to send his most faithful friends to Pontus <note>A region on the southern coast of the Black Sea</note> to fetch his image. He declared that this would bring prosperity to the kingdom, and that the place which received him would become great and famous. At the same moment, the young man was seen to be carried up into heaven in a great blaze of fire. Ptolemy, moved by this omen and miracle, revealed his nocturnal vision to the Egyptian priests, whose custom it is to interpret such things. But as they knew little of Pontus or foreign matters, he questioned Timotheus the Athenian, of the family of the Eumolpidae <note>A priestly clan in Athens who oversaw the Eleusinian Mysteries</note>, whom he had summoned from Eleusis to be a master of ceremonies, asking what this superstition was and who the deity might be. Timotheus, having questioned those who had traveled to Pontus, learned that there was a city there called Sinope, and not far from it a temple famous among the locals from ancient times dedicated to Jupiter Dis <note>The Roman name for the god of the underworld, equivalent to Pluto or Hades</note>. The rest of Tacitus's account is more long-winded and not particularly relevant to our purpose. The main point comes to this: Ptolemy, urged by repeated warnings, ordered ambassadors and gifts to be prepared for King Scydrothemis (who then ruled over the people of Sinope). The King, terrified by the threats of his opposing people, hesitated. Meanwhile, after three years had passed, Ptolemy did not cease his efforts or his prayers. Then a threatening vision appeared to Scydrothemis, warning him not to delay the God's destiny any longer. Nevertheless, the common people opposed the King, envying Egypt and fearing for themselves, and they surrounded the temple. A greater story has since handed down that the God himself, of his own accord, boarded the ships that had been brought to the shore. It is a marvel to tell: having crossed so much sea, they arrived at Alexandria on only the third day. A temple was built, suited to the greatness of the city, in a place called Rhakotis. There had been a small shrine there dedicated to Serapis and Isis in ancient times. These are the most famous accounts of the origin and arrival of the God.

### X. Regarding this narrative by Tacitus, I observe the following:

I. That it is not only the most famous account, but it originated from the Egyptian priests themselves, who, it is well known, were magnificent boasters of their own antiquities. 

II. That Serapis was not a native God of the Egyptians, but what the Athenians call <term>epithetos</term> <note>original: "ἐπίθετον" — meaning an added, foreign, or "adopted" deity</note>, or a resident alien summoned from Pontus. 

III. And that this was so recent that in the time of Ptolemy Lagides <note>Ptolemy I Soter, the founder of the Ptolemaic Kingdom</note>, both the divinity and the name of Serapis were unknown to the Egyptian priests themselves; for they confessed to the King that they knew little of Pontus and foreign things, even though it was their custom to understand such matters. 

IV. That the fame of this deity was so obscure among neighboring nations, even the most inquisitive ones, that those who were famous for their learning and were masters of ceremonies—such as Timotheus the Athenian—learned nothing of him until they had finally questioned those who had traveled to Pontus. These facts provide an invincible...

# BOOK II. CHAPTER III.

They enrich the argument that those most celebrated and ancient Teraphim <note>Hebrew: *Teraphim*, small household idols or cult images often used for divination</note> of the entire East cannot be derived from the ignoble and more recent Egyptian "Serapides" <note>The plural form of Serapis, a Greco-Egyptian deity</note>.

XI. I do not hide the fact that the final words of *Tacitus* <note>Publius Cornelius Tacitus (c. 56–120 AD), a Roman historian</note>, which we just praised, suggest that before that God was brought from *Sinope*, there was already a small shrine at *Alexandria* dedicated in ANCIENT TIMES to *Serapis* and *Isis*. But to one paying proper attention, it is clear that this passage lies in error; unless one can believe that such a sharp-witted writer would so ineptly and absurdly contradict himself within a short historical account. For if there had been a shrine of *Serapis* there in ancient times, how is it possible that the Egyptian priests were ignorant of what kind of deity *Serapis* was? Hence, I conjecture that the word *Apis* <note>The sacred bull of Memphis, a much older Egyptian deity</note> should be substituted for *Serapis*. <margin>Saturnalia, book 1, chapter 7.</margin>
> *The Egyptians,* he says, *received neither Saturn nor Serapis himself into the secret places of their temples until after the death of Alexander of Macedon. After him, pressed by the tyranny of the Ptolemies, they were forced to receive these Gods into worship after the custom of the Alexandrians, among whom they were chiefly honored. They obeyed the command in such a way, however, that they did not entirely confound the observed rites of their own religion—And after other matters—Therefore, no town of Egypt received a temple of either Saturn or Serapis within its walls.*

XII. Nor should it be a burden to us if, after the passage of so many centuries, we are ignorant of the origin of a foreign word. Certainly, it is not so important to me that I would wish to abandon my legal standing <note>original: "vadimonium deserere," a Latin legal metaphor for giving up a case</note> over it. In this sense, it could be referred to the Arabic* תרף <note>tarafa</note> *meaning "he made fruitful and affluent." This meaning is found in the Ethiopic language, where it signifies "to remain" or "to be a remnant," as in Matthew 14:20; hence* תרף לב <note>abundance of the heart</note> *in Matthew 12:34. ->CHAPTER IV.<-

### That in the doctrine concerning the Way of Salvation and the Supreme Deity, there is conflict rather than agreement between the Egyptians and the Hebrews; and that the entirety of Egyptian theology consists of mere absurdities.

*I. Many things are praised as similar in the dogmas of the Egyptians and Hebrews which are actually in opposition. II. The Egyptians were utterly ignorant of the way to true Happiness, let alone being the first to know it. III. Furthermore, the Greeks used that particular phrase no less than the Egyptians. IV. Indeed, even the Romans did. V. All Egyptian philosophy concerning Blessedness is, according to Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo, the influential Christian theologian</note>, more recent than Moses. VI. There is not even a semblance of agreement between the Egyptian and Hebrew doctrine regarding the Supreme Deity. VII. The "Intermediate Gods" <note>original: "Dii Medioxumi"</note> among the Romans are different from the "Mediators" <note>original: "Μεσίται"</note> of the Greeks. VIII. The Egyptians, exactly like other Gentiles, held to twin sets of Gods: some Celestial and Immortal, others Terrestrial and Mortal. IX. The prohibitions of the Egyptians and Hebrews regarding foreign worship have nothing in common besides the words themselves. X. The Greeks also commanded that the religion of one's fatherland be protected. XI. As did the Romans. XII. And even the Barbarian nations. XIII. The general prejudice of almost all nations opposes Plutarch <note>Greek philosopher and biographer</note> when he praises the religious decrees of the Egyptians. XIV. Plutarch himself confesses that they made their religion ridiculous and suited to persuading people toward Atheism. XV. This was not the madness of the common people alone, but a public insanity of the nation. XVI. The foul and shameful nature of their superstitions. XVII. Especially concerning the Goat of Mendes <note>A deity of ancient Egypt represented as a ram or goat, associated with fertility</note>. XVIII. These things cannot be excused by any pretense of Symbols or Enigmas. XIX. For such an interpretation is a more recent invention. XX. Nor do those Symbols rise any higher than the explanation of natural phenomena. XXI. In which matter, from the fables of the Greeks...*

# BOOK II. CHAPTER IV.

...are greatly surpassed by the [law] tables. XXII. *Plutarch* represents the *Egyptians* not according to truth, but from his own imagination. XXIII. The very Hieroglyphic of *Kneph* <note>A creator deity in Egyptian mythology, often depicted as a ram-headed man or a serpent</note> is a figure of this World.

I. **LET US NOW PASS TO THE SECOND CHAPTER** of the treatise we have undertaken, in order to show that in the dogmas, institutions, and rites approved by God, there is in reality not as much agreement as exists in the opinion of those most learned men; and that many things are proclaimed as similar which are either quite dissimilar or even fight face-to-face in opposition.

<margin>Compare Book 1, Chapter II, Section 3.</margin>
II. And to begin from that which is foremost in every religion—namely, the showing of that **WAY** by which one strives **TOWARD TRUE HAPPINESS** and the blessed fellowship of the deity—I truly do not see what similarity the doctrine of the *Egyptians* has here with the faith of the *Hebrews*. For if that general desire for attaining happiness is considered, there has never existed a superstition so absurd that it did not profess it. But if you mean the definition of true happiness and the showing of the way by which it is obtained, no follower of the Christian faith can doubt that *Apollo* <note>Referring to an oracular statement attributed to the god Apollo</note> lied when he asserted it was known and recognized by the ancient *Egyptians*. Certainly, the way in which the *Israelites* were commanded to proceed toward happiness is directly opposed to the ways of the *Egyptians*. *Leviticus* XVIII. 3. *Ezekiel* XX. 7. XXIII. 27.

III. I suspect that the most noble *Marsham* <note>Sir John Marsham (1602–1685), an English writer known for his work on ancient chronology</note> was pleased by that critical observation that "the way of the blessed" <note>original: "ἡ τῶν μακάρων ὁδὸς"</note>—the discovery of which *Apollo* ascribes to the *Egyptians*—agrees at least in phrasing with the language of our own [scriptural] instruments, where you may very frequently hear "the way of the Lord" mentioned. However, even that is not of such importance that it ought to have been mentioned. For *Apollo*—if indeed that poem belongs to *Apollo* and not to some idle little *Greek* <note>original: "Graculi," a diminutive for a Greek person, often used dismissively</note>—did not follow the *Egyptian* custom of speaking, but rather the *Greek*. Certainly, the *Greeks* no less than the *Egyptians* called the method of obtaining blessedness a "way to those above." The verses of *Diphilus* <note>A Greek poet of the New Comedy</note> are well known:

> For indeed we believe there are two paths in Hades,
> One the way of the righteous, and the other of the impious.
> <note>original: "Καὶ γὰρ καθ’ ᾅδην δύο τρίβους νομίζομεν, Μίαν δικαίων, χἀτέραν ἀσεβῶν ὁδόν."</note>

And it seems to me entirely that the oracle of *Apollo* was fabricated in the likeness of the poem of the *Ascraean* <note>Referring to the poet Hesiod, who was from Ascra</note>.

For at the time when Moses was born, it is found that the great astronomer Atlas lived, who was the brother of Prometheus and the maternal grandfather of the elder Mercury, whose grandson was that famous Mercury Trismegistus <note>original: "Trismegistus ille Mercurius." Hermes Trismegistus was a legendary Hellenistic figure associated with a syncretism of the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian god Thoth, credited with ancient sacred writings.</note>.

<margin>Compare Book I, Chapter II, Section 4.</margin>

VI. It is no less strange that the most noble *Marsham* <note>Sir John Marsham (1602–1685), an English writer known for his chronological studies of ancient history.</note> has searched for some appearance of agreement within such an immense discrepancy of opinions concerning the SUPREME DEITY <note>original: "SUMMO NUMINE"</note> that exists between the Hebrews and the Egyptians. To be sure, the Egyptians employed those many gods of theirs as *Intermediaries* <note>original: "Medioxumos." A term for deities of middle rank.</note>, by whom they might be led toward that *as it were supreme* one. They shadowed forth the power of that *One* with various symbols. And just as the *Israelites* abominate all foreign worship <gloss>foreign worship; original Hebrew: "Avodah Zarah"</gloss>, so also the *Egyptians* rejected whatever their ancestors had not shown them. Finally, the most learned Plutarch excused their religion from the absurdities and follies imputed to it.

VII. I do not wish at this time to disturb the fact that *Marsham* called those gods "Intermediaries" <note>original: "Medioxumos"</note> whom the Greeks called *Mesitas* <note>original Greek: "Μεσίτας," meaning mediators or middle-men.</note>; I do not know if this is according to Roman usage. For by the name of "Intermediary Gods," the Romans understood those who were considered *Middle* in power and dignity *between the Heavenly and the Infernal* gods. *Plautus in The Casket Comedy:*
<margin>Act IV, Scene I.</margin>
->And so may the Gods and Goddesses, those above and those below, and the Intermediaries.<-
A little later:
->May all the gods—the great, the small, and the platter-gods—<-
that is, the household gods <term>Lares: protective Roman spirits of the home</term>, and any similar to them who were worshipped with small platters <note>original: "patellis"</note> rather than sacrificial bowls. *Gyraldus, in "Of the Gods of the Nations," quoting from Martianus's second book "On the Marriage of Mercury and Philology,"* <margin>Composition XV, page 371.</margin> *has this to say: The Latins called them Intermediaries, all of whom are indeed of a less lucid and splendid nature than those celestial ones; yet they are not so corporeal that they can be perceived by human sight.* <margin>On the 8th book of the Aeneid, page 519.</margin> *Servius* explains somewhat more clearly: *The Poet called Hercules a "common God," between God and men; hence he is called "Medius Fidius" <note>A Roman oath invoking divine truth, often associated with Hercules or Jupiter.</note>. Or a medium of both natures, between mortality and Divinity. For there are some deities who are only celestial, some only terrestrial, and some middle ones, whom Apuleius calls Intermediaries—that is, those who become Gods from men.* From these things it is plain that they were called Intermediaries not in view of their office, but of their nature and dignity. I am not unaware, indeed, that according to the mind of *Apuleius*, certain divine middle powers were believed to be carriers of prayers from here and gifts from there between mortals and heaven-dwellers; but I deny that for that reason they were called Intermediary Gods...

...were designated, and that this specific duty belonged to those so named. However, this critical observation is of such small consequence that I am now almost ashamed and regretful of it, harmless as it may be.

VIII. But it is of greater importance that the most noble *Marsham* <note>Sir John Marsham (1602–1685), an English chronicler known for suggesting that Egyptian rites preceded those of the Hebrews.</note> has endeavored, by means of that distinction, to somehow excuse the shameful idolatry of the Egyptians. If this argument should prevail, there is nothing in Paganism so absurd that the "Wiser Men" among the Gentiles could not defend by the same reasoning. For this was the common refuge <note>original: κρησφύγετον (krēsphýgeton) - a place of retreat or a "loophole."</note> for all of them, from which they were so often driven out by the leaders of the Christian religion. Nor did the *Egyptians* hold anything more sound than others in their opinions regarding the divine. They had two types of Gods, as did almost all nations: *Some celestial and eternal; others terrestrial and mortal, who were translated into the number of the Gods after death.* *Diodorus* <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian of the 1st century BCE.</note> discusses both. First the *Celestial ones: the Sun, Moon, Spirit, Fire, Earth, Ocean, and Air.* Having explained these, he proceeds to the *terrestrial* ones with these words: *“Regarding the gods in heaven who have an eternal origin, the Egyptians say this much. But they say there are others from among these who became terrestrial, having been mortal by nature, but who attained immortality through their wisdom and common service to mankind. Some of these were also kings in Egypt.”* <note>The author provides the original Greek text followed by his Latin translation; both are rendered here into English.</note> Can these things be reconciled in any way with the Theology of the Hebrews?

IX. And what, finally, does the *Hebrew* prohibition against foreign worship have in common with the *Egyptian* prohibition against worship not handed down by their ancestors—except perhaps a similarity in words, yet with a most diverse, even contrary, meaning? For the worship which the *Egyptians* held as handed down from their ancestors was considered by the Hebrews to be the most foreign of all. And the worship which the Hebrews looked up to as handed down to them by the supreme deity of heaven was an abomination to the *Egyptians*. Thus, by these mutual prohibitions, religious commerce and mixing were strongly forbidden on both sides, and a similarity of institutions is by no means proven.

X. Unless perhaps you urge that general principle of defending the religion of one's fatherland. But *Egypt* held nothing exceptional in this. The same was true among the Greeks and Romans, and almost all nations, not even excepting the *Barbarians*...

It had been cautioned among the *Athenians* and *Romans* that no one should introduce new religions: for this reason *Socrates* was condemned at *Athens*, and the *Chaldeans* <note>Astrologers and magicians from the East</note> and *Jews* were expelled from the City [of Rome]. Regarding both, he speaks truly. In the *Attic Laws* as arranged by *Petitus* <note>Samuel Petit, a 17th-century scholar of Greek law</note>, this is the second in order: <note>original Greek: θεσμὸς αἰώνιος... πατρίοις</note> LET THIS BE THE MOST ANCIENT LAW AND OF ETERNAL AUTHORITY IN ATTICA: THAT THE GODS AND NATIVE HEROES ARE TO BE VENERATED PUBLICLY ACCORDING TO THE ANCESTRAL SANCTIONS. And such indeed was the fervor of the *Athenians* in this matter, <margin>Against Apion, Book II</margin> that (these are the words of *Josephus* <note>A Jewish-Roman historian</note>) <note>original Greek: ὥστε... κολάζειν</note> they would punish without any mercy even those who uttered but a single word against their laws concerning the Gods.

XI. The *Romans* possessed an equal care and severity. For they guarded against this excellently, even from the very birth of the city, by the *Law of Romulus*. And from that source *Cicero* drew <margin>On the Laws, Book II</margin> the Law which he proposes: NO ONE SHALL HAVE GODS SEPARATELY, NOR NEW ONES; NOR SHALL THEY WORSHIP STRANGE GODS PRIVATELY, UNLESS THEY ARE PUBLICLY ACCEPTED. The consul *Posthumius* speaks beautifully in *Livy* <margin>Book XXXIX</margin> in the oration where he exposes the shameful acts of the *Bacchanalia* <note>Secret, often wild festivals for the god Bacchus that the Roman Senate suppressed in 186 BCE</note>: *How often in the age of our fathers and grandfathers was the task given to the magistrates to forbid foreign rites? To prohibit sacrificing priests and soothsayers from the forum, the circus, and the city? To seek out and burn prophetic books? And to abolish every discipline of sacrificing except in the Roman manner? For those men, most wise in all divine and human law, judged that nothing was so effective at dissolving religion as when sacrifices were performed not by ancestral rite, but by a foreign one.* It was also observed by *Dionysius of Halicarnassus* that, although innumerable nations have come into the city, for whom it was entirely necessary to worship their ancestral Gods by domestic rite, yet this state has emulated no foreign sacred rites so as to have them publicly accepted. But even if any sacred rites, by the command of oracles, were at some time introduced into the republic, the citizens nevertheless worshipped them with their own [Roman] rites, having rejected all—

XII. And what nation does not share nearly this same zeal? *Aristotle* says, "To transgress ancestral customs is considered unjust among all people." <note>original Greek: τὰ πάτρια ἔθη... παρὰ πᾶσι παραβαίνειν ἄδικόν ἐστι</note> To change or violate ancestral rites is held to be a crime everywhere in the world. The response that Thespesion flings back will not be unpleasant to the Reader, should they wish to consult the cited passage of the Author. It appears, moreover, from the same Philostratus, that the Egyptians were able to give no rational explanation at all for this insane worship; regardless of how much Kircher <note>Athanasius Kircher (1602–1680), a Jesuit scholar who attempted to interpret Egyptian hieroglyphs as Christian mysteries before they were actually deciphered.</note>, after the lapse of so many centuries, imagines that he has discovered the mysteries of the entire Christian world in those monstrous gods. # EGYPTIAN MATTERS

<margin>Book 1.</margin>
*Cicero* had already set the tone when he discussed the nature of the Gods seriously and skillfully in his own manner: *With the error of the Poets, one may join the portents of the Magi, AND THE MADNESS OF THE EGYPTIANS IN THE SAME CATEGORY.* <note>original: "ÆGYPTIORUMQUE IN EODEM GENERE DEMENTIAM"</note> From this it happened that the *Romans* did not allow Egyptian sacred rites to be brought into the city until late, and then only with the indignation of the wiser men. *Servius*, commenting on that line of *Virgil*:

> And the monsters of gods of every kind.

He called them *monsters* because the *Romans* had not yet received Egyptian rites under *Augustus*. And *Varro* is indignant that *Alexandrian Gods* are worshiped at *Rome*.

<margin>Chapter 93. Book 51.</margin>
To *Augustus* certainly, as *Suetonius* testifies, the bull-god *Apis* was not of such great value that he would turn aside a little from his path to visit him while traveling through Egypt; adding this reason which *Dio* records: <note>original Greek: "θεὸς ἀλλ’ οὐχὶ βοῦς προσκυνεῖν εἰθίσθαι"</note> *that he was accustomed to worship Gods, not oxen.* *Persius* complains that Isis was received into the city:
<margin>Book 2. Elegy 33.</margin>

> Is Egypt with its dark-skinned nurslings not enough for you?
> Why has Rome been sought by you by such a long way?

<margin>Domitian chapter 1. Chapter 9.</margin>
*Suetonius* mockingly criticizes the petty priests of the same cult. In the morning, *Domitian* was hidden in the habit of an *Isiac* <note>A follower or priest of the goddess Isis</note> among the priests of a vain superstition. *Lampridius* writes, not without irritation and laughter, concerning *Commodus*: *He observed the rites of Isis, even to the point of shaving his head and carrying the statue of Anubis. But Commodus himself held those rites in ridicule, as they deserved. For while carrying it, he used to strike the heads of the Isiacs heavily with the face of the idol.* To the more severe men, however, these rites were so hateful that they were several times driven from the city. *Tertullian* says:
<margin>Apology chapter 6.</margin>
*Serapis, Isis, and Harpocrates with his Dog-headed attendant <note>The Cynocephalus, often associated with Thoth or Anubis</note>, having been prohibited from the Capitol—that is, expelled from the assembly of the Gods—were renounced by the Consuls Piso and Gabinius (who were certainly not Christians), who even overturned their altars; thus restraining the vices of shameful and idle superstitions.* Concerning *Tiberius*, *Suetonius* writes:
<margin>Chapter 36.</margin>
*He suppressed foreign ceremonies and Egyptian rites: compelling those who were possessed by that superstition to burn their religious vestments along with all their ritual gear.*

# BOOK II. CHAPTER IV.

<note>The text begins with a Greek passage from Plutarch's "Isis and Osiris," followed immediately by its Latin translation. Both are translated here into English.</note>

...nor have they struck the sacred rites with mockery and derision; but this is the least of the evils arising from such folly. For a terrible opinion takes root, which drives the weak and innocent into pure superstition, while in the more acute and bold, it falls away into atheistic and brutal reasonings. *But most of the Egyptians, by worshiping the animals themselves and treating them as Gods, have not only exposed almost the entire system of their sacred rites to mockery and derision (for this is the smallest evil that comes from that foolishness), but a powerful conviction is also bred in their minds, which induces pure superstition in the weak and simple; whereas it drives the more vehement and daring toward the denial of the Gods and toward beast-like thoughts.*

XV. Lest anyone should think this was the insanity of the common rabble alone, it is handed down by the same Plutarch that entire populations rushed together with hostile weapons on the occasion of a eaten fish or a killed dog:

> *In our own time,* he says, *when the people of Cynopolis <note>The "City of Dogs"</note> ate the Oxyrhynchus fish, the people of Oxyrhynchus <note>The "City of the Sharp-snouted Fish"</note> seized dogs and, having slaughtered them like sacrificial victims, ate them. Because of this, a war was kindled, and while the cities themselves inflicted heavy losses upon one another, they were later punished by the Romans, who imposed a penalty upon them.*

The account of Diodorus Siculus is consistent with this:

> *So deeply,* he says, *is that religion of animals impressed upon the minds of men, and so stubborn an affection does each person bear toward venerating them; that even at the time when King Ptolemy had not yet been declared a friend by the Romans, and the common people were applying every effort to treat those arriving from Italy with obsequious respect, and were striving out of fear to give them no handle for accusation or war: nevertheless, when a certain Roman killed a cat, and a rush of the people to his house occurred, neither the leading men sent by the King to plead for mercy, nor the common terror of Rome, could rescue the man from punishment, even though he had committed the deed without intent.*

Diodorus testifies that he reports this not from hearsay, but as something he saw with his own eyes during his travels to Egypt. He adds another detail, which might seem to exceed belief and be very much like a fable:

> *For when famine once pressed upon Egypt, they say that many were forced to the mutual devouring of human flesh; but no one was ever accused of having even tasted anything from the sacrosanct animals.*

He who considers these things, will he be persuaded that the Egyptians held the animals of their Nomes <note>Administrative districts of ancient Egypt</note> only as Symbols of the Divine power over all things?

# EGYPTIAN STUDIES

<margin>Page 330.</margin>
If one chooses, I will not say now that it clears them of superstition, error, or some absurdity, but rather of madness, insanity, and fury. For they did not only worship the most foul figures of beasts and cattle—**dog-headed, serpent-headed, donkey-headed, cat-headed, hawk-headed** <note>original: *Canicipites, Serpenticipites, Asinicipites, felicipites, accipitricipites*</note>, and six hundred other monsters of that kind, which we look upon to this day as witnesses of Pagan frenzy—but they also adored certain other things shameful to mention as if they were Gods. As *Minutius Felix* <note>A 2nd-3rd century Christian apologist</note> elegantly reproaches them: *Do they not fear the pungency of onions more than Isis? Do they not tremble more at the sounds expressed through the shameful parts of the body than at Serapis?* <note>A reference to the belief that Egyptians deified bodily functions or common vegetables</note> Besides *Minutius*, those who bring charges against this foolish and stinking religion include *Origen, Jerome, Caesarius, Clement*, and others.

<margin>Book II, chapter 46.</margin>
<margin>Preparation [for the Gospel], Book II, chapter 1.</margin>
XVII. And why do we beat around the bush? Could anything more monstrous be imagined than the infamy of the *Mendesian* people? They, worshiping a **Goat** <note>original: *Hircum*; likely referring to the god Banebdjedet</note> as a deity, were accustomed to prostrate women of the most excellent beauty to its lust. And—O, the faith of men!—as if they were agents of lewdness, they would instigate the beast against nature when it was ceasing by the law of nature. This matter is well known from *Herodotus*, who relates that it was done openly in his own time, as well as from *Pindar, Strabo, Plutarch’s Gryllus, Aelian, Aristides the Rhetorician*, and others. If anyone desires their exact words, let him consult *Bochart* <note>Samuel Bochart, a 17th-century biblical scholar</note> in his *Hierozoicon, part 1, book II, chapter 53*. Defending this irreligious religion of his people, *Asclepiades*, in his books *On Matters of Theology* <note>original Greek: Θεολογουμένων</note>, used to say that such **unlawful mingling** <note>original Greek: ἀθέμιτον μίξιν</note> ought not to seem so very wonderful, since histories testify that the greatest men have been born from such a union. See, if you please, *Casaubon* on *Suetonius’ Augustus, chapter 94*. What useful moral cause, then, can be assigned to such shameful infamy? What elegance, whether Historical or Natural, can be found in it? Shall we judge a religion so insane to be worthy of such extensive praise from a serious man like *Plutarch*? Or that it should be compared by a learned Christian man, such as the most noble *Marsham* <note>Sir John Marsham, who argued for the antiquity of Egyptian ritual</note>, with the chaste, holy, and wise discipline of the ancient *Hebrews*? How much better does *Eusebius* put it? **Such is the shameful godlessness, rather than Theology, of the Egyptians, which is so disgraceful that it is even foul to oppose it.** <note>The author provides both the original Greek and a Latin translation of Eusebius's scathing critique of Egyptian religion.</note>

# BOOK II. CHAPTER IV.

...they might understand; hence it happened that they judged them too unfavorably. <margin>Marsham, page 58.</margin> To be sure, the common people judge with their eyes: *they neglect hidden speculations*. We must pause here for a moment; and we must weigh a little more diligently how much value should be placed on that *Enigmatic* Theology. And first, I hope it will be granted to me by fair-minded judges of these matters, that *not everything* can be turned into enigmas and symbols of secret science; certainly not those foul and unspeakable things at the memory of which the soul shudders. Or, if those things too were shaped into images of Divine matters, what more notable injury can be done to the deity than that those things, which ought to be held only in the most holy and chaste manner, are marked by such nefarious displays?

XIX. Next, it should also be noted that *the first Theology of the Egyptians we possess was purely historical*, though patched together with fables; since later generations were ashamed of these, they gradually began to attach *mystical* meanings to them. *Eusebius* followed this argument skillfully. <margin>Preparation for the Gospel, Book 1, Chapter IX.</margin> He observes that *Osiris, Isis*, and others whom they deemed worthy of chief veneration, were human beings who had served the state well, whom they elevated to heaven as a testimony of their gratitude. *Philo of Byblos*, the Greek translator of *Sanchuniathon* <note>Sanchuniathon was a purported Phoenician author; Philo of Byblos claimed to translate his ancient history into Greek</note>, did not conceal this. <note>original Greek: "θεοὺς ἐνόμιζον μεγίστους..."</note> *The most ancient of the Barbarians, especially the Phoenicians and Egyptians, considered those who discovered the necessities for life, or who in some way did good for the nations, to be the greatest gods; regarding these as benefactors and the causes of many goods, they worshipped them as gods. To be sure, those whom they were persuaded were the authors of the most benefits for themselves, they endowed with divine honors.* Nor is there need for much argument here. <margin>Book III, Chapter III.</margin> <note>original Greek: "ὅγέ τοι ἀληθὴς λόγος..."</note> *The truth speaks for itself, and almost crying out with a loud voice, testifies that those of whom we treat were certain mortal men.* Furthermore, *Plutarch*, in that work which he left written concerning *Isis and the Egyptian Deities*, voluntarily and with deliberate effort declares the specific bodily shape and color of each one in these words: <note>original Greek: "Ἱσορῶσι γὰρ Ἀιγύπτιοι..."</note> *For the Egyptians relate,* he says, *that Hermes was short-armed in his body, Typhon was red in complexion, Horus was white, and Osiris was black-skinned, as being men by nature.* <note>This theory, that gods were originally historical human beings, is known as Euhemerism</note>

<summary>The author argues that Egyptian mythology originated from the historical veneration of human benefactors (Euhemerism) rather than secret mystical truths, suggesting that later "enigmatic" interpretations were merely attempts to cover up shameful or primitive fables.</summary>

# EGYPTIAN MATTERS

The Egyptians record that Mercury <note>The Greek/Latin name for Thoth</note> had one arm shorter than the other, Typhon <note>Set</note> was red-skinned, Mars <note>Horus</note> was quite fair, and finally Osiris was of a darker complexion: for they had, in fact, existed as men by nature. From this, Eusebius <note>A 4th-century Christian historian</note> judiciously infers that the entire **apotheosis** <note>original: θεοποιΐαν; the process of making a human into a god</note> or consecration of deities was nothing other than the worship of the dead; moreover, whatever secret meaning is believed to reside in their **Natural Philosophy** <note>original: Physiologiæ</note> was actually fabricated later by men of leisure. *So that from all these things it is clear that this wonderful and noble natural philosophy has touched upon no truth at all, nor does it truly introduce anything divine, but it possesses a revered yet deceptive outward appearance of solemnity, having begged for a dignified explanation from elsewhere.* <note>The author provides a Latin translation of the Greek text by Eusebius, which is here rendered into English.</note>

XX. But let us proceed further: That enigmatic Theology of the Egyptians, however much it is marketed as sublime, did not strive higher than the elucidation of natural and physical things. Nor could it have been otherwise. For besides those "Historical Gods" <note>Deified humans</note>, they recognized no others than the "Natural Gods," whom they declared to be the Sun, the Moon, and the rest of the fixed stars along with the elements. Philo of Byblos and Chaeremon <note>A Stoic philosopher and priest</note> teach this in express words within the works of Eusebius.

<margin>Preparation for the Gospel, Book I, Chapter IX.</margin>
Since this is of the greatest importance to this matter, it will be worth the effort to present the actual words of both authors. And indeed Philo, after he had said that they had bestowed the names of their Kings upon the elements of this universe and upon certain things to which they attributed Divinity, continues thus: *They recognized as the only gods the natural ones: the sun, the moon, the other wandering stars, the elements, and things connected to them; so that to them, some gods were mortal and others were immortal.* The former were the Historical gods, the latter were the Natural gods.

<margin>Preparation for the Gospel, Book III, Chapter IV.</margin>
Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher</note> writes concerning Chaeremon: *For Chaeremon and the others do not believe there is anything else prior to the visible worlds, placing this at the beginning of the Egyptian accounts; nor do they recognize other gods except the so-called planets, those that complete the zodiac, and those that rise alongside them.*

<meta>catchword: them</meta>

# BOOK II. CHAPTER IV.

...those who are introduced by the *Egyptians* place [these things] at the very beginning of their disputes; nor do they recognize any other Gods than those commonly called the wandering stars <note>The planets</note>, and those which fill the *Zodiac*; as well as all those [constellations] that rise in their vicinity. From this it follows that not even the secret *Theology* of the *Egyptians* themselves placed any beings in the rank of Gods besides the bodies of nature—much less did they employ their symbols to signify the hidden properties and perfections of some supreme and incorporeal mind.

XXI. And even in the sketching and figuring of these natural things, all the *Hieroglyphic* wisdom of the *Egyptians* falls far below the ingenuity of *Greek* fables. Let us give one example out of many, from which it can be gathered how crude and dull the rest are. The image of *Isis* was horned: because, evidently, she was a symbol of the *Moon*, which appears horned <note>crescent-shaped</note>, for which reason the *Cow* was also sacred to her. They crowned the head of the Goddess, as if with a royal diadem, with a type of asp that they call *Thermuthis*: because, since it breathes out a most immediate poison, it proved the immense power of the Goddess. She was depicted being carried in a ship, because the Moon is horned, and when it is such, it has the shape of a boat; and likewise, because the *Moon* has power over the waters: and we are carried through the waters by a ship: for which reason *Isis* was also put in charge of navigation. It wearies me to pursue the rest. For who would not feel a cold shiver <note>original: "catharrum sibi fluere," literally a flow of phlegm, implying a reaction to something tedious or nonsensical</note> at such chilling trifles?

<margin>On Idolatry, Book I. chapter v.</margin>
XXII. I am not unaware that *Plutarch* represented the *Egyptians* as a little wiser than they have been portrayed by us so far. But we exhibit them in their native appearance. He shows them only masked and adorned with *Greek* industry. This quality of his—whether it be praise or fraud—*Vossius* <note>Gerard Vossius (1577–1649), a famous Dutch scholar of classical religion</note> has excellently uncovered. To be sure, the *Egyptian* Priests understood by *Osiris* sometimes the *Sun*, sometimes the *Moon*, and sometimes the *Nile*; by *Typhon*, sometimes the *Sun* and sometimes the *Sea*; by *Isis*, sometimes the *Moon* and sometimes the *Earth*. Since that interpretation did not satisfy *Plutarch*, who contended that nothing corporeal and devoid of sense could be worshipped as a deity, he took pains to improve the more common opinion of the *Egyptians* regarding their Gods. Therefore, he bids us understand the *World* by *Isis*; and by *Osiris* and *Typhon*, great Gods or *Demons* <note>In the classical sense of "daimones" or guiding spirits, not necessarily evil</note>, by whose power the nature of things is governed. However, all that philosophizing of *Plutarch* is *Greek* rather than *Egyp*-

XXIII. Not even those things which were previously mentioned by us concerning Knephus <note>original: "Knepho"; a Greek rendering of the Egyptian deity Khnum or Amun-Re</note>, represented by a serpent with a hawk's head, seem to extend any further than to have figured some *Genius* <note>A guardian spirit or guiding essence</note>, which they conceive of as a *Spirit of the World* or a soul, which, joined to the coarser parts, constitutes one whole with them. Certainly, what *Eusebius* <note>A 4th-century Christian historian</note> relates concerning *Taautus* <note>The Phoenician equivalent of Thoth or Hermes</note> from the works of *Sanchuniathon* <note>An ancient Phoenician author</note> via *Philo of Byblos*, does not compel us to think of anything more sublime. And from this it seems to have happened that *they also expressed the visible world by the image of a serpent: whose scales denote the stars with which the heaven is dappled; its weight, the earth; its lightness and slipperiness, the water; and the annual shedding of its skin, the turning year.* These things are found in Horus <note>Referring to Horapollo, the supposed author of a treatise on hieroglyphs</note> in *Hieroglyphics, Book II*, in these words: <note>The following is a translation of the Greek passage provided in the text</note> "Wishing to write 'the World,' they paint a serpent devouring its own tail, marked with various scales; by the scales they obscurely hint at the stars in the world. This animal is very heavy, just like the earth; and very smooth, like water. Every year, casting off old age, it strips off its skin. In this way, the annual time in the world, making its change, becomes young again. But that it uses its own body as food signifies that all things which are generated in the world by Divine Providence, these again receive their diminution back into itself." *Wishing to describe the World, they paint a serpent devouring its own tail, punctuated with various scales, through which they obscurely suggest the stars of the world. And indeed this animal is very heavy, just like the earth: and just like water, it is exceedingly slippery. Every year also, as the serpent sheds its skin with old age, in no other way does the annual time, making its change, grow young again. But the fact that it uses its body as if for its own food signifies that whatever things are produced in the world by Divine Providence, these, once a reduction has been made, will be resolved back into the same.* Whatever the case may be, the enigmas of Egyptian Theology are so perplexed, obscure, and uncertain—often even absurd—that nothing solid or worthwhile can be hammered out of them. For those things which *Kircher* <note>Athanasius Kircher (1602–1680), a Jesuit scholar who famously but incorrectly claimed to have deciphered hieroglyphs</note> heaped together with great effort in his *Oedipus* <note>Referring to his work "Oedipus Aegyptiacus"</note>, the wiser sort see, and laugh at, as being for the most part empty fictions of a man abusing his own talent and leisure.

### CHAPTER V.
### It is wrongly argued from Hermes Trismegistus that the Trinity of Persons in One Deity was known to the Ancient Egyptians.

I. *Hermes Trismegistus is praised by Kircher beyond belief.* II. *As he is also by François de Foix de Candalle and Hannibal Rosselli.* III. *For the writings attributed to that Hermes are forged.* IV. *The first Hermes, who is said by some to be older than Moses, wrote no books.* V. *The volumes of the second Hermes are of a completely different subject matter than those praised today.* VI. *The modern Hermetic books are manifest forgeries <note>original: νοθείας (notheias) - meaning spurious or illegitimate</note>.* VII. *The Trinity in Egyptian theological principles belongs not to God, but to the World.* VIII. *The hieroglyphic of the winged circle and the serpent-offspring pertains to the same thing.*

<margin>Compare Book 1, Chapter III.</margin>
I. However, the things which the same *Kircher* introduces <note>original: isogẽ / isagoge - to introduce or lead in</note> regarding the mystery of the TRINITY in One Deity being known to the ancient *Egyptians* surpass all belief. Specifically, he claims a certain *Hermes*—who, because he spoke of the Trinity, was called *Trismegistus* or *Thrice-Greatest* according to the testimony of *Suidas*—was a contemporary <note>original: σύγχρον@ (synchronos)</note> of *Abraham*. Having been taught by the most ancient Patriarchs with whom he lived, he supposedly described many books on the contemplation of Divine matters in Hieroglyphic letters. From these were translated into the Greek language the works we have today, the *Poimander* <note>The Shepherd of Men, a foundational Hermetic text</note> and the *Discourse to Asclepius*: in which he is said to have shown in open words, and delivered to the Egyptians, the ruin of the ancient religion, the rise of the new faith, the coming of Christ, the universal judgment, the resurrection at the end of the age, the glory of the blessed, and—the matter we are now dealing with—the Trinity of Persons in the individual Unity of the Deity.

II. In that dedication, he places his *Hermes* before the other Prophets and even *Moses* himself. III. But such tasteless fabrications have long since been rejected by more sensible men; it is a wonder that in such an abundance of refined learning, mortals are found with such slow-moving jaws <note>a metaphor for being slow-witted or gullible</note> that such insipid delicacies should please them. We have no leisure, nor is there any desire, *to write the Iliad after Homer* <note>a proverb meaning to do unnecessary work that has already been done better by others</note>: only those things, according to the nature of our undertaking, must be briefly noted which prove that the tenets of that Hermetic doctrine are counterfeit <note>original Greek: ὑποβολιμαῖα (hypobolimaia)</note>.

IV. And first, it has indeed been observed by most learned men that *that most ancient Mercury*, who in the *Dynasty of Africanus* is called Athothis, the son of Menes the first King of the Egyptians—and whom the Egyptians call Thoth, the Alexandrians Thoth, and the Greeks Hermes—wrote no books, but only engraved certain stelae, or columns, in the sacred dialect. # BOOK II. CHAPTER V.

...innumerable species of animals, which they called Hieroglyphic letters. From these, the second Mercury <note>Hermes Trismegistus</note>, who was more recent than Moses, is said to have compiled his books. Manetho <note>An Egyptian priest and historian</note>, according to Syncellus, is reported to have written to Ptolemy Philadelphus *concerning the interpretation of the books of the second Hermes* <note>original Greek: περὶ τῆς ἑρμηνείας τῶν τοῦ δευτέρου Ἑρμοῦ βιβλίων</note>. He says that from the pillars placed *in the Seriadic land*—for which Valesius prefers to read *the land of the Syringes* <note>Subterranean tunnels or galleries in Egypt</note>—and inscribed in the sacred dialect and Hierographic letters by Thoth, who is the First Mercury, the Second Mercury (son of Agathodaemon and father of Tat) translated the books, which he deposited in the inner sanctuaries of the Egyptian temples. From these, Sanchuniathon translated his works into the Phoenician language, and Manetho translated his into Greek. From this it is clear that, since the first Mercury is never recorded to have written any books, those which we possess are wrongly attributed to him.

V. Indeed, they do not even belong to the second Mercury. For just as the first Mercury commanded that the pillars contain the genealogies of the Gods, and devised the kingdoms of the Gods after the manner of a great *restoration* <note>original Greek: ἀποκαταστάσεως; a cosmic cycle or "apocatastasis"</note>: so these same things and similar matters *are contained in the General Books of Hermes* <note>original Greek: ἐν τοῖς Γενικοῖς Ἑρμοῦ</note>, in the Genealogical books of the Second Mercury, *and are carried in the Cyranic books* <note>original Greek: καὶ ταῖς Κυρανίσι βίβλοις φέρονται</note>. Now, the *Cyranis* book is, according to the interpretation of Salmasius, a *miscellaneous collection*. Briefly, the Mercurial Books taught Medicine, Astrology, and the sacred Rites of the Egyptians—that is, the leadership of a most vain superstition. In these, there is nothing related to those things which Kircher <note>Athanasius Kircher, a Jesuit scholar known for his attempts to decipher hieroglyphs</note> proclaims so tiresomely with such a parade of words.

<margin>Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, Book VI, page 456.</margin>

It is loathsome to report more of the ways in which that impostor, like a shrew-mouse, betrays himself by his own evidence.

# BOOK II. CHAPTER VI.

I. <margin>Compare Book I, chapter 5.</margin> My mind now hastens toward other matters: specifically those which concern the **MORAL DISCIPLINE OF THE EGYPTIANS**. Diodorus Siculus <note>A Greek historian of the 1st century BCE known for his monumental 'Library of History.'</note> has certainly discussed this topic with great renown. However, what a wise judge of true antiquity ought to think of these things, I prefer to explain not so much in my own words as in those of *Jacques Cappel* <note>original: "Jacobi Cappelli"; a 17th-century French Protestant theologian and scholar.</note>, for I have despaired of finding any more effective or elegant. He, therefore, speaking on the Year of the World 1931, says the following: <margin>Sacred and Foreign History, page 47.</margin> *Furthermore, those famous laws which the Egyptians attribute to their ancestors in the writings of Diodorus are similar to the Cyropaedia of Xenophon <note>A biographical work about Cyrus the Great, often considered a "mirror for princes" rather than strict history.</note>, who teaches not what Cyrus was like, but what he ought to have been; so that Cyrus the Younger might become the kind of man he described his ancestor, Cyrus the Great, to be. I seem to see the gravity of a citizen of Memphis <note>original: "Memphitæ"; an inhabitant of the ancient Egyptian capital.</note>, pressing his finger to his lip, breaking out into almost these words: "There is no reason, Diodorus, for you to judge our ancestors based on the present state of affairs. It has been nearly five hundred years since foreigners—Macedonians and Persians—have ruled over us. Since the Tigris flowed into the Nile <note>A metaphor for Persian influence and conquest reaching Egypt.</note>, Persian luxuries, and then Greek ones, have defiled the customs of Egypt. Formerly, when Egypt lived by its own customs and was ruled by natives, it outpaced the happiness of all other provinces by many parasangs <note>A Persian unit of distance, used here to mean "by a great deal."</note>. In those blessed and truly golden ages, the whims of kings did not serve as laws, but only the prescriptions of the laws pleased the kings." And so, having offered this preface* <note>original: "φροϊμιάσας" (phroimiasas) - having prefaced or introduced.</note>*, the Memphite described the rites, laws, and deeds of kings long buried in oblivion according to his own whim. And Diodorus, intending to furnish his Library, selected those things which he thought most plausible. But there is no doubt that Diodorus, like Herodotus, often had his face smeared with lies <note>original: "os oblitum"; a Latin idiom meaning to be deceived or cheated.</note>. Indeed, Chemnis <note>The name used by Diodorus for Khufu/Cheops, builder of the Great Pyramid.</note> was able to harass three hundred and sixty thousand men for twenty whole years with impunity, just to erect a single monument of the vainest vanity. Yet he was not allowed to taste a thrush, nor a hare, nor any other meat except veal or goose; it was not lawful for him to touch his wife except on a prescribed day and hour. Thus are men accustomed to loathe the present, and to amplify the old days with false, useless, and silly proclamations. These things are noted by us,* so the most polished writer concludes, *not out of a desire to find fault, but lest Egyptian trifles <note>original: "næniæ"; literally "dirges" or "nonsense."</note> deceive anyone when they oppose sacred history; and so that you may remember that the Egyptians are as deceitful as the sacred Writers are truthful.*

II. But let us weigh more specifically those things which *Marsham* <note>Sir John Marsham, an English writer on chronology.</note> saw fit to note.

# EGYPTIAN AFFAIRS

<margin>
Compare Book 1, chapter 5, section 7.
</margin>
There are many such instances where the institutions of the Hebrews and the Egyptians—no matter how much skill one uses to try to reconcile them—clash head-on. That the Hebrew laws regarding **UNLAWFUL INTERCOURSE** were diametrically opposed to Egyptian customs is not only admitted by *Marsham* <note>Sir John Marsham (1602–1685), an English chronicler known for his work on Egyptian chronology.</note>, but also proven by him. Indeed, the facts speak for themselves. For, almost uniquely among all other nations, the Egyptians considered incestuous marriages between brothers and sisters—whether *uterine* <note>sharing the same mother</note>, *twins*, or *full siblings*—to be permissible or even praiseworthy. I did not say lightly that they felt differently from other nations in this matter; *Diodorus* also noted this. <margin>Book 1.</margin> <note>original Greek: Νομοθετῆσαι δὲ φασὶ τοὺς Αἰγυπτίους... translated below</note> *It was established by Egyptian law, **contrary to the common custom of other men**, that marriage should be entered into with sisters, because of the success Isis had in this regard; for she married her full brother Osiris.*

III. There exists a most beautiful dissertation by *Philo the Jew* <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher</note> on this matter, in his *Book on Special Laws regarding the sixth and seventh commandments of the Decalogue*; I would like to present it here, but in English only, as it is somewhat lengthy. *Next, he says, it is commanded that not even a sister is to be taken in marriage. This is a truly honorable precept, and one suited to self-restraint. Although Solon of Athens observed this only regarding uterine sisters, he left it free to marry those born of the same father. Conversely, the Lacedæmonian <note>Spartan</note> legislator did not forbid marriage with uterine sisters, but only with those born of the same father. But the Egyptian, laughing at the simplicity and half-baked decrees of both, loosened the reins on lust and increased the incurable evil of intemperance in bodies and souls by permitting the license to marry sisters—whether related through one parent or both, older or younger or of the same age—not even excepting twins, whom nature separated at birth but whom intemperance joined in an insatiable society and a poorly matched union. Moses, loathing these laws as utterly foreign to a well-ordered republic and as inciting every kind of baseness, prohibited in every way intercourse with sisters, whether they share both parents or only one.*

IV. Since these things were so excellently observed by Philo, I judge that the Egyptians are in no way to be excused, as if by a liberty granted through the law of nature—

V. But in truth, it is much better to believe that the prohibition regarding sisters is founded in *Natural Law*. Regarding uterine sisters, the Hebrews constantly decree this: among those things which they teach are forbidden to man by natural law, they count in the fourth place sexual intercourse *with a sister from one's mother* <note>original Hebrew: באחותו מאמו</note>. Nor does the reasoning appear to be different for a *full sister* <note>original: Germana</note>, since the degree of kinship is exactly the same. In the beginning, it was indeed necessary for a brother to be joined to a sister, since otherwise the human race could not be multiplied; but *the more ancient that practice was when necessity compelled it, the more damnable it became afterward when religion prohibited it*, as *Augustine* significantly puts it. Moreover, religion prohibited it not only through the Mosaic law, but even before. *Epiphanius* says: <note>original Greek: λοιπὸν οὐκ ἔτι τὰς αὐτῶν ἀδελφὰς πρὸς γάμους ἤγοντο, ἀλλὰ εἰς εὐνομίαν κατέστη, καὶ πρὸ τοῦ διὰ Μωυσέως ἐγγράφου νόμου, ὁ κατὰ τὸν σεμνὸν γάμον θεσμός.</note> *Furthermore, they no longer took their own sisters as wives; but the law concerning marriage obtained the force of right even before the Law written by Moses.*

# OF EGYPTIAN MATTERS

Nevertheless, Abraham called Sarah his *sister*, and the *daughter of his father* <note>original: "filiam Patris sui"</note>, according to a common Hebrew idiom, even though she was actually his father’s *granddaughter* through *Haran*, whom Terah (Abraham’s father) could have had by another wife. Indeed, the Scripture calls Sarah his <term>daughter-in-law</term> <note>Hebrew: כַלָּתוֹ (Kallato)</note>, that is, Terah’s daughter-in-law, in Genesis 11:31, and not his *daughter*, even though a daughter is more closely related to a father than a daughter-in-law is. Theologians of the greatest reputation defend this opinion. Among the Ancients: *Augustine*, *Jerome against Helvidius*, and *Chrysostom*. Among the Protestants: *Junius*, *Rivet*, and *Tarnovius*. Among the Catholics: *Lyranus*, *Tostatus*, *Pererius*, *Delrio*, *Cornelius a Lapide*, *Bonfrerius*, *Genebrard*, and *others*.

VII. But suppose—though it remains uncertain—suppose that *Sarah* was indeed Abraham’s sister <term>by the same father</term> <note>Greek: ὁμοπάτριον (homopatrion)</note>; can one derive a general law from this single instance? The Patriarchs of that age did not have a written law; and Natural Law easily fades away unless it is supported by the written word. Added to this was the zeal of the Patriarchs, which was not always equally prudent; in order to avoid marriages with foreigners, they preferred to take wives from their own family, even those closely related. Nor should we press too hard on the fact that we do not read of the authors of such marriages being rebuked by God. For Divine mercy tolerated many things of this kind among those ancients which Divine Holiness did not approve. XIII. Nor is it difficult to show how nature and right reason condemn fornication. For such a union of bodies by its very nature tends toward the procreation of offspring. Reason teaches that every parent should know, acknowledge, love, and raise their offspring for the glory of God and their own comfort. Nothing is more natural than for parents to perform these duties of piety for their children. This same natural reason dictates that it is fair for children to know, love, honor, and serve their parents, and to delight in their love. All these duties are overturned by fornication. For fathers are ashamed of such children, and they are a disgrace to their mothers. Nor can they be raised by both parents, since they do not live together. The children themselves are forced to be ignorant of their parents, or to keep them secret, lest they admit they are illegitimate—for which reason in the Laws they are called <term>fatherless</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀπάτορες" (apatores); a legal term for those without a legally recognized father</note>. Briefly, he who acts through fornication in a way that might produce children seems to procreate children whom he does not wish to acknowledge or love as his own, who may even hate and fail to honor their parents; and in the dishonoring of their parents, they dishonor God, from whom they received life through the very parents they dishonor. The meaning of these words is this: that whatever mixtures with women occur, even short of adultery, which are done outside the law, are all themselves shameful. For they arise from intemperance: since no one of a chaste mind, preserving their modesty, would endure to become familiar with a harlot, nor with a free woman outside of marriage, and—by heaven—not even with his own female slave. For there is nothing lawful or proper in such habits: but they are the height of baseness and a disgrace to those who pursue them. Having produced a similar <term>speech</term> <note>original: "ῥῆσιν" (rhesin) - a formal oration or passage.</note> from *Porphyry* (for it would be long to describe everything), he proceeds thus: *This natural suggestion stood in the way, preventing a wandering Venus <note>A metaphor for lust or sexual desire.</note> from breaking through the barriers of shame in a single impulse, or even without discrimination.*

And having praised the testimony of *Chrysippus* which we mentioned above, he writes that he relates it all the more willingly because what *Chrysippus* says is most true—that in ancient times prostitutes did not live in the cities, but in the fields (a custom of which traces have been found even among the *Peruvians* and *Tartars*), and they did not prostitute themselves openly but with a covered face—as appears from the narrative of *Moses* himself in Genesis 38:14. Among the *Romans*, anyone who defiled a free-born virgin was punished with the death penalty. Nor was a life of prostitution permitted except to those who had publicly declared that life; which laws they believed, as *Tacitus* says, were sufficient punishment through the shame itself. Therefore, regarding what the *Hebrews* note on the history of *Judah* and *Tamar*, that the use of a harlot was permitted before the Law, it can be granted if the question is about impunity from punishment: but not if the question is about what could be done without moral baseness. Thus far *Grotius* <note>Hugo Grotius, the famous Dutch jurist and philosopher.</note>. And these things had to be said by us in favor of ancient sanctity, against the pretended license for fornication before the *Mosaic* law.

# EGYPTIAN MATTERS

...and similar things which are clearly contrary to public safety, they considered a great sin. Nevertheless, they held many types of theft to be not only unpunished, but even permitted—indeed, almost honored; at least to the extent that by public decree, a portion of the stolen goods was awarded to the thief. *Aulus Gellius* <note>A 2nd-century Roman author known for his miscellany "Attic Nights."</note> and *Diodorus Siculus* <note>A Greek historian of the 1st century BCE.</note> provide evidence of this. The former says this regarding the Egyptians: *I also remember reading in a book by Aristo, a legal expert and by no means an unlearned man, that among the Ancient Egyptians—a race of men established to have been both clever in inventing arts and wise in investigating the knowledge of things—all thefts were permitted and unpunished.*

<margin>Book 11, chapter 18.</margin>
XX. Here, however, [Diodorus] is not a little more precise and accurate: <note>original Greek: Ὑπῆρχε δὲ καὶ περὶ τῶν κλεπτῶν νόμος παρ’ Αἰγυπτίοις ἰδιώτατος...</note> *There was also a most peculiar law among the Egyptians concerning thieves. For it commanded those who wished to practice this profession to register themselves with the Chief of Thieves, and to immediately report the stolen item to him.* There was, moreover, among the Egyptians a **MOST SINGULAR LAW CONCERNING THIEVES**: *For it ordered that those who wished to devote their labor to theft should declare their name to the Chief of Thieves, and promise to bring the stolen property to him immediately; so that those who lost items might likewise write to him regarding each lost thing, and concerning the place, day, and hour of the loss. In this way, the items being easily found, the one who lost them recovered his property after paying a fourth part of the value. For since it is impossible for everyone to abstain from theft, the lawgiver found a way through which the whole object might be saved by a small price of redemption.*

<margin>Book 1.</margin>
XXI. From these words of Diodorus, five points are clear: I. That the Egyptians had a law regarding theft that was as different as possible from the institutions and customs of other nations, and thus <term>most peculiar<note>original Greek: idiōtaton</note></term> or highly singular. II. That by this law, a certain guild of thieves was established, whose <term>work<note>original Greek: ergasia</note></term> and, as it were, "craft" was to steal. III. That it was open to anyone <term>who wished<note>original Greek: boulomenō</note></term>, provided they were willing, to devote themselves to this guild and craft, on the condition that they gave their name publicly. IV. That a leader was set over this guild by public authority, to whom an account had to be rendered by each individual. V. That one caught in the act of theft was not only not punished with any penalty or misfortune, but by the command of the law, retained a fourth part of the value for himself or certainly for the guild; with only three parts being returned to the rightful owner when he came to reclaim his things. It is unnecessary to prove how immensely far these things stand from the holiness of the Hebrew Laws, as this is well known to everyone.

# BOOK II. CHAPTER VII.

### CHAPTER VII.

->That the Hebrews owe nothing to the Egyptians in the ordering of Years and Months.<-

*I. Since the distinction of years and months prevailed before the flood, it is falsely established that the Egyptians were the authors of it. II. Many affirm that the Egyptians learned astrology <note>In this context, astrology refers to the general study of stars and celestial movements, which we now call astronomy.</note> from Abraham. III. The festivals of the Egyptians travel through all parts of the year: those of the Hebrews are each bound to their own specific seasons. IV. The Civil and Sacred year of the Egyptians has nothing in common with either year of the Hebrews. V. The mystery of the Sacred Year among the Hebrews. VI. What it could have taught the Israelites that God willed the sacred year to begin from that month which is called Abib or Nisan. VII. Jewish observations on this matter.*

---

<margin>Compare Book I, Chapter VI, Section 2.</margin>
I. **THOSE** things which are praised by Marsham <note>Sir John Marsham (1602–1685), an English writer known for his work on ancient chronology.</note> from *Herodotus* and *Diodorus* concerning the distinct calculation of **YEARS AND MONTHS** as if invented by the Egyptians are openly false; since the Mosaic history distinguishes the times of the first *Patriarchs* and even of *Adam* and *Eve* themselves by their own months and years: and before the flood, God prescribed a certain number of years to *Noah*, after which he would destroy the earth with waves. It is also established that those years had twelve months, since explicit mention is made of the first, second, seventh, and tenth month in Genesis 7:11 compared with 8:4, 5, 13. There the Divine calculation pauses: not because more months were not included in the year, but because in the following months nothing happened that was worth recording by *Moses* with a designation of time. It is likewise established that the months were circumscribed by thirty days: since from the seventeenth day of the second month, up to the seventeenth day of the seventh month, one hundred and fifty days are numbered in Genesis 7:11, 24 compared with 8:3, 4.

II. And if historians are to be heard in such obscure antiquity outside of the Scriptures, we have those whom we may oppose to *Herodotus* and *Diodorus*. *Berosus*, *Nicolaus of Damascus*, *Eupolemus*, *Alexander Polyhistor*,

# EGYPTIAN MATTERS

<margin>Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book IX, chapters 16, 17, 18.</margin>
*Artapanus* <note>A historian of Jewish subjects from the 3rd or 2nd century BCE</note>, whose fragments *Eusebius* has preserved for us, all praise *Abraham* with one voice as an exceptional man, and one "skilled in heavenly matters" <note>original Greek: καὶ τὰ οὐράνια ἔμπειρον</note>, *endowed with knowledge of celestial things*. They record that while traveling among the Egyptians, he was held in great esteem by them, and he taught them Arithmetic and Astrology <note>In this context, "astrology" refers to the general study of stars and astronomy</note> extensively and generously. "For before the arrival of Abraham, the Egyptians were ignorant of these things" <note>original Greek: Πρὸ γὰρ τῆς Ἀβραάμου παρουσίας Αἰγύπτιοι τούτων εἶχον ἀμαθῶς</note>, *for in these arts, before Abraham's advent, the Egyptians had been altogether strangers and foreigners.* *Polyhistor* <note>Alexander Polyhistor, a Roman scholar</note>, however, traces the discovery of these things back to Enoch. *He maintains that Enoch was the chief author of them, as he was the first of all to discover Astrology, and not the Egyptians.*

III. But from wherever the Egyptians may have derived the constitution of their Year, it is certain that more differences than similarities can be assigned between the years of the Egyptians and the Hebrews: especially if we look at the cycle of annual festivals, which pertains most importantly to matters of religion. For the Egyptians took care to ensure that their festivals traveled through all parts of the year, so that the same rite might be performed now in spring, now in summer, now in autumn, and now in winter; therefore, their priests were the most bitter enemies of *intercalation* <note>The insertion of leap days or months to keep a calendar aligned with the solar year</note>. This was entirely foreign to the institutions of the Hebrews. Indeed, their festivals—being tied to the ripening of crops, the harvest, and the gathering—had to recur always at the same season of the year: therefore, they were most diligent regarding *intercalation*. *Moses Maimonides* <note>The influential 12th-century Jewish philosopher and jurist</note> treated this extensively in a complete treatise on the Talmudic Title *Kiddush HaChodesh* <insert>Sanctification of the New Moon</insert>, or *on the consecration of the New Moons.*

IV. Likewise, the dual year of the Egyptians has nothing in common with the dual year of the Hebrews: For the *Civil* and *Sacred* year among the Egyptians is exactly the same, and is distinguished from the *Natural* or *Solar* year by only a quarter of a day. However, the *Sacred* and *Civil* year of the Hebrews differ greatly in *Time*, *Usage*, and *Mystery*. In *Time*: for the use of the *Civil* Year is the most ancient of all, and was perhaps coeval with the world; its beginning falls in the month of *Tishri* <note>original: Tifri</note>, which corresponds to our *September*, and begins from the new moon of the *Autumnal Equinox*. *Moses* described the times of the *Sacred* Year by the command of God, at the time when the Lord claimed the *Israelites* for himself from the slavery of the Egyptians:

For according to the Civil year, they calculate the ages of the world's creation, the years of rest <note>The Sabbatical year or Shmita</note>, and the Jubilee year. According to the Sacred year, the festivals were to be reckoned. Nor does this entire matter seem to be lacking in *mystery* <note>In this context, "mystery" refers to a hidden spiritual or prophetic meaning</note>.

V. For by this change of the New Year's Day, I. God indicated that He was the King and *civil ruler* <note>original Greek: πολῐτᾰ́ρχην (politarchēn)</note> of the Israelites. For the same reason, *Julius Caesar* in the Republic and *Gregory XIII* in the *Roman* Church changed the divisions of the year, so that each might assert supreme authority for himself by this act. II. He willed that month to be as a birthday for His Israel, in which He claimed them for Himself—raised, as it were, from civil death and delivered into liberty from the Egyptian workhouse; so that, being exempted from the slavery of men, they might serve the living God, which is the true life of the soul. III. It taught that the "New Year's Day" of a better year was to be expected in the liberty of the New Testament, to be proclaimed by the Messiah. Isaiah 61:2. IV. Compare 1 Peter 4:2-3.

VI. And since that first month of the Sacred Year is called *Abib*, Exodus 13:4—a word which signifies *fresh ears of grain* to the Hebrews, because it is the month of ripening crops, for which reason the Greeks also call it the *month of new fruits* <note>original Greek: μῆνα τῶν νέων καρπῶν (mēna tōn neōn karpōn)</note>—it is called *Nisan* by the Chaldeans. Josephus reads this as *Nisan*, derived from *Nissin*, meaning *military standards* <note>original Hebrew: נִסִּין (Nissin)</note>, because banners are usually brought out for battle in that month, 2 Samuel 11:1. From this also comes the Roman *March, named after Mars*. By this beautiful emblem the Israelites were taught that from the moment one begins to belong to God, from that time new seeds of good exercises and virtues must be brought forth to the honor of God; and an expedition must be courageously undertaken under the banners of our heavenly Commander against the most powerless <note>The author likely means "impotent" in the face of God, or perhaps "unrestrained" (impotens) in their malice</note> enemies of Divine glory and human salvation.

# OF THE EGYPTIANS

From the time the Holy One, Blessed be He <note>original: "Sanctus Benedictus," a Latinization of the Hebrew 'HaKadosh Baruch Hu'</note>, chose His world, He established in it the beginnings of months and years; and when He chose Jacob and his sons, He established among them as the beginning of months the month of redemption, because in it the Israelites were redeemed from Egypt, and in it they are to be redeemed hereafter; namely, by the Messiah, just as it was said in Micah 7:15: *According to the day of your exit from Egypt, I will show him wonders.* Note that, according to the mind of this Master <note>referring to the rabbinic source</note>: I. ## CHAPTER VIII.

### That the institutions of the Bronze Serpent and the Red Heifer, and the use of Hyssop in sprinklings, are wrongly claimed to be derived from Egypt.

I. Not only prudence, but also piety occasionally forbids comparing the trifles of the Egyptians with the most sacred institutions of God. II. Although the Egyptians and others may have used talismanic figures <term>Talismanicas: objects engraved with astrological signs believed to have magical powers</term> for the charming of serpents; III. Nevertheless, the bronze serpent was not made by Moses according to the model of those deceptions. IV. On which matter the Hebrew masters speak better than Marsham <note>Sir John Marsham, a 17th-century scholar who argued that Jewish rites were borrowed from Egypt</note>. V. It is not established whether, before the time of Moses, the Egyptians sacrificed red oxen out of hatred for Typhon <note>In Egyptian mythology, Set/Typhon was associated with the color red</note>. VI. VII. And even if it were established, the ceremony of the Red Heifer is not to be derived from there. VIII. A holier mystery is assigned to it. IX. There is something similar to it in the rites of the Gaurs <note>likely referring to the Guebres or Zoroastrians</note>. X. The Egyptians used hyssop in one way, the Hebrews in another. XI. The mystery of Hyssop in sprinkling.

Into this category <note>The author is referring to scholars who try to find pagan origins for biblical rites.</note> I place the comparison of Egyptian illusions in the charming of serpents with the bronze serpent erected by Moses at God’s command; and the comparison of the red oxen—which the Egyptians sacrificed out of hatred for *Typhon*, whom they believe was red-haired—with the *Red Heifer* <note>Numbers 19</note> whose ashes were mixed with the water of purification, as if no reason could be assigned for that color other than an emulation of Egyptian ritual. I also include the comparison of Typhonic rites with the goat of *Azazel* <note>The "scapegoat" of Leviticus 16</note> and the other sacred ceremonies used on the Day of Atonement; of Egyptian *Amulets* and most shameful *Phalli* <note>Symbols of fertility</note> with the Israelite *Totaphot* or *Phylacteries* <note>Small leather boxes containing scripture worn during prayer</note>; and finally, the comparison of the *Teraphim* <note>Household idols or figurines</note> to which the Israelites had become accustomed in Egypt, with the most sacred apparatus of the High Priest used in receiving and delivering oracles, which the Divine Scriptures call the *Urim*.

III. However, there is nothing in those illusions that deserves in any way to be compared with that wonderful serpent erected on a pole by the miracle-worker Moses at God’s command. For whatever was done here was not done by some "incantation," as the most noble Marsham <note>Sir John Marsham, who argued that Jewish rites were derived from Egypt</note> was pleased to say—since God most severely forbade such things to His people—but by the express mandate of God. It was not by the evil arts of the Devil, but by Divine omnipotence, summoned by the pious prayers of Moses for the help of the Israelites.
