Heaven is not further distant from the underworld than this miraculous specimen of Divine Goodness is from the local magic <note>original: "μαγείᾳ ἐπιχωρίῳ" (mageia epichōriō)</note> of the most impure Egyptians.

# BOOK II. CHAPTER VIII.

Since we learn from more recent ages that the *Egyptians* sacrificed only red oxen because *Typhon* <note>In Egyptian mythology, Typhon (Set) was associated with chaos and the color red.</note> is said to have been of a red color, must we consider that the entire reasoning for this commandment <note>Referring to the "Red Heifer" ritual in Numbers 19.</note> was founded on the permission of some ancient custom which the *Israelites* had drawn from Egypt? Who will guarantee such great antiquity for that custom? Who will judge the testimony of *Plutarch* <note>A Greek philosopher and historian (c. 46–120 AD) who wrote extensively on Egyptian religion.</note> to be sufficient for the proof of such an enormous demand? Is such a recent author a suitable witness for such hidden antiquity? Indeed, he is not even a witness of so ancient a rite. For while he reports the ceremonies of the *Egyptians* in his own manner, he does not ascend to the first origin of this matter. He does, it is true, base it on the opinion which the *Egyptians* conceived regarding the red color of *Typhon*, but as to when they began to derive this corollary <note>original: "πόρισμα" (porisma) - a deduction or consequence.</note> from that hypothesis, he does not touch upon it even with a word.

VI. Nor is it of great interest to us to investigate this laboriously. For even granted that the *Egyptians* from all remote antiquity sacrificed only red oxen, must the reason for this *Israelite* ceremony be summoned from there for that reason? But what cause, finally, can be given why—when in all other sacrifices clean animals were duly offered without distinction of colors—it was necessary for this lustral <note>Purification or cleansing.</note> cow alone to be red? Let all the cabinets of ancient customs now be shaken out, and let it be shown from them why, on account of the foolish and insane superstition of the *Egyptians* sacrificing only red oxen, God—in the purification of the unclean alone—did not merely "permit" (which is falsely said) but expressly commanded a red cow to be used by the *Israelites*, when nevertheless all other sacrifices had no designation of a certain color.

VII. Furthermore, there is no doubt that the red cow offered, slaughtered, and burned in this way according to the prescription of the Lord, was pleasing to God; since God himself calls sacrifices of this kind his own food. However, the *Egyptians* sacrificed red oxen not because they thought them more precious or more pleasing to their gods, but out of hatred and contempt. For they dictated that "that which is sacrificed is not dear to the gods" <note>original: "θύσιμον οὐ φίλον εἶναι Θεοῖς" (thysimon ou philon einai Theois).</note>.

VIII. How much better, holier, and more worthy of a *Christian* man it is to rise to the *mystery*, and in this entire ceremony of the lustral cow to recognize a *type* <note>A "type" is a person, event, or ritual in the Old Testament believed to foreshadow something in the New Testament.</note> of our spiritual *purification* through Christ?

They mention this above all: that at the command of an unbelieving king, he willingly and gladly threw himself into a bath of molten silver; when he emerged from it safe and sound, he filled everyone with admiration for himself and made them obedient to his teaching. And from this he was called *Zer-Ateucht*, which in their language signifies *Washed in Silver*. Therefore, those *Guebres* have nothing more sacred in their purifications than the *urine of a Cow*. Whenever someone has stepped on filth, or touched any unclean thing, or when someone from the priestly order has come upon a corpse and looked at it, it is necessary for him to be purified by this cow's urine. # BOOK II. CHAPTER VIII.

...they say, and with that urine, after a sufficiently rigorous penance of ten days, the priest—whom they call a *Cazi* <note>likely a reference to a 'Qadi' or judge, though here used for a ritual official</note>—sprinkles the sinner seven times; and he offers him a small amount of it to drink. Only then is he considered absolved of his crime. Indeed, they feign that the first origin of this rite is older than their Prophet <note>referring to Muhammad</note> and almost contemporary with the first-formed man <note>original: "protoplasto," referring to Adam</note>. But we have no desire to hunt for any praise of scholarship from the trivial details of such minor observations.

X. Nor do I see what it contributes to the advancement of Theology if—when we read that God commanded that for the sprinkling at Passover, and the purification of the leper, and elsewhere, a bundle or sprinkler should be used made of cedar and hyssop bound with a scarlet thread—it is then recalled to our minds that the priests of the Egyptians did not eat bread unless it was cut with hyssop, for they believed hyssop purged the excessive potency of the bread. To be sure, Chaeremon <note>A Stoic philosopher and historian of Egypt</note> testifies to this in the writings of Porphyry; yet Porphyry knew as much about what the Egyptian priests did in the age of Moses as those who are born today. But even if the Egyptians did this in the time of Moses: what has bread to do with a ritual sprinkler?

XI. Of far greater importance is that wisdom which David boasts God revealed to him in secret in Psalm 51:8-9. That ceremony contains a mystery, for the sake of whose significance the whole institution exists. Leprosy denotes the filth of sin, with which the soul is miserably infected. The purification of leprosy signifies the remission of sin and the sanctification of the mind. The material for the sprinkling was blood and living water. The fulfillment of both is in Christ: *who came by water and blood: not by water only, but by water and blood.* 1 John 5:6. Of these, the former can signify the Spirit of Christ, and the latter the power of his satisfaction and merit. The sprinkling figures the imputation of the righteousness of Christ and the application of his merits. The sprinkler itself undoubtedly did not lack its own significance. There are learned men who think that by the triple material of which it consisted—cedar, hyssop, and scarlet or purple—it was foreshadowed that by the will of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, the communion of the merit and death of Christ is given for righteousness and life. The cedar tree, on high mountains and on the ridge of Lebanon, tall, hardy, and most long-lived, can, they say, signify the Father. Hyssop, a humble sprout that grows on walls (1 Kings 4:33), signifies God the Son, Christ as man, humble and despised. The purple of the blood...

The color is red, indeed, it is even like *blood*. Blood is the vehicle of the *Spirit*. What then prevents it from hieroglyphically signifying the *Holy Spirit*, which, like scarlet, glows with the fire of charity, and the love of God and of all that is good? If, however, this should seem too subtle—as it may rightly seem—one may consider that *Christ* is figured by the entire *sprinkler* <note>The aspergillum used in ritual purification</note>, so that the cedar wood, by its hardness, vitality, and height, denotes the *eternity and excellence of the Divine nature in Christ*; and by its fragrance, the *manifestation of the Spirit in words and in obedience*. *Hyssop denotes the lowliness of human nature; the scarlet thread denotes the imputation of sin and the bloody passion.* Indeed, the Psalmist mentions hyssop alone, implying the rest, because all other things together with the human nature of Christ conspire toward the same efficacy, and because all certainty of that grace depends upon the incarnation of Christ. I would prefer to meditate on these things on the occasion of that ceremony, rather than to think of some Egyptian bread which their priests might have eaten with hyssop.

### CHAPTER IX.

#### Likewise, it is wrong to derive the ceremonies of the annual atonement, and the laws concerning Frontlets, from the sacred Egyptian averting-rites, amulets, or phalli.

I. *The word* Azazel <note>original: "עזאזל"</note> *does not denote Typhon <note>An Egyptian deity associated with chaos</note>, or any averting deity.* II. *The Hellenists seem to have called it the "sent-away" goat <note>original: "ἀποπομπαῖον" (apopompaion)</note> because it was released.* III. *God did not permit, much less command, a sacred goat to be offered to the Devil.* IV. *The reason for the sacred institution must be sought from the innermost shrines of Christianity.* V. *The scapegoat was not cast down from a cliff.* VI. *The imprecation upon the head of a piacular victim <note>A sacrifice offered in atonement</note> is an institution common to almost all nations.* VII. *It is a shameful thing to derive God's Law concerning Frontlets <note>Phylacteries or Tefillin</note> from the shameful phalli of the Egyptians.* VIII. *The three places in which mention is made of the* Totaphot <note>original: "τῶν Totaphot" - Hebrew term for frontlets</note> *or Frontlets.* IX. *To the Orientals, Totaphot were ornaments of the head or arms.* X. *God nowhere commanded the making of Totaphot, but gave His own words and deeds in place of Totaphot proverbially <note>original: "παροιμιωδῶς" (paroimiodos)</note>.* XI. *Petit <note>Samuel Petit (1594–1643), a French scholar</note> published an improbable notation of that and related words.*

BOOK II. CHAPTER IX.

<margin>Compare Book I, Chapter VII, Section 14.</margin>

I. **I** cannot bring myself to believe that anything other than an injustice is done to the most holy ceremonies of the annual <term>EXPIATION</term> <note>The Day of Atonement or Yom Kippur</note> when they are derived from the impure *Typhonic* rites <note>Referring to Typhon, the Greek name for the Egyptian god Set, associated with chaos and storms</note> and from those devoted animals which the Egyptians offered to their averting gods <note>Gods intended to turn away evil or bad luck</note>. For what, after all, is it that leads us to that opinion? Is it because it pleased the *Hellenists* <note>Greek-speaking Jews who translated the Old Testament</note> to translate the Hebrew word *Azazel* <note>original: לעזאזל</note> as "to the one sent away" or "for the sending away" <note>original: τῷ ἀποπομπαίῳ, vel εἰς τὴν ἀποπομπὴν</note>, that we are permitted to divine that this word is *Egyptian*, and signifies *Typhon*, or I know not what other *averting deity*? Did God permit his people—let alone command them—to recognize some averting spirit whom they might appease with sacred animals, or to do anything similar to the abominations of the Egyptians?

II. We have long since learned that for Greek writers, *apopompe* <note>original: ἀποπομπὴν</note> signifies the *driving away* of evils through sacrifices and prayers; but the simplicity of *Hellenistic* speech is not always to be measured by the elegancies of the Greeks. It is not certain—indeed, perhaps not even credible—that the Hellenists had that specific meaning in mind. They wished to say *apopompaios* <note>the one sent away</note>, which *Jerome* called the "emissary goat" <note>The Scapegoat</note>. *Cyril* teaches this in his *Glaphyra* <note>A commentary on the Pentateuch by Cyril of Alexandria</note>. <margin>Bochart, *Hierozoicon*, Book II, Chapter VI.</margin> *Of the named goats, one was for the Lord, and the other for the "Apopompaios," because it was sent away.* <note>original: Τῶν τραγῶν ὠνομασμένων, τοῦ μὲν ἑνὸς Κυρίῳ, τοῦ δ’ ἑτέρου Ἀποπομπαίῳ, διὰ τὸ ἀποπέμπεσθαι.</note> And *Theodoret* in his commentary on *Leviticus*: *The goat was called "apopompaios," as if being sent away into the desert.* <note>original: ὁ τράγος ἀποπομπαῖος ἐκλήθη, ὡς ἀποπεμπόμενος εἰς τὴν ἔρημον.</note> *Symmachus* translated it as *the departing goat* <note>original: τράγον ἀπερχόμενον</note>. And *Aquila* as *the goat released into the desert* <note>original: τράγον ἀπολελυμένον εἰς τὴν ἔρημον</note>. It is memorable that, when *Julian the Apostate* <note>The Roman Emperor who rejected Christianity</note> abused this passage of *Moses* to prove that he had written about the *apotropaioi*, or *Averting Gods*, *Cyril* set out to refute him at great length and with sharpness in his *Ninth Book against Julian*. But among the letters of the same *Cyril*, there exists one quite long letter to *Acacius*, Bishop of Melitene, concerning the *Apopompaios*, in which he argues vehemently against those who—because they read in the Greek version that lots were cast for two goats, one for the Lord and the other for the *apopompaios*—concluded that of the two goats, one was indeed assigned to the Lord for sacrifice, *but the other was sent to some "apopompaios," an evil and impure demon.* <note>original: τόνγε μὴν ἕτερον ἀποπομπαίῳ τινὶ, καὶ πονηρῷ, καὶ ἀκαθάρτῳ δαίμονι πεμφθῆναι</note>

III. And indeed, what could be imagined more absurd than that God, out of two consecrated goats, should designate one for Himself and the other for the Devil, and command it to be sacred, when He expressly forbids sacrifices to be made to demons? Both were equally sacred to the Lord, to be presented by the High Priest before Jehovah at the door of the tent of meeting: the difference consisted solely in the manner of offering; for one was to be slaughtered and burned, while the other *was to be presented alive before Jehovah to make atonement over it, and to be let go into the desert.* (Leviticus 16:7-10). I would not, for my part, wish to reject the opinion of those who think that the Devil was symbolized by *Azazel*; but to believe that he was considered by the Jews as some kind of guardian spirit who averts evil, or that the goat was sacred to him, is foreign to piety and religion. The scapegoat <term>caper emissarius: the goat sent out into the wilderness</term> was not offered to the Devil, but by the will of God was exposed to be harassed by the Devil.

How His various relationships <note>original Greek: σχέσεις</note> were figured through the twin goats, we have explained systematically <note>original Greek: πραγματικῶς</note> elsewhere, which there is no need to repeat here.

He is said to have been *set apart* for release, <note>original Greek: διεσταλμένῳ εἰς ἄφεσιν</note>. This is in the same manner as certain sacred animals, which the Greeks called "released ones" <note>original Greek: ἄφετα</note>, because they were let go free in honor of some God. Various testimonies or examples of this matter exist in the works of Plato, Athenaeus, Synesius, Harpocration, and others; whoever wishes to see them may consult Bochart <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a French Protestant biblical scholar</note> and Marsham <note>Sir John Marsham (1602–1685), an English writer on chronology and history</note> himself.

VI. THE PRONOUNCING OF CURSES UPON THE HEAD OF THE VICTIM <term>imprecatio: the ritual act of calling down a curse or transferring guilt onto a sacrificial subject</term> is established by Herodotus to have been an Egyptian rite. But whether it existed before Moses is difficult, or even impossible, to prove. "There is no doubt," says Bochart, "that a similar rite flowed from there <insert>the Hebrews</insert> to the Egyptians." However, not only the Egyptians, but most other nations as well, employed this: specifically because they substituted such sacrifices as substitutes for themselves; for which reason they were also called "soul-for-soul" <note>original Greek: ἀντίψυχα; implies a life given in exchange for another</note>. Nature itself almost dictating that sins must therefore be placed upon them by a certain ritual, and curses invoked, which otherwise awaited those making the offering. The Greeks observed this not only with cattle, but also with humans employed for expiatory sacrifices. To this, refer to those words of the Commentator on *Aristophanes*:

<margin>On The Knights.</margin>
> For the Athenians maintained certain very low-born and useless persons, and in a time of some calamity befalling the city—I mean a plague or something of that sort—they sacrificed these people for the sake of being cleansed from the defilement; these they also called "cleansings" <note>original Greek: καθάρματα (katharmata); refers to offscourings or people sacrificed to purify a community</note>.

Moreover, Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine Greek historical encyclopedia</note> teaches what they prayed over them, and with what formula.

<margin>On the word "offscouring" <note>Greek: περίψημα</note>.</margin>
> Thus they spoke to the one designated for the annual containment of evils: "Become our offscouring," that is, our salvation and redemption. And they cast him into the sea, as if paying a sacrifice to Neptune <note>The Roman name used here for the Greek god Poseidon</note>.

The people of *Marseille* did the same; whenever they suffered from a pestilence, one of the poor offered himself to be supported for an entire year on public and pure foods.

<margin>Servius's commentary on the Aeneid, Book III.</margin>
Afterward, adorned with sacred branches and garments, this man was led around the entire city with curses, so that the evils of the whole city might fall back upon him: and thus he was cast out. Therefore, the custom of invoking curses upon sacrificial victims was accepted among very many nations. Nor is it necessary

VII. But it is truly a shameful thing that *Samuel Petit* <note>Samuel Petit (1594–1643) was a French scholar known for his work on ancient laws.</note> has led his mind to explain the Law of God regarding the Hebrew FRONTLETS <note>The author refers to *tefillin*, ritual boxes containing scripture worn on the forehead.</note> by comparing them to the shameful amulets of the *Egyptians*. Is it really so, that because the Hebrews once protected their foreheads with the superstitious amulets of the Egyptians—and perhaps with shameful phallic symbols, or certainly with certain <term>ridiculous</term> <note>original Greek: γελοίοις</note> little images—that God therefore commanded them to wear certain more sacred parchments on their foreheads? And yet, Petit claims these very parchments retained that *shameful* name in the sacred tongue, being named not only from "mud," but from that part of the female body which cannot be honorably named? What will the vanity of the human intellect not devise to hunt for the praise of recondite erudition? Plain truths, it seems, are considered sordid. Something rare and unusual in its very sound must be brought forward, however <term>ridiculous</term> <note>original Greek: γελοῖον</note> and shameful it may be.

VIII. Let us say those things which are sound, sober, pure, and worthy of God and the people of God. We find mention of the <term>Totaphot</term> <note>original Greek: τῶν Totaphot; a Hebrew term for frontlets or phylacteries</note> exactly three times in the books of the Old Testament. Where, when God had given the precept concerning the consecrating of the firstborn to Himself, both of men and of cattle, He commands that parents impress the reason for that precept upon their children, by saying: *It happened when Pharaoh had shown himself stubborn in letting us go, that Jehovah slew every firstborn in the land of Egypt, both the firstborn of men and the firstborn of beasts; therefore I sacrifice to Jehovah every male from every beast that opens the womb, but every firstborn of my sons I redeem.* Which shall be (so the speech of the parents to the children continues) *for a sign upon your hand*, and for frontlets between your eyes <note>original Hebrew: ולטוטפת בין עיניך</note>, *and for frontlets between your eyes, because with a strong hand Jehovah led us out of Egypt.* Then in Deuteronomy 6:8, where Moses speaks thus concerning all the precepts which he was teaching the Israelites in the name of God: *And you shall bind them for a sign to your hand*, and they shall be as frontlets between your eyes <note>original Hebrew: והיו לטטפת בין עיניך</note>, *and they shall be for frontlets between your eyes.* Finally, in Deuteronomy 11:18: *You shall lay up these words of mine in your heart and in your soul, and you shall bind them for signs to your hand*, and they shall be as frontlets between your eyes <note>original Hebrew: והיו לטוטפת בין עיניכם</note>, *and they shall be for frontlets between your eyes.*

### BOOK II. CHAPTER IX.

...should we consider their use? They are an ornament of the head, and that word is used by the Chaldean <note>The author refers to the Aramaic Targum, an ancient translation/paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible</note> for a **Tiara**. Esther 8:15: *And above the crown were Tiaras.* <note>original: "Et supra coronam erant Tiara"</note> Ezekiel 24:17: *Your Tiara shall be upon you.* *Your Tiaras upon your heads.* Or even for a **bracelet** or ornament of the arms. 2 Samuel 1:10: *The bracelet which was on his arm.* <note>original: "Armilla quæ erat in brachio ejus"</note> Where in the Hebrew text it is <term>As'adah</term> <note>אצעדה - a Hebrew term for an armlet or anklet</note>. Not amulets, not phallic symbols, nor any such superstitious or shameful things; but objects which had a civil use, for honorable decoration, or even for memory. Whatever follies or even magical madness the storytellers of later ages may have added with their inventions is another matter.

X. It must be observed, however, that God nowhere commanded that they should make <term>Totaphot</term> <note>The Hebrew word often translated as "frontlets" or "phylacteries"</note> for themselves: or that they should carry their memorable deeds, or precepts, written on scrolls around their foreheads or arms. Rather, concerning His own great works which He had performed, and the precepts He had given to Israel, He said: *these shall be to you as Totaphot*, that is, these shall be in your mind, before your eyes, and always in your memory. You shall consider yourselves no less adorned by the pious and grateful remembrance of these things than all **lovers of beauty** <note>original Greek: φιλόκαλοι (philokaloi)</note> are by their bracelets or tiaras. God did not say, *“make for yourselves Totaphot”*; or *“carry the Ten Commandments written on little parchments on your foreheads”*; or *“let that be for you in place of Egyptian amulets,”* as the most learned **Petit** <note>Samuel Petit (1594–1643), a French scholar of ancient law</note> interprets the divine command. Instead, He said: *the things I have said, the things I have done, these shall be to you* **for frontlets**, *that is, as it is explained in Exodus 13:9, for a memorial.* It is a proverbial expression, the twin of which occurs several times in the Divine parables. Proverbs 1:8-9: *Hear, my son, the instruction of your Father, and do not desert the teaching of your mother: for they shall be a graceful addition to your head, and a chain for your neck.* And chapter 3:3: *Let not kindness and faith leave you: bind them to your neck, write them on the tablets of your heart.* And chapter 6:21: *Bind them to your heart continually, tie them to your neck.* Since God said all these things and others like them **proverbially** <note>original Greek: παροιμιωδῶς (paroimiōdōs)</note>—not regarding the Ten Commandments, as **Petit** thinks, nor regarding certain other small portions of the Law, as **Fagius**, **Cameron**, and others show following the Jewish opinion, but regarding all parts of heavenly teaching—it is not a matter of Divine command, but of Jewish superstition, that certain segments of the Law, with fixed rites according to their own judgment...

XI. Having duly weighed these matters, it will not be necessary for us to weary ourselves much regarding the etymology of the words <term>Totafot <note>Hebrew: frontlets</note></term>, <term>Tefillin <note>Hebrew: phylacteries</note></term, and <term>immovable <note>original Greek: asaleuta</note></term>. But, if I may speak with the permission of the most renowned *Petit* <note>Samuel Petit (1594–1643), a French scholar</note>, I remember finding no derivation anywhere that is less skillful than his own. That most learned man seems to have had a mind so full of the imagination of Egyptian <term>abominations <note>original Greek: bdelygmatōn</note></term> and <term>phalluses <note>Latin: phallorum</note></term> that when he approached this commentary, he could not drive those intrusive thoughts from his chaste breast. ### CHAPTER X.

#### That the Teraphim were nothing but instruments of superstition, and were never approved by God in His worship.

I. *The assertion that the Urim was a small image of the same function and form as the Teraphim is a monstrous claim.* II. *For the Teraphim served for Divination.* III. *And for Idolatry.* IV. *And for Magic.* V. VI. *Certainly in the speech attributed to those small images.* VII. *Hence they were hated by the godly.* VIII. *Nor is it credible that God made a similar little idol the messenger of His secrets.* IX. *It is more likely that He is believed to have given the Israelites a far different instrument for His Oracle.* X. *For He nowhere mentions the Teraphim as being used in any part of His worship.* XI. *On the contrary, He forbids them.* XII. *The nature of the Cherubim is entirely different.*

<margin>Compare Book I, Chapter VIII.</margin>
I. Now at last let us descend to the consideration of the <term>Urim</term> <note>original Greek: τῶν URIM; these were objects on the High Priest's breastplate used to determine God's will</note>, and let us examine whether they were small images of the same function and figure as the <term>Teraphim</term> <note>household idols or figurines often used for divination in the ancient Near East</note>, though under a different name. Since this is a monstrous assertion, it must be examined by us all the more diligently. And indeed in this order: so that we may show: I. That the *Teraphim* were the absolute and purest instruments of *Divination*, *Idolatry*, and *Magic*. II. That they were never commanded, praised, or approved by God as instruments of His worship; but were forbidden, and indeed with detestation. III. That the *Urim* was nothing less than a talkative little figure or idol of that sort.

II. In the construction of the first thesis, there is no need to be very lengthy: since it is confessed among all that the *Teraphim* of the nations were an abomination to God. That they served for *Divination* through an impure spirit is proved by the example of the Babylonian King in *Ezekiel 21:21*, who, lacking counsel and wavering in mind, is read to have stood at the head of two ways,

IV. The author of the *Jerusalem Paraphrase* holds the same. Nor does *Kircher* disapprove, who teaches that the idols of *Serapis* in the *Mithraic rites were made not without blood*. Truly, let those authors stand by their own words.

VIII. Those things which we have recounted create a great prejudice in the mind, lest we rashly believe that God wished to dedicate to His own worship—and even make them the most admirable part of it—those things which were instruments of such great crimes among profane nations. For the *Teraphim* <term>Teraphim: ancient household idols or figurines used for divination</term> would indeed have been such, if, when placed in the High Priest's breastplate, they had brought forth Divine oracles for Israel. God was not ignorant of how prone to idolatry the people of this new republic, which He was forming for Himself, were. What was that republic if not a *Theocracy*? Where the worship of any foreign deity whatsoever ought to be judged as *rebellion*, *treason*, and a *crime against the Majesty* of God. Therefore, God, the ruler of the Republic, had no greater concern than that the Israelites be kept as far as possible from idolatry and from everything that leads to it, or has even the slightest affinity with it. What, however, could more effectively instill the condemned veneration of the nations' *Teraphim* into their minds, or more strongly confirm that superstition in souls long accustomed to them and naturally inclined toward them, than if they saw that God had made a small image of the same nature and use—and, as *Alphonso de Castro* <note>A 16th-century Spanish theologian and jurist</note> says, a "little idol"—the messenger of His secrets?

IX. God did not want His Israelites to be inferior in any matter of sacred rites to the *Chaldeans*, from whom they drew their first origin; or the *Egyptians*, among whom they had lived for a long time; or finally the *Canaanites*, whose land they were now prepared to occupy through the munificence of the Deity. But He also wished to recall them from every superstition of the other neighboring nations, so that they might depend solely upon Him. And therefore, since those nations had various arts of divining, prophesying, and knowing and foretelling the future—for which the *Teraphim*, who are the subject of our current dispute, served—in place of all those, He granted His people more certain oracles. These were given not only through Prophets inspired by His Spirit, but also through the *Urim* <term>Urim: part of the High Priest's breastplate used to determine God's will</term>, which, whatever they may have been, certainly surpassed the lying loquacity of the *Teraphim* by the immense Divine certainty of their responses. # BOOK II. CHAPTER X.

These new instruments, by their all-encompassing excellence and utility compared to the others, were naturally suited to draw the minds of all to themselves, and to induce forgetfulness of other follies, or extinguish the desire for them.

X. But what need is there here for our reasonings? Let us consult the Best Divinity <note>original: "Optimi Numinis"; a reference to God</note> Himself; who indeed sets forth the entire apparatus of His worship expressly and distinctly, down to the smallest details (if it is permitted to speak so); yet He nowhere makes mention of *Teraphim* as being properly used in any part of religion. For as to what some assert—that they lie hidden *under another name*—since that is an insane demand, it ought *not to be merely dictated*, but proved by clear and peremptory reasons. This is all the more true because, since the Sacred Scriptures declaim so often and so vehemently against the *Teraphim* of the Gentiles, and yet some of them are supposed to have been pious and sacred; it would be necessary for the minds of the Israelites to remain in suspense as to what kind of *Teraphim* please or displease God, and what use of them might be lawful or unlawful, unless they were more distinctly taught about it. Surely the mere change of a name is not sufficient for a mind seized by a holy fear of the Divine to persuade it of the transfer of the same thing from idolatrous and magical superstitions to the worship of God, without any mandate of the Divinity, and without a Divine designation of legitimate use. Or, if any such precept of the Divine Law concerning *Sacred Teraphim* exists, or if celestial doctrine hands down any distinction between types of *Teraphim*; let those consultants of rare wisdom point them out. It has not yet been granted to us to find them. For those things which the most illustrious *Spencer* <note>John Spencer (1630–1693), an English theologian who argued that many Jewish rites were adapted from Egyptian or Gentile customs</note> produces are not precepts, nor dogmas, but examples, and those not praised, but rather blamed; we shall respond to those without difficulty shortly.

# EGYPTIAN MATTERS

XI. On the contrary, God clearly enough forbade the entire making and use of the <term>Teraphim</term> <note>household idols or cult images mentioned in the Old Testament</note> by the second commandment of the Decalogue: *You shall not make for yourself a carved image or any likeness.* <note>original Hebrew: לא תעשה לך פסל וכל תמונה</note> For the word "carved image" <note>Hebrew: pesel</note>, the Septuagint <note>the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> uses the word *idol* <note>Greek: εἴδωλον / eidolon</note>. However, the Greek Scholia <note>ancient marginal commentaries</note> note that other translators use the word *sculpture* <note>Greek: γλυπτὸν / glypton</note>. Indeed, the Septuagint translators themselves usually translated this Hebrew word with that same term. A carved image, as the Jesuit Lorinus <note>Jean Lorin (1559–1634), a prolific Jesuit commentator</note> well observes, was prohibited more distinctly and earnestly; <margin>In Acts 27:29.</margin> *because the worship of idols was concerned chiefly with a carved image, or a statue, which by the solidity and thickness of its parts more effectively represents the person presented for adoration than if it were merely expressed in colors on a surface.* Furthermore, the Hebrew interpreters of the Law, whose decrees Selden <note>John Selden (1584–1654), a renowned English jurist and polymath</note> explained in *On Natural Law and the Law of Nations, Book II, Chapter VI*, commonly teach that of all figures, none was more prohibited than the human form. This was so strictly held that they did not consider it lawful or right to fashion them even for the sake of decoration, even if without any thought of foreign worship. This was specifically to prevent those who were prone to error from wandering astray and thinking the images were made for foreign worship. Hence it happened that they would not fashion a human image from wood, lime, or stone—at least not one that was prominent or standing out <note>i.e., in three-dimensional relief</note>, such as the ornaments and figures usually placed in dining rooms and other things of that kind. And whoever fashioned an image of this sort was punished with lashes. Since, therefore, God forbade all images in matters of religion, especially *carved* ones, and among these especially those fashioned after the human figure, the *Teraphim* cannot fail to be included in the same prohibition, as all these characteristics apply to them. For they were *images*, and *carved*—whence they are sometimes called *sculptures* <note>Greek: γλυπτὰ</note> by the Greeks—and they were fashioned in the likeness of a *man*, and finally, they were employed in the business of religion.

XII. If you should object that the Teraphim are no more banished from religion by this general prohibition than the *Cherubim*, whose sacred use in the Tabernacle and the Temple is well established: I respond that the nature of each was entirely different. For first, the *Cherubim* were *Hieroglyphic* types, not images; for there is no thing, whether in heaven or on earth, which they expressed by their figure. Rabbi Isaac Mofaides <note>likely a reference to Isaac Aboab or a similar commentator cited by Selden</note> rightly says in the works of Selden: <margin>On Natural Law, Book II, Chapter VI.</margin> *The fashioning of the Cherubim is not included in the general prohibition, because their form is not found in any of the dwellings* <note>original Hebrew: אין מעשה כרובים בכלל שהרי אין צורתם נמצאת בשום אחד מהמדורים — referring to the celestial or terrestrial realms</note>.

# CONCERNING EGYPTIAN MATTERS

Indeed, he first fights his case using the example of *Rachel*, who stole her father’s *Teraphim* <note>Teraphim: small household idols or figurines used in the ancient Near East for divination or as symbols of family inheritance</note> out of a religious affection, so that she might possess for herself those things which were most dear to her family. He contends that it is clear that *Jacob* himself did not consider the *Teraphim* to be of no value, based on the fact that he offered the sacrilegious thief to *Laban* to face the death penalty if discovered. But he especially presses the example of *Micah*, who believed that everything was lost to him once his *Teraphim* were taken away; God himself seems to have approved of these by his own testimony, for when he was consulted by the *Danites* through the *Levite* (Micah’s minister), he issued his oracles through the *Teraphim*. The history of *Michal* <note>The daughter of King Saul and wife of David</note> also teaches that there were *Teraphim* in the house of *David*. It is not credible, however, that pious men would have had and kept images of that kind in their homes if they could have even suspected them to be idolatrous and hateful to God.

II. But there is no need for great erudition or eloquence to blunt these little quibbles. For even if I do not say now that a matter of religion is of too great importance to stand safely on examples alone unless Divine approval is added; the very examples which are brought forward are hardly valid for achieving what is intended. To begin with *Rachel*: since the sacred history does not explain with what intent she stole her father's *Teraphim*, no one can say for sure except by guessing. There are those who wish to believe she did it with a pious mind, so that by removing the instruments of superstition she might call her father away from idolatry. Others attribute it to fear; as if, fearing that her husband’s secret journey might be betrayed by those talkative little images, she preferred to take them with her rather than face that risk. To *Pererius* <note>Benito Pereira (1535–1610), a Jesuit theologian and commentator</note> it seems most probable that because they were precious—made of gold or silver, perhaps—she claimed them for herself, partly as payment for the wages of which the greedy *Laban* had defrauded her husband, and partly for the dowry owed to her and her sister.

III. But let us act candidly, and let us grant to *Spencer* <note>John Spencer (1630–1693), a scholar who argued that many Jewish rites originated in Egyptian customs</note> what he argues not improbably: that *Rachel* undertook all these things led by religion and love for the *Teraphim*. *Laban* had grown old in the veneration of them, held fast by ancient sluggishness and superstition. His daughters, imbued with the same opinion from their tenderest years <note>Latin: "a teneris unguiculis," literally "from their tender little nails," meaning from earliest childhood</note>, had lived until then in that region where the multitude of those wandering in error favored the mistake. It is probable that *Jacob*, having been better instructed by his father *Isaac*, beheld the superstition spreading among his kinsmen with great sorrow of heart, and opposed it both by example and by holy warnings. But

# BOOK II. CHAPTER XI.

Since he was alone in a foreign land, he was unable to persuade his father-in-law, nor even the women—whom nature seems to have fashioned with a prone disposition toward superstition—to utterly and suddenly cast aside an error so deeply rooted. It was, therefore, from the old leaven of that ancient superstition, and not from a zeal according to knowledge <note>A reference to Romans 10:2, implying her devotion was misguided</note>, that **Rachel** took it into her mind to carry the *Teraphim* <note>Household idols or cult figurines</note> away with her. Nor does it seem to have escaped her notice that this plan would have greatly displeased her husband; she was well aware that he was minded quite differently toward the *Teraphim* than she was. Therefore, with the greatest care, she kept the matter secret from her husband no less than from her father, fearing the just rebuke of both.

IV. As for the fact that **Spencer** <note>John Spencer (1630–1693), a scholar who studied Hebrew rituals</note> suspects **Jacob** also held the *Teraphim* in the highest esteem and honor, in this he speaks a reproach against a distinguished man. You would sooner draw water from a stone than elicit such a conclusion from the praised words of **Jacob**. Does he protest that he holds the *Teraphim* in veneration simply because he offers their thief up to death and misfortune? Surely nothing is further from the truth. Rather, being indignant at the troublesome suspicion of **Laban**, and conscious of his own innocence, he thought it unworthy of the sanctity of his family to be accused of theft—especially of a stolen object which, while of the highest antiquity to **Laban**, was of no use to himself or his family. With a certain impulse and fervor of spirit, he said: *“With whomever you find your gods, let him not live.”* In these words, there is a manifest contempt and a "treating as nothing" <note>original: ἐξουδενισμός (exoudenismos) — a Greek term for total devaluation or scorn</note> of those gods who were unable to protect themselves. He does not say "gods" simply, nor "our gods," but "your gods," which he opposes to the *God of his Father*, the *God of Abraham and the Fear of Isaac*, by whose guardianship he had remained safe against the frauds and violence of **Laban**. Genesis 31:32, 42. Furthermore, if those gods of **Laban** remained surviving in his family up to that time, he carefully buried them—along with the remaining instruments of idolatry which perhaps survived from the spoils of **Shechem** or elsewhere—under the oak near **Shechem**. Genesis 35:2, 3, 4. **Josephus** <note>Titus Flavius Josephus, the 1st-century Jewish historian</note> favors this 
<margin>Book 1, chapter XIX.</margin>
observation: *“God commanded Jacob by a vision to be of good courage, and ordered him to purify his tent. And so, while he was purifying it, he came upon the gods of Laban (for he had not known that Rachel had stolen them); having buried these in the earth under a certain oak at Shechem, etc.”*

V. Regarding the deed of **Micah**, there are many things in it which prove it to have been superstitious, idolatrous, and therefore utterly unpraiseworthy...

# ON EGYPTIAN MATTERS

...they may argue: so that no defense of the *Teraphim* <note>original: "Theraphim"; small household idols or oracular figurines mentioned in the Old Testament</note> can be sought from it. For whether we look at the origin and occasion of his deed, or the *time*, or the *thing itself* which he performed, or the *place*, or the *ministers* whom he took for himself, or the *consequence*; all things conspire to prove that he acted altogether badly and without counsel. The origin and occasion of the deed was the superstition of a powerless old woman; when her son *Micah* had stolen eleven hundred silver shekels from her for some unknown reason, she had cursed the thief with the most dire curses, ignorant of whose head they would fall upon. Then, having been informed by her son that the silver for which she had uttered the curse was in his possession, she suddenly changed her mind and declared him blessed by *Jehovah* <note>The Tetragrammaton, the name of God</note>, and dedicated that silver to the making of a carved and molten image. All this was done from impulse and lack of self-control, with nothing by deliberate counsel, nothing by weighing the Law, or by consulting the mouth of the Lord, which ought to have been done in a matter of religion; where nothing should be dared except by prescription. Behold the origin of the evil: a nearly frantic woman. As *Jerome* <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century Church Father and translator of the Vulgate</note> observed, most heresies are either started or propagated by women.

VI. The designation of the *Time* also creates a prejudice against the deed. *In those times, says the sacred text of Judges 17:6, there was no King in Israel: everyone did what seemed right in his own eyes.* This can be explained in two ways: either in this sense; that the authority of the legitimate magistrate having been removed, and the barriers of the laws broken—by which the audacities <note>original Greek: "τολμήματα" (tolmēmata)</note> of private individuals in matters of religion ought to be restrained—everyone, as usually happens in a state of anarchy <note>original Greek: "ἀναρχίᾳ" (anarchia)</note>, thought that what he pleased was permitted to him, with no one rebuking or inhibiting him. Or in this way; there was no prince or judge whom they served: no one hindered them from good, no one impelled them to evil; they were not solicited toward wicked things by the example or force of a leader who was himself seduced or seducing. There was a full use of liberty; so that each person was allowed to arrange his affairs according to his own mind's opinion. In either mode of interpretation, those words contain a disapproval of the deed.

VII. Since, therefore, such a deformed...*

# BOOK II. CHAPTER XI.

*...the face of the Church was wretched, Micah set his own example against the age; he acted as a supporter, so to speak, of religion, and decreed to worship God—if not as he wished, at least as he was able.* <note>The author is quoting an opposing view here which suggests Micah was trying his best in a lawless time.</note>

VIII. But all these things are said as thoughtlessly as they are magnificently. For you will never find that specific notation of time <note>The phrase "In those days there was no king in Israel" from Judges 17:6.</note> placed before any laudable deed; it should not be judged that he did well who is narrated to have done "what was right in his own eyes" because there was no king in Israel. But what I would especially wish to be observed by **Spencer** <note>John Spencer (1630–1693), an English theologian who argued that many Jewish rites were adapted from Egyptian customs.</note>; those times were not so infested with robberies as he asserts. Rather, the Israelites were living in a deep peace—which is the mother of security but the stepmother of religion—each following his own mind. This is gathered not only from the fact that the young **Levite** <note>The wandering priest Micah hired.</note> traveled freely through the land without fear of assassins, investigating a convenient place for his journey wherever chance might take him: but it is most evident from the fact that at the same time the **Danite tribe**, intent on seeking new possessions for the enlargement of their borders, undertook an expedition against the **Laishites** after first sending out scouts. To think about enlarging borders, as if at leisure, when you see everything at home besieged by robbers, is the mark of men providing for their affairs without foresight. Would not the robust hand of the **Danites** have rather expelled those most pestilential assassins from the fatherland before acting to acquire new seats for themselves; so that while they were away from home, their wives and children might live secure and safe?

IX. *The very thing which Micah made, namely the graven and molten image, is diametrically opposed to the Divine precept in Exodus 20:4: "You shall not make for yourself a graven image," and Deuteronomy 4:15-16: "Therefore take good heed to yourselves... that you do not corrupt yourselves and make for yourselves a graven image, the likeness of any figure." Deuteronomy 27:15: "Cursed is the man who makes a graven or molten image, an abomination to Jehovah, the work of the hands of a craftsman, and sets it up in a secret place."* Is not our **Micah**, with this deed of his, seemingly pointed out as if by a finger by this discourse? And indeed, lest we doubt whether he violated the precept of God, he himself calls that molten and graven thing his "gods" in *Judges 18:24*. Just as **Laban** once called his **Teraphim** <note>Household idols or cult objects mentioned in Genesis.</note> his gods. This was directly against the will of the Lord in *Exodus 34:17*: *"You shall not make for yourself molten gods."* Nor does it excuse **Micah** that he prepared all this equipment in honor of **Jehovah**; no more

X. Indeed, most learned men dictate that Micah <note>Referring to the story in Judges 17 of Micah’s private shrine.</note> wished to represent the two Cherubim of the Tabernacle with his carved and molten image. Since God, exercising his right, ordered two Cherubim—carved tokens of his presence—to be placed in his Tabernacle; the number of Micah's images and other circumstances of the story seem to suggest that Micah acted so that his private chapel and religion might correspond and agree with the Tabernacle and public worship, like a face reflecting a face in the water. XI. But what is this audacity of divination? Have these very learned men learned from any example of the sacred scriptures that the Cherubim sacred to God are referred to by the ominous and abominable name of a "carved" or "molten" image? Or because *Micah* formed two images for himself, must it be concluded from this that he wished to represent the twin Cherubim? If he had that in mind, why did he not make each little icon molten from solid silver, just as each Cherub in the Tabernacle was of solid gold? By what authority, finally, did these learned men learn that what the Scripture calls a "carved image" was made of wood covered with silver plates? Is it right to smear on paper and thrust upon others whatever comes into a dreaming mind? But let us grant it was so—which all modest men will, unless I am mistaken, confess with us that they do not know—what does this have to do with the Cherubim? Is it because several centuries later in Solomon's temple the Cherubim were formed from wood covered in gold, that *Micah*, perhaps foreseeing this by the inspiration of I know not what spirit, wished it to be prefigured by one of his Cherubim? # BOOK II. CHAPTER XI.

...Micah <note>original: "Michas"</note>, at the time he was forming these small images, had the *Cherubim* <note>The winged angelic figures atop the Ark of the Covenant</note> in mind; nevertheless, no suitable defense for his cause has yet been found. For with whatever intent *Micah* did these things, he certainly acted with the worst judgment. For it was not lawful for any private individual to manufacture the instruments or ornaments of public worship according to his own will. God had commanded a single Tabernacle to be established for Himself, where all Israel was to assemble for sacred rites.

XII. Therefore, *Micah* also sinned in this: that he performed in an unlawful place—within his own private house—those things which otherwise belonged to public worship. For God had commanded in *Leviticus 17:1, 9; Deuteronomy 12:14, 26, 27; and 15:20, that sacrifices were not to be offered privately in private homes, or in any other place that each person might choose for himself, but were to be brought to the priest, so that they might be sanctified by his ministry, with the blood poured out at the altar in the place which God had chosen for His name to dwell.* The sanctity of this place was once so strictly guarded that the other tribes decreed it should be defended even by war against the *Reubenites*, the *Gadites*, and the half-tribe of *Manasseh*, when they appeared to have violated it by building a great altar at the banks of the Jordan. *Joshua 22:10* and following. To this point belong those Hebrew traditions which *Outram* <note>William Outram, a 17th-century theologian</note> presents from the *Shields of the Mighty* <note>original: "Schilte Haggibborim," a rabbinic work by Abraham Portaleone</note>, and from *Isaac Abarbanel*, and *Rabbi Levi Ben Gersom* <note>Also known as Gersonides</note>.
<margin>On Sacrifices, book 1, chapter 11.</margin>
*While the people remained in the desert, it was provided by law that no one should sacrifice in mountain shrines; however, that law ceased to apply when they arrived at Gilgal; because in that place, as there was no certain and fixed seat for the sacred tent, so also the entire people were separated into various settlements. But once the Sanctuary at Shiloh was established—which was built with stone walls, even if covered with curtains—that law which was to be observed in the desert was again in force. For in this place, the sacred Ark had a fixed and certain seat. Thus it happened that this sanctuary is everywhere called the House of God.* These events of which we now treat, however, occurred while the house of God was in *Shiloh*; and therefore they were conducted wrongly.

XIII. But *Micah* also acted against the prescription of the law in that he employed as a minister of sacred rites first his own son, and then a *Levite*. This was not an extraordinary proof of his zeal for God and Divine law—that he "holily and religiously consecrated his firstborn as a priest according to the custom of the ancestors," as Spencer <note>John Spencer, a Hebraist who argued that many Jewish rites were adapted from Egyptian customs</note> puts it—and that he then resolved to hire a priest descended from the Levite race at any price...

introduced; and as if he were secure in the name of Divine favor, he greatly congratulated himself with these words: *Now I know that the Lord <note>original: "Jehova"</note> will do me good, seeing I have a Levite as my priest.* For regardless of how much the superstitious **Micah** congratulated himself, or how much **Spencer** <note>John Spencer (1630–1693), a scholar who argued that many Jewish rites were adapted from Egyptian customs.</note> applauds him; in both acts there was an open violation of Divine Law. Even if in the most ancient ages it was so arranged that not only the firstborn (as many maintain) performed the sacred rites, but every man was his own priest for sacrifices made for himself; nevertheless, by the more recent law given to the Israelites freed from Egypt, the right of performing sacred rites was restricted to the **Aaronic** family. *Them,* says **Moses**, speaking of the Aaronic Priests in Deuteronomy 21:5, *the Lord your God has chosen to minister to him and to bless in his name.* Add also 1 Chronicles 23:13. And indeed, God barred all others from the function of the Priesthood with such severity that he threatened the death penalty against those who rashly intruded. Numbers 3:10: *But appoint Aaron and his sons to attend to their priesthood; for any outsider who comes near shall be put to death.* Moreover, anyone from a tribe other than the **Levitical** was considered an outsider; indeed, even if he were from the **Levitical** tribe, he was an outsider if he was not from the family of **Aaron**. Therefore, by the rigor of the law, both the son of **Micah** and the **Levite** (who was not an **Aaronite**) incurred the penalty of death by performing sacred rites; it is so far from the truth that this should have been praised by **Spencer** as an outstanding proof of zeal for God and Divine law.

XIV. Finally, this matter had a most shameful and sad consequence. For as nothing spreads more easily or quickly than a bad example; so it shortly happened that the plague of that forbidden worship, creeping out from a private house, immediately infected an entire tribe of Israel. For the **Danites** snatched away these foul trifles of an old woman's superstition by force—while **Micah** struggled against them in vain—and for a long time, with remarkable perversity, they worshiped them as if they were most sacred relics in the city named after their tribe. This was in the very same place where **Jeroboam** later set up the golden calf, an act so often condemned by the Scriptures. But the Spirit of God also marked this matter with a black <term>Theta</term> <note>The Greek letter Theta (Θ) was used by ancient judges as a shorthand for 'thanatos' (death), marking a person or thing condemned.</note>, and it was ultimately the ruin of the **Danites**. XV. Be careful not to understand what is told here regarding the "migration" as referring to that which occurred in the time of *Tiglath-Pileser* <note>An Assyrian king who deported Israelites in the 8th century BCE</note> when the sons of *Gad* and the sons of *Reuben* were led away into captivity (2 Kings 15:29; 1 Chronicles 5:25-26); nor that other migration carried out by *Shalmaneser* (2 Kings 17). > *For they provoked him with high places, and* BY THEIR CARVED IMAGES *they stirred him to jealousy. When* GOD *heard this, he was enraged, and greatly despised Israel. So much so that, deserting the tabernacle of Shiloh, the tent which he had placed among men, he delivered his strength into captivity, and his glory into the hand of the enemy: and he gave his people over to the sword, because he was enraged against his own inheritance.*

From this sacred song we clearly perceive the low standing these carved images held with God—images for which *Spencer* <note>John Spencer (1630–1693), a scholar who argued that many Jewish rituals were adapted from Egyptian customs</note> has shown himself to be a more fervent than cautious patron. Therefore, since this entire institution of *Micah* was faulty on so many counts, full of superstition, and the source and beginning of public idolatry in Israel—by which God, stirred to jealousy, grew incensed against his inheritance—anyone who attempts to argue and gather a legitimate and holy use of the <term>Teraphim</term> <note>Household idols or cult objects</note> in sacred rites from that history of *Micah* is entirely in vain.

...since it can be covered by some appearance of truth. Namely, that the most holy Divinity seems to offer such an illustrious testimony to the religion of *Micah* <note>original: "Michæ"; referring to the story in Judges 17-18 regarding Micah's private shrine</note> by an *oracle given from the Teraphim* <note>Teraphim: household idols or cult objects used in ancient Near Eastern divination</note>. Regarding the *heavenly origin of its response, Spencer* <note>John Spencer (1630–1693), a scholar who argued that many Hebrew rites originated from Egyptian customs</note> *estimates that no room for doubt is left*: since it is established that the *Danites*, drawing courage from that joyful omen, gave it the most certain faith; nor does the religion of the *Levite* allow us to believe that he, hired for no small price, would have simulated a Divine oracle with such a bold face; and finally, the outcome of the events itself can be believed to have sufficiently fulfilled the faith of that oracle sent from heaven.

XVII. However, what is *undoubtedly true to Spencer*, seems to me most uncertain, and—to hide nothing—*false*, or certainly *very close to false*. For the sacred text asserts with not a single word that *God gave any response through the Teraphim*; but only this: *to the Danites, asking that God be consulted in His name, it was answered by the Priest of Micah: "Go in peace; your journey on which you go is before Jehovah." Judges 18:5-6.* He who says these words of the Priest *are the words of God, and indeed brought forth through the Teraphim*, adds something to the scripture; which I, for my part, do not dare to do.

XVIII. And truly, this was not the place where God had made His name to dwell, or where He wished to be approached and consulted. If the *Danites* had acted seriously in this—that they would not undertake this expedition unless God were brought into counsel—they should have approached the *High Priest of the family of Aaron at Shiloh* <note>original: "Silunte"; the site of the Tabernacle before the Temple was built</note>, who might present himself before God on their behalf with the *Urim and Thummim* <note>sacred lots used by the High Priest to determine God's will</note>. But now, since they performed these sacred rites by the wayside, and showed sufficiently that they were already certain of their destination; it is no wonder if, snatching up the "good words" of some storyteller <note>term: "aretalogi" - originally a teller of god's miracles, here used disparagingly for a braggart or religious charlatan</note> as if they were oracles of the divinity for favorable omens, they took courage for themselves from there.

XIX. Nor should it seem foreign to the character of our *Levite* that, by simulating the name of *Jehovah*, he would prophesy those things to the *Danites* which he knew would be pleasing. So are they accustomed to do who chase the popular breeze and sail toward their own advantages. ### That the Urim are nothing less than the Teraphim.

I. The Urim were commanded instruments of religion, while the Teraphim were forbidden.
II. Nevertheless, *Spencer* <note>John Spencer (1630–1693), a scholar who argued that Jewish rituals originated from Egyptian customs</note> contends that in Hosea 3:4, the latter stands in place of the former.

# BOOK II. CHAPTER XII.

*...history mentions neither. XXI. Teraphim is not the same as Seraphim. XXII. Conclusion.*

I. It now remains for us to prove, thirdly, that the *Urim* <note>The "Urim and Thummim" were sacred objects used by the High Priest to determine God's will.</note> was nothing less than a small image of the same shape and use as the *Teraphim* <note>Household idols or oracular figurines often condemned in the Bible.</note>. The determination of this controversy depends on what has come before. For if the *Urim* were a great and most sacred part of the High Priest's equipment, as is well established, while the *Teraphim* were profane, superstitious, and idolatrous images hated by God, as we have just proven; it follows that the *Urim* are not the *Teraphim*. But let us hear the reasons by which *Spencer* <note>John Spencer (1630–1693), a scholar who controversially argued that many Jewish rites originated from Egyptian customs.</note> comes to assert such an insane and great *paradox* <note>original: "παράδοξον"</note>.

II. And in the first place, he reasons from *Hosea 3:4* in roughly this manner. He bids us observe that by the name of the *Ephod* <note>A ceremonial vestment worn by the High Priest.</note>, one should not understand the common garment of a priest, but the much more restricted garment of the *High Priest*. Then, he argues there was a great connection between the *Ephod* and the *breastplate*, in which the *Urim* was enclosed, so much so that in the sacred scriptures the *breastplate* is more than once understood by the name of the *Ephod*. Furthermore, since the *Ephod* and *Teraphim* are presented here joined together and to be read as if in one breath, what is more fitting than that we interpret the *Teraphim* as the *Urim*, which is connected to the *Ephod* by such a holy bond? Especially since the Greek Elders <note>The translators of the Septuagint, the ancient Greek version of the Old Testament.</note> use the word *manifestations* <note>original: "δήλων" (delon)</note> here for the word *Teraphim*, and God could not count it among the misfortunes that the Israelite people would be without idols.

III. However, to one considering everything rightly and without prejudice, it will seem more solid and preferable to explain the *Teraphim* here—as elsewhere in the sacred scriptures—as *instruments of idolatry*; if not of the crudest kind, then certainly of a more subtle and wicked superstition. Truly, the word of the Lord leads us there, explaining what would happen to Israel first in figurative words, then in his own. *And I said to her, for many days you shall sit for me, you shall remain unmarried, until the convenient time comes for taking you back to me as a wife. You shall not play the harlot, you shall not defile yourself with the idolatry of the nations, as in the past:* <insert>and you shall not be for a man</insert> <note>original Hebrew: "ולא תהיי לאיש"</note>. *Pagninus* <note>Santes Pagnino, a Dominican philologist and Bible translator.</note> with others translates, *you shall not belong to another man*. But, says *Rivetus* <note>André Rivet, a French Huguenot theologian.</note>, it is better read absolutely, *you shall not be for a man*, to signify a state of widowhood. *To be for a man* is *to marry*. *Ezekiel 16:8:* <insert>and you became mine</insert> <note>original Hebrew: "ותהי לי"</note>, *that is, you married me.*

He therefore foretells for her a long period of widowhood, during which she would be pure from prostitution and yet lack the use of a lawful marriage bed, deprived of all intercourse with a man, whether licit or illicit; this was so that she might learn continence in the meantime. However, he adds another point for her consolation. For he who commands a woman to wait for him, and to sit meanwhile as if a widow, seems in turn to bind himself by new vows, with a promise of waiting until the time destined for her reclaiming has passed. IV. God further interprets this parabolic speech with a clearer and more literal explanation. In place of what he had said—*you shall not be for a man*—he says: *For the children of Israel shall sit for many days without a King and without a Prince, and without sacrifice, and without an Ephod.* <note>The Ephod was a priestly garment used for seeking divine oracles; its absence signifies a loss of direct communication with God.</note> They shall lack Governance, Religion, and Prophecy, in which they once held, both individually and collectively, certain pledges of my covenant with them. BOOK II. CHAPTER XII.

There was nothing else there but a certain rough stone, found there by chance. This stone **Jacob** <note>original: *Jacobus*</note> set up in memory of the Divine revelation which had happened to him in that place; with a vow that this stone would be for him the **House of God** <note>original: *Domum Dei*</note> (verse 22). That is to say, he would perform the worship of God there as soon as he was provided with those things which could be offered to God, of all of which he was then destitute. As he later, being admonished by God, fulfilled his pledge (Genesis 35:1 and following).

VI. It does not seem doubtful to me that the Patriarch did these things rightly and in order; since he erected this **Monument** <note>original: *Titulum*</note> for the memory of a remarkable event (which was also done at other times by the command of God, see Exodus 24:4, Joshua 4:5, 24:26); not so that he might worship it, or pursue it with any religious devotion. Nor was the worship performed there by **Jacob** unpleasing to God, as He testified in express words when He said: *I am the God of Bethel, where you anointed the stone* (Genesis 31:13).

VII. Nevertheless, that stone seems to have been a "stumbling block" to the neighboring Canaanites. For the Phoenicians, imitating **Jacob's** deed with a certain wicked zeal <note>original: *kakozēlia* (Greek: κακοζηλίᾳ)</note>, first worshipped that very stone which the Patriarch had anointed. At least the Jews report it thus: <note>original Hebrew: אף על פי שהייתה מצבה אהובה לפני המקום בימי האבות אחרי כן שנאה מפני שעשוה כנענין לחוק לעבודה</note> *Although that pillar was beloved by God in the times of the Patriarchs, afterward He hated it, because the Canaanites turned it into a rite of Idolatry.* Indeed, they anointed and consecrated other stones with the same ritual, which they named *Baetylia* and *Baetylos* in memory of the stone of *Bethel* (which the Greeks write as *Baithel* <note>original: βαιθήλ</note>) that had been erected. **Sanchuniathon** <note>An ancient Phoenician author</note> called them "animated stones" <note>original Greek: λίθους ἐμψύχους (*lithous empsychous*)</note> according to the version of **Philo of Byblos**, saying they were fashioned by the god **Uranus**. Paganism certainly believed this; perhaps with the Devil moving them and mocking the credulity of the common people with his delusions. <margin>In Photius, page 1062.</margin> **Damascius**, a highly superstitious Pagan writer in the age of **Justinian**, says: *I saw the Baetylus stone moving through the air.* In the same place, **Isidorus the Philosopher** says, *there is some demon by which it is moved.* Whoever desires more on these matters may consult **Scaliger** on Eusebius, **Vossius** on Idolatry, and **Bochart's** *Canaan*.

VIII. Since God wished His people to be as far removed as possible from this superstition, He commanded the pillars of the heathens to be overturned (Exodus 23:24, 34).

*If ever I beheld ribbons decorated with pictures on ancient trees, or a stone lubricated and stained with olive oil, I would flatter it as if a present power dwelt within, I would speak to it and ask for favors from the unfeeling trunk.* From all of this, unless I am mistaken, it is as clear as the rays of the sun when the sky is most bright, that even around the final times of the Jewish kingdom, and indeed long after them, the "idol-madness" <note>original: εἰδωλομανεία</note> of the Gentiles concerning titles, markers, columns, statues, or by whatever name one wishes to express the word *Matzeba* <note>Hebrew: מצבה, a standing stone or pillar</note>, was still flourishing. If this was the reason for the prohibition given to the Israelites regarding the making of such markers, it is only right that the prohibition remained as long as the cause remained.

XIII. Furthermore, the most illustrious *Spencer* <note>John Spencer, 1630–1693, a scholar who argued that many Jewish rites originated in Egypt</note> is not slightly deluded in his belief that in the final times of the kingdom, the Jews considered the use of statues consecrated to God to be lawful; for at no time did they abhor statues more. And that which was once an altar and an image in Egypt, or a *Matzeba*, they cursed as a pure plague upon religion. This fact is too well known for me to wish to waste words in vain.

XIV. Nor does reason fail him any less in his contention that *Maimonides* <note>The preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher</note> restricts the Law concerning statues only to those dedicated to some fictitious deity; since in express words it is otherwise...

# BOOK II. CHAPTER XII.

<margin>On Idolatry, chapter VI. section VIII.</margin>
Maimonides explains the intent of the Law. Let us hear him from the translation of Dionysius Vossius <note>Dionysius Vossius (1612–1633) was a Dutch scholar known for translating Maimonides' work on idolatry into Latin.</note>, to which Spencer <note>John Spencer (1630–1693), an English theologian who argued that many Jewish rituals originated from Egyptian customs.</note> appeals. Thus says that Master of the Hebrews: *A structure is considered a "pillar" prohibited by the law if it is one where everyone gathers together, even if it is done to serve the true God. For such is the manner of idol worship. Moreover, it is said in Deuteronomy 16:22: "Neither shalt thou set thee up any pillar." Whoever, therefore, sets one up, shall be flogged. Similarly, whoever bows down upon a figured stone <note>original: "lapide figurato," likely referring to the "maskit" stone mentioned in Leviticus</note>, of which the Law speaks, even if he does this to the true God, he shall be flogged. Because it is said: "Neither shall ye put any figured stone in your land, to bow down upon it." Leviticus 26:1. For it was the custom in the worship of idols that a stone was placed upon which they would prostrate themselves. And for that reason, it is a sin to do this in the worship of the true God.* Could anything be more clearly stated?

XV. And just as Spencer poorly understood the mind of Maimonides, so too he did not read the notes of Dionysius Vossius attentively enough. Vossius does not distinguish between pillars dedicated to the true God and those consecrated to false deities—as if teaching that the former were permitted and only the latter forbidden according to Maimonides—but rather between those that are **superstitious** and those that are **memorial**. The words are plain and not subject to any twisting: *This is the opinion of our writer: not that any pillars whatsoever are forbidden, but only superstitious ones; likewise, those which are placed in memory of some event are not forbidden.* Such was the pillar of Jacob in Genesis 28:22 and again in 31:52. Therefore, these words, *“thou shalt not set thee up any pillar, which the Lord thy God hateth,”* the Jews explain as referring to a *pillar established for superstition, not one placed for memory.* Excellent. But what is Spencer aiming at or measuring here?

XVI. From this observation by Dionysius Vossius, light shines upon the prophecy of Isaiah. This is certainly not to be explained as some material pillar to be placed in Egypt in honor of the true Deity, but as something spiritual and mystical, which can be represented by a pillar—and certainly a permitted one. Since, therefore, a pillar, or some monument, or a heap of stones erected in memory of the illustrious deeds of God was permitted, and sometimes even pious by God's command, it is consistent that we judge it to be an allusion to such a thing. With this intent, God promises that He will establish faith in the unique sacrifice of the Messiah and the spiritual worship of the Gospel (signified by the Altar) in Egypt; and in the propagation of saving doctrine, the conversion of the elect, and the sancti-

# ON EGYPTIAN MATTERS

...regarding the purification, consolation, protection, and growth of the Church, and the vengeance upon its enemies, God would produce such illustrious examples—destined to endure through the eternity of time by the fame of these deeds—that He might be seen to have established a memorial for Himself, like a monument <note>original: "cippi instar"</note>, within the borders of the Egyptians. I am not unaware of the more subtle commentaries others have written; however, the points we have made seem plain and clear. Since, therefore, the *sacred pillar* <note>original Hebrew: מצבה (matzevah); a standing stone often used for cultic purposes</note> is an instrument of forbidden worship, just like the *Teraphim* <note>household idols or cult images</note>, *Hosea* represents that state of Israel in which they were to be deprived of the exercise of religion—both that which was once commanded and that which was always forbidden. This, moreover, was what we had undertaken to prove.

XVII. But, you will say, how can God count it *among evils* that the Israelite people would be deprived of idols? To those who like to quibble in this way, let them, if they please, ask God what evil there is in His threat that the *calf of Bethel* would be carried away by *Shalmaneser*. *Hosea 10:5-6: The inhabitants of Samaria shall fear because of the calves of Beth-aven; for its people shall mourn over it, as well as its priests who rejoiced over it, because its glory has departed from it. It shall also be carried into Assyria as a present for King Jareb.* Truly, not everything that is taken away by God as a punishment for a crime is good and lawful in itself; it is enough that it seems good and is pleasing to the one who is deprived of it, and that they feel a loss from the removal of that thing. Nor is this, as *Spencer* <note>John Spencer (1630–1693), a scholar who argued that many Jewish rites originated from Egyptian customs</note> likes to mock, merely imposing a "fantastic" or imaginary punishment for a real evil. For it is no *imaginary* punishment to be brought to such a state that, along with the state, that which you held as your religion perishes at the same time; and that your enemies triumph not only over your goods and yourself, but also over your gods. In this, you may recognize the custom of ancient leaders. *Thus, when Babylon was captured, the idols of the Babylonians, Bel and Nebo, went into captivity. Isaiah 46:1-2. Likewise, when Moab was cut off by the Chaldeans, Jeremiah prophesied that Chemosh, the god of the Moabites, would go into exile, Jeremiah 48:7. And you may see the same predicted concerning Malcam, the god of the Ammonites, Jeremiah 49:3; Amos 1:15.* Following this same example, *Ptolemy Euergetes*, having defeated *Seleucus Callinicus and the Syrians*, led their gods captive into Egypt. *Daniel 11:8.* This very practice was also frequently employed by the Romans. Please see the learned collection on this matter by the great <note>original Greek: ὁ πάνυ (ho pany) - "the great" or "the famous"</note> *Bochart* <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a French Protestant biblical scholar</note>, in his *Hierozoicon, Part 1, Book 2, Chapter 34.*
