### BOOK II. CHAPTER XII.

XVIII. Furthermore, this is not the only response by which we are able to meet that minor objection. We add this: it is by no means necessary that we refer the prediction concerning the lack of a sacred pillar <note>original: "statua"</note> and **Theraphim** <note>Household idols or cult objects often associated with divination in the Old Testament</note> to a **threat** or curse. For indeed, those things contained in this prophecy are of a mixed kind; partly good, partly bad. Surely God portends nothing evil for Israel when He says, *you shall not play the harlot*. Moreover, this prediction corresponds to that: *you shall sit without a sacred pillar and Theraphim*. This much good shall be present in your miserable condition: that you will keep yourself pure from gross idolatry and the superstition of your ancestors.

XIX. As for the remaining minor observations of *Spencer* <note>Referring to John Spencer (1630–1693), a scholar who controversially argued that many Jewish rites originated from Egyptian customs</note>, if one may use his own words, they are *lighter than a feather or a helmet of chaff* <note>original: "pluma & palearum cassis leviores" — a Latin idiom for something trivial or without weight</note>. From these observations, if you conclude anything at all, it is certainly nothing more than that superstitious apostates substituted **Theraphim** for the most Divine sacrament of the **Urim** <note>The "Urim and Thummim" were sacred lots used by the High Priest to determine God's will</note>; so that when they were deprived of that thing through which God poured forth oracles, they might have some substitute in which wicked spirits might involve themselves for deception and fraud. Nor do we deny that just as in the true worship of God, the **priesthood**, the **Altar**, the **Ephod** <note>A ceremonial vestment worn by the High Priest</note>, and the **Urim**—and these indeed most especially—were joined by a certain bond of religion, so too in that worship which counterfeited the true, being composed in some measure after its likeness, there was a certain necessity between the idolatrous **Ephod** and the cursed **Theraphim**. Since idolaters believed these objects provided for them what the **Urim** once did for the Israelites, it is for the sake of this imitation <note>original: "μίμησιν" (mimesis)</note> that they were able to be expressed here by the Septuagint <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> with the word *manifestations* <note>original: "δήλων" (delon)</note>, and by *Aquila* and *Theodotio* <note>Translators of the Hebrew Bible into Greek in the 2nd century AD</note> with the word *illuminations* <note>original: "φωτισμῶν" (photismon)</note>. However, it matters little to us to inquire what moved those translators to interpret the name **Theraphim** in this place differently than they usually do. Certainly, not even all of *Spencer's* ridiculous arguments could extort from the prophecy of *Hosea* the idea that God understood His own **Urim** by the term **Theraphim**.

<margin>Judges 8:27</margin>
XX. There is even less support in the History of *Gideon*. There, mention is made of an **Ephod**, but none of the **Urim**, nor of the **Theraphim**. We do indeed confess it to be very probable that not only was some priestly garment made by Gideon; for how else could one thousand seven hundred shekels of gold—that is, according to the calculation of a Learned Man, *more or less seventy pounds of gold*—have been spent on a single garment? It is therefore credible that other things were added to that sacred apparatus, by which *Gideon* intended to celebrate the memory of the Divine favor.

# OF EGYPTIAN MATTERS

However, since whatever that object might have been, it is called neither *Urim* nor *Teraphim* <note>original: "Theraphim"; these were household idols or cult images mentioned in the Old Testament</note>; and since we, due to the silence of the Scripture, are forced to remain eternally ignorant of it, by what kind of argument can it be gathered from that narrative that the *Teraphim* and the *Urim* were of the same form and use?

XXI. As for the observations *Spencer* <note>John Spencer (1630–1693), a scholar who argued that Jewish rites had Egyptian origins</note> makes elsewhere regarding the agreement of *meaning* in the words *Urim* and *Teraphim*—for *Urim* denotes *inflammations* or *illuminations*, while *Teraphim*, according to the Chaldean dialect, stands for *Seraphim* (which is an ancient name for Angels), meaning *burning* or *inflaming* ones—while these remarks should not be deprived of the praise due to erudition, they cannot hold the place of convincing reason. For an argument from etymology <note>the study of the origin of words</note> is quite weak, especially if it is uncertain and much debated among the learned. Such is the derivation of *Teraphim* which *Spencer* commends here above others. We have provided another from *Louis de Dieu* <note>a Dutch Protestant theologian and orientalist</note>, which seems no less probable. And truly, if statues were built in ancient times as a symbol to celebrate the memory of angels or to signify their presence, and were therefore called *Teraphim* because it is the same as *Seraphim* (the name by which the *flaming* angels are noted): what reason can be given why we never find those images called *Seraphim*, and never find Angels called *Teraphim*? *Teraphim* is of Chaldean origin. However, the Chaldean *Teraph* <note>original Hebrew/Chaldean: תרף</note> and the Hebrew *Seraph* <note>original Hebrew: שרף</note> have no agreement in meaning. And those Angels who are called *Seraphim* by the Hebrews, I have seen proved by no example that they are called *Teraphim* by the Chaldeans, let alone by the Hebrews. Since, therefore, the Scripture always so carefully distinguishes each word and never alternates them as if they had the same meaning, I certainly would not dare to treat them as synonyms of the same origin or as one and the same thing.

XXII. And so I believe I have demonstrated that it is not without a notable injury to religion and piety that these follies and reproaches of the Egyptians—and, as the Scripture calls them, *shameful things* <note>original Hebrew: בוש (bosh), referring to idols or things that cause shame</note>—can be compared with the most sacred institutions of God.

### Concerning the Cherubim.

I. # EGYPTIAN STUDIES

<margin>
Compare Book I, Chapter IX, Section I.
</margin>

I. Regarding what we previously discussed concerning the *Attendant Spirits* of the deity *Hemptai*—of whom one had the form of a *Boy*, the second a *Dog-like* face, the third a *Hawk-like* countenance, and the fourth a *Lion-like* appearance—and the comparison of these with the *Cherubim* whom God willed to attend the throne of His glory upon the *Ark*; those ideas savor more of a playful wit than of anything worthy of serious consideration. For the *Hempta* of the *Egyptians* has nothing in common with the *God* <note>original: אמת "Emet"</note> *Truth*, whom the descendants of *Eber* <note>The biblical ancestor of the Hebrews.</note> piously worshipped, except for a certain similarity in the sound of the letters. And who can say at what time the worship of a deity by that name began among the *Egyptians*? Furthermore, the *Cherubim* placed upon the mercy seat of the *Ark* were not equal in number to those *Hemptaic* spirits, as there were only two of them; nor were they equal in form. Although the true appearance of the *Cherubim* remains uncertain and unknown to us, everyone knows they possessed neither a dog-like nor a hawk-like face. Nevertheless, since we have now fallen upon this subject—which, if any, deserves an accurate commentary—I do not think it should be held against us if we wander somewhat more freely in such a flowery meadow, and communicate those little flowers we have been able to gather <note>original: ἀφθόνως "aphthonos"</note> abundantly with our *Readers*.

II. Concerning the appearance of the *Cherubim*, many have offered many opinions by way of conjecture; but I do not remember finding anyone who supported his opinions with suitable arguments. Let us see how far we are able to progress through the meditation and comparison of the *Scriptures*, so that it may appear what is certain, what is probable, and finally where one must stop with a confession of not-unpraiseworthy ignorance.

III. The first mention of the *Cherubim* is in the history of the expulsion of our first parents from *Paradise*. Genesis 3:24: He placed at the East of the garden of *Eden Cherubim*, and a flaming sword turning every way, to guard the way that led to the tree of life. It is admitted by all that *Angels* are designated there by the term *Cherubim*; but in what form they appeared, or if they had any form at all, and likewise for what reason that name is attributed to *Angels*, *Moses* does not say. Therefore, to judge anything regarding their form belongs to diviners, which we do not dare to do. However, it is not improbable that some form was seen, because of what is added concerning the vibrating blade of the burning sword. Although, what that might have—

### BOOK II. CHAPTER XIII.

...remains in obscurity. Many suspect it was the appearance of a sword in a visible form, wielded by Angels stationed at the entrance of the garden. We read that they often appeared in this form when sent to execute the judgments of God: to **Balaam** <note>Numbers 22:22-23</note>, to **Joshua** <note>Joshua 5:13</note>, and to **David** <note>1 Chronicles 21:16</note>. **Grotius** <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a famous Dutch legal scholar and theologian</note> understands the "flaming sword" to mean perpetual fires and caverns overflowing with bitumen and sulfur, such as writers describe in the plains of Babylonia. Finally, others decree that this expression should be understood figuratively as the "fiery law of God" by which God prohibited man from entering Paradise, with angels added as the guardians and avengers of that law. They bid us compare this to Deuteronomy 33:2: *The Lord came from Sinai, from among his holy myriads, from whose right hand a fiery law went forth to them.* <note>original Latin: "Jehova ex Sinai venit... a cujus dextra ignis legis ipfis exftitit"</note> None of this is improbable, nor is it ignorant; yet all of it remains uncertain.

IV. But the reasoning behind the name <note>Cherubim</note> does not seem so obscure that a probable origin cannot be sought elsewhere. I believe everyone will easily grant me that it is not far from the truth that **Moses** wrote the history of *Genesis* along with his other books in the desert, after he had been commanded to make the Tabernacle with all its sacred equipment. This happened shortly after the law was given at Sinai. A certain part of that equipment consisted of those symbolic images to which the name of *Cherubim* was given; God intended these to be emblems of the heavenly spirits. Hence it seems to have happened that **Moses**, when making the first mention of those spirits, deemed it wise to designate them by this emblematic name; he was not looking at the appearance of the emblem itself, but at the reality signified by the emblem. We have a similar example in Psalm 18:11 and 2 Samuel 22:11: *And he rode upon a Cherub* <note>original Hebrew: וירכב על כרוב</note> *and flew upon the wings of the wind.* In this passage, one should not think of a specific appearance or shape, but simply of angels offering their obedience to God.

V. Furthermore, concerning the emblematic figure—such as it was on the "mercy seat" <term>propitiatory: the gold cover of the Ark of the Covenant</term> of the Ark—**Moses** relates two things in Exodus 25:18-20. First, that they had wings spread upwards, and that they covered the mercy seat with their wings; second, that they had faces turned toward one another, and also turned toward the mercy seat. From this it can be certainly concluded that they were winged living creatures; but as to what species they were, how many wings or faces they possessed, and what the form of the rest of the body was, there is a deep silence in the writings of **Moses**. Whether because that matter [was well known in those] times...

whether the [form] was sufficiently known to the Israelites; or whether some other more sublime and secret cause lies beneath it. This much is clear: Moses did not make the Cherubim according to the model of images he had formerly seen in Egypt, but according to the pattern shown to him on the holy mountain <note>Mount Sinai, where Moses received the divine blueprints for the Tabernacle</note>.

VI. Those **Cherubim** which **Solomon** fashioned in the Sanctuary of his Temple did not have exactly the same form, or certainly not the same placement of parts. For the **Mosaic** [Cherubim], as we have seen, had their faces turned toward each other and toward the mercy seat <note>The gold lid of the Ark of the Covenant</note>; and with their wings spread out, the wing of one touched the spread wing of the other on both sides; just as if two men were looking at each other and holding hands. This positioning of wings is contrary to the nature of all birds. The **Solomonic** ones, however, were not facing each other, but were side-by-side, with their faces turned not toward one another, but toward the east, so that each had the west at his back. And they spread their wings from their sides across the entire width of the Holy of Holies; so that one **Cherub** touched the southern wall with the tip of his right wing, while the other touched the northern wall with the tip of his left wing, and they touched each other with the two middle wings. This positioning of wings comes closer to nature. *1 Kings 6:27.* Thus far, nothing certain can be gathered, except that the **Cherubim** were statues with huge and outspread wings.

VII. **Ezekiel** leads us a little further; in depicting the **Cherubim** of his Temple, he distinctly sets forth how many and what kind of faces they had: *namely two, one Human and the other Leonine <note>Lion-like</note>. Ezekiel 41:18-19 <note>original: "Ezech. XLI. 20. 21." - the author's citation differs slightly from modern numbering</note>. And it was crafted with Cherubim and Palm trees. A palm tree was between two Cherubim; and each Cherub had two faces. Specifically, a Human face toward one palm tree on this side, and the face of a young Lion toward the other palm tree on that side.* However, because only two faces are recounted for each **Cherub**, it cannot be certainly inferred that there were not more elsewhere. For the learned observe that the **Cherubim** are described here as they appeared to the sight of onlookers when carved on a flat wall; by which circumstance it could happen that two other faces were cut off by the flat surface of the wall itself. This was only a "half-sculpture" <term>bas-relief: a carving where figures project slightly from a flat background</term>, in which many non-protruding parts must necessarily be hidden: parts which are seen distinctly in a separate statue that is exposed to view from all sides.

VIII. Occasion for this observation was given by the monstrous animals

# BOOK II. CHAPTER XIII.

...four living creatures, seen by the same Ezekiel; each of which had four faces, as many wings, straight feet, a sole similar to the sole of a calf's foot, and the appearance of human hands under the wings. These four faces were: *Human* on the front side, *Lion-like* on the right, *Ox-like* on the left, and *Eagle-like* on the rear side. The position of the *Wings* was different from both the *Mosaic* <note>Referring to the Tabernacle described by Moses</note> and the *Solomonic* <note>Referring to the Temple built by Solomon</note> designs: for they did not have them stretched forward like the Mosaic ones, nor expanded to the sides like the Solomonic ones; but some were extended upward, and others were drawn in to cover the body. Ezekiel 1:5 & following. There also appeared the *form of a man's hand under their wings*. Ezekiel 10:8. Furthermore, he emphasizes that these living creatures were Cherubim by frequently repeating the name in chapter 10, especially in verse 20:
> *This is the living creature that I had seen under the God of Israel at the river Chebar, and* I KNEW THAT THEY WERE CHERUBIM.

IX. But the matter is not settled even by this. For interpreters do not yet agree on the concept of this species. Hieronymus Prado, Pererius, Grotius, and others, do not understand the four <term>panim (פנים)<note>Hebrew for "faces" or "surfaces"</note></term> as countenances or faces, but as forms, figures, likenesses, or insignia. Just as the Hebrews call the appearance of the air, sky, and earth their "face." Therefore, according to them, there was in those living creatures a *Cherub face*, that is, the *form of a Man* in the countenance and the whole body; the *form of a Calf in the feet*, because they had a cloven hoof such as calves have; the *form of a Lion in the chest, neck, and shoulders*, because in these parts there were manes like those of *Lions*; and the *form of an Eagle*, namely the wings, on the shoulder. Imagine for yourself a *Man*, add to him on the neck and chest the manes of a *Lion*, add to the shoulders the wings of an *Eagle*, add the feet of an *Ox*; and you will have, according to *Prado*, the likeness of a *Cherub* such as Ezekiel saw, and such as were in the *Tabernacle* and *Temple*.

X. Others, however, give to each Cherub four faces or countenances, and consequently as many heads, or rather half-heads: so that the front part had the head and face of a man, as if primary and more eminent; to which on the right was inserted or annexed the face and head of a lion; on the left, the face and head of a calf; and from the back part—or, as those who follow the Vulgate version prefer, from above—the face and head of an Eagle. Thus, through these four heads, four animals were joined together into one body and head, as it were.

...truth very closely. For when the Prophet speaks of the Iris <note>the rainbow</note>, Amber <note>original: "Electro"</note>, the Firmament, and similar things which properly do not possess a face, he does indeed attribute to them *mar’eh* <note>Hebrew: מראה</note> *vision* or *appearance*, and *demut* <note>Hebrew: דמות</note> *likeness*, but not likewise *panim* <note>Hebrew: פנים</note> *face*. This serves as an argument that he is using this word now in a stricter sense. And indeed, he depicts the faces of his living creatures in such a way that he teaches clearly enough that by them he understands not *manes*, nor *wings*, nor *hooves*, but *countenances*; since he asserts that the face of the *Ox* was on the left, and the face of the *Lion* was on the right. For this cannot be said of manes and hooves, which a *Lion* and a *Calf* have on the right as well as on the left. Added to this is the fact that he openly distinguishes the wings, feet, and hands from the faces by a distinct description.

XII. But truly, of whatever figure these monstrous living creatures were; it does not follow from the fact that Ezekiel calls them *Cherubim* that the Cherubim placed upon the Ark and painted or fashioned in the Tabernacle and Temple had the same appearance. Nor was it Ezekiel's intention to teach the form of the Mosaic Cherubim, when he testifies that he finally recognized that the living creatures he had seen were *Cherubim* (Chapter 10:20). Indeed, one might rather conclude the opposite from this. For what would have prevented him from recognizing the form of the *Cherubim* immediately in the first vision—a form so noble, so notable, and finally so well-known at that time, which every Jew (at least the priests, such as *Ezekiel* was) saw daily on the walls and gates of the temple? Was it then so unrecognizable that a repeated vision was needed to produce the idea of it in the Prophet's mind? Could he, who so accurately delineated the faces, wings, and feet after the first sight, not have compared living creatures of such unusual appearance with the form he had observed a thousand times with his own eyes in the temple? What then? Ezekiel is not discussing the *figure* when he relates that he recognized them as *Cherubim*; but rather the reality signified through that *Hieroglyphic* <note>The author uses "hieroglyphic" here in the broad 17th-century sense of a sacred, symbolic image or emblem</note> symbol. That is to say, he perceived that those wonderful living creatures—whose purpose in their prodigious appearance he had not yet fully grasped—he now perceived, I say, that they were *emblems* of the heavenly *Angels*; and that the same thing was signified by them as by the sacred *Cherubim* of the temple. However, it is not necessary that things which are symbols of the same reality must also agree with each other in exact likeness.

# BOOK II. CHAPTER XIII.

XIII. Nevertheless, it seems that something can indeed be learned from this prophecy of *Ezekiel* regarding the form of the *Cherubim* dedicated in the holy temple of God. This is especially true if we pay attention to chapter 10, verse 14: *Each one had four faces: the first face was the face of a* CHERUB; *the second face was the face of a Man; the third the face of a Lion, and the fourth the face of an Eagle.* It is clear that the Prophet, under the name of "faces," is describing some external and visible form here. Therefore, it is impossible for us to interpret the name *Cherub* here as referring to an Angel <note>The author argues that "Cherub" must refer to a specific physical shape rather than a spiritual being in this context</note>, since it is necessary to understand it as a likeness that meets the eyes, just like the likeness of a *Man, a Lion,* or an *Eagle*. But what is that specific likeness of a *Cherub*? *Ezekiel* leaves us in no doubt; in chapter 1, verse 10, when enumerating the same faces of the same living creature, he records the face of an Ox in place of the face of a CHERUB. Furthermore, what reason can be imagined—even in one's dreams—why he would designate an *Ox* by the name of *Cherub*, unless it was well-established among the Israelites that the *Cherubim* primarily displayed the form of an ox?

XIV. The etymology of the word supports this: for the root *KRB* <note>original Hebrew: כרב</note>, from which the name *Cherubim* is derived, signifies *to plow* among the Chaldeans, Syrians, and Arabs; and oxen are the animals most especially used for this task. *Cherub*, therefore, denotes a <term>Plowing Ox</term> <note>original Greek: Βῦν Ἀροτῆρα</note>. To this is added the reasoning that God is several times said to sit upon a *Cherub* or be carried by a *Cherub*, and that *Angels* are frequently called the *vehicle of God*, as in Psalm 68:18: *The chariots of God* <note>original Hebrew: רכב אלהים</note>. And in Zechariah 6:1 and following, where the four *chariots* <note>original Hebrew: מרכבות</note> *are the four Spirits of God sent out into all the earth.* And indeed, in this very vision of *Ezekiel*, they are joined with wheels. Anyone can see that all these things suit a *beast of burden*—for instance, an *Ox*—better than any other form. Led by this argument, I easily agree with those most learned men who contend that the *Cherubim* displayed various animal forms in such a way that they most closely approached the form of an *Ox*.

XV. And these are the things we have been able to gather concerning the figure of the *Cherubim* by comparing the testimonies of the sacred records. They were, without doubt, *unusual living creatures*, representing the appearance of an ox's body for the greatest part of themselves, equipped with large wings (it is uncertain how many), and at least two faces: *Lion-like* and *Human*. I believe we must stop here. For who, while the Scripture remains silent, could describe the rest? For the things which more recent teachers have handed down are vague, uncertain, and some even false, smelling of the foul temperament of the [later] Jews <note>A common period expression reflecting the author's bias against post-biblical Rabbinic traditions</note>.

...finally, such things upon which you cannot safely plant your foot <note>The author is critiquing unstable or speculative theories about the appearance of these beings</note>. *Josephus* paid tribute to a prudent modesty, finishing his description of them thus: *winged living creatures, similar in form to none of those seen by men*, which *Moses* had seen represented on the throne of God <note>original Greek: ζῶα πετεινὰ, μορφῇ οὐδενὶ τῶν ὑπὸ ἀνθρώπων ἑωραμένων παραπλήσια</note>. The descriptions of *Moses* sketching his Tabernacle and *Ezekiel* sketching his Temple spontaneously suggest that same idea to us.

XVI. Akin to the Cherubim of *Ezekiel* are those living creatures which *John* saw between the throne of God and those surrounding the throne. There were four of them in number, full of eyes in front and behind. *And the first living creature was like a Lion, and the second living creature like a Calf, and the third living creature having a face like a Man, and the fourth living creature like a flying Eagle. And the four living creatures each had six wings around them, and within they were full of eyes.* Revelation 4:6, 7, 8.

XVII. *Joseph Mede* in his *Apocalyptic Key*, and other learned men with him, think that in this vision of *John* there is an allusion to the camps of the Israelites in the desert, which were divided under four banners <term>vexilla: military standards or flags used to identify tribal divisions</term>, each having its own signs. Indeed, *Moses* himself mentions this in Numbers 2. The Hebrew Masters add that the animals shown here to *John* were painted on the banners. On the banner of *Judah*, a *Lion*; on the banner of *Ephraim*, an *Ox*; on *Reuben's* banner, a *Man*; on *Dan's*, an *Eagle*. It is worth the effort to hear from *Aben-Ezra's* commentaries on the aforementioned passage of *Moses* what reasoning and arguments they hold for this matter. He says: *Our predecessors said there was on the banner of Reuben the form of a Man, according to the symbolic power of the Mandrakes* <note>original Hebrew: וקדמנינו אמרו שהיה בדגל ראובן צורת אדם; referring to the mandrakes Reuben found in Genesis 30</note>; and on the banner of *Judah*, the *figure of a Lion*, because *Jacob* compared him to a Lion in Genesis 49:9. On the banner of *Ephraim*, the figure of an *Ox*, because it is said of *Joseph*, the father of *Ephraim*, in Deuteronomy 33:17: *The beauty of his firstborn Ox is his.* Finally, on *Dan's* banner, the figure of an *Eagle*, so that it might be similar to the Cherubim which the Prophet *Ezekiel* saw. *Chizkuni* and *Bar Nachman* hold similar views in their comments on Numbers 3.

XVIII. Nor can it be doubted that this observation is beautiful, provided the matter itself were certain and proven. # BOOK II. CHAPTER XIII.

*Bochart* and *Heidegger* <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667) and Johann Heinrich Heidegger (1633–1698) were prominent Protestant scholars of biblical natural history and theology.</note> argue that the claims made regarding animal symbols on the tribal banners are nothing but a foul invention of modern teachers. For since **Moses** mentions nothing of the sort, nor does the Scripture elsewhere, nor **Josephus** where he pursues the history of the **Jews** in a more liberal commentary, nor **Philo** in his *Books on the Life of Moses*—indeed, not even in the **Talmud** itself has this been detected by the most learned men—who then revealed such a great secret to these "new-wine" <note>Latin: *musteis*, implying fresh or inexperienced</note> interpreters born only yesterday or today, nearly three thousand years after these events took place?

XIX. As for those who drag into this debate a passage from *Psalm 68:10* <note>Verse 11 in the original Latin text's numbering</note>, <term>Your congregation dwelt therein</term> <note>original Hebrew: *Chayatecha yashevu vah*</note>, as if it refers to the wilderness in which **Israel** lived for several years—whom the **Psalmist** would supposedly call "God's animals" because of the four animals depicted on the banners—that argument is driven far from all reason. For that passage does not deal with the stay of **Israel** in the desert, but with their dwelling in their inheritance, that is, the land of **Canaan**. Furthermore, it is not necessary to translate <term>Chayatecha</term> as "your animals," since the word <term>Chayah</term> also signifies a "company" or "congregation," as seen in *1 Samuel 23:11, 13*, and that definition is exceedingly fitting in this context. And so almost all the **Hebrew** scholars understand it: **Rabbi Solomon** <note>Rashi</note>, **Aben Ezra**, **Kimchi**, **Pomarius**, and from our own crowd of interpreters, everyone except **Pagninus** and **Arias Montanus**. The construction of a plural verb with a singular collective noun also favors this. Finally, even if the **Israelites** were called the "Animal" or "Animals" of God, it does not follow from this that the prophet is alluding to the **Jews'** "beast-themed" banners. Since the **Church** is everywhere called the "Flock of the Lord" or "Sheep of the Lord," why should it not also be called the "Animals of the Lord," because it is animated by the Lord through the **Spirit**, without any reference to banners?

XX. Moreover, among the reasons brought forward for the figures on each individual banner, only the one concerning the symbol of **Judah** <note>The Lion of Judah</note> has any appearance of truth; the others are either non-existent or ridiculous. It is absurd to claim the **Ephraimites** had the figure of an **Ox** on their banner because of the final words of the dying **Moses** concerning **Joseph**. For these banners were raised in the second year after the Departure (*Numbers 1:10 & 2:2*), thirty-eight years before the death of **Moses**. It is much more absurd to attribute an **Eagle** to the **Danites** because of the vision of **Ezekiel**, which is both nine centuries later and says not a single word <note>Latin: *ne gry quidem*, literally "not even a grunt"</note> about the **Danites**, nor indeed about the other tribes. XXI. Finally, it is utterly inconsistent with any likeness of truth that *Moses* would have erected images not only of an *Ox*, but of other animals, for those very people whom God had recently punished so severely for worshipping the image of a *Bull* <note>The Golden Calf</note>, or that he would have voluntarily placed this stumbling block before a people so prone to idolatry. Added to this is the fact that when *Vitellius* <note>A Roman Governor of Syria</note> was about to move war against the Arabs and lead his army from *Ptolemais* through *Judea*, the leading Jewish men ran to him and pleaded against the passage through their region. They pleaded that their ancestral rites did not permit them to overlook images being brought into their territory, as there were many images attached to the standards; <note>original Greek: "Ὀυ γὰρ ἀυτοῖς εἶναι πάτριον περιορᾷν εἰκόνας εἰς ἀυλὴν Φερομἑνας, πολλὰς δ' εἶναι σημαίας ἐπικειμἑνας"</note> they argued that their laws did not allow the introduction of any images, which most Roman standards possessed. This pretext would surely have been vain and lying, nor would it have deceived the Romans, if the Jews themselves had possessed signs of animals on their own banners.

XXII. From all of this it is manifest that the vision of *John* <note>In the Book of Revelation</note> is not to be compared with the painted banners of the Israelites in the desert, since those are fictitious; rather, it should be compared with the apparitions made to *Ezekiel*, with which *John's* visions will be seen to have great agreement by those who examine them. There is a twofold observable difference here. First, that those things which were shown to *Ezekiel* under the appearance of a single four-faced Living Creature appeared to *John* as four distinct animals, each having one head, which was therefore more distinct, more perfect, and more visible.

XXIII. The commentary of *Grotius* <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a foundational Dutch jurist and theologian</note> is worth mentioning. *In the Tabernacle*, he says, *in the Temple of Solomon, and in the vision of Ezekiel, there are two equal figures composed of the forms of four animals; here, however, as the following things teach us, there are four distinct forms of animals.* Why is that? Because all things in the New Testament arise more distinctly than in the Old. Perhaps he meant *are known* <note>The author is correcting a possible typo in Grotius's Latin from "nascuntur" (are born) to "noscuntur" (are known)</note>: Ingenious and clever. Except that he seems to take more upon himself than is right in determining the species of the Cheru—

BOOK II. CHAPTER XIII.

Concerning the Cherubim of the *Tabernacle* and the *Temple*; whether they were endowed with the forms of four living creatures, as we have shown above, is not entirely clear. Regarding the fact that in the Vision of Ezekiel he posits only two figures, even though the text expressly counts four living creatures in Ezekiel 1:5, corresponding to four wheels, such that each single wheel was beside each one of the Cherubim (Ezekiel 10:9): Truly, if anyone wishes to be a scrupulous interpreter of the Scriptures, as is only right, where the text says, *The likeness of four living creatures*, he will not dare to offer as a gloss: *Of two Cherubim, who each had the parts of four living creatures*. And where the Holy Spirit says: *Four wheels beside the Cherubim: one wheel beside one Cherub, and one wheel beside another Cherub*, that is—as Vatablus <note>François Vatable (d. 1547), a renowned French humanist and Hebrew scholar.</note> well observed from the natural character of simple Hebrew idiom—as if He had said, *the individual wheels were beside the individual Cherubim*: there were as many wheels as there were Cherubim. One must not substitute a commentary based on a rashly conceived hypothesis: <term>Enallage</term> <note>A grammatical term for substituting one grammatical form for another; here used to argue the text says "four" but means "two".</note> is present: for he wishes to say, concerning the two wheels which were on the two sides, that each was so close to the Cherub of that side that it was touched by it. Furthermore, the reason he assigns for this diversity does not seem to be rejected. Cornelius a Lapide <note>A prominent Jesuit exegete (1567–1637) known for his encyclopedic biblical commentaries.</note> put forward things not unlike this. The cause, he says, why Ezekiel’s living creatures had four faces each, but John’s <note>Referring to the Book of Revelation (the Apocalypse).</note> had only one each, is because *the symbols of Divine matters, which in the Old Testament were convoluted, covered, and obscure, are exhibited in the New Testament as divided, distinct, plain, and explained*.

XXIV. But the most excellent Launaeus <note>Pierre de Launay (1573–1661), a Reformed theologian and biblical scholar.</note> organizes it differently; he thinks that John’s living creatures were no less four-formed than Ezekiel’s; however, John described only that single face of each which, turned toward him, appeared in full. The cause of this may perhaps be that John saw the living creatures standing in a circle around the throne, always keeping the same position; Ezekiel, however, saw them running out, returning, and moving themselves hither and thither, whence he could more easily discern their diverse faces. But this does not seem solid enough. For besides the fact that something is added to the Word of God when four faces are attributed to that living creature of which Scripture praises only one: it is not evident that John’s living creatures always kept the same position, since they were introducing him to the contemplation of the mysteries contained in the first four seals.

XXV. Another distinction lies in this: that the living creatures of *Ezekiel* were equipped with only four wings, whereas those of *John* had six—just like the *Seraphim of Isaiah (chapter 6:2)*, who also assigns a specific use for each pair of wings. *With two they covered their feet, in confession of their own weakness <note>original: ἀδενείας (weakness/frailty)</note> before God; with two they flew, being most swift in executing His commands.* The reason for this diversity in the number of wings seems to be sought in the location where the creatures were seen. Truly, *John and Isaiah* saw them as *surrounding the Throne of Glory*, and consequently needing wings to veil their faces—yet not so veiled that they could never be seen in any way. *Ezekiel*, however, perceived his creatures beneath the expanse, below the Throne, where that particular use of wings was not required. *Ezekiel 1:22, 23, 26.*
<margin>Prologue to the Hebrews, Exercise 22, § 17.</margin>
Unless you prefer the acute observation of the most learned *Owen* <note>John Owen (1616–1683), a prominent English theologian.</note>: that in *Isaiah’s* vision, Christ is represented (*John 12:41*) alongside the mystery of the calling of the Gentiles and the rejection of the Jews—a mystery which the Angels were once unable to look into or fully understand. In *Ezekiel*, however, is represented the counsel and will of God in the works of common Providence, which they contemplate with an uncovered face.

XXVI. Furthermore, this commentary of ours would be quite barren unless we strove for something deeper. It is not enough for a pious mind to have learned anything by scrutinizing the external form of the *Cherubim*, or the appearance of the "monstrous" <note>In the classical sense of "portentous" or "supernatural" rather than "evil."</note> creatures which God showed to His servants; it is not enough to know that these sacred emblems were not given to God's people in imitation of *Egyptian* superstitions. We must investigate further what Divine Wisdom wished to teach us through these hieroglyphics <note>The author uses "hieroglyphics" here to mean sacred symbols or encoded spiritual truths.</note>.

XXVII. Let us begin, therefore, with those *Cherubim* who overshadowed the Mercy Seat of the *Ark of the Covenant*. It seems there should be no doubt that through those images, whatever their form may have been, the holy *Angels* were signified. For we have proven above that they are called *Cherubim*. The Psalmist sings that *Sinai was in the Sanctuary (Psalm 68:17)*; that is, those things were symbolically shadowed in the *Sanctuary* which actually took place on Mount Sinai. There the Son of God appeared with the awesome signs of His present Majesty, surrounded by myriads of *Angels*, who stood around Him like an army drawn up in battle array when He proclaimed the sacred *song of the law* in the assembly of the Israelite people. *Deuteronomy 33.*

BOOK II. CHAPTER XIII.

<margin>Acts 7:53</margin> And here God sat among the *Cherubim*, placing his Throne upon the top of that Ark where the Tables of the Law were kept. By this arrangement, what else was signified but that the ministering *Angels* stand by *Christ*? These angels offered their obedience to him everywhere even before the incarnation, and descended upon him while he lived on earth (John 1:51), and now surround him by their thousands while he sits on the Throne of glory (Isaiah 6:2; Daniel 7:10). Finally, they shall accompany him when he returns to pronounce the final sentence upon all mortals according to the law he brought forth (Matthew 25:31).

XXVIII. Furthermore, these *Cherubim* were made of *Gold*, to signify the excellence, constancy, and eternity of the *Angelic* nature and blessedness; by these qualities, they approach as closely as possible to that Divine excellence of the Son of God. *They were made of beaten work from the mercy seat itself*; because *Christ*, through his atonement, causes the chosen from among men to grow together with the *Angels* into one heavenly commonwealth. *For by his benefit, we have come to the heavenly Jerusalem and to myriads of Angels* (Hebrews 12:22). *They spread out their wings, overshadowing the mercy seat*; not only because the mysteries of grace in Christ were at that time covered by many veils of figures and riddles even for the faithful themselves—let alone for the carnal Israelites (2 Corinthians 3:14-15)—but also because, on account of *Christ’s* merits, they provide strong protection to all those who are members of his mystical body. This is alluded to in Psalm 36:8: *The sons of men take refuge in the shadow of your wings.* And Psalm 61:5: *I will dwell in your tent forever; I will take refuge in the secret place of your wings.* Furthermore, *with downward faces the Cherubim gazed upon the Ark*: for the *Angels* also desire <term>parakypsai</term> <note>original: παρακύψαι; to stoop down and look into</note> the mysteries of our redemption (1 Peter 1:12). *There were two of them, with faces turned toward one another*, yet in such a way that each also *looked toward the Ark*: by this position, it may be believed they prefigured the duty of the faithful of both the Old and New Testaments, who, with eyes of <term>isotimō</term> <note>original: ἰσοτίμῳ; equal value or privilege</note> faith and mutual love, look indeed at one another, yet look together at *Christ*. For the *Angels* are frequently set before the faithful as an example.

XXIX. Nor do I think the *living creatures* of Ezekiel, which he himself calls *Cherubim*, pertained to anything else. From this, it is plain that *Angels* were signified by them. Specifically *Archangels*, who are set over other *Angels*...

Nevertheless, it should not be denied on that account that some were superior to others in rank, dignity, and the excellence of their duties; since God employed them to perform extraordinary works in the government of both the world and the Church. Moreover, they were *four* in number; just as many chariots were seen by *Zechariah*: to whom, when he asked what those chariots were, the *Angel* replied: *These are the four spirits of heaven, going out from where they stood before the Lord of all the earth.* *Zechariah 6:5.* <note>The original citation says VI. 6, but the text quoted is verse 5.</note> Truly, as many as there are *parts of the world* or *cardinal points*, as many faces as are described in the *Temple*, *Ezekiel 48:30 and following*, as many sides as *John* attributes to the *New Jerusalem*, *Revelation 21:13*, so many *Angels* are represented here, through whom it pleased God to carry out his wonderful works in the world and the Church.

XXX. Joined to the *Cherubim* were *four wheels*, by which the various revolutions of the world, and the changes of affairs in the Church to be governed by *Angels*, are designated. *The appearance of the wheels* and *their work was like Tarshish*, that is, like *Sardonyx* <note>original: "Sardonychis"</note>: for so the great Interpreter has proved by probable arguments. Now, in *Sardonyx* there is whiteness and brightness, but tempered with redness. By this can be noted the tempering of Divine *love for mankind* <note>original Greek: "philanthropia"</note> and justice, with the holiness that shines back in both, which virtues God clearly shows in the care of his Church. The wheels abounded with *eyes*, so that we may know all these changes of things are not carried along by a blind impulse, but are governed by the highest wisdom and vigilance, and are directed with certainty toward their ends. The terrible *height* of the rims marks that inscrutable and unspeakable depth of Divine counsels; at which one must exclaim: *How great are your works, O Jehovah! how deep are your thoughts!* *Psalm 92:5.* *O Jehovah, your mercy is in the heavens; your faithfulness reaches to the clouds above; your righteousness is like the great mountains; your judgments are like a great abyss.* *Psalm 36:5-6.* <note>The author uses the numbering from the Latin Vulgate or Hebrew, which may differ by one verse from modern English Bibles.</note> A *wheel within a wheel* signifies the most full agreement of Divine works, which are all carried toward a single end; performed by the same Spirit, who both rules the *Angels* and dispenses the labors of the *Angels*.

# BOOK II. CHAPTER XIII.

The face of the **Man** signifies the reason, humanity, gentleness, and *love of mankind* <note>original: "Φιλανθρωπια" (philanthropia)</note> of the *Angels*. Through the **Lion**, strength, nobility, and terrifying Majesty are shown. For the *Lion* is the symbol of these things. Proverbs 30:29-30, Isaiah 31:4, 1 Chronicles 12:8. Such do the *Angels* show themselves toward the enemies of the Church. Psalm 35:5-6. The face of the **Ox** denotes constancy, patience, firmness, and diligence in performing the duty commanded to them by God, as well as the remarkable usefulness they provide to men. Proverbs 14:4. Add to this the strength for defeating enemies. Compare Deuteronomy 33:17. Finally, the **Eagle-like** face signifies the vigor of their heavenly nature. Compare Psalm 103:5, Isaiah 40:31; their supreme agility, Jeremiah 4:13; their incredible insight; and their striving toward or dwelling in heavenly things. Job 39:30.

XXXII. Nor should we omit what has been observed by most learned men: *that two of these are wild, the Lion and the Eagle; and two are tame, the Man and the Ox: the former to terrify the rebellious, the latter to be a comfort to the godly.* Among the wild ones, the *Lion* pursues prey on the earth; the *Eagle* does so even in the air and the midst of the clouds: so that we may know these spirits attack not only wicked men who crawl upon the ground, but also *the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places.* <note>original: "τὰ πνευματικὰ τῆς πονηρίας ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις"</note> Ephesians 6:12. *The two tame ones, the Ox and the Man, are terrestrial*, because the protection of *Angels* is necessary for us while we are here on earth; it is not so in heaven, where there are no enemies and no impending evils.

XXXIII. For it is even said in a proverb that the *Ox* sets its foot down strongly. Furthermore, their feet were *sparkling like glowing brass*, or *polished steel*, by which is signified holiness, zeal for Divine glory, and charity—a charity that is shining and closest to the virtues of God. Compare Daniel 10:6, Revelation 1:15. The *Wings* denote speed: for they dashed out and returned like the appearance of a most violent flash of lightning. With two other wings they covered their bodies: for the sake of modesty, and to teach the invisibility of the Angelic nature. Moreover, *each one went straight forward toward the area facing them; without turning back or circling around, they did not divert as they went.* For in the ways of God there is no retreating; there is no curved path. XXXIV. Of the same significance, in our view at least, were the *living creatures* seen by *John*; by which we believe that not the *assembly of the faithful*, as many assert, but four exceptional Angels were represented. This is indeed worthy of celestial spirits: but it would be an unworthy thing if "those standing before and the leaders" <note>original Greek: "οἱ προεϛῶτες καὶ οἱ ἡγούμενοι" - referring to the church hierarchy</note> only began their songs following the example of the Church. 
II. Because they are guides for *John* toward the knowledge of Divine mysteries. Revelation 6:1, 3, 5, 7. That is truly the work of *Angels*. Daniel 8:16, 9:21, 10:11, and frequently in *Zechariah*. 
III. One of the four living creatures gave to the seven *Angels* seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God, who lives forever and ever. Revelation 15:7. This is much more suitably understood as an *Angel* delivering the commands of God to other *Angels*, rather than as the *Church*.

XXXV. But if we pay proper attention, we will see that it is not necessary to conclude that this sacred song was spoken to God by the living creatures. For it is possible that one part of this passage applies to all the subjects together, while another part applies only to some. Clearly, the first part of verse 8, *the four Living Creatures and the twenty-four elders fell down before the Lamb*, applies to both...

# BOOK II. CHAPTER XIII.

<margin>Regarding Chapter IV, verse 6.</margin>
...rightly applies. But regarding what follows—*each having harps, etc.* and in verse 9, *And they sing a new song, etc.*—we are not forced to understand these as referring to anyone other than the twenty-four elders. For it is the duty of the Elders, or the Overseers, to lead the Church in celebrating the praises of God, just as the Levites used to do in ancient times, equipped with harps and other musical instruments. It is also their duty to bring the prayers of the faithful to God, just as the priests of old presented bowls full of incense to the Lord morning and evening. For they are no less the mouth of the people toward God than they are the mouth of God toward the people. Nor should it seem strange to anyone that when a discourse mentions several groups together at the beginning of a prayer, the things said as it progresses are not applicable to all, but only to some. For the common proverb holds true here as well: "the predicates reveal their own subject." <note>A logical principle meaning that the actions described in a sentence help identify which specific person or group is being talked about.</note> Similar examples are not lacking. In Nehemiah 13:1–2 it is said: *it was found written that no Ammonite or Moabite should enter the assembly of God, because they had not met the Israelites with bread and water, but had hired Balaam against them, etc.* The first part—that they did not meet Israel—is common to both the Ammonites and the Moabites; but the latter part, concerning the hiring of Balaam, could be blamed on the Moabites alone, as is clear from Numbers 22:3. Similarly, in Jeremiah 21:7: *I will deliver Zedekiah king of Judah, and his servants, and the people themselves, etc. into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, etc. who shall strike them with the edge of the sword.* What is said at the beginning about the delivery of Zedekiah, his servants, and the people is true of everyone; but what is added next—*who shall strike them with the edge of the sword*—must be understood as referring to the servants and the people of Zedekiah, not to the king himself, since he died a natural death <note>original: "sua et sicca morte," literally "his own and dry death," meaning a non-violent death in captivity.</note> in Jeremiah 52:11. If anyone desires more examples of this kind, let him consult *Jean de la Buy’s commentary on the Apocalypse*. It remains settled, therefore, that by those "living creatures," in the writings of *John* no less than *Ezekiel*, we must understand the *Angels*.

If one fills their mind with these observations, they will certainly not have wasted their effort as much as if they were to idly invent many stories about I-know-not-what monstrous spirits of the Egyptians.

### CHAPTER XIV.

### That the Egyptians knew nothing in the Doctrine of Creation which other nations did not also draw from the same source of Reason or Tradition.

I. *Whatever good the Egyptians held in Religion, other nations for the most part drew from the same source.* II. *Both the Greeks and the Barbarians <note>In this context, "Barbarians" refers to any non-Greek speaking peoples, such as Persians or Scythians.</note> professed that God is the maker of the world.* III. *The Greeks no less than the Egyptians called Him "Mind."* IV. *And "Word" <note>original: "sermonem," likely referring to the concept of the Logos.</note>.* V. VI. *Maximus of Tyre elegantly taught that He made all things by His nod.* VII. *Regarding the order of creation, they also brought forth many things that agree with the Mosaic accounts <note>The writings of Moses in the Bible.</note>.* VIII. *And they did not have these from the Egyptians, but from the Hebrews by way of the Phoenicians.* IX. *Orpheus traces his own ideas back to the Chaldeans.* X. *From which it is concluded that the Egyptians have nothing unique here.*

I. We now gird ourselves for the THIRD head of the undertaken treatise, by which it must be proved that those either *dogmas of religion*, or even *rites* and *ceremonies*, in which the *Egyptians* agree with the *Hebrews*, are for the most part such that the *Egyptians* held them in common with other more civilized peoples: having arisen, clearly, from a common source, either of *Reason* or of *Tradition*; both of which—at least in these matters—were purer and more unpolluted among the Hebrews.

<margin>Compare book 1, chapter IV, section 1.</margin>
II. Let us begin from the Doctrine of CREATION. Whatever is brought forward as praiseworthy from the monuments of the *Egyptians* concerning it, we find all those same things, and sometimes even a little more clearly, in the writings of other Gentiles. Not only the *Greeks*, but also the *Barbarians*, almost all agree in this: *that God is the author and maker of the world*. That the world *was truly established through Divine providence* <note>original Greek: "τῇ ἀληθείᾳ διὰ τὴν τοῦ Θεοῦ γενέσθαι πρόνοιαν"</note>, was not said by Plato alone:

# BOOK II. CHAPTER XIV.

But indeed, almost all the wise men of the nations, as Lactantius <note>Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius (c. 250 – c. 325), an early Christian author who advised Constantine I.</note> says, testify with one Spirit and a single voice, and almost all philosophers agree on this point. Not even the Indians are excepted, whether the ancients or those of more recent times, to whom the report of this matter has spread. *Strabo, citing Megasthenes, says of the Ancients*: <note>original Greek: Περὶ πολλῶν καὶ τοῖς Ἕλλησιν ὁμοδοξεῖν... / Latin: De multis eos cum Græcis sentire...</note> They agree with the Greeks on many things: for they say that the world had a beginning and is perishable, and that it is spherical in shape. Furthermore, they believe that God, the maker and governor of the world, pervades the whole of it; and that the various elements of all things are different, but water was the beginning of the world's creation. And to mix recent things with the ancient, *Richard Whitbourne* <note>An English colonist and traveler (1561–1635) who wrote about Newfoundland.</note> records that the inhabitants of *New England in North America* believe the whole world, and everything contained within it, was created by a certain supreme divinity they call *Kichtan*. <margin>See Tobias Pfanner, System of Gentile Theology, chapter 5, section 11.</margin> And a Priest of a certain place in the *Kingdom of Pegu* <note>Modern-day Bago, Myanmar (Burma).</note>, when questioned about the creation of the world, replied in the presence of the Portuguese traveler *Fernão Mendes Pinto* that nature had no other origin than the will of God.

# BOOK II. CHAPTER XIV.

But how this might be done is not easy for me to say. Homer, however, secretly hints at it when he says:

VI. There are many things in this discourse that are quite excellent. I. That it is a study most worthy of man to inquire into the source and author of all goods. II. That this is learned no better than from the mouth of God himself. III. Yet this truth—that God is the father and maker of all—is of such great evidence that it ought to be considered almost to meet one's very eyes, and there seems to be scarcely any need for an oracle to create faith in it. IV. That the Maker is a solid and incorruptible mind. V. That he made all things not with hands or machines, but by a nod.

VII. Nor is anything brought forward from the Egyptians concerning the order of creation that agrees with the Mosaic narrative, for which most learned men have not shown similar things to exist among the Greeks. Just as *Moses* begins the creation of things from the making of heaven and earth; so also *Plato* derives the beginnings of things from fire and earth <note>original: "ἐκ πυρὸς καὶ γῆς"</note>. That earth which *Moses* calls *Tohu Vabbohu* <note>Hebrew: "without form and void"</note>; the Poets call *chaos*, *a rough and unordered mass*. And that darkness preceded light was the philosophy of *Thales*, who, when someone asked whether night or day was made first, said, *Night was one day earlier* <note>original: "ἡ νὺξ ἔφη μιᾷ ἡμέρᾳ πρῶτον"</note>. In the same manner *Aristophanes* in *Lucian's* *Philopatris*:

The *Breath* <term>Flamen: a Latin term for a gust or divine breath</term>, *Love*, and the *egg* correspond to the Spirit "hovering" or "incubating" <note>original Hebrew: מרחפת (merachephet), used in Genesis 1:2</note>. VIII. You may say that the *Greeks* received all these things from the *Egyptians*. But from where did the *Egyptians* get them? Certainly not from some particular cleverness of their own mind, in which they surpassed all other nations. For however much you may contend that they were powerful in intellect, they would never have discovered the *order of creation*, nor those things we have heard concerning the *Word* <term>Verbo: The Logos or creative Word of God</term> as the craftsman, through their own reasoning. It is necessary, therefore, that these things flowed from an ancient tradition, proceeding first from those to whom it pleased God to reveal more of Himself than what is learned with nature as a teacher. What, then, stands in the way of the *Greeks* having been able to receive these traditions from their own ancestors, just as the *Egyptians* did? *Plato* says excellently: *And indeed the ancients, who were better than us and dwelt closer to the Gods, handed down this report.* <note>original Greek: Καὶ οἱ μὲν παλαιοὶ κρείτονες ἡμῶν...</note> Unless we prefer—as we certainly do—that both the *Egyptians* and the *Greeks* drew the matters we are now discussing, whether more or less directly, from the godly posterity of *Shem* <note>The biblical son of Noah</note>, whom God made the depository of sacred instruction. *Grotius* has shown that commerce existed between the *Phoenicians* and the ancient inhabitants of *Attica*, the oldest of the *Ionians*. The ancients record that *Linus* <note>A legendary figure in Greek music/poetry</note> came from *Phoenicia*. And *Orpheus* drew his ideas from the *Phoenicians*. The *Phoenicians* drew theirs from the *Hebrews*.

VI. Therefore, this most true, most ancient, and most universal tradition flowed from the first parents (for from where else could it come?) to almost all the more civilized peoples, no less than to the Egyptians. VII. As for the fabrication of **METEMPSYCHOSIS** <term>Metempsychosis: the transmigration of souls, or reincarnation</term>, if it is of such great value, I easily allow it to be claimed by the Egyptians; but those things which they discussed concerning the **PLACE DESTINED FOR SOULS** after death are from a most ancient tradition, of which the Egyptians were neither the sole nor the first guardians. Rather, the most ancient mortals, having drawn these ideas from Noah, impressed them upon their own descendants; these ideas, as usually happens, were gradually covered by many layers of fables, yet they retained some marks of their ancient simplicity. And there is scarcely any nation so barbarian, and so far removed from all refinement, that it does not show some traces of this tradition. ### VIII.

## CHAPTER XVI.

### Concerning Blasphemy, Holidays, and Festivals, Purifications, sacrifices, the hatred of swine, and sacred Lamps; that the Egyptians held nothing unique in these matters above many other nations.

I. Just as nature was able to teach the Egyptians that one must abstain from BLASPHEMY <note>The act of insulting or showing contempt for God or sacred things.</note>, so it taught others: who, if they heard anything by report concerning the Mosaic precept on this matter, were soon compelled to agree with it as being most just. That saying of Socrates in Plato is memorable:

<margin>In the *Philebus*, near the beginning.</margin>

<margin>On the Laws, Book XI.</margin>

Indeed, there is excellent praise with which Plutarch honors Socrates; who, after citing a certain saying of his from Plato’s *Theaetetus*, proves it was not uttered in jest or play by the fact that he had mentioned the Divine name in it.

<margin>Platonic Questions: at the beginning.</margin>

III. The solemnities of HOLIDAYS AND FESTIVALS <note>original: "FERIARUM FESTORUMQUE"</note> are so closely joined with the worship of the deity that wherever we find the latter, we also find the former. Nor did the *Egyptians* possess anything unique in this matter. Truly, since human life consists almost entirely of action, and some actions are sacred and religious while others are manual and pertain to animal and civil life—and since all these actions cannot exist without time—God therefore distinguished and adapted time for the actions of man. Even in the pagans, those sparks of the knowledge of God remained, so that according to human actions, some days were sacred and others were profane. The former served the exercise of external religion, while the latter served labor and the manual arts. And from this it happened that some fixed time for religion was always designated among even the most savage peoples.

<margin>Book 1 of the *Saturnalia*, Chapter XVI.</margin>
IV. Hence arises that distinction of days, the author of which is praised by *Macrobius* as being *Numa* <note>Numa Pompilius, the legendary second king of Rome, credited with establishing Roman religious rites.</note>, into *Festal, Profane, and Divided* days. *Festal days* <note>original: "Festi"</note> were dedicated to the Gods. *Profane days* <note>original: "Profesti"</note> were granted to men for the administration of private and public business. *Divided days* <note>original: "Intercisi"</note>, however, are common to both Gods and men. For on certain hours of those days it was lawful <note>term: "fas" (divine law/permission)</note>, and on others it was not lawful, to administer justice. Furthermore, there were four types of *Holidays for the Romans*. Some were *Fixed* <note>original: "Stativæ"</note>, common to the whole people, occurring on certain and established days and months, and noted in the calendars. Others were *Conceptive* <note>original: "conceptivæ"</note>, which were appointed every year by magistrates and priests on either fixed or even uncertain days. Others were *Imperative*, which the consuls or praetors proclaimed at their own discretion. Finally, others were the *Market Days* <note>original: "Nundinæ"</note>, which belonged to the villagers or rustics, on which they assembled to look after their own business or merchandise.

V. Natural reason dictates this: since man is a social and political animal <note>original: "ὁμιλητικὸν καὶ πολιτικὸν" (homiletikon kai politikon)</note>, God must be worshiped not only privately, but also publicly and *in assembly*. For this purpose, it is necessary to designate certain places where the gathering may occur, and to establish a set time for when it happens. Furthermore, on those days consecrated to the worship of the deity, this worship must be the focus; one must *attend to this one thing* and no other, and apply the mind fully to it.

<margin>Petit, Attic Laws, Title 1, Law XI.</margin>
Hence, it is written in the *Attic Laws*: <term>While all Athenians are observing a sacred month, let no one wrong another either privately or publicly during this time, nor transact any business that does not pertain to the festival.</term> <note>original Greek: "ἁπάντων τ’ Ἀθηναίων ἀγόντων ἱερομηνίαν..."</note> *On a festival day of the Athenian people, let no injury be done to anyone, whether privately or publicly; nor let any assembly be held concerning matters other than those pertaining to the religious observance of the festivals.*

<margin>Book II, On the Laws.</margin>
The Roman Laws in Cicero agree: REMOVE DISPUTES FROM HOLIDAYS: AND LET THE SERVANTS OBSERVE THEM ONCE THEIR TASKS ARE COMPLETED. Which he explains thus: *The system of holidays and festal days provides for the free citizens a rest from lawsuits and quarrels;*

<margin>Saturnalia, Book I, Chapter XVI.</margin>
*and for slaves, a rest from works and labors.* In Macrobius, the priests affirm that holidays are polluted *whenever, once they have been proclaimed and undertaken, any work is performed.* Furthermore, it was not permitted for the *King of Sacrifices or the Flamens* <note>High-ranking Roman priests</note> to see work being done on holidays. And for that reason, they announced through a herald that no such thing should be done, and anyone negligent of the command was fined. *Beyond the fine, it was affirmed that he who had done something on such days unintentionally must offer a pig as an atonement; however, Scævola the Pontifex affirmed that he who acted intentionally could not be purified.* Yet that law of <term>idleness</term> <note>original: "ἀργίας" (argias) - cessation from labor</note> had its own certain exception, *which equity dictated.* For, as found in the same Macrobius, Umbro denied that a man was polluted who had performed work either PERTAINING TO THE GODS OR FOR THE SAKE OF SACRED RITES, or who had BUSIED HIMSELF WITH SOMETHING REGARDING THE URGENT NECESSITY OF LIFE. Finally, Scævola, when consulted as to what was permitted to be done on holidays, replied: THAT WHICH WOULD CAUSE HARM IF NEGLECTED. *If an ox had fallen into a pit and the head of the household freed it by employing labor, he was not seen to have polluted the holiday; nor was he who saved a house from imminent ruin by shoring up a broken roof beam. Maro <note>The poet Virgil</note>, skilled in all disciplines, knowing that a sheep is washed either for the sake of cleaning the wool or curing the scab, pronounced that it was permitted for a sheep to be submerged during holidays if this were done for the sake of a remedy.*

By adding the word *healthful*, he shows that this was permitted only for the sake of averting disease, *and not for the sake of profit or the cleaning of wool*. These matters agree closely with the *Law of the Sabbath*, and the explanation of it given by our Lord in the Gospel.

VI. Thus far, almost all nations are in agreement. Nor was it necessary for one to be the leader of another in this matter, since they all drew it from the common fountain of reason. However, the specific distribution of sacred times was established by the leaders of each nation according to their own character, or because they were deceived by the evil arts of demons. And just as each nation excelled in character and was cultivated by better disciplines, so much more orderly did it distinguish its own solemnities. Nor do I think there is any reason why the *Romans* should yield to the *Egyptians*, or to any other nation, in this regard. Furthermore, if it happened that some nation was renowned for the greatness of its kingdom, wealth, authority, and reputation for wisdom, it could easily happen that neighboring nations would adopt the same rites. And so perhaps the *Greeks* took over some things from the *Egyptians*; since their republic was more recent and weaker in antiquity than that of the *Egyptians*, it is not surprising if the *Egyptian solemnities are called ancient, while the Greek ones are called recent by Herodotus*. *Regarding the seven-day cycle and the Sabbath, we shall speak in its proper place below.*

<margin>Compare Book I, chapter VII, section 3.</margin>
VII. Reason teaches almost everyone to use WATER in initiations and purifications <term>lustrations; ceremonial washings to remove ritual impurity</term>. Sir John Marsham confidently asserts this, as if on the authority of *Diodorus Siculus* <note>Diodorus Siculus was a Greek historian of the 1st century BCE known for his monumental universal history.</note>. Whether this is true or false, certain or doubtful, matters little to us. But it must be known that *Diodorus* does not support that narrative on his own credit, nor with certain arguments; rather, he merely presents to his reader the boastings of the *Egyptians*—most of them vain and futile—exactly as he had received them. For with the same arrogance, they used to boast that the *Babylonians*, *Jews*, *Athenians*, and *Argives* were their own offshoots and colonies, based on certain flimsy conjectures. ### BOOK II. CHAPTER XVI.

For the Greeks, out of an ancient superstition, considered those for whom a funeral and burial had been performed as if they were deceased to be profane; they were barred from religious assemblies and sacrifices. A certain *Aristinus*, being bound by this religious restriction, sent to Delphi to pray for a way to extricate himself from these difficulties in which he was entangled by the authority of the laws. The *Pythia* <note>The high priestess of the Temple of Apollo at Delphi who delivered oracles.</note> answered him:

->Whatever a woman in labor performs at the bedside,<-
->Perform those things again and sacrifice to the blessed Gods.<-

->*Having perfected in order whatever a woman in childbirth observes,*<-
->*Let him stain the sacred altars of the Heaven-dwellers with animal sacrifices.*<-

Therefore *Aristinus*, having correctly understood the oracle, offered himself to women to be washed, swaddled, and nursed as if he were reborn. Others, who had met with the same fate, imitated this. Some, however, believed this custom to be older than *Aristinus*. But I have seen no one who would trace its origin to the *Egyptians*.

<margin>See Johannes Macarius in *Abraxas*, section 3, page 12.</margin>
X. First among the initiations into the mysteries of *Mithras*—the supreme deity among the *Persians*—out of eighty other rites, was *Baptism*. The ancients noted that the sacred rites of this God were very similar to Christian rites. For they also dipped them in a washing, marked them on the forehead, and had a form of the *Eucharist* <note>The Christian sacrament of Holy Communion.</note>, as well as an imitation of *martyrdom* and a belief in the *resurrection*. If learned men had found these things among the *Egyptians*, what applause would they not have given?

For this purpose, they had basins not only in temples, but also in the forum and at crossroads. And they made *sprinklers* <term>aspergilla: brushes or branches used to sprinkle holy water</term> from laurel, or from a branch of the fruitful *olive* tree: just as the *Hebrews* used *hyssop*. > —- the steam of lambs and of perfect goats.
> <note>original Greek: ἀρνῶν κνίσσην, αἰγῶντε τελείων</note>

Truly, as Eustathius <note>A 12th-century Byzantine scholar and commentator on Homer.</note> brilliantly remarks there: *To the divine ones, as they are perfect, perfect things must be brought.* <note>original Greek: Τοῖς θείοις ὡς τελείοις προσάγειν χρὴ τέλεια</note> Now, a victim is called "perfect" in which nothing is lacking. Solon called such sacrifices "simple" or "unblemished" <note>Greek: ΑΦΕΛΗ (aphele)</note> in the *Axones* <note>Wooden tablets inscribed with the laws of Solon.</note>, according to the testimony of Pollux. <margin>Book I, Chapter I</margin> He lists them as: *Sacred, sacrificial, sound, uncut, whole, healthy, unmaimed, having all members, having the full number of limbs, neither stunted, nor disabled, nor mutilated, nor distorted.* Solon named those that were not disabled "unblemished." Therefore, in Apollonius, Jason—about to perform sacred rites to Apollo before his departure—orders servants skilled in these matters: <margin>Argonautica, Book I</margin>

> —- to drive from the herd oxen, having selected them well.
> <note>original Greek: βόας ἀγέληθεν ἐϋκρίναντας ἐλάσσαι</note>

Megasthenes also reports concerning the Indians (with Strabo and Arrian as witnesses) that they held it a divine violation to offer a flawed or maimed victim to God. And Pliny stated it was noted that a limping calf does not obtain a favorable omen, nor are the Gods appeased by an inferior sacrifice. Worthy of note is the observation of Macrobius: <margin>Saturnalia, Book III</margin> **EXCEPTIONAL** (*Eximii*) is not a poetic epithet in sacrifices, but a priestly term. For Veranius teaches in his *Pontifical Questions* that victims were called "exceptional" because they are "exempted" or "selected out" from the flock for the purpose of sacrifice; or because they are chosen for their exceptional appearance as things to be offered to the deities.

**XVI. THE SWINE** was perhaps no more hated among the Egyptians—and possibly even less so—than among other nations. For the Egyptians alone among men used the labor of the pig in the cultivation of their fields. Eudoxus, as cited in Aelian: <margin>Book 4, Symposiac Questions 5.</margin> *After they have finished sowing, they lead in herds of swine, which tread the seed of the grain deep into the moist earth so that it remains viable and is not consumed by birds.* *Plutarch* records the same. Yet to the rest of mortals, the pig was hateful as an animal hostile to crops and vines. For this reason, swine were sacrificed to Ceres <note>The Roman goddess of agriculture</note> and Bacchus <note>The god of wine</note>, <margin>On The Frogs, Act 1, Scene 7.</margin> *as they are destroyers of the gifts of the two Gods* <note>original Greek: ὡς λυμαντικοὶ τοῖν Θεοῖν δωρημάτων</note>, as the commentator on *Aristophanes* observes. Indeed, if we believe the ancients, <margin>Metamorphoses, book 15.</margin> this was the very first of all sacrificial victims.

> --- the sow is thought to have been the first
> victim to deserve death, because with her wide
> snout she rooted up the seeds, and cut off the hope of the year.

But many other peoples besides the Egyptians abstained from eating swine. The incomparable Bochart, in his usual thorough manner, proves this extensively regarding the Arabs, Phoenicians, the women of Barca in African <margin>Hierozoicon, Part 1, book 2, chapter 57.</margin> Cyrenaica, the Ethiopians, and the Indians. The cause for this hatred could have been the animal's filthiness: it is believed to grow fattest when it wallows and rolls in the mud, which, as *Varro* says, is their rest, just as bathing is for men. Hence, in common proverbs, it is a symbol of a shameful man.

**XVII. LAMPS** were frequently used in the rites and festivals of many nations, even in broad daylight, as can be learned from Lipsius, and more fully from Fortunio Liceto in his excellent work *On the Lamps of the Ancients*. Whether the first lighting of them for religious purposes is owed to the Hebrews or the Egyptians, I could not easily say. Perhaps it is older than both. *Josephus* attributes it to his own Hebrews. <margin>Page 303.</margin> *Clement of Alexandria* attributes it to the Egyptians: but he speaks in that manner by which other things are ascribed to the Egyptians as inventors which it is certain were not invented by them—such as the division of the year into twelve months, which we have previously shown to be older than the Great Flood. And truly, if we accept what *Manetho* <note>An ancient Egyptian priest and historian</note> relates concerning the origin of the Festival of Lamps among the Egyptians, it is clear that the events which took place in Egypt during the time of Moses gave occasion for the festival. <margin>Egyptian Oedipus, Volume...</margin> I am pleased to set this forth in the words of Athanasius Kircher. *What truly,* he says, *was the sacred reason for which such a great festival was instituted, Mane—*

# BOOK II. CHAPTER XVI.

As Syncellus <note>George Syncellus, a 9th-century Byzantine chronicler</note> teaches; Typhon, having slain Osiris, covered all of Egypt 
<margin>Hieroglyphic Collection, Book 20, Chapter 1</margin>
with darkness and thick gloom. Terrified by this omen, the Egyptian priests consulted an oracle, which responded that the darkness spread over the land would not cease unless they appeased Osiris—who had been killed by Typhon—with the frequent brightness of lamps. Once this was done, the darkness was soon dispersed and the longed-for light returned; and thus the festival of the lighting of lamps was instituted, celebrated with the greatest zeal by those deceivers <note>The author likely refers to the pagan priests as "impostors" from a Christian perspective</note>. There are some, however, who wish to claim that the origin of the festival of the lighting of lamps was drawn from the ten plagues of Egypt, with which Moses struck Egypt by Divine power, among which the "nearly palpable darkness" <note>A reference to the "darkness that could be felt" in Exodus 10:21</note> was one. I do not disagree with these people, especially since we have shown throughout this entire work that **THE EGYPTIANS BORROWED MOST THINGS FROM THE HEBREWS AND MADE THEM THEIR OWN**, even if they were corrupted by various fables and fabrications. Thus far Kircher <note>Athanasius Kircher, the famous 17th-century Jesuit scholar</note>.

XVIII. John Baptist Casalius, in his book *On the Profane Rites of the Egyptians*, speaks 
<margin>Chapter 25</margin>
somewhat differently, and perhaps no less aptly. If, he says, one were permitted to divine the truth regarding this festival of lamps worshiped by the Egyptians with tears and wailing, I would say it was performed in memory of that slaughter which God himself brought upon the firstborn of all Egyptians, both of men and of cattle, in order to lead away the children of Israel. For then King Pharaoh, in the middle of the night, and all of Egypt, sprinkled with grief and tears, rising from their beds and lighting lamps, lamented their slain sons and compelled the children of Israel to go out from the land of Egypt; as found in Exodus 12:29-30. Indeed, it could have happened that the firstborn of Pharaoh who died was called Osiris; for everyone speaks of the Egyptian Osiris. And furthermore, Apuleius <note>Author of *The Golden Ass*</note> is a witness that this festival day of lamps was celebrated during the full moon. Just as the sacred oracles <note>The Bible</note> have handed down that the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt happened at the time of the full moon in March. These are the words of Casalius. To these observations I add this: that the entire fable of Typhon was distorted from the Mosaic history; and therefore those Typhonic shadows, which Manetho <note>An ancient Egyptian priest and historian</note> mentions, are not different from the Mosaic ones: as I shall prove more at length in the proper place.
