# ON EGYPTIAN MATTERS

by which it may be demonstrated that most of those things which the Egyptians held to be praiseworthy and which were consistent with the institutions of the Hebrews, flowed to other nations as well from a common source of either *Reason* or *Tradition*. Thus, the Egyptians possessed nothing particularly extraordinary in this regard, whereas the Hebrews possessed much that was superior to them, as God deigned to make the Hebrews the guardians of the most ancient and purest traditions.

XX. These things are not said by us with the intention of denying that many things passed from the Egyptians to other nations. We are not so foolish as to wish to deny that the sun shines at midday. The fame of Egyptian wisdom, joined with the glory of a most flourishing kingdom, brought forth many followers. We embrace with both arms <note>A Latin idiom meaning to welcome something enthusiastically</note> what Diodorus Siculus testified:
<margin>Book 1, chapter 59.</margin>
> *many ancient customs of the Egyptians were not only approved by the natives, but also came to be held in great admiration among the Greeks; for this reason, all the most celebrated among the learned devoted themselves to travels in Egypt, so that they might attain a knowledge of the laws and studies there as matters of great importance.*

However, that excursion into Egypt could not have been as frequent in the most ancient times—when the region denied entry to strangers—as it was in more recent times, from the point when Psammetichus <note>Psammetichus I (reigned 664–610 BCE), the pharaoh who opened Egypt to Greek trade and settlement</note> was moved to power. He was the first of all the Kings of Egypt to show himself liberal and kind toward foreigners migrating there of their own accord.

# ON EGYPTIAN AFFAIRS

We must do this twice over, examining with great care whether it can truly be proven that *the pious and laudable institutions of the Egyptians are older than the Hebrew laws concerning Religion.* Learned men put this forward with great spirit; but, unless my judgment fails me, they support their claim with very thin and weak reasoning. This controversy belongs to that class of questions which consist of facts; therefore, it must be proven not by subtle reasoning or bold guesswork, but by suitable witnesses—those who either lived in that age themselves, or were closest to it, or at least drew their information from such sources without a mixture of mythical stories. Since this matter is of great importance to religion as a whole, it should not be considered a fault in us if we desire solid and soul-convincing arguments, and refuse to allow the matter to be passed over with slight conjectures. Let us see, therefore, which witnesses these most learned men are able to praise.

II. Whatever we know of the ancient institutions of the *Egyptians*, if we set aside what we have been taught from our own Sacred Monuments <note>The author refers here to the Bible</note>, is almost entirely collected from *Dio Cassius, Lucian, Plutarch, Strabo, Diodorus Siculus, Chaeremon, Herodotus,* or the fragments of *Manetho and Sanchuniathon*. But not one of all these is of such antiquity or authority that he could provide proof of such great age—I will not say to a stubborn man, but even to one who is only moderately prudent.

III. As for DIO CASSIUS, he lived quite late, in the age of *Marcus Antoninus the Philosopher* <note>The Emperor Marcus Aurelius</note>, and under *Marcus’s* son *Commodus* and the succeeding emperors, enjoying the dignity of a Senator at that time. He was raised to the consulship by *Alexander*, the son of *Mamaea*, which he held alongside the Emperor himself in the year of the City 981 <note>229 AD; the author uses the Roman dating 'Ab Urbe Condita'</note>. He brought his history down as far as this *Alexander*. Furthermore, that which learned men bring forward from *Dio* in their favor is very meager indeed: namely, that assigning the individual days to the planets was an invention of the *Egyptians*. See above, *Book 1, Chapter 6, Section 7.* Regarding this matter, I have no desire to argue. I wouldn't give a straw for it <note>original: "Ciccum non interduim" — a Latin idiom meaning to care very little for something</note>.

IV. LUCIAN belongs to the same era; he lived under *Marcus Antoninus* and after him. Indeed, he mentions the war waged by *Marcus* against the *Marcomanni and Quadi*, and calls *Marcus* "Divine," which proves that the Emperor had yielded to nature and been placed in heaven <note>A reference to the Roman practice of deifying deceased emperors</note>. And the things he tells of the *Egyptians* at the beginning of *The Syrian Goddess*, he neither relates with any certainty, and they are openly false...

The words of *Lucian* <note>Lucian of Samosata (c. 125–180 AD), a Syrian-Greek satirist and rhetorician.</note> himself are as follows: *The Egyptians are said to be the first of men, of whom we have knowledge, to have gained a conception of the Gods.* <note>original Greek: Πρῶτοι μὲν ὧν ἀνθρώπων, τ̄ ἡμεῖς ἴδμεν, Αἰγύπτιοι λέγονται Θεῶν τ̄ ἐννοίην λαβεῖν; Latin: Primi itaque hominum, QUOS NOS SCIMUS, ÆGYPTII, DICUNTUR Deorum notitiam percepiffe &c.</note> Pay attention to the phrases, *They are said*, and, *of whom we have knowledge*. If he had examined or believed those things which *Moses* set forth, he would have found that long before the *Egyptian* state existed, the knowledge of the divine and the understanding of sacred names had flourished. Furthermore, *Lucian* himself sufficiently shows how much credit should be given to those narratives with which almost every nation is accustomed to boast of its own antiquity—more out of ambition than truth—when he writes: *When I inquired about the years of how long this temple had lasted, and about the Goddess, whom they themselves thought she was, many stories were told; some were handed down as sacred, others were open and plain, while others on the contrary were quite fabulous. Again, some were Foreign, others in agreement with the Greeks; all of which I shall report, but I by no means approve of them.* <note>original Greek: ἱϛορέοντι δὲ μοι ἐτέων περὶ... δέχομαι δὲ δ̄αμᾶ; Latin: Inquirenti mihi de annis... haut quaquam autem approbo.</note> Is one who speaks in this way to be thought to supply solid reasons by which such an insane postulate might be proven?

V. PLUTARCH flourished chiefly under Nerva and Trajan; and that which he tells in fables concerning *Isis*, *Osiris*, and *Typhon* from the traditions of the *Egyptians*, we shall show in its proper place to be a significant part distorted from the sacred history of *Moses* and corrupted by foolish fictions.

VI. STRABO was in *Egypt* when *Cornelius Gallus* was governor of that Province, and he wrote his Geography in the fourth year of the reign of *Tiberius Caesar*.

### VIII. CHÆREMON,

frequently praised by *Porphyry* <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher</note>, you may best learn who and what sort of man he was from *Vossius* <note>Gerardus Vossius, a noted 17th-century scholar</note>. He was an Egyptian, to be sure, who committed the Hieroglyphics and Egyptian matters to writing. He was the teacher of *Dionysius of Alexandria*, the one who taught from the time of *Nero* until *Trajan*. But we know *Chæremon’s* age primarily from the fact that he followed *Aelius Gallus* into *Egypt* when he was sailing from *Alexandria*, as <margin>Book XVII.</margin> *Strabo* relates. However, he was a man of ignorant *arrogance* and a most *unreliable* writer. On this account, he was rejected not only by *Josephus*, but by others as well. *Josephus*, indeed, in the first book against *Apion*, cites and refutes several of *Chæremon’s* foolish lies concerning *Jewish* matters. *Strabo* moreover reports that, although he professed expertise in *Philosophy* and *Astronomy*, he was an object of ridicule because of his ignorance and arrogance. *Vossius* also uncovered the man's vanity from *Tzetzes* <note>A 12th-century Byzantine poet and grammarian</note>.

### IX. HERODOTUS

is the oldest of all *Greek* historians who survive today: yet he is more recent than *Moses* by many centuries: for he flourished in the times of *Darius Hystaspes*, *Xerxes*, and *Artaxerxes* who was called *Longimanus*, or *Long-handed*, around the three-hundredth year from the founding of the City <note>Rome</note>. With what faith and judgment he wrote of Egyptian matters, you may gather not only from *Josephus*, who <margin>Book 1 against Apion.</margin> argues from the writings of *Manetho* that *Herodotus frequently lied about Egyptian matters through ignorance* <note>original Greek: πολλὰ Ἡρόδοτον τ’ Αἰγυπτιακῶν ὑπ’ ἀγνοίας ἐψευσμένον</note>: but also from *Diodorus*; whose words are worthy of being <margin>Book 1, chapter LXIX.</margin> displayed here. Thus he says: "As for those things which *Herodotus* and some of those who compiled the deeds of the Egyptians have fabricated and written, having voluntarily preferred the telling of marvels and myths over the truth..." <note>original Greek: Ὅσα μὲν οὖν Ἡρόδοτος καὶ τινες τῶν τὰς Αἰγυπτίων πράξεις συνταξαμένων ἐσχεδιάκασι...</note>

# BOOK III. CHAPTER I.

<note>original: "πλάττειν ψυχαγωγίας ἕνεκα, παρήσημεν"</note> to fashion stories for the sake of entertaining the soul, we shall pass over. As for us, we shall set aside those monstrous narratives which **Herodotus** and several writers of **Egyptian** affairs have babbled—willingly embracing fables as truth and devising myths for the sake of pleasure. The author **Suidas** <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedist</note> is our authority that a certain **Aelius Harpocration** wrote a book <note>original: "περὶ τοῦ καταψεύσασθαι τὴν ἡροδότου ἱσορίαν"</note> *on proving the falsehoods of Herodotus's history*.

X. Since these things are so, I appeal to the tribunal of all those who are not occupied by a prejudice for the cause: whether writers so recent—the oldest of whom is removed by so many centuries from the times of which we dispute; who are more than once convicted of vanity by each other and by others; who, even when they have used all their skill and integrity, sometimes confess they are narrating uncertainties in which they themselves scarcely have faith, drawn as they were from **Egyptian** priests (who felt no religious scruple in sailing toward the glory of their own nation with ambitious lies); who, finally, either held the affairs of the **Hebrews** as entirely unknown or learned them too late, after the fame of the **Egyptians** had filled the world—let any wise man, I say, judge whether such writers are fit witnesses from whom you may solidly and validly argue for the antiquity of **Egyptian** ceremonies as being older than the age of **Moses, Joseph,** or **Abraham**.

<margin>Sacred Origins, book 1, chapter II, section VIII.</margin>

XI. But perhaps **MANETHOS** will supply more certain things—an **Egyptian** himself, and one who drew his material from the most ancient columns and sacred books. Let us see. **Manethos** was of the **Sebennite** nation, by function a <note>original: "Ἀρχιερεὺς τῶν ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ εἰδώλων"</note> *High Priest of the idols in Egypt*, as **Eusebius** says, or as **Syncellus** puts it: <note>original: "τῶν ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ μιαρῶν ἱερῶν ἀρχιερεὺς"</note> *High Priest of the impure rites in Egypt*. He translated the entire **Egyptian** history, and specifically those things pertaining to the **Theology** of this nation, extensively into the **Greek** language, both in the sacred work he wrote and in other commentaries. He lived under **Ptolemy Philadelphus**, to whom he dedicated his history, and was somewhat more recent than **Herodotus**. He says he drew his material partly from columns placed in the **Seriadica** land, upon which sacred marks were engraved in a sacred dialect by **Thaut**, or **Mercury**, and partly from books written by the grandfather of **Mercury Trismegistus** <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure combining the Greek god Hermes and Egyptian Thoth</note>, and others which are preserved by priests in the inner sanctuaries of the temples. And this happened most especially to *Manetho* when he narrated those Egyptian affairs in which the affairs of the Hebrews were in some way entangled. Nor indeed is that surprising. For since he was an Egyptian, he judged himself to have many causes for hatred and envy against the *Jews*: and since he was a priest of most impure demons, he envied the God of Israel whatever contributed to His glory. Nor can you gather more clearly from anywhere else than from this *Manetho* himself how either ignorant of true antiquity, or malevolent dissemblers of it—nay, truly wicked corrupters—the Egyptians were; provided one chooses to compare those things which the sacred scriptures brought forth concerning the arrival of the Israelites in Egypt and their departure from Egypt with those things which the peddler of trifles *Manetho* consigned to his writings, and which *Josephus* learnedly refuted.

XII. But at least, you might say, more accurate and more ancient than *Manetho* is 
->**SANCHUNIATHON OF BEYRUT**<-
who wrote the history of the *Phoenicians* in his native tongue, and mixed into it many things by which the antiquities of the Egyptians and Hebrews are illustrated in a wonderful way. The man's accuracy is attested by his very surname. For, as *Theodorus* <note>Theodorus of Gadara</note> says from *Porphyry*: *Sanchoniathon* in the dialect of the Phoenicians means "Lover of Truth" <note>original Greek: Σαγχωνιάθων ὁ κατὰ Φοινίκων διάλεκτον Φιλαλήθης</note>. In Hebrew you would write it *Sankineatho* <note>original Hebrew: סנקנאתן</note>, that is, a friend of the *Law*, or of the truer doctrine: or if you render it word for word, *The Law is his zeal*. *San* <note>original Hebrew: סנ</note> is shortened from *Sanna* <note>original Hebrew: סנא</note>. This was the same for the Phoenicians as *Sanna* <note>original Arabic: סנא</note> was for the Arabs: *Law*, or *Doctrine*. Hence the Phoenician city is called in one way *Kirjath-Sepher* <note>City of Books</note> in Judges 1:11-12, and in another way *Kirjath-Sanna* <note>City of Instruction</note> in Judges 15:49. We owe this etymology to the incomparable *Bochart* <note>Samuel Bochart, a famous 17th-century French Protestant scholar of biblical geography and animals</note>.

# BOOK III. CHAPTER I.

...he is said to have been the author of these commentaries: partly from those things which he had received from *Jerombalus*, a Priest of the God **IEVOU** <note>original: "IEVOU" - likely a Latinization of the Hebrew Tetragrammaton, Yahweh</note>, as *Eusebius* records from *Porphyry*—though *Theodoret* reads this as **IAO** <note>original: "IAO" - a common Greek rendering of the Divine Name</note>—and partly from the commentaries of individual cities and the monuments of temples, which were found stored in the inner sanctuaries, written in the *Secret letters of the Ammoneans* <note>referring to a cryptic or priestly script used in Phoenician temples</note>, of which very few men attained knowledge. XIV. Truly, the *antiquity* of this writer is remarkable: for he is said by *Porphyry* to be older than the *Trojan* war, approaching very nearly to the age of *Moses*, and to have lived while *Semiramis* was reigning among the *Assyrians*, whom they record to have been either older than or contemporary with the times of the *Iliad*. Indeed, *Vossius* (following *Scaliger*) intervenes here; to prove that *Sanchuniathon* is more recent than the *Phoenician* annals suggest, they observe that he mentions the time when *Tyre* was founded, and mentions it as a thing already ancient. And yet *Tyre* was not built just one year before the fall of *Troy*, as *Justin* falsely handed down in the eighteenth book of his *Epitome*; nevertheless, it was founded no more than 76 years before 그hat destruction, as *Vossius* thinks, or 65 years according to the calculation of *Louis Cappel*. However, to blunt that objection, *Bochart* bids us observe that the name of *Tyre* was common to many cities in *Phoenicia*: of which that most famous one, which was on the island near *Palaetyrus* <note>Old Tyre</note>, was not the most ancient. For it is clear from the name itself that *Palaetyrus* was older than it. For *Palaetyrus* is nothing other than *Old Tyre*. Therefore, mention is made of *Palaetyrus* in the book of *Joshua*, chapter 19:29. For there, the <term>מבצר צור</term> <note>Hebrew: Mibzar Tzor</note> *fortified city of Tyre*, the border of the *Asherites* by the sea, not far from *Sidon*, cannot be any other than *Palaetyrus*. Furthermore, *Bochart* contends that it was *Palaetyrus*, not the insular *Tyre*, that was discussed in those words of *Sanchuniathon* upon which the entire argument of *Scaliger* and *Vossius* rests. But the Most Reverend *Stillingfleet* refutes *Bochart* with arguments not to be despised in his *Sacred Origins, Book I, Chapter II, Section IV*. ...he [the author] foolishly guesses that he lived a little before; whereas it is well established that she <note>Likely referring to Semiramis or a similar figure mentioned on the previous page</note> preceded the *times of the Trojan War* by about eight hundred years. XV. But here also many things come to be observed. 1. Whatever kind of man *Sanchuniathon* may have been, and of whatever age, all evidence proves that he was more recent than *Moses*. *Josephus* <note>Flavius Josephus, the 1st-century Jewish historian</note> sets his calculations such that he thinks the *Exodus of the Israelites* from *Egypt* under the leadership of *Moses* preceded the *Trojan War* by almost a thousand years: and the Ancient Christians accepted this computation of *Josephus* with the greatest zeal. Hence *Justin Martyr* places *Moses*, the leader of the Jews, in the times of *Ogyges* and *Inachus*. Now, *Inachus* is believed to have formed a new kingdom at *Argos* in the *Peloponnese* in the year 2857 of the *Julian Period*. *Ogyges* reigned a little later in *Attica*, and in his age the flood occurred which is named after him, and which was recorded by *Acusilaus* to have preceded the first *Olympiad* <note>The four-year periods used by Greeks to track time, starting in 776 BCE</note> by one thousand and twenty years. *Theophilus* followed *Josephus*; *Tatian, Tertullian, and Africanus* followed *Justin*; *Clement of Alexandria* followed *Tatian*, as is his custom; and *Epiphanius* and *George Syncellus* followed *Africanus*. Nor was anyone found before *Eusebius*, as our own *Marsham* confesses, who dared to detract from the antiquity of *Moses*. *Eusebius*, however, subtracted 284 years from the ancient *Mosaic* chronological advancement <note>original: "προχρονισμῷ" (prochronismo) - referring to the practice of dating an event earlier than it actually occurred</note>. *Scaliger, Petavius, Marsham*, and many among the more recent chronologists follow him: whether rightly or wrongly, I do not care to inquire at this moment. But let us grant that *Moses* was nearly three hundred years younger than *Josephus* contends (who was perhaps more studious of antiquity than of truth in this matter): and let us suppose that he flourished in the age of *Cecrops*, the first *King of the Athenians*, in the year 3156 of the *Julian Period*; he certainly would have preceded the fall of *Troy* by almost four centuries. For this event, as *Petavius* says, most certainly fell in that year which is *Julian Period 3530*. From this it follows that if it is true, as *Suidas* recorded along with *Porphyry*, that *Sanchuniathon* existed at the time of the *Trojan War*, he is younger than *Moses* by almost four hundred years; if we agree with *Vossius* and *Scaliger*, he is younger by many more. And shall this *Sanchuniathon* be a fit witness for us of those antiquities which surpass the age of *Moses*?

XVI. But, they say, he drew his information from the most ancient monuments.

### BOOK III. CHAPTER I.

Tell me then, by what means? From the *records*, you say, *of individual cities and temples*. But who can guarantee their reliability? Even if someone did, what do those *Phoenician monuments* possess that could prove the antiquity of *Egyptian* ceremonies over *Hebrew* ones? You continue: "But he collected other wonders with marvelous industry from the *secret books of Thoth*." <note>Thoth, or Hermes Trismegistus, was the Egyptian god of wisdom to whom many mystical and scientific works were attributed.</note> However, what should be thought of those books of *Thoth* has already been explained by us at great length above; more must be added shortly.

XVII. But regardless of where *Sanchuniathon* <note>A purported Phoenician author whose works are lost but were said to predate the Trojan War.</note> obtained his information, who actually possesses *Sanchuniathon*? Whatever he wrote in his own language—that is, the *Phoenician* tongue—has long since perished. It is true that *Philo* translated it into the *Greek* language—not that *Jew* from *Alexandria*, but a certain *Pagan* from *Byblos* who was a contemporary <note>original: "σύγχρονος" (synchronos)</note> of the Emperor *Hadrian*. But who can say with what skill or what faithfulness he did so? Furthermore, nothing remains of that *Philo* except for fragments <note>original: "ἀποσπάσματα" (apospasmata)</note> found in *Eusebius* and perhaps one or other author, where among many fables you might perceive some truths as if through a mist. And indeed, I remember nothing of any real weight produced by those most learned men that would go toward confirming that monstrous assertion that the religion of the *Hebrews* is to be summoned from the sacred rites of the *Egyptians*. And so I believe I have now shown that those historians, upon whose testimony these learned men chiefly rely, are not sufficiently serious or suitable authorities for such a great matter.

XVIII. Much less can it be established from the oracle of APOLLO—which *Marsham* <note>Sir John Marsham (1602–1685), an English writer who argued for the Egyptian origins of Jewish law.</note> saw fit to place at the head of his other observations—that Divine philosophy, which demonstrates the path to blessedness, proceeded from the school of the *Egyptians*. *Eusebius* certainly had his own reasons, and weighty ones at that, for using this testimony (which the *Pagans* accepted as a Divine oracle) to fight against the *Pagans*. Among us, however, who regard oracles of that celebrated kind either as the inventions of crafty men or as the deceptive songs of evil demons, that weapon is utterly powerless. Let us be permitted to answer *Marsham* with the words of *Clement of Alexandria* in his *Exhortation to the Pagans*: *Tell us also of the useless oracles of the other divination, or rather of insane vanity: the Clarian, the Pythian, etc.* <note>original: "Διήγησαι ἡμῖν καὶ τῆς ἄλλης μαντικῆς, μᾶλλον δὲ μανικῆς ἄχρησα χρηστήρια, τὸν Κλάριον, τὸν Πύθιον &c."</note> *These are truly the insane inventions of faithless men.* <note>original: "μανικὰ ταῦτα ὡς ἀληθῶς ἀνθρώπων ἀπίστων σοφιστήρια."</note>

<margin>I.</margin>
We might be considered finished with this argument now that we have shown that Marsham and those of the <term>same opinion</term> <note>original: "ὁμοψήφοις" (homopsēphois) - those who vote the same way</note> find little or no protection in those authors and testimonies which they consider the strongest bulwarks of their cause. But it does not please us merely to weary the opponent's arms by dodging his blows; having become bolder in battle, we turn against him the very machines he had deployed against us. From the oracles with which he attempted to strike terror into us—from Sanchuniathon, Manetho, Diodorus, Plutarch, and his other veteran reserves—we shall borrow arguments to prove that even the most ancient <term>Theological Principles</term> <note>original: "Theologumena" - discourses or traditions concerning God</note> of the Egyptians which are so praised, are nearly equal to, or rather later than, the Hebrew ones.

IV. But let us also look at SANCHUNIATON <note>A Phoenician author whose work survives only in fragments; he was believed to have written before the Trojan War.</note>. He is said to have this in common with *Manetho* <note>An Egyptian priest and historian</note>: that both drew their writings from certain very ancient monuments of *Thoyt* or *Taaut*, whom the *Greeks* call *Hermes* and the *Latins* call *Mercury*. But who that *Mercury* might be lies hidden in such an obscure cloud of fables that it is quite difficult to extract historical truth from it. *Augustine* teaches that he was more recent than *Moses*. Indeed, at the time when *Moses* was born, there is found that *Atlas*, the great Astrologer and brother of *Prometheus*, who was the maternal grandfather of *Mercury the Elder*, whose grandson was that *Mercury Trismegistus* <note>"Thrice-Great Hermes," a legendary Hellenistic figure associated with magic and alchemy.</note>. *Artapanus*, an ancient author whose fragments *Eusebius* has preserved for us, relates that *Moses* was the infant of a *Judean* woman, but was adopted by the daughter of *Palmanothes*, King of the *Egyptians*, and handed down many things most useful to the human race. *For these reasons, therefore, Moses was loved by the crowds, and having been deemed worthy of god-like honor by the priests, he was addressed as Hermes, because of his interpretation of the sacred writings.* <note>original Greek: Διὰ ταῦτα οὖν τὸν Μωϋσον ὑπὸ τῶν ὄχλων ἀγαπηθῆναι, καὶ ὑπὸ τῶν ἱερέων ἰσοθέου τιμῆς καταξιωθέντα προσαγορευθῆναι Ἑρμῆν, διὰ τὴν τῶν ἱερῶν γραμμάτων ἑρμηνείαν.</note> By these deeds, he not only won the love of the people for himself, but also easily obtained honor equal to the gods from the priests, who called him *Hermes*—that is, *Mercury*, or *Interpreter*—on account of his *interpretation* <note>original Greek: ἑρμηνείαν (hermēneian)</note> of the sacred letters. If these things are true, that fabled *Theut* or *Mercury* of the *Egyptians* would be *Moses* himself.

# BOOK III. CHAPTER II.

*Justin* <note>original: "Justinus"; referring to the Roman historian Marcus Junianus Justinus</note>: *Whom, besides the paternal inheritance of knowledge, even the beauty of his form commended.*

<margin>Book 36.</margin>
Mercury was the God of Shepherds, and they say that he himself pastured sheep. Moses led a pastoral life, and tended the sheep of his father-in-law Jethro, and he stood at the head of the Israelites, who declared themselves to have been shepherds of sheep from their very origin. The ancients called Mercury *Nomion* <note>original: "Νόμιον"; a Greek title meaning "The Pastoral One"</note>: which some indeed derive from the pasturing of cattle, but Phurnutus <note>Lucius Annaeus Cornutus, a Stoic philosopher</note>, as cited in Josephus, more suitably derives it from the bringing of Laws <note>A wordplay on the Greek "nomos" (law) and "nomios" (pastoral)</note>. And this fits Moses aptly, who is the most ancient and noble of all Lawgivers.

<margin>Book 1 against Apion.</margin>
Mercury is portrayed as a trickster: was this perhaps because of the wonders performed by Moses throughout the entire course of his life? The Caduceus of Mercury is much celebrated, being a rod, entwined with serpents, the worker of portents: surely it is like that miraculous rod of Moses which, when cast upon the ground, crawled like a serpent, swallowed the rods of the Egyptian sorcerers, and thereafter performed wonderful works. Mercury was held to be thievish, and the God of thieves. Moses was the authority for the Israelites to cheat the Egyptians of their gold and silver vessels and much clothing. Whence Trogus <note>Pompeius Trogus, a Roman historian</note> says of Moses: *Having become the leader of the exiles, he carried away the sacred objects of the Egyptians by theft.*

VI. Mercury was considered and called the God of Ways, or the God of Paths, and the presiding deity of journeys. Phurnutus is the authority for him being called *Hegemonion* <note>original: "Ἡγεμόνιον"; meaning "The Leader" or "Guide"</note>. Moses showed himself as the leader of the way for the Israelites through the desert and pathless places for forty years. Mercury was held to be the messenger and mediator <term>sequester: a middleman or agent</term> of gods and men, who reported the commands of the Gods to men, and the prayers of men to the Gods: Moses was also a *mesites* <note>original: "μεσίτης"; Greek for "mediator"</note>, an intermediary between God and the Israelites, and his frequent journeys, and long stays on the summit of Mount Sinai, and his frequent conversations with the deity, and the commands of God brought to men, and the vows and promises of the Israelites reported back to God, are celebrated in the sacred writings. The Egyptians attributed the invention of all things and of universal wisdom to their Mercury <note>referring to Hermes Trismegistus</note>. Moses, however, embraced the beginnings of all things in his books, not only of the world and nature, but also of Religion and Theology, as well as the history of the human race and of animals, Geography, Politics, military discipline, and many other subjects.

<margin>Miscellanies, Book 1.</margin>

Therefore, those things which are consistent with truth and piety, and are said to have been inserted into the writings of *Sanchuniathon* and *Manetho* from the written commentaries of *Mercury*, we can opine—not without reason—to have been sought from the fountains of *Moses*. For what would you expect from a man who had no certain knowledge of where the Israelites originated, nor by what occasion they came into Egypt or departed from it; nor who Moses was, whether Hebrew or Egyptian; nor had he learned to distinguish the times of David (in which Jerusalem was finally occupied by the Jews and built up and enlarged) from the time of the exit from Egypt? Many *Canaanites* were driven by the same necessity of avoiding famine as *Abraham*. Certainly *Josephus* <note>Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Jewish historian</note>, in *The Jewish War, Book VI, chapter XI*, joins an almost infinite multitude to him as companions on his journey. Although these descriptions may smack of <term>rhetorical flourishes</term> <note>original Greek: τὰς τῶν ῥητόρων ληκύθους; literally "the oil-flasks of the rhetoricians," meaning over-embellished speech</note>, they would not have been phrased this way if *Abraham* had descended alone with only his immediate family. *Polyhistor*, quoting *Artapanus*, adds: <term>many of those who came with him remained in Egypt because of the prosperity of the land</term> <note>original Greek: τῶν τέτῳ συνελθόντων πολλὲς ἐν Ἀιγύπτῳ καταμεῖναι διὰ τὴν ἐυδαιμονίαν τῆς χώρας</note>. *Of those who had descended with him, not a few, enticed by the richness of the region, stayed in Egypt.*

VII. *Manetho* <note>An ancient Egyptian priest and historian</note> continues, stating that these foreigners took possession of *Egypt* <term>easily and without a fight</term> <note>original Greek: ῥᾳδίως καὶ ἀμαχητὶ</note>. You might not absurdly understand this as referring to *Abraham*; for both for the sake of Sarah (as the Scripture says) and because of the singular reputation for wisdom which he imparted to the *Egyptians*—as *Nicolas of Damascus, Eupolemus, Artapanus*, and others testify in the works of *Eusebius*—he was raised to such great wealth that he could be said to have, in a sense, *plundered Egypt*. This happened, says *Manetho*, under *King Timaus*, against whom <term>God blew a contrary wind</term> <note>original Greek: ὁ Θεὸς ἀντέπνευσεν</note>, and was opposed to him. Who does not recognize in this *Timaus* that *Pharaoh* whom the Lord struck with great plagues because of *Abraham* and *Sarah, Abraham's wife*? (*Genesis 12:17*). *Manetho* continues: they brought great disasters upon the *Egyptians*. He errs not in the core of the matter, but in certain circumstances of the event. For this should not have been attributed to the injustice of others, but to the intemperance of *Pharaoh*. Nor was *Abraham* the cause, yet he was the occasion for the calamity brought by the Divine. What sort of calamity it was, the Scripture does not express. *Josephus* is the authority that it was a plague and a popular sedition; *Philostratus* says it was unusual diseases and horrendous tortures; *Polyhistor*, quoting *Eupolemus*, says: <term>It happened</term>, he says, <term>that both his house and the people were destroyed</term> <note>original Greek: Συνέβη δὲ φθείρεσθαι ἀυτῶ τὸν οἶκον καὶ τὸν λαὸν</note>.

# BOOK III. CHAPTER III.

...it is said that those who were called shepherds were also named "captives" in their own sacred books; this also fits the Israelites exactly. For, as **Josephus** <note>Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian</note> rightly notes, they were not called captives by the **Egyptians** without reason, since **Joseph** himself described himself as a captive to the King of the **Egyptians**; and the Israelites were subsequently held as captives by the Pharaohs and treated most poorly. If we refer these events to the age of **Abraham**, contrary to what was done by **Eusebius** <note>An early Christian historian and Bishop of Caesarea</note>, who preferred to refer them to **Joseph**, then the difficulties which **Scaliger** <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger, a 16th-century scholar of chronology</note> raised regarding the dates of these dynasties are, if not entirely removed, certainly greatly diminished. Nor is it necessary to trim everything to the quick <note>original: "ad vivum omnia resecare" - meaning to be overly precise or literal</note>, since truth must be searched for amidst innumerable lies.

X. Furthermore, regarding the story that under King **Alisfragmuthosis** the defeated shepherds lost the rest of **Egypt** and lived for a time confined within the narrow limits of a certain place; this much agrees with the truth: that while the **Hebrews**, during **Joseph's** lifetime, held (so to speak) all of **Egypt** under the kings; after his death, as if driven from the rest of **Egypt**, they took refuge in the land of **Goshen** <note>original: "Gessen"</note>. They contained themselves within the borders of that province, which was indeed fertile for grazing, but very narrow. The force applied by **Thummosis** <note>original: "Themosi"</note> to besiege, conquer, and destroy them corresponds to those most unjust and cruel afflictions by which the **Pharaohs** endeavored to exterminate the entire race. The rest—concerning the treaty by virtue of which the shepherds departed **Egypt** freely with all their possessions, the journey through the desert, the arrival in **Judea**, and the building of **Jerusalem**—designate the **Hebrews** so clearly that there seems to be hardly any room left for doubt. The fables attached concerning the lepers, and whom they might refer to, will be explained shortly.

XI. It was not difficult for **Marsham** <note>Sir John Marsham, an English writer on chronology</note> to collect many discrepancies by which the foolish fables of **Manetho** <note>An Egyptian priest and historian who wrote in Greek</note> recede by a very long distance from the truth of the **Mosaic** history. However, even if these discrepancies were many more and greater, he will not prove that the same event is not being narrated by both. Moses relates it truly and without bias, as it happened in his own time and that of his parents; whereas Manetho, a mere infant compared to **Moses**, has shrouded much in a dark cloud of fables, partly from ignorance of antiquity and partly from malice <note>original: "ærugine" - literally 'rust' or 'canker', implying spite or ill-will</note>.

# EGYPTIAN STUDIES

The venerable name of *Marsham* <note>Sir John Marsham, a 17th-century English chronicler</note> is not a tribunal to be feared in deciding this little dispute. Therefore, that famous *Grotius* <note>Hugo Grotius, the influential Dutch jurist and theologian</note>, when he had said in Book 1 of *On the Truth of the Christian Religion, Section XVI*, that regarding the departure of the Israelites from Egypt, not a few things could be brought forward from the Egyptians Manetho, Lysimachus, and Chæremon; he speaks thus in his Notes:

> The passages are found in Josephus's *Against Apion* <note>A famous defense of Judaism by the historian Flavius Josephus</note>, full of lies, as they originated from a nation always most hostile to the Jews; from which source Tacitus also drew his own accounts. It appears, however, from all these sources compared among themselves, that the Hebrews originated from the Assyrians, took possession of a part of Egypt, and there led a pastoral life: but being later oppressed by servile labors, they departed from Egypt, with certain Egyptians even accompanying them, under the leadership of Moses, and through the lands of the Arabs they finally arrived in Syrian Palestine, **AND THERE THEY FOLLOWED INSTITUTIONS CONTRARY TO THE INSTITUTIONS OF THE EGYPTIANS.** Furthermore, how the Egyptian writers—some among themselves, and each within their own accounts—conflict with one another in the lies they have sprinkled into this history, and by how many centuries those accounts are surpassed by the antiquity of the books of Moses, the most learned Josephus excellently demonstrates in that book.

Thus far *Grotius*.

XIII. No less appropriately to the present matter writes *Nicolaus Abramus* <note>Nicolas Abram, 1589–1655</note>, an interpreter of Sacred Scripture at Pont-à-Mousson, a learned chronologist and historian from the Society of Jesus. He, unless my mind utterly deceives me, has hit the nail on the head and judiciously uncovered the origin of the entire fable.

> *The Egyptians*, he says, *attempted to obscure the affairs of the Hebrews—from whom no small infamy redounded upon their own nation—with fables and lies, if they could not abolish them entirely. Since they could not confess without infamy to their own nation that the Hebrews (whose ancestors had both saved a starving Egypt from destruction and raised the kings of Egypt themselves to the highest wealth through the wisdom of Joseph) had been most unjustly reduced to slavery by their descendants, and that the entire name of the Egyptians was afflicted by various disasters and almost deleted by slaughter because the Divine Power was avenging the injury inflicted on the Hebrews; lest they be believed to be either enemies of God or defeated by slaves and vile bondsmen, for that reason they attempted to disguise such clear truth with various deceptive fables. Therefore, since they could not deny that shepherds setting out from Syria had ruled the kingdom for some time, and had returned to that same Syria by right of recovery, and yet they did not wish to confess that Joseph had obtained the deputy-kingship in Egypt by virtue and benefits rather than by force and injuries—*

### BOOK III. CHAPTER III.

...that their dignity had been compromised, they invented a story that Egypt had been harassed and occupied by certain most obscure shepherds. They claimed that these shepherds—once the spirits of the Egyptians had been raised to recover their liberty—were eventually forced to leave the borders of Egypt and migrated into Palestine in Syria. There, they supposedly founded Jerusalem. Later, they were said to have been called back to help by certain leprous and polluted Egyptians who had been condemned to the stone quarries and were rebelling under the leadership of Moses. These groups together allegedly afflicted Egypt with great disasters until they were finally expelled by the Egyptians, retreated, and admitted those leprous Egyptians into their own city.

XIV. They therefore fabricated two separate departures. The first was after the death of Joseph, following the end of the "Shepherd Dynasty" <note>The author refers to the Hyksos, whom Josephus and others identified with the early Israelites</note>; this was likely because at nearly that same time, the Ephraimites (descended from Joseph) set out from Egypt into Canaan and invaded the territories of the Gathites with arms. However, as it is said in 1 Chronicles 7:21: *The men of Gath who were born in that land killed them, because they came down to take away their livestock.* It seems a pretext for this lie was sought from this excursion of the Ephraimites. The second departure they claimed was not of shepherds, but an expulsion of lepers, whose leader was Moses. This was a truly crafty fabrication. They did this not only to claim Moses for themselves, but also to shift blame. Just as the Italians call the "venereal plague" <note>Syphilis</note>—which arose at the time the French held Naples—the "French disease," while the French conversely call it the "Neapolitan disease," so too did they want to claim the first origin of leprosy came not from themselves (where it had actually arisen), but from the Hebrews. In reality, the disease had been sent upon the Egyptians by God's vengeance for the wrongs they did to the Hebrews. Artapanus, a very ancient writer cited in Eusebius, is the authority for the claim that the Pharaoh who sought to kill Moses was the first of all mortals to be seized by elephantiasis or leprosy, and thus breathed out his unhappy soul. This punishment even overflowed to his descendants. For as Pliny writes: <margin>*Preparation for the Gospel, Book IX, Chapter XXVII*</margin> *This evil is peculiar to Egypt; and when it falls upon Kings, it is a funeral knell for the people. For in the baths, they used to warm themselves in human blood as a medicine.* <margin>*Natural History, Book XXVI, Chapter I*</margin> *These are the words of Nicolaus Abramus.* <note>Nicolaus Abramus (1589–1655) was a Jesuit scholar known for his work on biblical chronology and history.</note>

XV. I have not been reluctant to insert these accounts here, however lengthy they may be; both because they lend excellent light to antiquity, and because they greatly support the case we are making. For all these things are gathered to prove that the Egyptians of a later age, who became famous for the monuments of history they wrote, were deceptive regarding the antiquity of the Hebrews...

# BOOK III. CHAPTER IV.

The Egyptians, and the Greeks who were ignorant of the truth, seem to have taken a great part of these stories from the history of *Moses*: although they are wrapped in so many fables that they cannot easily be carved out <note>original: "exsculpi," meaning to extract the truth from the surrounding myth</note>. Not that I would dare to claim the entire fable of *Osiris* and *Typhon* is more recent than *Moses*; for I have already deduced above that the *Israelites'* calf in the desert was derived from the worship of *Osiris*. But rather, as usually happens, they interpolated the ancient fable with many additions of fiction, the causes of which later generations understood very little. With wonderful skill and incredible sagacity, *Bochart* <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a famous French Protestant scholar of biblical geography and zoology</note> uncovered the hidden truth; I could never speak so magnificently of that man's praises that his erudition would not surpass it. Let it not be a cause of resentment if we provide in summary what he pursued more extensively.

II. They tell that *Typhon*, the brother of King *Osiris*, born of the same mother though from a different father, plotted many things against the king, having recruited seventy-two men into a conspiracy, and attempted this with the help of the Queen of *Ethiopia*, who stood by him. They say that after various crimes, *Typhon* finally fled riding on a female donkey; and having escaped, he fathered sons named *Hierosolymus* <note>Jerusalem</note> and *Judæus* <note>Judah</note>. Under these fictions, *Moses* lies hidden. They derive *Typhon* from a royal lineage and from the same mother as the king because *Pharaoh's* daughter had adopted the infant *Moses*; that *Pharaoh* under whom *Moses* (now eighty years old) performed so many miracles could have been her son. They imagine seventy-two men conspired because seventy elders were added to *Moses* and *Aaron* to rule over the *Israelites* <note>The author accounts for the extra two by including Moses and Aaron in the count</note>. The Queen of *Ethiopia*, his companion, was the wife of *Moses*, whom the most ancient versions of Scripture call an *Ethiopian woman*, and whom *Jewish* histories assert was the daughter of the King of *Ethiopia*. The flight of *Typhon* is the departure of *Moses* from *Egypt*. They say he was carried by a donkey, which is how *Moses* is described in *Exodus* 4:20. And they say he fled for seven days, just as *Tacitus* writes of the *Jews* fleeing from *Egypt*, and *Trogus* writes of *Moses*. This error was born from the fact that the Law designates the seventh day for rest. Above all, it is ridiculous that they assign *Hierosolymus* and *Judæus* as sons to *Typhon*. Yet even from this, you may gather that the leader of the *Israelites* is signified by the name of *Typhon*, by whom they were led out of *Egypt* into the borders of *Canaan* and finally became masters of *Jerusalem* and thus of all *Judea*.

III. But nothing is more impudent than that they impute the crimes of their own king to *Typhon*—that is, to *Moses*. The King had ordered by edict that all the sons of the *Israelites* should be thrown into the *Nile*. Against this edict, the mother of *Moses*...

# EGYPTIAN MATTERS

...an obedient life, when she placed him, enclosed in an ark, upon the bank of the river. But in *Plutarch* <note>Plutarch (c. 46 – 120 AD) was a Greek philosopher and biographer whose work "On Isis and Osiris" is a major source for Egyptian myth.</note> on the contrary, as if the roles were reversed, *Typhon* casts King *Osiris* into the *Nile* enclosed in an ark. And so that you may know the same event is being discussed under changed names, *Osiris* is said to have been cast in through the *Tanitic* mouth of the *Nile*, and from there carried to *Byblos*. Truly, *Moses* is also believed to have been exposed near *Tanis* <note>original: "Tanim"</note>, where the Royal Palace then was (Psalm 88:12), and there he was found by the king's daughter. And the ark lay hidden in *Suph* (Exodus 2:3), that is, in the *Nilotic seaweed* <note>original: "alga Nilotica"</note>, which is *papyrus* in the broader sense of the word. Indeed, the ark itself was a *papyrus ark* <note>original Hebrew: "tebat gome"</note>. *Josephus* <note>First-century Jewish historian.</note> calls it a "woven papyrus vessel" <note>original Greek: "plegma byblinon"</note>. *Suidas* calls it a "little chest made of papyrus" <note>original Greek: "kibotion ek byblou"</note>. *Clement of Alexandria* calls it "a vessel made of the local papyrus" <note>original Greek: "ek byblou tēs epichōriēs skeuos"</note>. For there the *Byblos*, or papyrus, grows in great abundance. From this was born the fable that this ark was carried from the *Tanitic* mouth to the city of *Byblos*, and found there by *Isis*. Whereas in reality, it was "in the papyrus" <note>original Greek: "en tē byblō"</note>—that is, in the papyrus thicket—and in a "chest of papyrus" <note>original Greek: "thibē ek byblou"</note>, that *Moses* was both placed and found.

IV. Furthermore, they say that *Typhon* was red in color: perhaps attributing this to the *leader of the Hebrews* because the Scripture attributes it to the *Father of the Idumeans*, who was called *Edom* from his red color (Genesis 25:30). Truly, there is no one who does not know that *Idumeans* and *Jews* are sometimes referred to interchangeably. But there is no need to resort to that: if *Artapanus* <note>An ancient historian of Jewish origin who lived in Alexandria.</note> truly asserts in the works of *Eusebius* that *Moses* was "tall and ruddy" <note>original Greek: "makron kai pyrrhakē"</note>. Nor does it stand in the way that he is praised everywhere, in both sacred and secular literature, for the extraordinary beauty of his form. For although the color of *red* hair is placed by others among the signs of an evil mind, it is nonetheless established that it was approved by the ancients from what is said of *David* (1 Samuel 16:12): *He was ruddy, and beautiful to look upon, and of a handsome face.* With which these words of *Festus* <note>Sextus Pompeius Festus, a 2nd-century Roman grammarian.</note> are in harmony: *"Rutilius"* signifies red, a color which even ancient women were fond of.

V. Nor is it without purpose that one reads that *Typhon* tore *Osiris* into fourteen parts. For *Moses* had torn away just as many parts—that is, just as many peoples—from the body of the kingdom. For from the twelve sons of *Jacob* were born thirteen tribes; namely, one from each, except that from *Joseph* two arose, specifically *Ephraim* and *Manasseh*. These thirteen tribes are just as many parts torn from the body of *Osiris*. To which is added a fourteenth, namely the "mixed multitude" <note>Referring to the non-Israelites who left Egypt with Moses (Exodus 12:38).</note>...

->BOOK III. CHAPTER IV.<-

...many, who went up with them. Exodus 12:38. The Hebrews prove from the *Tanchuma* <note>A collection of Jewish homilies on the Torah</note> that these numbered up to forty thousand, and had as leaders *Jannes and Jambres* <note>Traditionally identified as the Egyptian magicians who opposed Moses</note>.

VI. To this same *Typhon* they attribute evil and noxious animals: because *Moses* used frogs, lice, dog-flies, and locusts for the destruction of the Egyptians. Nor are there lacking those who think the shadow of the earth, into which the Moon falls when it eclipses, should be designated by the name of *Typhon*. This is because it came to mind that he had brought three days of darkness upon Egypt. Furthermore, the Egyptian priests detest the sea, and call salt the "foam of *Typhon*," forbidding it to be placed on the table. They are surely mindful that at *Moses’* command, the flowing sea overwhelmed the king and all the king's forces in such a way that not even one survived as a messenger of the disaster. From this, it may be believed that the name of *Typhon* was bestowed upon *Moses* by the Egyptians. For just as in Hebrew <term>צוּף</term> (*tzuph* <note>meaning to flow or overflow</note>), so in Syriac <term>טוף</term> (*Tuph*) means to inundate, and <term>טופן</term> (*Tuphan*) denotes an inundation to both Syrians and Arabs. It is therefore consistent with the truth that the Egyptians, who borrowed many words from the Syrians and Arabs, used that very word and named *Moses* from it; because by the overflowing of the Red Sea, he had drowned the King and the Nobles, as well as an immense multitude of their common people.

VII. Nor should we omit here what the Scripture teaches briefly, yet in express words: that on the night the *Israelites* departed from *Egypt*, the Lord executed judgments against all the Gods of *Egypt*. Exodus 12:12; Numbers 33:4. However, it did not express what kind of judgment this was. The *Chaldean Paraphrast* <note>The Targum, an Aramaic translation/interpretation of the Hebrew Bible</note> relates four judgments: that idols of cast metal were melted, those of stone were shattered, those of clay were broken into pieces, and those of wood were reduced to ashes. Others explain it differently. It shall suffice to know that the true God, through the ministry of *Moses*, severely punished the fabricated deities of Egypt: since the memory of the punishment then inflicted lasted for many ages, although buried and nearly overwhelmed by portentous fables. For it pertains to this that they fabulously claim the Gods, out of fear of *Typhon*, hid for some time in the forms of various animals. By this fable, it seems to be signified that the Egyptians, out of fear of *Moses* and the *Israelites* departing from *Egypt* in troops, removed their idols from the temples and hid them in cattle stalls and dung-heaps, or even in the dens and lurking-places of wild beasts, so that they might lie hidden more safely.

->E G Y P T I A N  M A T T E R S<-

VIII. However it may be, the Egyptians—having been punished in so many ways by Typhon, or *Moses* <note>The author identifies the Egyptian monster Typhon with the biblical Moses to show how the Egyptians demonized their former adversary</note>—nevertheless worshipped him in some manner, driven by a slave-like fear; but they did so in the same way the *Romans worshipped Fever* and the *Greeks the Furies*, namely, so that they might not cause harm. And so they were inconsistent and varied in his worship. For sometimes, as *Plutarch* is the authority, they soothe and soften him with sacrifices, but conversely, at other times during certain festivals of theirs, they degrade him and heap insults upon him.

IX. Who would deny that this comparison has been quite ingeniously established by that most learned man? Although it may not hold the force of a full demonstration in a mind stubborn in its purpose, it nevertheless seems much preferable to the cold commentaries of those who claim that certain ceremonies of the *Israelites* in their atonement rites were summoned from *Typhonic* <note>original: "Typhonicis"</note> sacred rites. Truly, that opinion was refuted by us long ago. Our intention now was merely to infer that it cannot be proven from *Diodorus* and *Plutarch* that the *Hebrews* took their sacred rites from the *Egyptians*; but on the contrary, those religious antiquities of the *Egyptians* which they narrate reek of *Mosaic* history, though—according to the genius of that nation and the custom of those times—they are wrapped in idle and hateful fables.

# BOOK III. CHAPTER V.

...by that name Noah is signified. Truly, when the men of the first generation, being exceedingly insolent, perpetrated wicked deeds—neither observing oaths, nor receiving guests, nor being touched by any mercy for suppliants—for that reason they were punished with an incredible calamity. For immediately the earth poured forth much water, and there were great rains, and the rivers ran down larger than usual, and the sea rose up until everything was inundated by the waters, and everyone perished. *Deucalion* <note>In Greek mythology, Deucalion is the son of Prometheus and the survivor of the great flood, serving as the Hellenic counterpart to Noah.</note> alone, however, was left among men for a second generation, on account of both his prudence and his piety. He was saved in this manner: he climbed into a certain large *Ark* which he possessed, having placed within it both his children and his wife. Furthermore, as he was entering, there came to the same place boars, and horses, and kinds of lions, and serpents, and whatever else feeds upon the earth, all in pairs of every kind. He received them all to himself. And these animals did not harm him at all, but there was a great concord among them—*Jupiter* <note>The Roman name for the king of the gods, used here to translate the Greek 'Zeus'.</note> so disposing it—and they all sailed together in one ark as long as the water prevailed. These are almost the exact words of *Lucian* <note>Lucian of Samosata (c. 125–180 AD), a Syrian-Greek satirist who described the flood of Deucalion in his work 'On the Syrian Goddess'.</note>. Who, then, is so dull-witted <note>original: "obesæ naris," literally "of a fat nose," a Latin idiom for lacking discernment.</note> that he does not smell the *Mosaic* history of *Noah* here?

II. ### CHAPTER VI.

### That Circumcision did not pass from the Egyptians to the Hebrews.

I. SO FAR, unless I am mistaken, we have shown by no slight reasons that it cannot be proven that those things prescribed by God in the sacred ceremonies of the *Hebrews* were more ancient among the *Egyptians*: both because those who are praised as witnesses in this cause are many centuries more recent than *Moses*: and because they themselves occasionally admit that they have discovered nothing certain regarding that most ancient antiquity: finally, because they narrate many things about *Egyptian* antiquities which even a moderately sharp-eyed person would easily perceive were taken from *Moses*. But they also attribute some things to the *Egyptians* as *inventors* which it is manifest were in use among the *Hebrews* before the *Egyptians*. Among these, the rite of CIRCUMCISION stands out.

# ON EGYPTIAN MATTERS

That circumcision was given by God to *Abraham* as a seal of the covenant, yet some choose to side with *Herodotus* and *Diodorus* <note>Herodotus and Diodorus Siculus were ancient Greek historians who claimed the Egyptians practiced circumcision before the Hebrews.</note> on this matter, is truly a wonder to hear and must not be passed over without indignation. Unless all faith and reverence for the Sacred Scriptures has perished among us, we holily acknowledge that *Abraham* did not cut away his foreskin by his own counsel or out of a desire to emulate the *Egyptians*, nor was he the author of doing the same, but that it was done by Divine command.

III. Nor was there any reason for God to wish the genitals of his servant to be cut according to the example of the *Egyptians*. *Abraham* was not so stiff-necked, nor seized by such an insane love for *Egyptian* rituals, that it would have been fitting for Divine mercy and wisdom to gratify him by indulging in this ceremony—lest, forsooth, He should lose a servant accustomed and addicted to such things. Such are the inventions of very learned men <note>A reference to scholars like John Spencer or Maimonides, who argued that some Mosaic laws were concessions to existing pagan customs.</note> regarding the *Israelites* of a later age. But a ninety-nine-year-old man, after he had set aside all family ties for the sake of the Deity out of obedience and love for religion, could only be compelled by the mandate of that same Deity to set aside shame and undertake the sacrament given to him by God. His age was quite unfit for such an action and more inconvenient for healing, and his person was seemingly too dignified to allow himself to be stripped bare before his household.

IV. And so far was God from intending to bind a servant already devoted to Him to religious constancy by the lure of some customary or "decorous" and desired rite—as some believe was done in other cases—that, on the contrary, by this entire institution He cast reproach upon all such worldly and insane wisdom. Indeed, the hidden wisdom of God appears in this matter: He willed a rite so blush-inducing and almost shameful to be the seal of His grace in the Old Testament, just as in the New Testament He placed the foundation of that same grace in a thing even more shameful; namely, the cross of Christ, so that He might thus put all wisdom of the flesh to shame. Our *Calvin* <note>John Calvin, the Protestant Reformer.</note> says, in his characteristically bold way: *At first glance, this command could seem very absurd and ridiculous. A sacred covenant is being treated, by which righteousness, salvation, and happiness are promised, and by which the seed of Abraham is distinguished from the rest of the nations so that it may be holy and blessed. Who would say it is fitting for the badge of such a great mystery to be placed in the private parts? But it was necessary for Abraham to become a fool [in the eyes of the world], so that he might show himself obedient to God—*

...reports that of all people, the Colchians <note>An ancient region on the Black Sea, modern-day Georgia.</note>, the Egyptians, and the Ethiopians were circumcised "from the beginning" <note>original: ἀπ' ἀρχῆς</note>, that is, from ancient times. He claims the Phoenicians and those Syrians who live in Palestine admit they received this custom from the Egyptians. First, he is mistaken in imagining that the Colchians practiced circumcision "from the beginning." Bochart has proved with many great arguments that these Colchians are the same people Moses calls the Casluhites <note>Genesis 10:14</note>, who were descendants <note>original: ἀπογόνους</note> of the Egyptians and ancestors <note>original: προγόνους</note> of the Philistines. Yet it is certain the Casluhites migrated from Egypt before the time of Abraham; for the Philistines who sprang from them had already driven out the Avvites and possessed Palestine (Genesis 10:14) and had their own kings, with whom Abraham and Isaac made treaties. The very fact that the Philistines were *not* circumcised proves that the rite of circumcision was not in use among the Casluhites at the time the Philistines branched off from them. However, it is believable that the Colchians—who were well aware they were of Egyptian stock, as Herodotus expressly states—adopted this rite several centuries after their migration so that they might "act like their fathers" in this regard. Diodorus confirms this, explicitly stating that the Colchians, being of Egyptian descent, took the rite of circumcision from them, "the ancient custom remaining among the colonists" <note>original: διαμονῇ & νομίμῳ παρὰ τοῖς ἀποίκοις</note>.

IX. Secondly, Herodotus is also quite mistaken when he says that the Syrians in Palestine admit they have circumcision from the Egyptians and Colchians. As Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, the Jewish-Roman historian.</note> rightly observed, among those in Palestine, only the Jews are circumcised. Nor did Josephus dodge the accusation by merely noting this, as Marsham <note>Sir John Marsham, an English writer on chronology.</note> suspects. For the conclusion is easy: the Jews admit nothing less than that they owe their circumcision to the Egyptians; on the contrary, they claim the Egyptians learned it from Joseph.

### BOOK III. CHAPTER VI. 227

X. The third error of Herodotus is his assertion that the *Phoenicians* adopted circumcision from the *Egyptians*. By *Phoenicians*—distinguished here from the Syrian inhabitants of Palestine—Ammonius, in his work *On the Difference of Words*, understands the *Idumeans*. <note>Ammonius of Alexandria was a 4th-century grammarian.</note> *The Idumeans were not originally Jews, but Phoenicians* <note>original Greek: Ἰδουμαῖοι δὲ τὸ ἐξ ἀρχῆθεν οὐκ Ἰουδαῖοι, ἀλλὰ Φοίνικες</note>. Truly, the Idumeans received circumcision not from the *Egyptians*, but from *Esau* (who is also called *Edom*).

XI. Therefore, if we wish to speak the truth, this is the actual progression of circumcision. *Abraham* was the first to receive it from God. From *Abraham*, through *Ishmael*, the *Arabs* received it, and perhaps the *Ethiopians*; through the sons of *Keturah* <note>Abraham's second wife</note>, other nations descended from them received it. Through *Isaac* came the *Edomites* (the posterity of *Esau*) and the *Israelites* (the descendants of *Jacob*). As for where the *Egyptians* obtained it, I will not say with absolute certainty. Some credit the *Arabs* here; others suspect the *Israelites*. This latter view seems more probable to me for reasons to be alleged in their proper place. From the *Egyptians*, the *Colchians* <note>An ancient kingdom on the Black Sea, modern Georgia</note> have it. From the ancient *Arabs* and *Ishmaelites*, the same rite of circumcising flowed down to the *Saracens*.

<margin>From the Saracens to the Turks.</margin>

They held them in greater veneration, professing a shared kinship with them. On this matter, I call the daughter of Pharaoh as a most wealthy witness; when she found Moses on the bank of the flowing river, she immediately recognized him as circumcised and declared him a child of the Hebrew race. Now, if the custom of circumcising had likewise belonged to the Egyptians, how could she have come to that knowledge by this sign? From this, one may also suspect that such mutilation was not the practice of all Egyptians, but only of the priests, so that they might be separated from the profane; whereas among the Hebrews, it was always observed by the whole people. Thus far Pierius <note>Pierio Valeriano, a Renaissance humanist</note>: let wiser men judge the force of his arguments.

# BOOK III. CHAPTER VII.

<margin>The story of Jephthah</margin> ...translators have transferred the history of *Jephthah* to this subject, which is specific to him. XIII. The historical *Saturn*, according to *Theophilus* <note>Theophilus of Antioch, a 2nd-century Christian apologist</note>, is only 322 years older than the *Trojan* war, which makes him nearly a contemporary of *Moses*. XIV. *Arnobius’s* learned calculation regarding the age of *Saturn*. XV. And yet even this, in the opinion of *Schotanus*, is more generous than is just. XVI. *Petavius’s* calculation. XVII. *Typhonic* rites <note>Rites associated with the Egyptian chaos-god Typhon/Set</note> contribute nothing to this matter.

I. It is of no great importance to the cause we are discussing whether *human sacrifice* <note>original: "ἀνθρωποθυσία"</note> was in use among the *Phoenicians*, *Egyptians*, or other neighboring peoples before that temptation by which God wished to test the faith and obedience of *Abraham*, or whether instead the nations were seduced by the illusions of *Satan* into such unspeakable sacrifices by taking an example from the history of *Abraham*. For although God tested the obedience of his servant by the command of this thing, since he prevented the outcome, he showed by that very act that the libation of human blood is displeasing to him: and he forbade the *killing of children* <note>original: "παιδοκτονίαν"</note> to his people under penalty of death. Leviticus 20:2. However, because it pleased *Marsham* <note>Sir John Marsham, an English writer on chronology</note> to affirmatively decide the first part of this question, come, let us follow him along his own path, and examine the reasons he produces in order.

II. In the first place, he mentions those whom *Philo the Jew* makes mention of, who contended that nothing new was practiced by *Abraham*, and he praises *Philo* himself, who confesses that the sacrificing of sons was an ancient superstition among the *Barbarians*. But truly, this is to play games with the reader, since *Philo* has nothing in that passage which is not entirely prepared to refute *Marsham’s* opinion. We shall exhibit the matter according to the truth, as becomes honorable men. *Philo*, therefore, after he had praised that excellent deed of *Abraham* in an ornate and copious manner, complains that there is no lack of *malicious calumniators, accustomed to vituperate rather than to praise* <note>original: "φιλαπεχθήμονας καὶ πάντα διαβάλλοντας, οἷς ψόγοι πρὸ ἐπαίνου τιμᾶν ἐθίζονται"</note>, to whom this deed does not seem so great and wonderful, since various examples of it exist everywhere and have existed from of old. This accusation of theirs *Philo* calls the *pursuit of the envious and bitterness* <note>original: "βασκανίαν καὶ πικρίαν"</note>: and he refutes it with many reasons.

# EGYPTIAN MATTERS

III. Finally, the matter comes down to this. Those who once sacrificed their children did so partly out of *custom*, as is said of some Barbarians, and partly because they could not otherwise ward off great *evils* and calamities that resisted human help from their cities. Of these, some offered their own *unwillingly*, being forced by those more powerful. Others were driven by the *fear* of men, and others by a *desire for glory* and fame. Then, in order, he shows that *Abraham* was far removed from all these causes. I omit other points as being foreign to our purpose; that which he discusses regarding *custom* is what we must now consider. He proves that *Abraham* did not do this out of custom: because <note>original Greek: "ἔθος μὲν οὖν τὸ ἐπὶ παιδοκτονίᾳ..."</note> *certainly the custom of sacrificing children was accepted neither in Babylon, nor in Mesopotamia, nor by the Chaldean nation, among whom he was educated and spent the greater part of his life; let no one think that the imagination of that evil seemed lighter to him due to being accustomed to it.*

IV. A little later, sticking to the same observation, he expands the point thus: <note>original Greek: "Ἔπειτα οὐκ ὄντος ἔθους..."</note> *Furthermore, since there was no custom in that region—as there perhaps is among some—of sacrificing humans, which through continuity usually weakens the perception of such horrors, he himself was going to be the first to begin a most new and unusual example, which it seems to me no one would have endured, even if his soul had been fashioned of iron or adamant.* <note>Adamant refers to an unbreakable, diamond-like stone.</note> Let the fair reader now judge whether there exists anything in this discourse of *Philo the Jew* <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish philosopher who sought to harmonize the Torah with Greek philosophy.</note> that *Marsham* <note>Sir John Marsham, a 17th-century chronicler who argued that Jewish rituals were derived from Egyptian ones.</note> can seize for his own argument, unless perhaps it is the bitter attack of those detractors and envious people whom *Philo* refutes; which in itself ought to create no small prejudice against a cause that is not very probable.

V. *Philo of Byblos* <note>A writer who claimed to translate the works of the ancient Phoenician Sanchuniathon.</note> follows *Philo the Hebrew*, who, on the authority of *Sanchuniathon*, traces the first <term>child-sacrifice</term> <note>original Greek: υἱοθυσίαν (huiothysian) - specifically the sacrifice of a son.</note> back to *Saturn*. But how much credit should be given to *Sanchuniathon*—a fabulous writer and, if compared with the age of *Abraham*, a newcomer—whenever he prattles about such ancient matters, has been explained by us more extensively above. And who, after all,

# BOOK III. CHAPTER VII.

Who was that *Saturn*? If we set aside the falsehoods of fable and pursue the truth of history, either there was truly no *Saturn* in the nature of things, or *Noah* lies hidden under that name. Following *Goropius Becanus*, *Vossius*, and countless others, *Bochart* <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a French Protestant biblical scholar</note> has demonstrated this with so many arguments that there is scarcely room for doubt.

<margin>Phaleg, Book I, Chapter I.</margin>
However, that *Noah* sacrificed any of his sons to God is as false as anything can be. What then? Poets often confused several individuals into one: just as they wrongly attribute the deeds of many *Hercules* figures to the single Theban one. Hence it happened that the Patriarch *Abraham* was also worshiped in the guise of Saturn. Certainly, the things *Sanchuniathon* <note>An ancient Phoenician author whose works survive only in fragments</note> relates here concerning Saturn do not fit *Noah*, but *Abraham*; and many points prove that *Abraham* is indeed designated here by *Saturn*.

VI. First, this *Saturn* of *Sanchuniathon*, who *offers his only-begotten son as a burnt offering* <note>original Greek: τὸν ἑαυτοῦ μονογενῆ ὁλοκαρποῖ</note>, and *is also circumcised in his private parts, forcing his comrades-in-arms to do the same* <note>original Greek: καὶ τὰ αἰδοῖα περιτέμνεται, ταυτὸ ποιῆσαι καὶ τοὺς ἅμ᾽ αὐτῷ συμμάχους καταναγκάσας</note>. Furthermore, the manuscripts of *Eusebius* constantly maintain that *Saturn* was called *Israel* by the Phoenicians. However, he confuses the *Grandfather* with the *Grandson* <note>i.e., Abraham with Jacob/Israel</note>. Just as we saw above in the Orphic verses that *Abraham* is called *Only-begotten* <note>original Greek: μονογενῆ</note>. There, *Abraham* and *Isaac* are confused, just as here *Abraham* and *Jacob* are. Or, if we wish to follow *Marsham* (who follows *Vossius*) and read *Ilus* instead of *Israel*—because elsewhere *Sanchuniathon* mentions that *Saturn* was called *Ilus*—*Il* is derived from *El*, or *Elohim* <note>Hebrew names for God</note>. We might then reasonably think of what the Phoenicians or *Canaanites* said to *Abraham*:

<margin>Genesis 23:6.</margin>
> *You are a Prince of God in our midst.* <note>original Hebrew: נשיא אלהים אתה בתוכנו</note>

Nor is it surprising if a fabulous posterity turned a *Prince of God* into a prince *God*. Thirdly, the son of this *Saturn* was called *JEUD*, which in the Phoenician language signifies "only-begotten." This is surely that epithet *JEHID* <note>original Hebrew: יחיד (Yachid)</note>, with which *Isaac* was distinguished in Genesis 22:2.

<margin>Genesis 22:2.</margin>

VII. But it is also worthwhile to hear *Grotius* here. After he had presented the entire discourse of *Sanchuniathon*, he proceeded thus: *By which words the man of Tyre <note>Sanchuniathon</note>, distorting the sacred history in many ways—as happened to almost all non-Jews who handed down Jewish affairs—named Israel instead of Abraham, that is, the grandson instead of the grandfather: saying that he was Saturn, doubtless because his descendants kept their holidays on the day of Saturn <note>The Sabbath/Saturday</note>. Moreover, unless I am mistaken, he called Sarah "Anobret," which is "the chosen one" <note>original: "חניכת" (Chanikat) / "ἐκλεκτὴν" (eklektēn)</note>. For "Jeod" instead of "Jeeid" <note>original: "’Ιεὸδ" / "’Ιεείδ"</note> is more a matter of dialect than a corruption of the word.*

VIII. However, *Marsham* interposes. *The discrepancy,* he says, *is too great.* But what, I ask, and how great? Let us count and weigh them.
*1. He writes "Israel"; what does that have to do with Abraham, who was Israel's grandfather? 2. The "Jeud" of Saturn was truly sacrificed, but Isaac was not. 3. His epithet was indeed "Jehid" <note>meaning "only-begotten" or "beloved"</note>, but that is a common title, not a proper name: whence Aquila <note>a 2nd-century translator of the Bible into Greek</note> translated it not badly as "Beloved" <note>original: "’Αγαπητὸν" (Agapēton)</note>. Thus Solomon was the "only" son of David, that is, the most beloved.* 1 Chronicles 29:1.

IX. But truly, such a small discrepancy cannot seem great except to one whose interest it is that it should seem so. For we do not dispute with *Marsham* regarding the name of *Israel*: it is all the same to us whether he prefers to read *Israel* or *Ilus*. And the difficulty that might appear here has been removed by us in that manner. Nor is there an insane difference between a *common epithet* attributed to someone by way of excellence <term>by way of excellence: (kat’ exochēn) referring to a title so fitting it becomes a name</term> and a *proper name*. What is easier than for a proper name to be formed from such a notable epithet over the lapse of time by those not particularly skilled in the facts? Especially if that epithet brings more weight to the matter at hand than the usual proper name. For this reason, we see it repeated again and again in the sacred history: Genesis 22:2, 12, 16; Hebrews 11:17.

X. Finally, the difficulty he moved in the second place must be explained at greater length. *The Jeud of Saturn,* he says, *was truly sacrificed: but not so Isaac.* Learned men responded long ago: the Devil wanted it to be believed that he was truly sacrificed, so that the event might serve as an example <note>i.e., to justify the pagan practice of human sacrifice</note>. # BOOK III. CHAPTER VII.

It is not lacking in probability that the savage custom of slaughtering humans spread from this very principle of the <term>sacrifice of a son</term> <note>original Greek: υἱοθυσίας (huiothysias)</note> by Abraham: the devil striving in every way to seduce the nations through a wicked imitation of that deed. For just as they consecrated the seventh holiday to **Saturn**—that is, the Sabbath day which was sacred among the **Jews**—so they also sacrificed their own sons in a damnable <term>perverse zeal</term> <note>original Greek: κακοζηλίᾳ (kakozēlia)</note> so that they might imitate **Abraham**. Furthermore, whereas God, having abundantly tested the faith and obedience of **Abraham**, prohibited him from the slaughter of his son, **Sanchuniathon** and **Porphyry** <note>Ancient historians of Phoenician and Neoplatonist traditions</note> nevertheless report that **Saturn** truly slaughtered his own son.

XI. Added to this is the fact that God, whom that <term>readiness of mind</term> <note>original Greek: προθυμία (prothymia)</note> of **Abraham** pleased immensely, valuing the intent as the effect, speaks of this act in the Holy Scriptures as if **Abraham** had truly sacrificed his son: by saying, *you have not withheld your son, your only son, from me.* Genesis 22:12. Which **Paul** amplifies in Hebrews 11:17: *Abraham, when he was tested, offered up Isaac through faith: he offered up, I say, that only-begotten one.*

<margin>Page 3. 4.</margin>
The same was skillfully observed by **Philo the Jew**: *This deed, although the end result did not follow, is nevertheless recorded and inscribed as complete and perfect, not only in the sacred books, but also in the minds of those who read them.* <note>The author provides both the original Greek and a Latin translation, here rendered into English.</note> Nor less elegantly does **Gregentius, Archbishop of Tephren**, state in his Disputation with **Herban the Jew**:

<margin>Page 7.</margin>
*For Abraham, being led to sacrifice Isaac for the love of God, by his will and purpose both slaughtered him and did not slaughter him; he completed it, and did not complete it. For he brought him back alive from the unexpected.* In which matter he observes a mystery. For in this way, he says, *the Lord God, for the salvation of the world, slaughtered His own Son: but He, rising on the third day, although He was slaughtered, was nevertheless not slaughtered: and if He died, yet He did not die.* I shall say nothing for now of the **Mohammedans**, who commonly call **Isaac** <note>original Arabic/Hebrew script: דביח אללה (Dhabih Allah)</note> *the one sacrificed to God.*
