# EGYPTIAN MATTERS

Confusing the story of **Abraham** with their own tales, the Gentile myth-makers transferred elements belonging to him into their own stories. For they tell that **Iphigenia** was offered by her father **Agamemnon** to **Diana** <note>The Roman name for Artemis, goddess of the hunt</note>. And they say that when she was just about to be slaughtered by the ministry of **Calchas** <note>The Greek seer during the Trojan War</note>, a voice was sent forth from the grove: *the deity spurns this kind of sacrifice, and for that reason the body of the maiden must be spared. Therefore, they should see to it that whatever they noticed was offered in place of the maiden should be sacrificed.* Meanwhile, while everyone was deliberating what and where this thing was that was ordered to be sacrificed, a doe of wondrous physical beauty stood fearlessly before the altar itself. Thinking it to be the foretold victim, offered by Divine power, they seized it and soon sacrificed it. So says **Dictys of Crete**. Others write that a different animal was slaughtered instead of **Iphigenia**. Some even claim she herself was slaughtered, as **Calchas** does in **Virgil**:

> With blood you appeased the winds, and with a maiden slain. <note>original: "Sanguine placastis ventos, & Virgine cæsa." From the Aeneid, Book 2</note>

But there **Servius** <note>A 4th-century commentator on Virgil</note> notes: *With a maiden slain—not in truth, but as it appeared.* And it should be known that in sacred rites, simulated things are accepted for true ones. Thus the **Greeks** mixed fragments of the **Abrahamic** history into their fables, though interpolated in their usual fashion—specifically this part of the history: that by the command of a deity, another animal was substituted for the intended human victim. Therefore, nothing prevents us from believing, along with the most learned authors of our age, that the mythical <term>sacrifice of a son</term> <note>original Greek: υἱοθυσίαν (huiothysian)</note> by **Saturn** was derived from the history of **Abraham**. From this, to use the words of **Tacitus**, came the *horrendous origins of Barbarian rites*; consequently, it can by no means be proven from that narrative of **Sanchuniathon** <note>A Phoenician author whose works are mostly lost</note> that the rite of sacrificing humans was practiced in **Phoenicia** before the age of **Abraham**.

XIII. But this argument can also be proven weak in another way. Let us grant that the Gentile writers, when discussing **Saturn**, thought nothing of **Abraham**. Yet at what time did the historical **Saturn** live according to their own calculation? **Theophilus**, in his *To Autolycus, Book III*, says: *For indeed Thallus mentions Belus, who ruled the Assyrians, and Saturn the Titan; saying that Belus waged war with the Titans against Jupiter and those who were called gods with him.* <note>original Greek: Καὶ γὰρ Βήλου ὁ Ἀσσυρίων βασιλεύσαντος καὶ Κρόνου τοῦ Τιτᾶνος Θᾶλλος μέμνηται... ### BOOK III. CHAPTER VII.

According to the history of Thallus <note>original: "κατὰ τὴν τοῦ Θάλλου ἱστορίαν" — Thallus was an early historian, likely of the first century, whose works are now lost but cited by early Christian authors</note>, Belus is found to be 322 years older than the Trojan War. XIV. Do you wish that Faunus, Latinus, and Picus lived one hundred and twenty years each? For it is denied that a human life can be extended beyond that. The estimate is fair and clear. There are, therefore, three hundred full years, and sixty years after these. The matter is exactly as the computation indicates. Whose father-in-law was Latinus? Aeneas's. He was the father of Ascanius. Of whom? The founder of the town of Alba. How many years was it ruled at Alba? Four hundred and nearly twenty. What is the age of the City of Rome indicated to be in the Annals? It numbers one thousand and fifty years, or not much less than these. Therefore, from Jupiter—who is the brother of Picus, and who is the Father of the lesser and remaining Gods—to these times, there are nearly two thousand years, or (as others read, 'not') full years, even if we are generous with the age."**

## CHAPTER VIII.

### The Law of Levirate Marriage is not from Egypt.

### I. Onan is the first of all who is recorded to have married the widow of a deceased brother. II. Yet that custom is older than the age of Onan, arising either from the Law of the Sons of Noah <note>The "Noachide Laws" considered by theologians to be the universal moral code given to humanity before the Mosaic Law.</note> or from the institution of God himself. I. **L**et us subjoin here something concerning the law of **LEVIRATE MARRIAGE** <term>Levirate: from the Latin 'levir' meaning brother-in-law; the practice of a man marrying his deceased brother's childless widow</term>, or the marrying of the widow of a brother who died without offspring, which Marsham endeavors to derive from Egypt through strange and winding paths of reasoning. The first mention of that custom is in the history of the Patriarchs, and an example occurred in the family of Judah regarding the widow of Er. When Er had been slain by God on account of his wickedness, Judah said to his other son, Onan: "Go in to your brother’s wife <insert>and perform the duty of a brother-in-law to her</insert> <note>original Hebrew: "ve-yabbem otah"</note> and raise up offspring for your brother." For the right of it was known not only to Judah, but also to Onan, since he knew that the children born from such a union would be born not for himself, but for his deceased brother.

The *Hebrew Masters* derive it from the law of the *Noachides* <note>The "Seven Laws of Noah" believed by Jewish tradition to be binding on all humanity</note>: but they do not admit this into the number of the commandments, whether *Major* or *Minor*. Nor do they take it as anything other than a chapter of civil law which was added to the Noachide law at the pleasure of the rulers, as seen in the example of *Onan* <note>Genesis 38:8-10</note>, as *Abravanel* <note>Isaac Abravanel, a 15th-century Jewish statesman and philosopher</note> expressly states. See *Selden, On the Law of Nature and Nations, Book VIII, chapter III.* Our own scholars derive it from the ancient custom of the holy *Patriarchs*, the origin of which was either from *Divine revelation*, or certainly from the בית דינו של שם *Consistory of Shem* <note>original: "Beth Din shel Shem," referring to a legendary court or academy of the biblical Shem</note>, as the *Hebrews* call it, or even from *Adam* himself. So says the illustrious *Heidegger*.

III. *Marsham* <note>Sir John Marsham, an English chronicler known for his secular approach to biblical history</note> interrupts: *It was born in Egypt*, he says. To prove this, two things had to be established: first, that this custom once flourished in *Egypt*; second, that it existed in *Egypt* earlier than the times of *Judah*; and if we wished to test him strictly, a third point should be added: that *Judah* had such intimacy and familiarity with the *Egyptians* that he had sufficiently suitable and grave reasons for adopting such an Egyptian institution into his own family. But *Marsham* did not even think of that. Nor do we wish to be so pedantic now as to cut everything to the quick. Let us only see how he confirms those first two assertions. He attempts to prove that the law of *Levirate marriage* <term>Leviratio: the practice of a brother marrying his deceased brother's widow to continue the family line</term> prevailed in *Egypt* until the times of the Emperor *Zeno* based on a certain *Law of Zeno* found in the *Code of Justinian, Book V, Title V, Law VIII.* He cites it in this manner:

> *The Egyptians, says Zeno, joined the wives of their deceased brothers to themselves in marriage for the reason that they were said to have remained virgins after their deaths; they judged, as it pleased certain lawmakers, that when they had not come together in body, the marriage did not seem to have been contracted.*

IV. But several things can be observed by us regarding that Law. I will not press the point now that, since this constitution is very recent, it in no way proves such a great antiquity of *Egyptian* law as is now under dispute. But I first advise that the Emperor is indeed recounting what was practiced at some time in *Egypt*; but not what ought to have been done by ancestral law or institution in a certain case. Furthermore, he does not even say that this was a received and common custom among the *Egyptians* to join the wives of deceased brothers to themselves in marriage: but rather that of certain private individuals...

Therefore, *Marsham* <note>Sir John Marsham (1602–1685), an English writer known for suggesting that Jewish rituals were derived from Egyptian ones.</note> has proved nothing so far: since that action of certain *Egyptians* is entirely different in kind from the law of the *Levirate* <term>Levirate: from the Latin 'levir' meaning brother-in-law; the practice where a man marries his deceased brother's widow</term> as it prevailed among the *Hebrews*.

Is it therefore *true* that the law concerning the marriage of sisters-in-law arose from the opinion of *Metempsychosis*, just because it pleased certain *Teachers*—those worthless men—to rave in such a way? Does it appear that the ancients judged so, just because more recent men, whom sanity and the Spirit of God itself seem to have deserted, rave so childishly? Do you yourself, *Marsham*, believe that this opinion of *Metempsychosis* gave origin to this law? If you do not believe it, as I know well enough you do not, why do you commit the reputation of your solid erudition and refined judgment to such a foolish argument?

God: regarding the law which God ordained in *Deuteronomy* <note>Deuteronomy 25:5-6</note> concerning the wife of a deceased brother being given to the later brother, that law was then first delivered in writing; but it already held sway among the people by some Divine revelation. Therefore, that law of *Deuteronomy* is not a recent institution, but a confirmation and sealing of an ancient observation. Moreover, the author of this observation must be considered the same as its confirmer. The cause for instituting it was the continuation of the Divine blessing upon the family; according to which blessing two prerogatives also belonged to the firstborn: one of the priesthood for the worship of the Lord, and the other of power pertaining to earthly blessing. For the firstborn were both priests in the entire family and heirs of a double portion. And this matter was indeed ceremonial, by which—from the founding of the world—the dignity of *Christ*, who is the firstborn among many brothers, was foreshadowed. 

But just as the reason for that blessing was ceremonial, so also was its continuation; according to which it first happened that the firstborn from the firstborn should obtain the birthright; then, if a firstborn died without children and without a wife, the second son would seem to be divinely adopted into the place of the firstborn; finally, if any firstborn should die without children but leaving a wife, the following brother would take this same wife for himself, along with the blessing transferred from the deceased firstborn. And this matter was otherwise not permitted by law, but excepted solely for the sake of this blessing. Thus a most learned man <note>likely referring to Franciscus Junius the Elder</note> reveals the origin and causes of this institute; certainly far more wisely than if we were to resort to some unknown opinion of *Egyptian Metempsychosis* <note>The Greek concept of the transmigration of souls or reincarnation</note>.

VII. *Rivetus* <note>André Rivet (1572–1651), a French Huguenot theologian</note> agrees with *Junius*. He says, "I would not think that this custom prevailed among other nations, or was taken from the customs of the *Canaanites* or neighboring peoples: but was introduced by a peculiar reason into the families of the patriarchs, so that the right of primogeniture <term>Primogeniture: the right of the firstborn child to inherit the family estate</term> might remain, to signify Him who is the firstborn among many brothers, and at the same time that the inheritance might be preserved in the families of that people, which was afterwards necessary after the division of the promised land." Moreover, although it was not commanded before *Moses* by any written law; it is nevertheless certain that it prevailed by the manner and custom of the ancestors, which *Pererius* <note>Benito Pereira (1535–1610), a Jesuit theologian</note> rightly observes is not rashly thought to have had its first origin from Divine inspiration.

## CHAPTER IX.

### That the seven-day cycle and the Sabbath did not originate from Egypt.

---

> *I. The method of counting by weeks is the oldest of all. II. The naming of the days after the planets is perhaps an Egyptian superstition, but the observation of the week is of an older and more sacred origin. III. Marsham <note>Sir John Marsham, a 17th-century English chronicler who argued for Egyptian priority in religious customs.</note> does not prove that the Egyptians held every seventh day as a festival.*

---

<margin>Compare Book 1, Chapter VI, Section VII. On the Creation of the World.</margin>
I. **But** neither was the SEVEN-DAY CYCLE OF DAYS first observed by the Egyptians and passed from there into the customs of other nations; rather, as *Philo* <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish philosopher who sought to harmonize Greek philosophy with Jewish scripture.</note> well said, that observation was *universal and born with the world* <note>original Greek: "πάνδημος καὶ τῷ κόσμῳ γενέσιος"</note>, accepted by all nations and contemporary with the world itself. From the *Chronology of George Syncellus*, *Salmasius* <note>Claude Saumaise, a renowned French classical scholar.</note> observed that before the method of calculating by months and years had been invented by astrologers, those ancient fathers distinguished spans of time only *by weeks* <note>original Greek: "καθ' ἑβδομάδας"</note>. And in the *Annals of Michael Glycas* it is read: *George* <note>referring to Syncellus</note> relates that *Seth* <note>The third son of Adam and Eve.</note> was the first to discover Hebrew letters, the celestial signs, the revolutions of the years, the months, and the WEEKS. But it is better that we ascend higher, to *Adam* himself, as *Rabbi Judah* does in the dialogue called the *Book of the Kuzari* <note>original: "Sepher Cozri," a famous 12th-century work by Judah Halevi.</note>. <margin>See Selden, On Natural Law, Book III, Chapter XI.</margin> *Adam*, he says, was driven out of Paradise on the eve of the Sabbath, and from there began the numbering of the days, which rests upon the six days of creation. And there *Adam* began to impose names upon the days. And when the earth was later inhabited by his increased descendants, it was the custom of men to number the days just as *Adam* had arranged them: from which it happened that men do not disagree concerning the seven-day number of the Week.

II. I would not stubbornly deny that the naming of the days from the seven planets is an *invention* <note>original Greek: "εὕρημα"</note> of the Egyptians; yet the observation of the week itself has a far more sacred and ancient origin. *John Philoponus* <note>An Alexandrian Christian philosopher and scientist.</note>, praised by *Photius* in his Library, says quite beautifully: <margin>On the Creation of the World, Book VII, Chapter XIV.</margin> *This at least is agreed upon by all men, that there are only seven days, which, by cycling back into themselves, constitute the whole of time.* <note>original Greek: "Ἐκεῖνο γὲ μὴν συμπεφώνηται πᾶσιν ἀνθρώποις, ἑπτὰ μόνας εἶναι ἡμέρας, αἵτινες εἰς ἑαυτὰς ἀνακυκλούμεναι τὸν ὅλον ποιοῦσι χρόνον."</note>

### CHAPTER X.

### That the construction of the Temple is wrongly derived from Egypt.

I. *The first origin of Temples is in obscurity.* II. *Most people trace it back to tombs.* III. *Others, however, more probably attribute it to the veneration of the Divine Power, to whom it is fitting that all magnificent things be consecrated.* IV. *Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an influential Early Church Father known for his preaching.</note> is mistaken when he claims the Temple of the Hebrews was built so that the people would not be touched by a wicked desire for Egyptian things.* V. *For David, Solomon, and God Himself teach that a different end was proposed for it.* VI. *Not even in the construction of the Tabernacle was attention paid to the customs of the Egyptians.* VII. *But God, as the King of Israel,* VIII. *Wished to dwell in the Temple as if in some magnificent Palace: with all things arranged according to the form of a certain August Royal Court.* IX. *As has been beautifully observed by the Masters of the Hebrews <note>Referring to Jewish Rabbis and scholars.</note>.* X. *But there were also other mysteries of both the Tabernacle and the Temple.* XI. *The Tabernacle was not built according to a certain Egyptian form, but according to the pattern shown by God.* XII. *As was the Temple also.* XIII. *And that matter was also* mysterious <note>original: "μυστηριώδης" (mysteriōdēs) - full of hidden spiritual meaning.</note>. <margin>Compare Book I, Chapter VI, Section 10.</margin> IV. Truly, I would not hesitate to confidently contend that the "Golden-Mouthed" Bishop <note>original: "aurei oris Episcopum" referring to St. John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), famed for his eloquence</note> was mistaken when he argued that *God ordered a temple of immense magnitude to be built for Himself—one which, in the magnificence of its materials, the elegance of its craftsmanship, and the form of its structure, would have no equal in the entire world—on the occasion that the people, recently departed from Egypt, still carried many remnants of impiety with them and were addicted to the point of madness to sensory things; this was done so that they would not later be touched by a longing for those things they had experienced among the Egyptians.* This, I say, *Chrysostom* argued not without some error. For that temple of immense wealth was not built at the time when the people, recently liberated from the Egyptian crowds and the barbarian tyranny of Pharaoh, still possessed much of the remaining Egyptian dregs: but rather several centuries thereafter.

V. And at the time when it was built, neither *David*, who first conceived the plan of building it, nor *God*, who permitted *David* to have the work he intended completed by his son *Solomon*, nor finally *Solomon*, who executed his father’s plan and God’s will, make even the slightest mention of *Egypt* as having provided the occasion for this matter. *David* judged it unworthy of the Majesty of the divine, and unbecoming of those benefits by which he confessed himself bound to the immortal God, that while he himself lived in a house of cedar, the Ark of God remained among curtains <note>i.e., within the Tabernacle tent</note>: and thus, moved by the sight of his own Palace which God had given him, he was stirred to dedicate a magnificent Temple to the supreme King of the heavens. 2 Samuel 7:2. Nor did God consider this as a remedy for the remnants of Egyptian impiety, but rather held it as a pleasing sign of extraordinary pious affection. And so far is it from the truth that He commanded such a house to be made for Himself because of the temples the Israelites had seen in Egypt, that on the contrary—at the time when the memory of Egyptian temples was fresh in the minds of their ancestors—He protested that He had said nothing regarding such a building. 1 Chronicles 17:5-6. *Since I have not dwelt in any house from the time I brought up Israel even to this day, but have gone from tent to tent, and even outside a tabernacle: wherever I went in all Israel, did I speak anything to any of the jud—* <note>The text cuts off mid-word "judicum" (judges) at the page break.</note>

VI. Indeed, soon after the Exodus of the Israelites, God commanded a sacred Tabernacle <note>The portable earthly dwelling place of Yahweh used by the Israelites from the Exodus until the building of Solomon's Temple.</note> to be constructed for Himself; but we are taught in the sacred scriptures that in its construction there was no regard for the customs of the Egyptians. To seek wisdom outside of the scriptures in these matters is to know nothing at all. Truly, if we look at the essence of the matter, the reasoning for the Temple and the sacred Tent was exactly the same. God held both as a domicile, in which He, as the King of the Hebrews, might dwell as if among His subjects. Concerning the Tabernacle, He Himself said in Exodus 25:8: *They shall make me a Sanctuary, and I will dwell in the midst of them.* Concerning the Temple, Solomon said in 1 Kings 8:13: *Building, I have built a house for your most firm dwelling, your throne forever.* This, therefore, was the distinction between that domicile and the synagogues built later: that in the latter God was only worshipped, while in the former He was both worshipped and dwelt there in a singular manner.

VII. For this is how the matter stands. Moses, being about to establish a Republic <note>original: "Rempublicam" — referring to the organized body of the Israelite people.</note> which was to be the holiest on earth, deferred the supreme power of all things to the Divine. And while others find other names, as the case may be, and call it now a monarchy, now an oligarchy, and sometimes a democracy, he understood that none of these would suit the nature and character of such a great empire. Therefore, he established a certain mode of government, which Flavius <note>Flavius Josephus, the 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian.</note> in his work *Against Apion* says can be significantly called a THEOCRACY <note>original Greek: ΘΕΟΚΡΑΤΙΑΝ — a term coined by Josephus to describe a government where God is the sovereign authority.</note>, as if you were to describe a state whose sole president and ruler is God.
<margin>Antiquities, Book IV, Chapter VIII.</margin>
And it is from this that the same Flavius introduces Moses instructing his Hebrews in these words: *Let no desire for another form of government seize you, but cherish this one. Having the laws as your masters, perform each thing according to them. For it is enough for God to be the leader.* <note>original Greek: Μὴ λάβοι πόθος ὑμᾶς ἄλλης πολιτείας, ἀλλὰ ταύτην στέργετε. Τοὺς νόμους ἔχοντες δεσπότας, κατ᾿ αὐτοὺς ἕκαστα πράττοντες. Ἀρκεῖ γὰρ ὁ Θεὸς ἡγεμὼν εἶναι.</note> Gideon certainly observed this religiously; when the Israelites offered him the empire, to be passed down to his son and grandsons, he said, *I will not have dominion over you, nor shall my son*

### BOOK III. CHAPTER X.

*“My son shall not have dominion over you; Jehovah shall have dominion over you.”* Judges 8:23. <note>original: "filius meus habebit dominium in vos; Jehova habiturus est dominium in vos." This refers to Gideon's refusal to take the crown, affirming God as the true King.</note>

VIII. Since, therefore, Jehovah was the King of Israel in a singular manner, He also willed—according to the Economy <note>The "Economy" here refers to the specific divine arrangement or administration of the world at that time.</note> of those times—that everything be arranged for royal pomp and magnificence. Jerusalem was thus chosen as the metropolis of the kingdom. Psalm 48:3; Matthew 5:35. There, every person in the kingdom who had completed their twentieth year was bound to pay a half-shekel of the sacred currency to their King, as a kind of annual tribute. Matthew 17:25, 26. The Temple took the place of the Royal Palace; divided into various courts and chambers, it provided suitable rooms for the people, the royal ministers, and finally for the King Himself. *“A glorious throne, exalted from the beginning, is the place of our Sanctuary.”* Jeremiah 17:12. In the courtyard, the entire populace gathered to perform sacred rites to the King. Closer by, the Priests—the King’s ministers—labored alongside the Levites. The Sanctuary <note>The Holy Place</note> truly seems to have been set apart as the Royal Presence Chamber; indeed, access to it was open only to the Priests, as they were servants of the inner admission and, as it were, courtiers of the highest rank <note>original: "purpuratis," literally those dressed in purple, signifying high-ranking officials or nobles.</note>. But God dwelt especially in the innermost shrine <note>The Holy of Holies</note>, where He had erected a Throne of Grace between the wings of the Cherubim, upon the golden mercy-seat of the Ark of the Covenant; entry was granted to no one except the High Priest, and then only once a year. For a *table*, He had the altar; for *food*, the sacrifices and grain offerings; for *drink*, the libations; for *perfumes*, the incense; for *musicians*, the Levite singers. In short, the entire design of the house was composed according to the idea of the most exquisite pomp and most magnificent splendor, reflecting the proud palace of some most powerful Monarch. This was what Solomon wrote to Hiram, the King of the Tyrians. 2 Chronicles 2:4, 5.

> Behold, I am about to build a house to the name of Jehovah my God: and that house which I am about to build will be great: for our God is greater than all gods.

<margin>Book 1, chapter III.</margin>
IX. These things were not hidden from the teachers of the Hebrews; whoever wishes may seek their testimonies in Outram’s <note>William Outram (1626–1679), an English theologian known for his work on sacrifices.</note> learned work on sacrifices. We shall provide one from among many. Rabbi Shem Tov, who commented on Maimonides’ *Guide for the Perplexed* <note>original: "Doctorem perplexorum," the Latin title for Maimonides' famous philosophical work, Moreh Nevukhim.</note>, left these remarks among <margin>On Part III, chapter XLV.</margin> others: *“God, to whom be praise, ordered such a house to be built for Himself as a royal house is accustomed to be. In a royal house, all these things are found: namely, some who guard his palace; others who perform duties pertaining to the Royal dignity; those who prepare the feasts, and others—”*

FOR HE IS THE GREAT KING, TO BE FEARED BY ALL NATIONS.**

X. There were also other mysteries underlying both the Tabernacle and the Temple; some common to both, some unique to each. And <term>Abravanel</term><note>Isaac Abravanel (1437–1508), a celebrated Jewish statesman and biblical commentator.</note> said with good judgment that the entire apparatus of the tabernacle is *like a book of higher wisdom, and a glorious matter to which those things are directed.* <note>original Hebrew: "כספר חכמה עליונה וענין נכבד אשר עליו יתישרו"</note> But it is not our present purpose to follow every detail part by part. Let it suffice to have observed in general that both the Temple and the Tabernacle signified all those things in which God deigns to dwell: first, the holy *flesh of Christ*, in which the Divinity was to appear as if in a temple (John 2:19); then heaven, the seat of Divine glory, in which the flesh of Christ was to sit (Hebrews 9:24); and finally the Church, in which God is equally present (1 Corinthians 3:16). Moreover, that God first ordered a portable Tabernacle to be made for Himself, in which all things were of less value, and then a house of more solid and majestic structure, the magnificence of which almost surpasses belief; this suggests the distinction between the *Jewish and Christian Church, or even the Church Militant and Triumphant.* <note>The "Church Militant" refers to Christians currently living and struggling on earth, while the "Triumphant" refers to those in heaven.</note>

XI. But this also is quite far from the truth: the idea that either the Tabernacle of Moses or the Temple of Solomon were constructed according to the **FORM OF THOSE BUILDINGS** which the Israelites had previously seen in Egypt. For the Supreme Deity allowed no human counsel to intervene, nor any idea to be borrowed from those works which had hitherto occurred to the senses—

# BOOK III. CHAPTER X.

...had run. When the *Tabernacle* <note>The portable earthly dwelling place of God used by the Israelites from the Exodus until the building of the Temple.</note> was to be constructed, God willed that *Moses* be with Him alone on the mountain, and He accurately showed him beforehand the entire form of the *Tabernacle* with all its equipment; adding a strict command:
> ACCORDING TO ALL THAT I SHOW THEE, THE PATTERN OF THE TABERNACLE, AND THE PATTERN OF ALL THE INSTRUMENTS THEREOF, EVEN SO SHALL YE MAKE IT.
*Exodus 25:9.* And again in verse 40:
> LOOK THEREFORE AND MAKE THEM AFTER THEIR PATTERN, WHICH WAS SHEWED THEE IN THE MOUNT.
Which is far different than if it had been said: make it according to the idea of those things which you saw in *Egypt*.

XII. Likewise, when God had consented to the construction of the Temple, He did not want *David* or *Solomon* to form a likeness or type for themselves from foreign works, or from the skill of architects, or from their own genius, but He Himself delineated all things with His own hand. *1 Chronicles 28:11, 12.* Then *David* delivered to *Solomon* his son *the pattern of the porch and of the houses thereof*—finally *the pattern of all that he had* INFORMED BY THE SPIRIT, *of the courts of the house of Jehovah*. And he said in verse 19:
> ALL THIS, SAID DAVID, THE LORD MADE ME UNDERSTAND IN WRITING BY HIS HAND UPON ME, EVEN ALL THE WORKS OF THIS PATTERN.

XIII. Nor was this matter without a mystery. For since God showed beforehand with such accuracy every detail to both *Moses* and *David* which He willed to be observed in the construction of the *Tabernacle and the Temple*, by that very act He showed it to be a sin for man to act by his own judgment in the business of Divine worship, or to think that he can please God by a thing which He Himself did not command. And since He gave to *Israel* the type of no pre-existing structure as the model for His own dwelling; by this He taught *Israel* that religion is not to be composed according to the whims of other men; and that whatever is of human invention is rejected by Him, nor does He want *Israel* to follow foreign rites in His worship. Finally, since this entire delineation of the sanctuary descended from heaven, the *Israelites* were taught that those earthly things are <note>original Greek: ὑποδείγματα καὶ σκιὰν τῶν ἐπερανίων</note> *copies and shadows of heavenly things. Hebrews 8:5.*

# OF THE EGYPTIANS

...and the Temple of Jerusalem. However, it must by no means be inferred that the former served as the model for the latter. For there is no evidence to prove that the things seen by Strabo <note>Strabo (c. 64 BC – 24 AD) was a Greek geographer and historian whose descriptions of Egyptian temples are often compared to biblical accounts.</note> in Egypt were more ancient than the Temple of Jerusalem. Indeed, since the fame of the Jerusalem Temple was renowned not only among neighboring peoples but also among more distant nations—as the sacred pages expressly record in 1 Kings 8:41-42—why should we be reluctant to believe that other nations built their own shrines according to that most beautiful form? It is surely probable that whatever is most excellent in its kind will serve as an example for others.

<margin>Concerning Justinian's Buildings, Book I.</margin>
XV. Truly, just as the ancient Christian temples were not unlike the Temple of Jerusalem, so the even older temples of the Gentiles <note>Non-Christians, specifically Greeks and Romans.</note> were not unlike those of the Christians. The temples of the Christians, especially those of the Greeks, were formerly divided into three parts in imitation of the Jerusalem Temple. The first part was called the *Pronaos*, or the **Portico**; the second the *Naos*, or the **Nave** <note>original: "Gremium," literally the "lap" or "bosom" of the church.</note>; the third the *Bema*, or the **Choir**. The **Portico** was situated at the doors of the temple, where in the *Narthex* (in Latin, the **Rod** or **Staff**), stood the *penitents*, who sought the intercessions of the faithful as they entered. Likewise, the *Catechumens* <note>Those receiving instruction in the faith but not yet baptized.</note> remained there as *listeners* before they became *candidates* for baptism. Finally, *Jews*, *Pagans*, and *Heretics* stood there if ever the desire seized them to observe the Christian rites from a distance. In the **Nave**, the faithful sat to perform their divine service, with men and women separated, and among the women, the young girls were set apart from the wives and widows. Procopius <note>A prominent 6th-century Byzantine scholar and historian.</note> noted double porticos, shining with vaulted ceilings and gold, one of which received the men and the other the women for prayer. The **Choir** (*Bema* or *Hierateion* <note>The "priestly place."</note>) was the innermost part of the temple, separated by veils, curtains, and steps, and ordinarily admitting only the Clergy. In this part were the **Altar**, the **Pulpit**, the **Bishop's Chair**, the **Seats of the Priests**, the **Benches of the Deacons**, and the **Mats** of the other Clerics.

<margin>Book I, Chapter III.</margin>
XVI. Furthermore, Polletus <note>François Pollet, a 16th-century legal scholar.</note> teaches in his *History of the Roman Forum* that the temples of the ancient Gentiles were of nearly the same form. For he says they consisted of a "Holier Chamber," which **we call the Choir**; this Holier Chamber was distinguished from the Basilica and the Porticos by a screen and a sort of second Fore-temple; **we might well call this the Pulpit, because it is raised in the manner of a stage or platform.** The Basilica, however, is **what we call the Nave or the Hull**; the walkways that are on both sides are entirely the porticos of the Ancients, which are like the aisles in the "Hull" of the church. The Chamber...

# BOOK III. CHAPTER X.

The holier part <note>referring to the *Cella* or inner sanctuary</note> was destined solely for sacred rites. However, the Basilica, the Portico, and the *Pronaon* <note>the vestibule or front porch of a temple</note> were frequently exposed to profane uses. For in those places, markets for merchandise, the brokering of contracts, marriage introductions, and business negotiations were conducted—much as they are among us today, quite impiously. What, I ask, does Strabo relate regarding the Egyptian temples in this matter, that Polletus does not likewise say of the Romans?

<margin>Book IV. chapter IV.</margin>
XVII. But this seemed to me especially memorable: that **Vitruvius** <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, a Roman architect and author of the influential "De architectura"</note> **handed down certain rules regarding the proportion of length to width, to be observed in the construction of sacred buildings according to the Doric discipline, which—if you subtract a very few details—agree marvelously with the measurements of Solomon’s Temple.** **The length of the building,** he says, **is distributed so that the width is half of the length, and the Cella itself is one-fourth longer than the width, including the wall where the folding doors are placed. Let the remaining three parts of the Pronaos extend to the *Antae* <note>pilasters forming the ends of the side walls</note> of the walls, which Antae ought to have the thickness of the columns.** *Louis Cappel* <note>a French Protestant scholar and expert on Hebrew texts</note> shows that the calculation of this proportion was maintained in the Temple of Solomon in his most learned description of the Jerusalem Temple. **The width of Solomon’s Temple was 46 cubits: the length, however, was 92 cubits. Now, 46 is half of 92. Again, a fourth part of this width is 11 1/2 cubits. Let those be added to the 46 cubits of width, and they become 57 1/2. Add to these the thickness of the wall of five cubits, and they become 62 1/2, which is the length of the Cella (that is, the Holy Place along with the Holy of Holies), which was 60 cubits long.** **What Vitruvius adds—that the remaining three parts of the Pronaos extend to the Antae of the walls—did not have a place in Solomon’s Temple, in which the Vestibule, and the open-air space before the vestibule where the Altar was, served in the stead and place of the Pronaos.**

XVIII. Furthermore, the ratio of the width and height of the Holy Place and the *Adytum* <note>the innermost sanctuary or Holy of Holies</note> in Solomon’s Temple, by the measurement of the same Cappel, corresponds accurately to that ratio which **Vitruvius** delivers in **Book VI, chapter V, where he discusses Dining Rooms and chambers. For he says: However great the width of the dining rooms shall be, the length ought to be twice as much (he delivers the same regarding the Cella of a Temple in Book IV, chapter VII: The lengths of the Cellas are double the widths.) The heights of all chambers that are oblong should have their ratio calculated so that the measure of the length and width are added together, and half is taken from that sum, and however much that is, so much is given to the height. But if the *Exedrae* <note>recessed seating areas</note> or the *Oeci* <note>main halls or salons</note> are square, the width—**

# EGYPTIAN MATTERS

...by adding half of the width, the heights are derived. According to this ratio, the Temple of Solomon was constructed: for the length of the Holy Place was double its width. Specifically, it was 40 cubits long and 20 wide. Moreover, its width and length combined together give 60 cubits. Half of this, namely 30 cubits, constitutes its height. The Inner Sanctuary <note>original: "Adytum"; the Holy of Holies</note> was square, being 20 cubits long and wide. Therefore, half of the width, namely 10 cubits, added to the length makes thirty cubits. This was the height of its wall, equal to the height of the Holy Place; but with a ceiling placed at a height of 20 cubits, the upper 10 cubits were cut off up to the roof, so that the interior was only 20 cubits wide, long, and high—made a perfect cube, as is held in 1 Kings 6:20.

XIX. Is not the agreement of this *Doric Architecture* with the *Solomonic* wonderful? What then? Shall we say that Solomon formed his own model by taking an example from the Temples of the Dorians, or—what is much more foolish—that God borrowed His? Far be it. Let us rather say that the incomparable structure of the Jerusalem Temple, designed by the most wise Divinity, embraced within itself all forms of art; which art the most skilled craftsmen of buildings among the Gentiles emulated, as far as each was able to achieve. *Villalpandus* <note>Juan Bautista Villalpando (1552–1608), a Spanish Jesuit known for his reconstructions of Solomon's Temple</note>, the eminent Theologian and Mathematician of our age, was certainly of this mind; he asserts that the entire, more perfect system of Architecture flowed entirely from the proportions of the *Hebrews* in the Temple of Solomon and its other structures, through the *Greeks* to the *Romans*, and finally into the books of *Vitruvius* <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, the Roman author of 'De architectura'</note>. See him in *Ezekiel, Volume II, Part II, Book V, Disputation I, Chapter XIII*. *Selden* <note>John Selden (1584–1654), an English jurist and polymath</note> agrees with Villalpando in *On Natural Law, Book 1, Chapter 11*. And let these things be said concerning the Temple: for I have sufficiently demonstrated, unless I am mistaken, that the Israelites did not have it from Egypt, neither in regards to the thing itself, nor the form of the Building.

## CHAPTER XI.

# That the Thummim was not given to the Hebrews as a copy of that gemstone which the High Priest of the Egyptians once wore suspended from his neck.

I. What the Urim and Thummim actually were *seems to have been unknown during the time of the Second Temple*, based on the silence of ancient authors. II. *Moses* himself, not without purpose, shrouded the matter in a wonderful brevity. III. It is not improbable that it was something fashioned immediately by God himself. IV. It is not sufficiently clear whether the Egyptian *Truth* <note>original: "᾿Αλήθεια" (Aletheia); the Greek word for Truth, used here to refer to a specific Egyptian amulet</note> was a single gemstone or several. V. Certainly, it does not agree with the Hebrew *Thummim*, either in the meaning of the word or in number, VI. VII. however much *Spencer* <note>John Spencer (1630–1693), a scholar who argued that many Jewish rituals were adapted from Egyptian customs</note> may exhaust himself in vain. VIII. Nor does it agree in the reason for its naming. IX. Nor in its use. For the Egyptian wore the *Truth* in his capacity as a *Judge*; the Hebrew wore it as a *High Priest*. X. Indeed, it was possible for the Hebrew High Priest not to be a judge. XI. According to *Spencer*, the *Thummim* was hidden within the fold of the breastplate; but the Egyptian wore the *Truth* in the sight of everyone. No probable reason is offered for this difference. XII. Nor can it be proven that the use of that Egyptian medallion is older than the time of *Moses*: since not even *Herodotus*, nor those who immediately followed him, made mention of it. XIII. The arguments *Spencer* brings forward for its antiquity are mere divinations. XIV. It is concluded that the *Thummim* was not given to *Aaron* in imitation of that medallion. XV. The Egyptians imitated the affairs of the Hebrews: but as children imitate the affairs of Men.

---

I. WHAT the URIM and THUMMIM were within the sacred vestments of the High Priest is shrouded in such thick darkness that even the most keen-sighted have despaired of perceiving it. There is scarcely any interpreter who has not exhausted his industry in the investigation of that matter; however, when you have consulted even the most distinguished among them, you will return much more uncertain than before. Not even *Spencer*, with all his diligence, has dispelled the shadows: who, by his *Conjectures*, as he himself frequently calls them, has indeed won for himself a reputation for genius and erudition;

# EGYPTIAN MATTERS

But he did not bring much light to the matter he had undertaken to treat. My reasoning is such, and I am so persuaded in my mind, that those who think they will find something certain in so uncertain a matter are wasting their efforts. The more recent Hebrew masters <note>referring to Rabbinic scholars</note>, as many as excel the rest in judgment and candor, ingenuously confess that they do not know what the *Urim* and *Thummim* <note>Lights and Perfections: sacred objects used by the High Priest to determine God's will</note> were. <margin>On the Life of Moses, book 3.</margin> *Philo the Jew*, where he treats the Pontifical vestments and the gems of the breastplate, leaves the reader's expectations unfulfilled when he reaches this point, giving nothing but words from which you can hammer out nothing solid. *Flavius Josephus* describes the Pontifical finery several times, and in doing so mentions the gems repeatedly, but makes no mention of the *Urim* and *Thummim*. From this we gather that the knowledge of them perished during the time of the Second Temple.

II. Everything must therefore be learned from the commentaries of *Moses*. But there, while other things are handed down at length, distinctly, and clearly, those things which regard the *Urim* and *Thummim* are shrouded in a wonderful brevity. Piety and a just estimation of God's wisdom bid us believe that this was not done without purpose. Doubtless He wished to place a restraint upon our curiosity: so that we might learn to be content not to know those things which it did not please the Supreme Master to reveal. <margin>Oration on the Priestly Vestments.</margin> Modestly, following others, *John Prideaux* says:

> *But who could conveniently explain to us the material of those stones upon which the Ten Commandments were inscribed; or the nature of the Manna, which melted in the sun and hardened in the fire; or the origin of that fire which, having glided down from heaven, devoured the sacrifices—unless that Spirit reveals it, who blows where He wills, and we know not whence He comes or where He goes? It is sufficient, therefore, to have observed that the Urim and Thummim were delivered by God, received by Moses, and were enclosed within the fold of the breastplate <note>original: "rationalis duplicitatem," referring to the doubled fabric of the High Priest's pectoral</note> as if in a certain case. Whoever rashly asserts anything beyond this should see to it that by peddling his knowledge, he does not owe a mockery to the unskilled and the wise alike.*

III. If, however, the Reader should absolutely demand of me what I think can be most probably established, I will say this: the opinion of those who observe that it was not a work of human art or hand seems likely to me; but rather something fashioned by God Himself, placed secretly by Moses within the fold of the breastplate, and perhaps never seen by the rest of the Israelites. <margin>In the Oration on the Ephod.</margin> The most illustrious *Jacobus Alting* has followed this line of thought with great learning. To be sure, God accurately enumerated what—

But he also seems to have reserved something for himself, with no human art or hand intervening. Nor was it done otherwise. The chosen workmen finished the weaving of the breastplate, as well as the engraving of the gems, and the setting of these into the golden sockets woven into the fabric, along with its bands and fasteners: and thus was Aaron clothed at his consecration. But the *Urim and Thummim* <note>The Urim and Thummim were mysterious objects used by the High Priest to determine God's will.</note> were not yet present. Regarding these, what did God command the craftsmen? Nothing. What did he command Moses? This one thing: *And you shall put in the breastplate THE Urim and THE Thummim.* <note>Exodus 28:30</note> But who shall make them? Who but God himself? Just as he delivered the Tables of the Law written by his own hand to Moses to be enclosed in the Ark, so also whatever this was, manufactured by his own wise omnipotence, he gave to the same Moses to be hidden in the secret folds of the breastplate. For this reason, they are even called with the definite article <note>original: "את האורים ואת התומים"</note> *THE Urim and THE Thummim*, for the sake of excellence. Moreover, *Urim* is named from "light," and *Thummim* from "perfection." Evidently, they had this use: that they might illuminate the consulted Priest toward the understanding of a hidden matter, and might perfect his speech to rightly announce what was understood: or rather, they were symbols of the Divine presence and direction, imbuing the Pontiff <note>The High Priest</note> in doubtful and secret matters with knowledge and eloquence for the instruction of those consulting him. The Greek words *Manifestation and Truth* <note>original: "Δήλωσις καὶ Ἀλήθεια"</note> are indicators of the thing itself rather than the vocabulary; the former seems to pertain to the *manifestation* for the priest's information, the latter to the *truth* for the information of the inquirers.

The nature of the *Thummim* <note>A sacred object used by the Hebrew High Priest to determine God's will; the author is comparing it to Egyptian amulets of "Truth."</note> is quite different. For the *High Priest* of the Egyptians wore that gemstone in his capacity as a *Judge*, to signify the integrity of that office; a fact clearly attested by both *Diodorus* and *Aelian* <note>Ancient Greek historians.</note>. However, there is no evidence that any of the *Hebrew Judges*, as such, ever wore the *Thummim*. This was the regalia of the High Priest, who represented the people before God, not that of a *Judge*. Nor was the High Priest of the Jews always the President of the supreme court, as was the case among the Egyptians according to *Aelian*. Indeed, far from being the head of the Sanhedrin <note>The supreme legal and religious council of ancient Israel.</note> by virtue of his priesthood, he was not even a member of it unless he was invited due to his expertise in handling affairs. *Maimonides* <note>A preeminent medieval Jewish scholar.</note> testifies that he was admitted <insert>to the council</insert> <note>original Hebrew: "אם הוא ראוי בחכמה"</note> *if he were wise and not unskilled in taking counsel.* Otherwise, it was lawful to reject him. For he did not enter the senate by his own right, but was admitted by vote. This fact is well known to scholars and is assumed as such by *Selden* <note>John Selden, a famous 17th-century English jurist and scholar of Jewish law.</note>: *The High Priest or chief priest, insofar as he was distinguished only by his sacred function, did not preside with authority by that primary institution; so that one might rightly say that matters of Order pertained fully to the High Priest, but matters of Jurisdiction pertained to the Princes and the Sanhedrin.*

XV. Regarding the other matters in which the apparatus of the Egyptian Pontiff is said to have agreed with the sacred vestments of Aaron, one may respond to Spencer <note>John Spencer (1630–1693), a scholar who argued that many Hebrew rites originated in Egypt</note> with the words of the distinguished Prideaux:

<margin>Oration on the Vestments of Aaron.</margin>
> I have neither the time nor the desire to pursue the superstitions <note>original: "δεισιδαιμονίας" (deisidaimonias)</note> of the Heathens in this matter. Just as they were the "Apes of the Church" in other things, so in that sacred solemnity of vestments they seem to have omitted nothing by which they might win either reverence for their persons or religious awe for their mysteries, according to the nature of the place or the worshipers. For who has not read in Herodotus, Pliny, Plutarch, and others, that the Egyptians employed their linen and hyacinth-colored <note>likely referring to a deep blue or violet dye</note> tunics, their breastplates, and even their sistrums <note>a type of musical rattle</note> clattering with a sharp tinkling in their more solemn rites? Corresponding to the two Onyx stones conspicuous upon the shoulders of Aaron, Alexander ab Alexandro mentions that there were certain corals among the Indian priests. How common are the terms for bands, mitres, and tiaras among Apuleius and other profane authors? William Stuckius, in his description of gentile rites, considers that breeches were neglected by none: because it was a sin among very many to strip oneself in a shrine or temple, as Plutarch is the author. Thus, nature itself dictated that Divine worship must not be performed without any refinement: but that some ceremonies are conducive either to the solemnity of the event, the distinction of persons, or the shaping of morals.

I. The *most learned Spencer* <note>John Spencer (1630–1693), a theologian who argued that Hebrew rituals were derived from Egyptian ones—the opposite of our author's view.</note> protests indeed with a great straining of his lungs, and contends that it is utterly incredible, considering the genius of both nations, that the *Egyptians* should have adopted so many things from the *Hebrews* into their own religion. But what seems incredible to him, is to me—following others most famous for their erudition and judgment—highly probable: the very genius of the *Egyptians* persuading me of it. For in this the most excellent authors agree: that the *Egyptians* were accustomed to follow with the greatest esteem those whom they saw were superior in wisdom and virtue, and by whom they remembered themselves to have been moved by great benefits; so much so, indeed, that they held such mortals to be *Divine beings* <note>original: "Divis"</note>, not only after they had died, but even while they were still living.

II. Clement of Alexandria <note>A Christian theologian and philosopher (c. 150–215 AD) who sought to reconcile Greek philosophy with Christian faith.</note> states it is clear that the Barbarians <note>In this context, "Barbarians" refers to non-Greeks, specifically the Egyptians and Persians.</note> always held their Lawgivers and teachers in exceptionally high honor, even calling them GODS. Among the Barbarians, the Egyptians excelled most in this practice. <note>original Greek: Καὶ τὸ τῶν Αἰγυπτίων γένος ἐθεολόγησαν ἀκριβῶς τὰ ἐκείνων.</note> **FURTHERMORE, THE EGYPTIAN RACE MOST DILIGENTLY RECORDED THEM AMONG THE GODS.**

Darius, the father of Xerxes, is said to have applied his mind to the laws of the Egyptians. For, detesting with no small hatred the impiety of Cambyses <note>Darius's predecessor, known for his erratic and often sacrilegious behavior in Egypt.</note> toward the Egyptian temples, Darius devoted himself to kindness toward men and piety toward the Gods. For he entered into friendship with the priests of Egypt and was made a participant in their <term>Theology</term> <note>The study of divine nature and the religious systems of the Egyptians.</note> and the matters recorded in their sacred volumes. Having been taught from these how great the ancient kings were in spirit and humanity toward their subjects, he adjusted himself to the imitation of their lives. <note>original Greek: Καὶ διὰ τοῦτο τηλικαύτης τυχεῖν τιμῆς...</note> Because of this, he obtained such great honor **THAT WHILE STILL ALIVE HE WAS ADDRESSED AS A DIVINE BEING, a distinction which happened to no other king,** and after his death, he received honors equal to those who had ruled Egypt most lawfully in ancient times.

V. Since the *Egyptians* were endowed with such a spirit, is it strange or incredible that they held *Abraham*, *Joseph*, and *Moses*—men whose equals in wisdom, virtue, and merit scarcely any age has produced—in great veneration? And is it not likely that they absorbed the noble teachings these men delivered concerning the Supreme Deity and all branches of both sacred and secular Philosophy, at least to the extent that a certain "tint" or trace of them survived in later centuries?

VI. ABRAHAM was equipped by God with such great gifts, increased by so much wealth and means, and so renowned for his reputation for wisdom and piety, that he was highly venerable to kings as if he were some Prince of God. This was true even for the *Egyptian Pharaoh*, who, captivated by the beauty of Abraham's wife, heaped many benefits upon him. Yet, through his own experience and that of his household, the Pharaoh recognized that Abraham was remarkably dear to God above all other mortals; for God preserved his family as most holy and inviolable. (Genesis 12:13-14). By that reputation, he was known to his neighbors and celebrated even by foreign writers. *Eupolemus* <note>A Jewish historian of the 2nd century BCE who wrote in Greek.</note> in the works of *Alexander Polyhistor* <note>A Greek scholar and compiler.</note>, whom *Eusebius* <note>The "Father of Church History" (c. 260–339 AD).</note> cites, praises him <margin>Preparation for the Gospel, Book 9, Chapter 17.</margin> <note>original Greek: ὡς εὐγενείᾳ καὶ σοφίᾳ πάντας ὑπερβεβηκότα...</note> *as one who surpassed all in nobility and wisdom, who indeed discovered both Astrology and the Chaldean arts, and who, having applied himself to piety, was well-pleasing to God.* Our belief in the piety of this illustrious man compels us to believe that he discussed divine matters with the King of the *Egyptians*, the nobles, the Priests, and the Philosophers. Furthermore, both his prevailing reputation for wisdom and the *Egyptians'* reverence toward "theologian-men" <term>Theologos: here referring to men who possess divine or sacred knowledge</term> persuade us that he was heard with favor and admiration.

For because* THE EGYPTIANS DELIGHTED IN DISCORDANT CUSTOMS, *and some disparaged the rites of others, and were held in mutual hatred for that reason, he [Abraham] conferred with each of them...*

VIII. It is superfluous to mention how great were the merits of JOSEPH toward the Egyptians, and how great was his authority. Furthermore, it is only natural that the things he communicated were accepted with minds all the more ready, as he himself was dearer to the king, more closely tied to the priests through marriage, and more pleasing to the whole people. Additionally, what he said agreed with sound reason far more than the diverse decrees of all the others, with the memory of his great-grandfather Abraham also playing a role. Therefore, whatever religious elements the Egyptians held in common with the most ancient Hebrews, from what better source can we derive them than from this instruction by Abraham and *Joseph*?

# ON EGYPTIAN MATTERS

But certainly not under such a law that no discourse concerning religion was mingled in. For it is not possible that a mind so full of the divine could restrain itself to such a degree. It is true, indeed, that the Egyptians remained obstinate in their superstition. However, if there was anything of truth and holiness in the midst of those superstitions—such as those beliefs concerning the creation of the world, the immortality of souls, the varying states of the deceased, and many more things of that kind which are mentioned—who could doubt that these were impressed upon them, repeated, and confirmed by Joseph? And perhaps from that time when Joseph took a wife for himself from the Egyptian priestly family, his relatives first, and then the rest of the priests, adopted circumcision following the example of so illustrious a man.

X. That Moses also—adopted by the King’s daughter, raised in the court to the highest hopes, endowed with a mind capable of all things, and gifted with admirable virtues—held great authority among the Egyptians, is both spoken of by the facts themselves and attested with one voice by almost all writers who mention him. We heard previously from Artapanus <note>A Hellenistic Jewish historian who wrote a history of the Jews in Egypt</note> that by his outstanding merits toward the state, he won for himself not only the favor of the people, but even attained honor equal to the gods from the priests.
<margin>Antiquities, Book III, chapter XIII, and Book I against Apion.</margin>
And Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, the 1st-century Jewish historian</note> says that Moses was considered so wonderful and divine by the Egyptians that they claimed him for themselves and falsely asserted he was a citizen of Heliopolis. Cyril <note>Likely Cyril of Alexandria</note> also asserts more than once that the virtue of Moses and his wonderful wisdom were held in the highest admiration among the Egyptians; and that he affected with the name of God not only the Jews, but also some of the Egyptians; they being aware, perhaps, of what God had said: *Behold, I have made you a god to Pharaoh.* Exodus 7:1. Let us grant that there is some hyperbole in these expressions. But this, I think, ought not to be called into controversy: that during the time he had not yet incurred the king's indignation, his name was illustrious and venerable to the Egyptians. And who would believe that a man endowed with such piety and such zeal taught the Egyptians nothing of religion, whether by his words or his example? Or that the Egyptians allowed themselves to be persuaded of nothing by that man, in whom they could neither be ignorant of nor wish to hide that something Divine resided—especially when they still held all causes of hatred and envy far away?

He proved his mission from God through wonders, so that all of Egypt trembled. These wonders, since they were joined with the slaughter and destruction of the Egyptians, were able to kindle the stubborn minds of those impious men with hatred toward Moses and toward God, whose servant he was; but at the same time, they struck a fear that is sometimes the very beginning of religion. Furthermore, Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine Greek encyclopedia of the ancient Mediterranean world.</note> records that one of the Sacred Scribes predicted to the Egyptian king that it would come to pass *that one day someone would be born among the Israelites, outstanding in virtue and merit, who would cut down and depress the dominion and power of the Egyptians, but would greatly advance the affairs and glory of the Israelites:* by which roundabout words he designated Moses. If these things are true, they certainly could feel nothing but what was majestic and immense concerning him whose birth they had learned was foretold by God to their ancestors. That nation was certainly prone to pursue with a kind of religious awe those things which it perceived to be either very useful or very harmful to itself. Both of these qualities met in the person of Moses.

XII. But also the fame of those Laws—which God had promulgated with His own voice partly in the assembly of the entire Israelite People, from the midst of thunders and lightnings and terrifying wonders, and partly had delivered to His servant Moses in the secret of the holy mountain to be prescribed for Israel—permeated far and wide through the nations neighboring Palestine. It filled them with an estimation of singular wisdom and holiness, by which these laws far surpassed the institutions of other peoples. Indeed, Moses predicted it would be so: Deuteronomy 4:6, 8. *You shall observe therefore and do them: for this is your wisdom and prudence before the eyes of the peoples: who, hearing all these statutes, shall say, "Surely this great nation is a wise and prudent people." For what great nation is there that has statutes and judgments as just as this whole law which I set before you today?*

XIII. Let the words that Rahab of Jericho said to the Israelite spies serve as an example for us, Joshua 2:9, 10, 11. *I know that Jehovah has given you this land: both because the terror of you has fallen upon us, and because all the inhabitants of this land have melted away with fear of you. XV. Furthermore, no one will deny that the affairs of the Israelites were most flourishing under the reign of **David** and **Solomon**. ...[the patriarchs] Abraham, Joseph, and Moses, lived among them with a great reputation for wisdom and virtue; furthermore, that the Religion of the Hebrews was confirmed by stupendous miracles, a great part of which the Egyptians themselves experienced; moreover, that the King of the Hebrews <note>Solomon</note>, who had no equal in wisdom among mortals and who raised his religion to the highest peak of majesty, was linked by marriage to the royal family of the Egyptians: if, I say, we weigh all these things together, we will wonder why more institutes of the Most Holy religion were not propagated among the Egyptians. # BOOK III. CHAPTER XIII.

XIV. XV. *Cadmus brought his contributions into Greece not from Egypt, but from Phoenicia.* XVI. *The general negligence of the Greeks before the Babylonian Captivity does not diminish the diligence of Pythagoras.* XVII. XVIII. XIX. *The objections raised regarding the Hebrews' aversion to foreigners are not universally true, and can easily be turned back against the Egyptians.*

I. NOR were the *Egyptians* the only ones who drank from this fountain, but *Greece* itself—that parent of letters and arts and the common Teacher of Europe, *Greece*—owes a great part of her wisdom to the *Hebrews*. The plan of our undertaking requires us to speak on this matter here: although the subject has been so exhausted by the commentaries of the most learned men that scarcely anything is left for new observations. Truly, the *Hebrews* were regarded by the ancient sages of *Greece* not as *Apes* <note>original: "Simiis"; a reference to John Spencer’s skeptical view that Hebrew rituals were merely imitations of Egyptian ones</note>, as *Spencer* seemed to playfully suggest to himself, but as distinguished *Philosophers*, and they were held in high esteem for their great erudition. Along with the *Egyptians*, the *Magi*, and other *Philosophers* of the East, the ancient *Jews* are frequently listed as leaders and foremost figures in *Barbarian Philosophy* <note>The term "Barbarian" here is used in the classical sense to mean "non-Greek."</note>.

He teaches that Pythagoras flourished between the 50th and 52nd Olympiads <note>roughly 580–570 BCE</note>. From this, it is the opinion of certain ancients that *Nazaratus*—or as others write it, *Zabratus the Assyrian*—who was the teacher of Pythagoras, was the very same person as *Ezekiel* <note>The author is linking the biblical prophet Ezekiel to the legendary teacher of Pythagoras</note>. Whatever the case may be, it is clear that during the time Pythagoras spent in Egypt, Jews were not lacking there; either Jeremiah was living there at the time, or at the very least, his memory was still fresh. Furthermore, when Pythagoras was in Babylon—whether during the Babylonian Captivity or just after its end—he found many Jews of great renown there. Who would say, or who would believe one saying, that he did not inquire into their sacred rites, when a pure desire for learning had kept him traveling for so many years? See *Ussher’s Annals, Book 1, page 151*. Augustine continues: *Socrates is found in the Chronicles after Ezra. Not long after, Plato was born.* Indeed, Socrates, as *Apollodorus* testifies, was born in the 4th year of the 77th Olympiad—nearly forty years after the Jews were ordered by Darius to repair the Temple and the city. Plato was born in the 88th Olympiad. Thus, the Jews with whom both interacted in Egypt had moved there long before the time of the Ptolemies. Regarding the Jews who lived there in even older centuries, there are clear testimonies in the Sacred Scriptures, specifically Jeremiah 44. This provides us with a new argument: the communication between the Jews and the Egyptians was not non-existent, nor was the Jewish name so hated or despised as <insert>Sir John</insert> *Marsham* and <insert>John</insert> *Spencer* would have it.

# EGYPTIAN MATTERS

Philo, in his treatise on the Jews, first doubts whether the work belongs to the Historian <note>Hecataeus of Abdera</note>, and secondly says that, if it is indeed his, it is likely he was carried away by the persuasiveness of the Jews and agreed with their doctrine. *There also exists a book by the Historian Hecataeus concerning the Jews, in which he so approves of the wisdom of this nation that Herennius Philo, in his own commentaries on the Jews, first doubts whether this writing belongs to that Historian; then he adds that if it is his, he seems to have been seized by the persuasions of the Jews and to have approved of their teachings.* <note>The author provides the same passage in both Greek and Latin to ensure accuracy for the reader.</note>

<margin>
Book 1, Against Apion.
</margin>
According to the testimony of *Josephus*, *Hecataeus of Abdera* was a philosopher and a man most capable in active affairs, who flourished during the time of King Alexander and was an associate of Ptolemy, son of Lagus. *A man not only a Philosopher, but also most fit for conducting business, who flourished in the time of King Alexander and was an intimate of Ptolemy, son of Lagus.*

XI. It is truly a wonder that *Scaliger* <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609), a famous scholar of historical chronology</note> placed this *Hecataeus* among the monsters of <term>spurious writers</term> <note>original: ὑποβολιμαίων (hypobolimaion) - forged or substituted works</note>, such as *Dares the Phrygian* and *Dictys of Crete*. It is even more wonderful that he thinks it can be clearly gathered from the cited passage of *Origen* that *Hecataeus* was fabricated by the Hellenists <note>Greek-speaking Jews</note> in ancient times. Yet *Origen* says nothing of the sort, as will be evident to anyone looking at the words. For *Origen* was not attempting to bring forward a forged writer in defense of the Jewish cause; rather, he cited Philo’s judgment on *Hecataeus* for this reason: so that the almost incredible agreement of *Hecataeus* with the Jews might be established more certainly. Indeed, the agreement was so great that *Herennius Philo* thought he should doubt whether he ought to attribute these commentaries to *Hecataeus*; yet if he had to—as he surely did, since he had no other reasons for doubt—he pronounced him "corrupted" by the Jews. <margin>In the Annotations on Origen.</margin> But *Spencer* <note>John Spencer (1630–1693), an English theologian</note> rightly corrected *Scaliger* on this point.

XII. These matters, so clear and so eloquent, confirmed by the testimonies of so many *Jews*, *Christians*, and *Pagans*, cannot be evaded by a single saying of *Lactantius*. He, disagreeing with all these others, wonders <margin>Divine Institutes, Book 4, Chapter 2.</margin> why, although *Pythagoras* and *Plato* had penetrated as far as the *Egyptians*, the *Magi*, and the *Persians* out of a love for investigating the truth, they nevertheless did not approach the *Jews*, with whom alone wisdom then resided, and to whom they could have traveled more easily. For that *Lactantius* erred splendidly when he wrote this is proved not only by the testimonies we have produced;

BOOK III. CHAPTER XIII.

Indeed, the facts themselves speak clearly, provided we compare the teachings of *Pythagoras* with the dogmas of the *Jews*. Graven images were forbidden to the *Jews*. *Pythagoras* also forbade the image of *God* to be inscribed on a ring. *Pythagoras* even transferred the law against eating the flesh of animals that died naturally into his own precepts. When he ordered that sacred rites be performed with bare feet, does he not seem to have had in mind the command given to *Moses* regarding the burning bush? Just as has been noted by *Ambrose*. <margin>Letters, Book III, Letter XX</margin> *Pythagoras* also represented the entirety of *Moses’s* precept in which he forbade the cutting down of fruit-bearing trees. That *Pythagorean* saying, *one must not pass through the place where a donkey has collapsed*, also seems to have originated from the story of *Balaam* and the *Donkey*. I will omit other points for now, noted by us elsewhere, in which there is a manifest harmony between the *Pythagorean* and *Jewish* decrees.

XIII. From this, a response is easy to those petty arguments of *Marsham* <note>Sir John Marsham (1602–1685), an English writer on chronology who argued for Egyptian influence over Jewish law.</note>, by which he strives to build faith in that anomalous and paradoxical statement <note>original: ῥήσει (rhese) - a Greek term for a speech or saying</note> of *Lactantius*. For as to what certain people object to in *Josephus*—that the constitution of the *Jewish Republic* seems to be a recent thing, since nothing was said about it by *Greek* writers—this is false in every way. We have the annals of no Republic more ancient than theirs: since everyone admits that the times preceding the *Trojan* war, if you look at other nations, are fabulous <note>meaning "mythological" or "legendary" rather than factual</note>. And the testimonies we have just brought forward make it plain that many of the *Greeks* not only remembered the *Jews*, but remembered them with extensive praise.

XIV. If it were true, as *Marsham* contends, that before the Babylonian captivity, or the age of the Seven Sages, the *Greeks* were so indifferent not only to Philosophy but to their own affairs (and even more so to foreign ones) that they had no commerce with the Hebrews; let him explain to me how it happened that such a great intimacy existed between those "indifferent" people and the *Egyptians*, as he proclaims everywhere. For if you say that *Cadmus* brought many Egyptian things with him from *Egyptian Thebes* into *Greece*, you would be greatly mistaken. *Cadmus* was not *Egyptian*, but a *Phoenician*; which his very name proves. Furthermore, these *Kadmonites* were the same as the *Hivites*. After the return from *Babylon*, the name of the *Jews* was not so vile that they were not numbered among the most excellent Philosophers of the East. Nor should more credit be given to the insults of *Tacitus* <note>Cornelius Tacitus, a Roman historian known for his critical view of the Jews</note>, who showed himself to have been quite ignorant of Jewish affairs, than to the unforced testimonies of more ancient writers in praise of the *Jews*.

XVII. Furthermore, regarding the objection that *Marsham* <note>Sir John Marsham (1602–1685), an English chronicler who argued that Jewish customs were derived from Egypt.</note> raises from *Josephus*—namely, that the *Jews* had no dealings with other nations and that, due to their unique way of life, there was nothing in ancient times to facilitate interaction with the *Greeks*—this should not be understood in an absolute or simple sense. Rather, it should be viewed in comparison to the more frequent travels of other nations for the sake of trade. For otherwise, it is recorded in the Holy Scriptures that *Solomon* conducted commerce by sending his ships to foreign and distant regions. Nor was *Josephus* so lacking in judgment or so forgetful of his own purpose that, while intending in this entire dispute against *Apion* to assert the antiquity, nobility, fame, and primacy in true wisdom of his own nation, he would strike down all his own forces with this single blow. Indeed, he himself produces many crowded testimonies from foreigners, including *Greeks*, concerning the affairs of his nation.

XVIII. What is added regarding the *Jews'* reluctance to share their Law with other nations and their avoidance of commerce with the Gentiles can easily be turned back against the *Egyptians*. For, as we heard above from *Herodotus*, not only were *Greeks* repelled from the kiss of an *Egyptian* man or woman, but the *Egyptians* could not even bear to use a *Greek* spit, knife, or pot, nor eat the pure flesh of an ox if it had been cut with a *Greek* knife. According to the testimony of *Chaeremon* <note>An Egyptian Stoic philosopher and historian of the 1st century AD.</note>, they were no less strict than the *Jews*, for they "associated with no one of a foreign worship" <note>original Greek: τῶν ἐξωτικῶν τῆς θρησκείας οὐδενὶ συνεσίαν</note>. Indeed, so great was the inhospitality of the ancient *Egyptians* that they would not even admit foreigners into their region. <margin>*Diodorus Siculus*, Book I, p. 61.</margin> *Psammetichus* was the first of all; who "showed himself liberal and kind toward those foreigners who voluntarily migrated into *Egypt*" <note>original Greek: εὐηργέτει τῶν ξένων τοὺς ἐθελουσίως εἰς τὴν Αἰγυπτον ἐπιδημήσαντας</note>. He was certainly the first of all the kings of *Egypt* to open the foreign marketplaces of the region to other nations and provide great security for the voyages of outsiders. For those who held power before him made *Egypt* inaccessible to foreigners, punishing those who landed there with slavery. Indeed, the inhospitality of the nation rendered the impiety of *Busiris* <note>A mythical Egyptian king who sacrificed foreigners to end a famine.</note> so famous among the *Greeks*. This did not actually happen in truth, but their extreme cruelty gave rise to the invention of the fable. Now, *Psammetichus* reigned in *Egypt* at the same time that *Manasseh* reigned in *Judah*, nearly seven centuries before the birth of the Lord. But even after those times, the Priests of the *Egyptians* remained mystical and uncommunicative;

XIX. Furthermore, the Jews have often been too spitefully accused of being *unsociable and uncommunicative* <note>original: "τὸ ἄμικτον καὶ τὸ ἀκοινώνητον" — terms often used by Greek and Roman critics to describe Jewish separation from Gentile customs</note>, even though they have received proselytes into the communion of their faith and Church in every age. For as many as have chosen to live by our laws, he receives all of them most lovingly; thinking that this communion is maintained not by race alone, but also by a voluntary association in our way of life. However, those who would approach them only in passing, or while occupied with other matters, he did not wish to be admitted into intimate familiarity.*

Therefore, Prudence <note>The author personifies "Prudence" as a guiding principle of governance.</note> suggested that many rites which were seen to be in common use among neighboring nations—and which God knew to be more tolerable follies—should be left to the people, provided they were slightly changed and redirected toward the significance of more majestic mysteries. This was done lest an excessive appearance of novelty should offend them. A new Commonwealth <note>original: "Respublica"</note> was indeed to be established, but minds had to be enticed toward it through some shadowy remnants of the old ways. This follows the precept of the most cautious Politics: *The secret of a new state is the image of the old.* <note>A common early modern political maxim suggesting that people accept radical change more easily if it looks like tradition.</note> Furthermore, the Reformation <note>original: "Reformatio"</note> which God was undertaking never proceeds more happily than when it is established step by step; not by immediately abolishing everything from old custom, but by tolerating whatever can be conveniently tolerated. Finally, unless God had established it so, there was a fear that the Israelite people, seized by a zeal for their old vanities, might wish to offer worship to the Demon through those rites if they were not permitted to do so for God. But God also showed consideration for the *Gentiles* <note>Non-Jewish nations</note> by this retention of ancient rites: for a certain degree of agreement between them was naturally suited to foster a favorable inclination among the Gentiles toward the Jews and their religion.

II. But in truth, however much these arguments may have the appearance of civil Prudence, they are all spoken without the word of God; they are the inventions of the human mind, hardly worthy of the Majesty of the Divine power. Surely, cautious and clever mortals in this world measure God by their own disposition: they place the secret arts of ruling and the crafty tricks of politicians—which the earth would scarcely approve—into heaven. As if indeed He, who holds the hearts of mortals in His hand and turns them wherever He wills, requires those winding paths of cunning to form and strengthen a people for Himself. I do not deny, certainly, that God, acting with men as with rational creatures, employs suitable means to persuade them, and displays a truly admirable wisdom in the choice of those means. Nevertheless, that most holy wisdom of God cannot be compared with the deceits and craftiness of politicians without significant insult to Him.

III. Just as He was truly undertaking a new Commonwealth, so He wished it to appear new to the Israelites, exactly as it was. For its form or appearance was not fashioned from the ruins of Canaanite or Egyptian rites, but had descended from heaven, having first been shown to Moses on the holy mountain, so that according to that pattern all things in Israel might be composed—
