VI. And hence it happened that God inserted many things into His ritual laws that were <term>parallel opposites</term> <note>original Greek: ἐκ παραλλήλου</note> to the institutions of the Egyptians, the Sabians, and the Canaanites. This was done not only in those matters which seem to have some natural reason of goodness or malice, but also in those of which Maimonides says, <term>if the Law did not exist, those things which oppose them would not be evil at all</term>. <note>original Hebrew: שאילמלא התורה לא היו רעות כלל</note> Whence the same Maimonides confesses: *that the reasons for many laws became known to him only through the knowledge of the faith, worship, and rites of the Sabians, to which they were directly opposed.* Various examples of this matter have been cited by us elsewhere. Now we shall add others.

VIII. # OF EGYPTIAN AFFAIRS

<margin>XII. It was</margin>

to entice the Gentiles to the Commonwealth of Israel by a similarity [of rituals]. But of this, more fully soon.

X. We will not be able to more certainly refute these fabricated causes for the Mosaic rites than by assigning the true ones; which were dictated not by a rash estimation of Divine wisdom, or the love of a hypothesis once adopted, but by the Spirit of God himself, in the monuments of the Sacred Scriptures which know not how to deceive. Therefore, God had this as his *primary* purpose in the commanding of rites: that by these laborious exercises he might subdue the untamable ferocity of the people, as if by a *most difficult yoke*. For indeed, *Israel appeared before God as an infant or a child, who, as he did not know the path for himself, so being petulant by nature and of a stubborn disposition, was harsh toward his monitors.* <note>The author uses a metaphor of a rebellious child to explain why the Old Testament laws were so strict.</note> Too mild an indulgence was not suitable for that state; it would have been a fuel for insolence rather than a remedy. Hence he gave the law to the people as a pedagogue <note>term: pedagogue. From the Greek 'paidagogos', a tutor or guardian who escorted children to school and supervised their behavior with strict discipline.</note>, who, armed with a rod and a staff, might restrain the impulses of their fierce passions. Galatians 3:23. *And although Israel was a son, and the heir of all things, God nevertheless treated him so that he seemed not to differ much from a slave. Removed from paternal embraces and flatteries, He ordered him to be under tutors and curators. And He reduced him to servitude under the elements of the world.* Galatians 4:1, 2, 3.

XI. Which was emphatically stated by the Apostle. For he calls the ceremonies *elements* <note>original: "elementa"</note> because of their rudeness or imperfection; a metaphor taken either from nature or from art. And indeed, they are *Elements of the World*, either because they were earthly, taken from the world, and consisted of those things which worldly men held in common with the pious, and which do not contain in themselves the blessing and the goods of the inheritance: or because God, wishing to instruct the world, that is, the inhabitants of the world, began from those thin principles, a lower school having first been opened in only one corner of the world. To these elements of the world the Israelites were <term>enslaved</term> <note>original Greek: δεδουλωμένοι (dedoulōmenoi)</note>. For they were given with a severe threat, lest they should be either neglected or used otherwise than had been commanded: and Princes and Elders were added, having power, sitting in the Chair of Moses, who might hold and drive them to the observation of the rites: and finally, the observation itself reflected something slavish, inasmuch as in it was a reproach of childhood, since it consisted of tiny precepts and dogmas, such as are prescribed to little boys: *do not eat, nor taste, nor touch.* Colossians 2:21.

### BOOK III. CHAPTER XIV.

XII. Furthermore, within that immense multitude of rituals, enjoined upon Israel with such severe threats, there was a **heavy burden** and a **yoke difficult to bear** <note>Acts 15:10</note>, which the Apostle calls the **yoke of slavery** <note>Galatians 5:1</note>. By this, the neck of that untamed heifer <note>A metaphor for the rebellious nature of the people</note> was pressed down, so that it might be driven toward obedience. This is true whether you look at the **matter of the rituals**, which consisted of **weak and beggarly elements of the world** <note>Galatians 4:9</note>—which were not able *to make the comers thereunto perfect* <note>Hebrews 10:1; original Greek: τοὺς προσερχομένους τελειῶσαι</note>, and in the observation of which there was no inherent holiness, nor the image of God, nor rational worship—or whether you look at the **multitude** of rites by which they were exhausted; or the **observation** itself, which was for the most part burdensome, joined with the undertaking of pain, immense expense, and a scrupulous attention to minutiae; or the **rigor** with which all things were demanded under the threat of a curse and the menace of being cut off; or finally, the **significance** of it all. For they were compelled to issue a confession of their own **impurity** through washings, and of their **guilt** through sacrifices—a guilt, indeed, not yet fully atoned for, as shown by the frequent repetition of those sacrifices. Thus, they were forced **to sign a handwritten bill of indictment against themselves** <note>Colossians 2:14; referring to the "handwriting of ordinances" that stood against the sinner</note>. In all these things, there was a burden and a yoke perfectly suited to restraining childish petulance.

XIII. Nor was it only a burden, but also a <term>guard</term> <note>original Greek: φρουρὰ (phroura)</note>. For so says the Apostle: *Before faith came, we were kept under guard by the law, shut up* <note>Galatians 3:23; original Greek: ὑπὸ νόμου ἐφρουρούμεθα, συγκεκλεισμένοι</note>. To be sure, God had chosen the Israelite people out of all nations to be a special people for Himself. Therefore, He willed them to be most thoroughly separated from the rest of the nations. For this purpose, He placed the law like a <term>guard</term>, or a kind of prison or fortress, in which they were enclosed and disciplined. These views differ greatly from that **indulgence** imagined by <term>Spencer</term> <note>John Spencer (1630–1693), a scholar who argued that many Jewish rites were adapted from Egyptian customs to accommodate the people's weaknesses</note>, who suggests that God, by yielding to the petulance and impudence of the people, granted them permission to keep Egyptian customs.

XIV. Furthermore, this was also God’s intention in the commanding of rituals: that by their observation, as if by a **partition wall**, He might remove them far from fellowship with the Gentiles. Let us hear the Apostle again: *For He is our peace, who has made both one, and has broken down the middle wall of partition between us; having abolished in His flesh the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances; for to make in Himself of twain one new man, so making peace* <note>Ephesians 2:14-15</note>.

# EGYPTIAN MATTERS

When he speaks of the *barrier of the dividing wall*, he seems to allude to the double *barrier of the Temple*. The outer of these, within which the Jews who were ritually clean gathered for the sake of religion, had a parapet <note>original: "loricam"</note> in which small columns were arranged at equal intervals. These were inscribed with Greek and Latin letters, by which it was signified that no foreigner was permitted, under penalty of death, to enter that parapet and break into the inner enclosure. Likewise, in the *inner enclosure*, there was another similar parapet by which the people were kept back from the entrance of the Temple and the Court of the Priests. *Louis Cappel* <note>A 17th-century French Protestant clergyman and Hebrew scholar.</note> observed this from the writings of *Josephus* <note>Titus Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian.</note> and skillfully applied it to this saying of the Apostle. The Ceremonies can be compared with both of those barriers or parapets: they removed the *Gentiles* from the *Jews*, by which name they were similar to the *parapet of the first barrier*; and they also removed the *Jews* themselves, in a certain way, from *God* and familiar access to Him.

XV. Furthermore, when he calls the *Law of commandments in rituals "enmities,"* he suggests among other things that it was a symbol and instrument of division and hatred between *Israel* and the *Gentiles*. For the *Jews*, proud of the rituals instituted by *God*, despised the *Gentiles*, who were enslaved to human or even Diabolical superstitions. In turn, many ceremonies of the *Jews* were hated by the *Pagans* <note>original: "Ethnicis"</note> and seemed absurd and ridiculous to them. And from this arose the mutual hatreds of the nations; not indeed commanded by the Law, but nevertheless established in a certain way by it. For this reason, the nations frequently reproached the *Jews* for their unsociable way of living. *Apollonius Molon* <note>A Greek rhetorician known for his anti-Jewish sentiments.</note> objected that *they do not admit those who think differently about God, nor is anything in common for them with those who differ in their institutions.* Similarly, the friends of *Antiochus* in the writings of *Diodorus* <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian.</note> accuse them, *that they alone of all nations are unsociable in their mixing with any other nation, and they regard everyone else as enemies* <note>original Greek: "μόνους ἁπάντων ἐθνῶν ἀκοινωνήτους εἶναι τῆς πρὸς ἄλλο ἔθνος ἐπιμιξίας, καὶ πολεμίους ὑπολαμβάνειν πάντας"</note>. This flowed from the contrariety of their rituals. <margin>History, Book 5.</margin> *Tacitus* <note>A senator and historian of the Roman Empire.</note> says: *Moses, so that he might strengthen the nation for himself in the future, introduced new rituals contrary to the rest of mortals. All things are profane to them which are sacred among us. Again, those things are permitted among them which are incestuous to us. And after some other remarks: These rituals, in whatever way they were introduced, are defended by their antiquity. Other institutions, sinister and foul, have prevailed through their depravity. Then: The custom of the Jews is absurd and filthy.* *Christ* destroyed this enmity of the Jews and Gentiles by making peace, removing the barrier by which they were separated, and by abolishing—

### BOOK III. CHAPTER XIV.

and by the law of rites; and thus he made *both one* <note>original: "τὰ ἀμφότερα ἓν" (ta amphoteria hen). A reference to Ephesians 2:14.</note>, namely one new man, who should serve God not in the oldness of the letter, but in the newness of the Spirit.

XVI. From this it is plain that *Spencer* <note>John Spencer (1630–1693), an English theologian who argued that many Jewish rites were adapted from Egyptian customs to make religion more palatable to the Israelites.</note> errs by the width of the entire sky when he contends that the system of Mosaic rites was so arranged that the Gentiles, noticing some agreement between those rites and their own, might have more favorable inclinations toward the religion of the Jews; and that this communion of sacred things, however great, might more easily and charmingly join their minds to the worship and fellowship of the Jews, and keep them bound to it. On the contrary, the Apostle teaches that the Law was given as a "partition wall" to separate the Jews from the Gentiles, and was an occasion for mutual enmity, which could not be ended unless that Law was abolished.

XVII. Finally, this also was the goal of the Ceremonies: *that they might be figures and shadows of spiritual things*, and that there might exist in them a skillful *picture of Christ* and of the grace to be obtained through him (Colossians 2:17). And truly, this was the remarkable happiness of Israel: that at a time when it pleased God to propose his mysteries only through enigmas, parables, and figures, they had these pictures of Divine goodness and of the coming Savior continually before their eyes. All the more so because they were instructed by the Patriarchs, the Prophets, and those taught by them, concerning the mystical significance of these things, according to the measure of those times (1 Peter 1:10, 11, 12). However, it is not probable that God made pictures of spiritual and heavenly things out of the impious and Diabolical rites of the Egyptians, out of ancient vanities, out of "tolerable trifles," or out of imitations of the Magic art. It is certain that most learned men would have spent their labor much more usefully, and more gloriously for God, if they had attempted to assign the exact agreement of the ceremonies commanded by God with the things they signified, rather than with certain gloomy trifles of the Egyptians.

XVIII. Yet, because Spencer thinks he has found something in the sacred writings which he judges should be brought forward to support his opinion, let us now briefly examine that as well. First, therefore, he urges what God says in Ezekiel chapter 20:25: *I gave them statutes that were not good, and laws by which they could not live.* From this he assumes for himself that by *statutes that were not good*, the ritual Laws are understood; which statutes [were] not good...

# EGYPTIAN MATTERS

...they are called so, not only for other reasons, but especially by reason of their *origin*, because they owed their birth to the customs of the age; enacted, of course, so that they might remove some of those customs marked by vice from their midst, while tolerating others with the greatest caution. But *Spencer* <note>John Spencer, a pioneer in the comparative study of religion</note> cannot be ignorant of the fact that the meaning of that passage is highly controversial; and the one he chose—because it seemed to serve his hypothesis, albeit timidly and with a hesitating mind—is rejected by most interpreters for reasons that are not to be despised. However, because there are even among our own people very learned men who are so far pleased by his explanation that they understand "ritual laws" by the phrase "statutes that were not good," I do not wish to argue over that matter now. It will be better for the common cause of piety to show that, even if that interpretation is granted, the conclusion for which *Spencer* fights does not follow.

XIX. Those who affirm that the precepts which are called dogmas, or decrees—commonly termed ceremonial—are called *not good* here by God, produce these reasons for that naming: They are "not good" because: I. They are not those in which the image of God and the true holiness of man consist. II. They are not pleasant, because they are a heavy and unbearable yoke. III. They are not those in which there is life. IV. Because as long as those precepts are incumbent, a "reformation" <note>original Greek: διόρθωσις (diorthosis), meaning a making straight or setting right</note> or a change *for the better* is expected; a "better hope" <note>original Greek: κρείττων ἐλπίς (kreitton elpis)</note> is excluded, through which we draw near to God; nor is the inheritance of the world given, and that joy which would otherwise arise from the communion of nations is taken away. However, they consider it foreign to their piety to say they were "not good" because they drew their origin from the evil customs of the age, or because they admitted something from them, even if with caution.

XX. And rightly so. I. For not only does God not suggest by even a little word that he gave these things to the stubborn character of the people—as if yielding somewhat to their hardness by indulging the use of certain rites to which they had become accustomed—but he repeatedly emphasizes his Royal authority and Masterful power, to which they ought to be obedient without any exception.
> Verse 19. *I am Jehovah your God; walk in my statutes, and keep my judgments, and do them.*
Unless they did so, he swore with an uplifted hand,
> *that he would pour out his fury upon them in the very wilderness to consume them.* Verses 13, 15.

...hardness <note>referring to the "hardness of heart" of the Israelites</note> that He [God] transcribed certain things from the customs of the Egyptians into His own, so that He might command them to be as far as possible from the customs of the Egyptians. He who established things thus does not teach that He indulged certain Egyptian rites for the sake of a stubborn people.

XXII. III. It must be explained more accurately in what way those statutes are said to be "not good" by reason of their origin. For if they arose from the good customs of the Egyptians and are in harmony with them, then by that very name they are certainly good. For whatever agrees with the good is good. If they arose from evil customs and are in harmony with them, they will certainly not be good statutes, nor would they be the statutes of God. For He cannot command anything unless it is good, or by commanding it, He makes it good. If *Spencer* <note>John Spencer (1630–1693), a scholar who controversially argued that Jewish rituals were adapted from Egyptian ones to accommodate the Israelites' habits.</note> wishes to claim that these institutions owed their origin to the customs of the age insofar as they were intended to correct them, he says what is true; but he neither proves what he undertook to prove, nor gives a reason why those statutes are called "not good." On the contrary, they are good for the very reason that they remove rites marked by some vice. According to the old proverb: *Good laws [are born] from evil customs.* Therefore, the speech of the Lord in Ezekiel helps Spencer not at all here.

### CHAPTER XV.

->A Response to the Authorities Cited Against Us.<-

*I. Certain general observations on the testimonies praised by the opposing side. II. First: Since the Greeks were acquainted with Egyptian affairs before those of the Hebrews, and believed the Egyptians when they boasted of their antiquity, it followed that they too liberally attributed many things to them. III. The same must be observed in certain Christians, who handled secular studies before sacred ones. IV. Second: Certain ecclesiastical writers said more than Marsham <note>Sir John Marsham, a chronicler who argued for Egyptian priority</note> or Spencer would wish. V. Third: Since they are recent, their authority on the most ancient matters is not valid unless supported by reasons; which are often weak <note>original: "ficulneæ" - literally 'made of fig-wood,' a Latin idiom for something brittle or worthless</note>. VI. And reckless. VII. Fourth: Some testimonies say only that which is agreed upon by both sides, and do not decide the dispute. VIII. Fifth: The principal authors among those they praise stand with us rather than with the opposing side. This is shown by example. IX. Of Maimonides. X. XI. XII. Of Origen. XIII. XIV. And of Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius, the famous Dutch jurist and theologian</note>. XV. Epilogue of the work.*

### BOOK III. CHAPTER XV.

...they lead forth a phalanx of those who, as the saying goes, "all go together into the same opinion" <note>original: "in eadem omnia... secum euntium" — a Latin idiom referring to people who blindly follow a consensus or a specific leader's vote.</note>. However, we do not consider it necessary to respond with excessive diligence to every single Author and their cited testimonies. It will suffice to set forth certain general observations by which we believe all doubts, if any remain, can be removed from the minds of the Readers.

II. And first, indeed, I would wish it to be observed: since the affairs of the **Egyptians** were most celebrated among the **Greeks** at a time when the name of the **Hebrews** was scarcely known to them, and almost all **Greek** Writers—from whom learning flowed down to others—scrutinized **Egyptian** antiquities much earlier and more diligently than **Hebrew** ones, it easily happened from this that whatever they understood to have been anciently received among the **Egyptians**, they believed to have also been invented by them. And if they later detected anything in some way similar to those things in the institutions of the **Hebrews**, they suspected it had been derived from the **Egyptians** to them. In this suspicion they were greatly confirmed, partly by the proud **boasting of the Egyptians**, who, swollen with the reputation of their wisdom, were excellent displayers of their own affairs; and partly by that tradition which had occupied the minds of many, that the **Hebrews**, and even **Moses** himself, the leader of the people, were descended from the **Egyptians**. 

Certainly **Herodotus** knew nothing at all about the **Hebrews**; **Diodorus Siculus**, **Plutarch**, and others had received only a few or erroneous things about them. **Egyptian** monuments, however, had long since filled their minds; and therefore, being entirely devoted to preaching those things, they impressed upon their Readers that opinion which they themselves had rashly adopted. If they had known that which we know from the Divine Scriptures—that the **Hebrews**, descended from the ancient Patriarchs and instructed in their sacred discipline, came into **Egypt** as dear and venerable to kings and princes, and thereafter received their system of rituals from God himself—they would not have attributed all those things to the **Egyptians** as inventors, which they have now too liberally attributed to them.

III. And this observation is valid not only against those **Gentiles** <note>In this context, "Gentiles" refers to the non-Christian, classical Greek and Roman authors.</note>, but also against certain **Christians**: who, since they had diligently handled secular studies before they obtained an exact skill in sacred history, and were oftentimes not very accurate searchers of origins or calculators of times; for...

# OF EGYPTIAN MATTERS

Those who approach sacred matters while their minds are still occupied by the prejudices of secular <note>original: "fanarum," referring to non-religious or pagan history</note> antiquities have sometimes judged them with too little skill. They have rashly believed that whatever they learned first must also have been the most ancient.

IV. Furthermore, it must also be noted that *Ecclesiastical* writers were sometimes so burdened by a presumption regarding the antiquity of the Gentiles <note>non-Christian or pagan nations</note> that they said considerably more about them than even *Marsham* or *Spencer* <note>Sir John Marsham and John Spencer, 17th-century scholars who argued that Jewish law derived from Egyptian ritual</note> would wish. Take, for example, *Chrysostom* <note>St. John Chrysostom, an influential Early Church Father</note>; he asserts that all the ceremonies of the *Jews*, all their rites, sacrifices, purifications, new moons, the Ark, and even the Temple itself, drew their origin from the crude ways of the Gentiles. *Spencer* himself admits that in making this assertion, *Chrysostom* sacrificed neither to modesty nor to truth as he ought. From this it follows that one should not grant them credit in such matters without scrutiny <note>original: "ἀβασανίσως" (untested/without examination)</note> and without an examination of their reasons.

V. Thirdly, it must be observed that since they speak of things far more ancient than their own age, their authority here is invalid unless they support their words with clear evidence. However, the evidence they bring forward is either irrelevant or highly uncertain. Let us recall what we heard *Chrysostom* arguing above: to prove that God granted the Jews many things for which they had developed a longing while in Egypt, he mentions as an example the structure of so <margin>Compare Book III, chapter 10.</margin> magnificent a temple. Although this was not disapproved of by *Marsham* and *Spencer*, we have established above by many arguments that it is quite irrelevant. Likewise, that which *Cyril of Alexandria* relates regarding the custom of the Gentiles *growing their hair long* and nourishing it for *Demons*, or offering it to *Nymphis* or a river, is highly uncertain. It is uncertain, I say, whether that custom was so ancient and so widely accepted among those nations with whom the Israelites had dealings that it could have given origin to the Divine laws concerning the Nazirite vow <note>A Jewish vow of consecration involving abstaining from cutting hair</note>. Would it not be more probably said that these laws were opposed to the custom of the *Zabians* <note>A group often identified by medieval scholars as ancient star-worshippers</note> of whom <margin>Guide for the Perplexed, Part III, chapter 47.</margin> *Maimonides* <note>The preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher</note> says:
> *they held all things separated from the body, such as hair, nails, and blood, to be unclean; hence all barbers were unclean to them because they touch blood and hair. Whoever allowed a razor to pass over his flesh was compelled to wash himself in clear, limpid spring water.*

VI. Nor simply because Spencer could find no other reason for the Divine precept regarding the *Nazirite vow*...

# BOOK III. CHAPTER XV.

reason occurs to us, for that reason we must embrace the opinion of the most excellent *Cyril* <note>Saint Cyril of Alexandria, a 5th-century Church Father known for his Christological works.</note>. For why do we little men allow ourselves so much, that we not only demand to explain the reasons for all Divine Laws, but even—if perhaps only one reason comes to our mind, and that one (as we ourselves would not dare deny) is quite weak—we rashly assert there is no other reason besides it? If legal consultants of human law defer so much to their elders as to say that many things were established wisely by them, even if the reason for them cannot be rendered by posterity; how much more is it right for us to think this of Divine Laws: that their most wise and holy reasons are always clear to God, even if the dark stupor of our own intellect cannot grasp them? Precepts of this kind are <term>decrees</term> <note>original: "δόγματα" (dogmata). In this context, it refers to laws that depend solely on the will of the lawgiver rather than on obvious natural reason.</note>, depending on the mere will of the Legislator, by which He wished to exercise the obedience of His people, so that they might learn to rest in the authority of the one commanding alone, without demanding a reason for the command. Meanwhile, it must be held by faith that whatever is commanded is just and good for the obedient: and that beneath that external precept lies something secret, the fulfillment of which must be sought in Christ and His mystical body. The most learned *Spencer* <note>John Spencer (1630–1693), a pioneer in the comparative study of religion who argued that many Jewish rites were adapted from Egyptian customs.</note> would have served us better had he explained the spiritual significance of the precept concerning the hair of the Nazirites—first being grown, then burned—by comparing the Scriptures.

VII. ***Fourthly***: *Spencer* praises several things as if they supported his own opinion, which are nevertheless conceded by both sides and are outside the question now being disputed. For we also have no doubt that God prescribed anew to the Israelites many things contributing to the outward display of worship—things formerly used in the world, but instituted and approved by God Himself through either general or specific mandates, and later corrupted by the gentiles—so that through these He might gradually lead them by the hand toward greater, spiritual, and heavenly things. To this extent He accommodated Himself to the unrefined state of the people, who could hardly be transferred in a single leap from the visible things to which they were accustomed to purely spiritual things, which are to be apprehended only by meditation of the mind and sublime faith. For this reason, Paul calls those ceremonies the "beggarly elements of the world." To this category can be referred Sacrifices, Altars, Temples, the distinction of Days, and many more of that kind, which were used by the ancestors and which God willed to be observed in the religion of the Israelites as well. But those things to us...

# EGYPTIAN MATTERS

The dispute is whether, because of the Israelites' familiarity with the Egyptians, God transcribed many things from Egyptian superstitions into His own worship—though slightly corrected and diminished—lest the stubborn people cast off all reverence for the Divine if this had not been granted to them. However, we do not find this in the lengthy *discourse of Maimonides* <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent Jewish philosopher and scholar.</note> that is cited. He indeed teaches that Priests, Sacrifices, Temples, and Altars—such as the Gentiles had impiously dedicated to the Sun, Moon, and other fabricated deities—were, by Divine command, transferred from created things and phantasms (which have no truth) to His own name and divinity. But he by no means teaches that the reasons for Mosaic rituals are to be explained by their agreement with Egyptian follies, or that God wished to be worshiped with those things which they had wickedly devised for their idolatrous cult. *And thus, that testimony of Maimonides does not oppose our opinion.*

VIII. We add **Fifthly**: That several authors are praised by *Spencer* <note>John Spencer, author of "De Legibus Hebraeorum," who argued that Jewish law was a reaction to or adaptation of Egyptian ritual.</note> who actually stand with us rather than with him. From many, I shall bring forward three examples of Illustrious men who, because of their exceptional erudition and uncommon skill in these matters, may represent all. These are, from the Jews, **MAIMONIDES**; from the Ancients, **ORIGEN** <note>An early Christian scholar and theologian (c. 184–253 AD).</note>; and from the more recent, **GROTIUS** <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch jurist and theologian.</note>.

<margin>Part III, chapter XLV.</margin>
IX. **MAIMONIDES**, to begin now with him whom we most recently heard speaking, explains his mind on this controversy we have at hand in these very words, and in that same chapter which *Spencer* cites for himself. *Of all these things*, he says, *there is one and the same intention, namely*, **THAT WE SHOULD NOT WORSHIP HIM IN THE MANNER IN WHICH IDOLATERS WERE ACCUSTOMED TO WORSHIP THEIR FICTITIOUS DEITIES**; *which thing He prohibited generally and universally, by saying*, **DO NOT SAY, "AS THOSE NATIONS WORSHIP THEIR GODS, SO WILL I ALSO DO."** Deuteronomy 12:30. *He means to say, they ought not to do so for God, and that for the cause which He subjoins*: **BECAUSE EVERY ABOMINATION TO THE LORD WHICH HE HATES THEY HAVE DONE FOR THEIR GODS.** *Moreover, he proves this by the introduction of many examples. It was*, he says, *a common superstition at that time to adore the sun and hold it as God; hence it happened, without a doubt, that they turned toward the East to worship. Abraham, however, turned himself toward the West on Mount Moriah, so that his back—*

With the Persians, because both sacrifice to Jove <note>original: "Jovi" — here used by Celsus to mean the supreme sky-god</note> on the highest mountains, by which name they understand this whole vault of heaven. Furthermore, he teaches that in the republic of the Hebrews we have a <term>pattern of a heavenly city <note>original Greek: παράδειγμα πόλεως ἐπουρανίας (paradeigma poleos epouranias)</note></term>, which Plato indeed tried to imagine, but Moses and the other Prophets after him actually formed—dedicated to God, purely educated, and far from all superstition.

### BOOK III. CHAPTER XV.

"Either that," he says, "or, what is more credible, this." 11. He judiciously mentions the Syrians; since the Hebrews originated from them, it is not surprising if they retained certain rites handed down from their ancestors, which those ancestors held from the most ancient Patriarchs. This is a point we have often emphasized. 111. From the same source, the Egyptians could have obtained similar rites, which, having become corrupted as superstition spread, were later corrected by Moses.

<margin>Section 15.</margin>
XIV. Whatever the case may be, the same **Grotius** <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a towering Dutch jurist and theologian</note> is clearly on our side elsewhere. In his notes on Book 1 of *On the Truth of the Christian Religion*, he explicitly teaches that most of those things which **Marsham** <note>Sir John Marsham (1602–1685), an English writer who argued for Egyptian influence on Hebrew law</note> derives from the **Egyptians** were actually sought from Moses; they passed from the **Hebrews** to the **Phoenicians**, and from the **Phoenicians** to the **Greeks**. He demonstrates with many arguments that **Pythagoras** drew his ideas from the **Jews**. He proves with various examples that the most ancient **Attic Laws** <note>The laws of Athens</note>—from which the **Roman** laws were later taken—drew their origin from the laws of **Moses**. Finally, dealing a fatal blow to **Spencer's** <note>John Spencer (1630–1693), author of 'De Legibus Hebraeorum', the primary target of this critique</note> cause, while discussing the Oracle that shone forth from the High Priest's breastplate, he says: THE EGYPTIANS IMITATED THIS, BUT ONLY AS CHILDREN IMITATE THE AFFAIRS OF MEN.

XV. We have deemed these observations necessary regarding those authorities whom **Spencer** cites in his favor. Since he brings them forward solely for the purpose of *not appearing greedy for novelty in Theology*, he sufficiently admits himself that the contrary opinion is by far the more widely accepted. Therefore, I would be wasting my effort if I busied myself enumerating the most learned and serious men who, disagreeing with him in all things, walk the same path as we do. And what is the heart of the matter: this controversy ought to be debated, and this lawsuit decided, not so much by the authority of a few recent writers, but by the evidence of reasons and arguments. Since these have now been produced by both sides, let the judgment be left to the impartial reader. Tired of writing, and called away to other duties of my laborious office as the holidays come to an end, I lift my hand from the page. Thus I finished, five days before the Kalends of February <note>January 28th</note>, in the year 1683 of the common era.

Often, and with no small pleasure of mind, I return to the memory of that time, ADRIAN PAULI, when we as very young men <note>original: "juvenes admodum"</note> were laboring in *Sacred Letters at Groningen* under the leadership of the most celebrated MARESIUS <note>Samuel Des Marets (1599–1673), a prominent French Protestant theologian who taught at the University of Groningen.</note>. At that time, I counted it as no small part of my happiness that I was granted the opportunity to find you there, to know you, and to enjoy your familiar company. For I looked up to your talent, I venerated your Piety, I embraced your Modesty, I emulated your Diligence, and I set before myself as an example those other Virtues, by which as a youth—

You were easily the foremost leader among the Academic youth. From all these qualities, I gathered into what a great man you would grow, and how many excellent things the Church of Christ could promise itself from you. Nor did the outcome fail that expectation. For, having completed the course of your studies, you first performed the duty of a Teacher <note>original: "Doctoris"</note> in the *Gymnasium of Hamm* <note>The Hammonense Gymnasium in Westphalia, a prestigious secondary school</note> with the highest praise; soon after, you proved yourself—and still prove yourself—to be a *Scribe* in the *Church of Danzig* <note>original: "Gedanensi Ecclesia"; modern Gdańsk, Poland</note>, a truly Evangelical man, well-practiced in the mysteries of the heavenly kingdom, who brings forth both Old and New things from the good treasure of his heart. You are an enemy of vices, a conqueror of errors, the beloved of the pious, the terror of the wicked, an example for the age, the honor of the Fatherland, and the glory of Christ.

I, meanwhile, living in the country and scarcely known to my neighbors, was feeding the little church committed to me by the Lord—I will not say in what manner, but certainly with a tender affection of piety. But the enjoyment of that leisure was not granted to me for long. It pleased the supreme Arbiter of our affairs <note>God</note> to drag this man of the shadows out from his hiding places into the light; and after frequent changes of stations, finally to move me to the *Chair of Theology* in more than one *Lyceum* <note>A term for a university or high-level academy</note>. Since I had undertaken this Province <note>A metaphorical "field of duty"</note> with a trembling soul—being unequal to such a mass of affairs—in addition to the Ecclesiastical labors of the Ministry; yet having experienced the incredible beneficence of the Divine power, which supplies strength to the weary, I have now sustained it for eight years.

When I was in the early stages of that work, being then devoted to my **FRISIANS** <note>The people of Friesland, a coastal region in the Netherlands and Germany</note>, you, Most Illustrious Man, wished to refresh the most pleasing memory of yourself. After no communication had passed between us for many years, separated as we were by a great distance of places, you were the first to greet me with your most kind letters; since then, you have testified several times that my specimens of study, such as they are, have not displeased you. How pleasant that—

Since this has happened to me, I am pleased to testify to it not only to you privately, but also publicly: and if posterity believes that the little book I now offer was written with any self-respect, it will likewise believe that I have pursued the honor of **ADRIAN PAULI** <note>Adrianus Pauli: likely a contemporary scholar or patron of the author</note> with great veneration. But there were also other underlying reasons why I ought to address you at the threshold of this *Exercise* <note>original: "Exercitationis" – a common term for a scholarly dissertation or formal academic essay</note>. Truly, I must offer an excuse and a justification for having dared to comment on the **Ten Tribes of Israel** after you. You handled this subject long ago with such erudition, judgment, and abundance that you taught many things not only to the moderately learned—such as myself and those like me—but even to the most highly educated. Following in a portion of your labor was that most distinguished man, formerly your colleague but my most deeply missed friend, **WILHELM WILHELMS** <note>Wilhelmus Wilhelmius: a deceased scholar whose work the author respects</note>, with an elegant dissertation on this very same argument; in which, calling forth the various opinions of the most learned men, he judged what was to be praised or blamed in each with no less modesty than foresight. And who, finally, am I, that I should dare to step into the arena after such great men? I am like a **pedestrian beside a Lydian chariot** <note>original Greek: "πεζὸς παρὰ Λύδιον ἅρμα" – a proverb for someone attempting a task far beyond their speed or ability</note>, a crude and rustic Thracian or follower <note>term: "secutor" – a type of gladiator armed with a sword and shield</note>, and some sort of Myrmillo or blindfolded fighter <note>term: "Andabatarius" – a gladiator who fought in a helmet without eye-holes</note> after so many prize-winning gladiators. But you will grant me pardon, I know well, most distinguished Sir; and our friend *Wilhelms* would have granted it if he were alive, once I have publicly professed that I have been greatly aided by your observations, led through obscure and rugged paths by your torch, and—sitting upon your shoulders like some dwarf or little boy—I have perhaps looked out a bit further. So much so that, if there is anything of good in this *Exercise*, I wish it to be credited to you both; for you either pre-formed these thoughts for me, or certainly provided the occasion and the entrance to them. Nor...

And yet, I say all these same things with you, though not in the same manner or order. And although I follow the same path, there are places where, departing a little, I turn aside into another track. Whoever would take this liberty away from the learned would, according to that most accepted saying from the Senate, **VOTE FOR ALL OTHER THINGS AND** <note>original: "QUI ALIA OMNIA," a Roman senatorial formula for total agreement; here used metaphorically to mean "rejecting everything else."</note> **at the same time remove the sun from the sky.** It is certainly for you to establish the methods of your own work and order. For me, however, this was the primary purpose: to present the complete history of the ten tribes of Israel, divided into specific periods and joined in a continuous series—as far as that was possible—until reaching the white chalk line <note>original: "candidam calcem," a classical metaphor for the finish line of a race.</note>. Meanwhile, I have taken care to compare the sacred songs which the prophets sang concerning each period with the actual outcome of events. From this, I had to explain many sections <term>pericopæ: specific passages or selections of Scripture</term> of the prophecies, some of which were touched upon by you; but others were omitted by a deliberate judgment because the nature of your undertaking was somewhat different from mine; and some, if you will permit me, were explained a little differently. Whatever I have achieved in this part, I offer to you, most illustrious **ADRIAN**, to be judged and corrected; I ask for you as my judge. *You shall determine*

> Whether this work of ours was spent in vain or for some use.

And I earnestly implore you, again and again, that you fulfill that hope you gave me—that you would return to us your own more enriched reflections <term>lucubrationes: literally "work done by lamplight," referring to scholarly study</term> on this subject with renewed care—and that by the same effort you might call me back to the path wherever I have wandered. Now, having said these introductory words, let me set forth the chapters of the history themselves piece by piece.

### CHAPTER I.

### The Separation of the Ten Tribes from the House of God and of David.

I. *The history of the ten tribes has four distinct periods.* II. *The beginning of the first period starts with Jeroboam, who tore the ten tribes away from the kingdom of Judah.* III. *God had predicted this revolution in affairs long ago.* IV. *Jeroboam, in order to secure the kingdom for himself, forbade his people from sharing the same sacred rites with the Jews in the same Temple.* V. *However, he did not think it wise to change the entire face of religion by leading the people away to foreign deities.* VI. *Instead, adapting himself to the character of the people, he designated a convenient place for worship.* VII. *Adding a visible sign as if of a present divinity.* VIII. *For this purpose, he chose golden calves.* IX. *Was it because that figure had once been dedicated to Joseph, from whom Jeroboam traced his descent?* X. *To which the name Serapis <note>An Egyptian deity often depicted as a bull</note> is believed to pertain, as if you were to say "Father Ox"; because Joseph, the Father of the King—*

<margin>I.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial O featuring foliate patterns and scrolling acanthus leaves within a rectangular frame.</image-desc>
The entire history of the TEN TRIBES OF ISRAEL is comprised of four periods, as it were. The FIRST is from their separation under JEROBOAM, both Sacred and Political; as much from the house of God as from the house of David: by which it happened that they began to establish a Church no less separate than their Commonwealth: and this runs until the ASSYRIAN DEPORTATION. The SECOND, beginning from there, extends to the BABYLONIAN CAPTIVITY OF JUDAH. The THIRD begins from the RETURN of the people from the Babylonian captivity, and lasts until the final DESTRUCTION of the ISRAELITE POLITY <note>The term "polity" refers to their organized political existence and self-governance</note> by the Romans. The FOURTH flows from then until the hoped-for and longed-for RESTORATION OF ALL ISRAEL.

<margin>II.</margin>
II. The beginning and sequence of the FIRST period are as follows. *Jeroboam*, a man shrewd, restless, and greedy for power, and

# THE TRIBES OF ISRAEL. CHAPTER I.

Having been educated from his earliest years in those arts by which minds are incited to the pursuit of great fortune, and after the death of *Solomon* and the succession of *Rehoboam*—whom he correctly guessed was unequal to such a great burden—he himself, full of vast hope, began to plot a revolution. Supported, therefore, by the favor of the aristocrats and the zeal of the common people (who, being naturally stubborn toward their rulers, are driven to rebellion by the slightest impulse), he sought, under a plausible pretext, to reduce the burdens long ago imposed upon the people. *Rehoboam* did not consider that the beginnings of a reign are most difficult; in which, since you neither can nor should fulfill the desires of everyone, such convenience and courtesy of manners must nevertheless be observed in your choices so that no good man may complain of having departed saddened by the face or speech of the prince. Therefore, scorning the advice of the elders—whom long age, experience in business, and familiarity with the most wise *Solomon* had made fit for giving counsel, and who urged with one voice that he should purchase a firm and lasting empire with a single day's compliance—he was egged on by his peers and those unskilled in affairs, and responded fiercely:

> *His little finger would be thicker than his father's loins; he would increase the weight of the yoke; his father had punished them with whips, but he would punish them with scorpions <note>original: "scorpionibus" — likely referring to a type of knotted or spiked whip</note>; and thus he would subdue that stubbornness of asking and complaining.*

A more desired opportunity could not have arisen for *Jeroboam*, who was watchful for everything. For ten out of the twelve tribes, exasperated by such harsh responses, made a secession from the House of David and willingly submitted themselves to *Jeroboam*, the supposedly excellent patron and defender of liberty. Such was the end of youthful and hot-headed counsels, which, though they seem joyful at first glance, are found to be hard in the handling and sad in the outcome.

III. God had foretold such a great change of affairs long before, both to *Solomon* and to *Jeroboam*. He addressed the former with a threatening voice:

> *Because this has been with you, that you have not kept my covenant and my statutes which I commanded you; I will surely tear this kingdom from you, and will give it to your servant. 1 Kings 11:11.*

To the latter, however, when *Ahijah the Shilonite* happened to meet him on the road, he took the new garment he was wearing and tore it into twelve pieces; ten of these he gave to *Jeroboam*, adding:

> *Thus says Jehovah <note>The Latin uses "Jehova," the traditional Latinization of the Tetragrammaton</note> the God of Israel: behold, I am about to tear this kingdom out of the hand of Solomon, and will give ten tribes to you. ibid. v. 29, 30, 31.*

In vain did *Solomon*, struggling against fate, enter into plans for killing *Jeroboam*. He survived, and having gained the king—

[Page 310]

It is a great matter. *Indeed, those things which are fixed by fate are not avoided, even if they are signaled in advance.* <note>original: "Quippe quæ fato manent, quamvis significata non vitantur." A reflection on the inevitability of divine decree.</note> The very foolish imprudence of Rehoboam served the counsel of God, so that what happened might also seem to have happened deservedly. O Wisdom, and the wonderful *power of hidden fate!* <note>original: "potentia fati"</note> which directs and bends all things in such a way that we nevertheless seem to have gone there of our own accord; and by our own counsels and deeds, we build for ourselves the step toward that fated fall or ascent.

IV. The next care for *Jeroboam* was now to strengthen the nation and the kingdom for himself. For he did not trust in the promise of God made through the prophet <note>The prophet Ahijah, who foretold Jeroboam's rise.</note> that his throne and his descendants would be established, provided he adhered to God with a pious inclination of mind. He turned instead to the usual trickeries of kings. He made it his primary effort to ensure the people did not travel to *Jerusalem* on feast days, or hold common sacred rites with the Jews from then on. For this, whichever way he turned, seemed to be a task full of dangerous risk. The center of religion converged in the city of *Jerusalem*, occupied by the kings of Judah. Access to it was impossible unless those kings permitted it. Therefore, either religion had to be abandoned, or submission had to be undertaken. If the people went by any means, *Jeroboam* had to either be present as a companion of the religious journey or be absent. In both cases, there was equal danger. For if absent, he could appear as a despiser of the deity and devoid of all religion: a thing which, above all else, a prince who demands to please his people must strenuously avoid. Nor was the fear absent that the Israelites might be incited to defection by their former King and their recently deserted brothers—but especially by the Priests and Levites—and that, captivated by the splendor of the Temple and the royal city, and stirred by the memory of *David and Solomon*, they might deprive *Jeroboam* not only of his dignity but of his life. Yet it was not permitted for him to be present himself. For the way was not open. Nor, if it were open, was it safe in enemy territory. And even if it were safe, it was not consistent with his dignity to be placed below the King of Judah: nor was it to be hoped that both would perform sacred rites with equal honor in the same house. The *Talmudists* <note>Scholars of the Talmud, the body of Jewish civil and ceremonial law.</note> have followed these reasonings of a profane but shrewd man not inaptly.

> *They had learned,* they say, *that no one has the right of sitting in the court of the temple except the kings of Judah, who are of the house of David. If therefore,* Jeroboam said to himself, *they see me standing while Rehoboam is sitting, they will decide that one is the king and the other the servant: or, if I should sit, that I am a rebel against the king: and thus, having killed me, they will immediately adhere to him. The words of the Talmud.*

# THE TRIBES OF ISRAEL. CHAPTER I.

Rashi <note>original: "Jarchius"; Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki, a preeminent medieval French rabbi and commentator</note> and Kimchi <note>original: "Kimchius"; David Kimchi, a medieval rabbi and Hebrew grammarian</note> maintain this in their commentaries. Therefore, although Jeroboam ought to have committed the entire matter to God—who, having raised him to the kingdom by His own divine power, could easily have preserved him safe and sound amidst so many dangers—he instead fled to evil arts. Following the wicked custom of rulers, he cunningly twisted religion to suit his own advantages, so that he might stabilize his dominion under its pretext.

V. Furthermore, he would have committed a most imprudent and rash deed if he had attempted to lead the people away from that God whom they recognized as the author of their liberation from Egypt toward foreign deities. For it is difficult to tear from the soul that which, handed down by the fathers, has fixed deep roots over time—especially in the matter of Religion. <margin>Cicero, Oration 10 against Verres.</margin> *For all men (as Cicero says) are moved by religion, and they judge that the ancestral Gods whom they received from their forefathers must be diligently worshipped and retained by them.* Wisely, therefore, Jeroboam did not wish to alienate the people from that which was ancestral and deeply instilled. He merely changed the place, the RITES of worship, as well as the MINISTERS and the TIME of worship; and he did this so astutely that the Israelites seemed to be recalled to the most ancient customs of all, rather than being initiated into new institutions.

VI. For the PLACES of worship, he selected those which recommended themselves both by notable convenience and by the memory of the ancients: namely, BETH-EL and DAN. Of these cities, the former was to the *South*, the latter to the *North*. BETH-EL indeed had long been famous because Jacob, the prince of the nation, having seen God there once and again, had solemnly dedicated an altar in that place. The name itself, signifying the *House of God* and the gate of heaven, was so illustrious that no part of the earth could be called by a more majestic title. <margin>Judges 18:30.</margin> DAN, however, was famous on account of the idol of Micah, erected there by the Danites not long after Joshua, and worshipped religiously by the inhabitants for a long time. Therefore, the minds of men could most conveniently be driven toward these locations.

VII. Moreover, it seemed advantageous to hold the minds of the Israelites with some VISIBLE SIGN, which would be a monument to the invisible God and an instrument of His worship. He therefore made two calves, or young bulls, of gold, of which he said: "It is enough for you to have gone up to Jerusalem until now; *Behold your Gods, O Israel, who led you out of the land of Egypt.*" As if he were saying: "There is no reason, Israelites, why you should, at great expense,

# CONCERNING THE TEN
<note>Referring to the Ten Tribes of Israel who followed Jeroboam</note>

...and by troublesome journeys, you should betake yourselves to Jerusalem three times a year: for that same true God, who led your fathers out of Egypt and promised that he would dwell in the midst of Israel, wishes to be sought and can be found here no less than at Jerusalem. You are not ignorant that He, by the immensity of His nature, is in every place—as Solomon declared, not even the highest heavens can limit His Majesty—and if you require symbols of His special presence, behold them in the calves which I have set up.

VIII. But why did he choose these symbols for himself rather than any others? The commentary of Hugo Grotius <note>A famous 17th-century Dutch jurist and theologian</note> is quite ingenious; however, much as he polished it himself, he owes it to the Hebrew interpreters. *He wished*, he says, *God to be worshiped in that figure which had formerly been dedicated to Joseph, the servant of God (from whom Jeroboam was descended), and which formed the principal part of the Cherubim: so that by that sight the people might be kept in veneration of the posterity of Joseph, and might more easily believe that the kingdom was owed to those who were descended from him, whose benefits toward all Israelites had been greatest. Thus the Julian house <note>The family of Julius Caesar</note> wished the praises of Aeneas to be sung by all the Poets, so that the people might more gently endure that empire, as if it were granted by the fates.*

<margin>Book I, chapter 29.</margin>
IX. For the understanding of this observation, it must be known that Grotius adopts the opinion of those who record that the memory of Joseph was worshiped by the Egyptians in the form of oxen, and who trace the entire fable of Apis and Serapis <note>Egyptian deities often depicted as or associated with bulls</note> back to this origin. Regarding this matter, Vossius <note>Gerardus Vossius, a noted scholar of classical history</note> treats it with primary erudition and at great length in his work *On the Origin and Progress of Idolatry*. And there are indeed many things which make that conjecture probable. It is known to anyone from the Mosaic history that there was no kind of honor with which the King of Egypt did not wish Joseph to be adorned. Furthermore, it was the Egyptian custom to propagate the memory of those who served them well to posterity through sacred symbols. Now, truly, no sign was more suitable for expressing the benefits of Joseph than the ox. For since he interpreted Pharaoh's dream of the seven fat cows which were devoured by as many other cows, foul in appearance and consumed by thinness—in which was the symbol of fertility and sterility—and since, on account of the man's Divine wisdom, he was appointed prefect of the grain supply <term>annona: the management of the city's grain stores and food supply</term> and provided excellently for the Egyptians in a time of famine: he could be honored by no symbol more fittingly than that of the ox. For the system of the grain supply depends in large part upon agriculture...

# THE TRIBES OF ISRAEL. CHAPTER I.

...depends; in which the ox is man's partner in labor; for this reason, it was called the "servant of Ceres" <note>Ceres was the Roman goddess of agriculture and grain</note> by Varro, and the "animal of agriculture" by Pliny. Hence also among the Romans, *L. Minutius*, the Prefect of the Grain Supply, was presented with a gilded ox outside the Trigeminan gate—not even against the will of the common people—because <margin>Livy, Book IV.</margin> he distributed the grain of Maelius to the people, valued at a mere penny per measure. Added to this is the fact that *Joseph*, according to the opinion of many, is called an "Ox" in Deuteronomy 33:17 according to the Hebrew codices; or at least, according to the Vulgate translator, he is compared to an ox.

X. Nor is the name *Apis* or *Serapis* <note>Apis was the sacred bull of Memphis; Serapis was a major Greco-Egyptian deity</note> inconsistent with this: for since among the Hebrews אב (*Ab*) denotes Father, שור (*Sor*) denotes ox, and שר (*Sar*) denotes Prince; from this *Joseph* could be called *Apis*, that is, "Father," just as he is called the "Father of Pharaoh" in Genesis 45:8. Likewise, he could be called *Sarapis*, "Prince Father," since he presided over all Egypt; or *Serapis*, "Ox Father," that is, the Father of the Egyptian kingdom designated by the symbol of the ox. Who would deny that these things were acutely devised by the distinguished *Vossius*? And if they are as solid as they are ingenious, what stands in the way of our agreeing with *Grotius*, who urges this as the cause for the calves erected by *Jeroboam* <note>Jeroboam was the first king of the northern Kingdom of Israel who set up golden calves at Dan and Bethel</note>: so that by the sight of them, the *Israelites* might be reminded of the excellence of *Joseph*, who was so extensively honored by the *Egyptians*? Moreover, why should *Jeroboam* himself—a descendant of such a great man—be considered any less worthy of imperial power than anyone from the line of *David*?

XI. But indeed, the most learned *Bochart* intervenes with strong reasons, so that we do not dare to place faith in a dissertation that is otherwise so erudite. For just as *Joseph*, while alive, would not have suffered those honors to be shown to him which were not far removed from Divine honors—which he foresaw would at least easily degenerate into idolatry—so too the memory of him after death quickly perished among the ungrateful *Egyptians*. For soon another king arose who "knew not Joseph" (Exodus 1:8), and who, having no regard for him, his brothers, or his descendants, exercised a most heavy tyranny over them. Other kings, equally hostile to the *Israelites*, succeeded him.

XII. Added to this is the fact that the worship of *Serapis* among the *Egyptians* was neither so ancient nor native, but more recent, and, as the Athenians say, *epidemos* <note>original: ἐπίδημος</note>, or "foreign/immigrant." *Herodotus*, who wrote so much about the gods of the *Egyptians*, says not a single word about *Serapis*. Nor does anyone else before the times of *Alexander the Great*. And most [say he was brought] from *Pontus* into *E-* <column-break/> -gypt...

The highly praised <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a famous French Protestant biblical scholar.</note> *Bochart* pursues this argument at length and defends it against the objections of *Vossius*. > They join to the statue the sign of a three-headed creature, which expresses in the middle—and also the largest—head the likeness of a Lion. On the right side, the head of a Dog rises up with a gentle, fawning appearance; but the left part of the neck ends with the head of a ravenous Wolf: and a Dragon connects these animal forms with its coils, its head returning to the God's right hand where the monster is seen.

One may consult *Athanasius Kircher* regarding this image and its mystical exposition in his *Egyptian Oedipus, Treatise III, chapter 5.* Furthermore, he contends that in the Egyptian language <term>sor</term> <note>original: σωρ</note> signifies a <term>chest</term> and <term>an</term> signifies an ox; he praises the observations of *Varro* and *Nymphodorus*, who recall that the dead bull *Apis*, placed in a *Sorus*—which in Latin we call an ark or coffin—was first called *Sorapis*, and thereafter *Serapis*. If these points are admitted, that Hebrew derivation from <term>Ab</term> <note>Father</note> and <term>Shor</term> <note>Ox; referring to the theory that Serapis was the patriarch Joseph</note> entirely collapses.

XIII. And truly, if we love to speak the facts, nothing is more uncertain than conjectures of this kind; they easily win for their authors an enviable reputation for erudition and <term>shrewdness</term> <note>original: ἀγχινοίας (agchinoias)</note>, but they can hardly obtain the assent of a judicious reader. The most excellent *Huet* <margin>Huet, *Demonstration of the Gospel*, book 1, prop. 4, ch. 4, para. 4 & 5.</margin> <margin>Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, book 9.</margin> did not merely try to "make a Mercury out of any piece of wood" <note>A Latin proverb meaning to make something great out of nothing.</note>, but set his mind to making *Moses* out of all the mythical Gods of the ancients; and he commanded all his vast learning to serve him in this direction. Therefore, in *Apis* and *Serapis* he also found *Moses*. Nor is he destitute of his own arguments. Indeed, in the writings of *Eusebius*, *Artapanus* relates that when *Nacherotes the Egyptian* asked *Moses* what might be truly useful to men, he replied: the breed of oxen which plow the earth. Therefore *Chenephres*, King of Egypt, named a bull *Apis* and ordered a temple to be built for it. What was easier for posterity than to confuse *Moses* with *Apis*, since his saying was the reason why *Apis* was consecrated with this worship? But hear also another etymology for *Serapis*, no less probable than that of *Vossius*. *Tacitus* in his *Histories, book 4, chapters 83 and 84*, reports that *Serapis* appeared to *Ptolemy Lagides* in a dream, being lifted into heaven in a great fire. Hence the origin of the name. For <term>saraph</term> <note>original: שרף</note> means to burn. From which also the <term>Seraphim</term> <note>original: שרפים</note> are named, that is, the burn-

XIV. Or finally, having long been accustomed to the calves in *Egypt*, where he had lived for many years under King *Shishak* (*1 Kings 11:40*), he may have judged it wise to transfer them into the sacred rites of the Israelites, whose fathers had once before been gripped by that same madness.

XV. This indeed seems to be the simplest explanation for everyone to think and say. For *Jeroboam* spoke of his calves in the very same words (*1 Kings 12:28*) as the Israelites spoke of the calf of *Aaron* (*Exodus 32:4*): *These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt.* They had truly drawn the superstition of the calves from *Egypt*: as *Stephen* bears witness (*Acts 7:39-40*): *In their hearts they turned back to Egypt, saying to Aaron, "Make us gods to go before us."* And this is the reason why God, through *Ezekiel* (*Chapter 23:8*), reproaches *Oholah*—that is, Israel—*that she did not leave behind her harlotries brought from Egypt*, following, of course, the worship of the calves. Added to this is the fact that the *Egyptians* from ancient times had two oxen, one of *Memphis* and the other of *Heliopolis*. It is probable that *Jeroboam* also looked toward this twin deity with his own calves. *Jerome* <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century scholar and Bible translator.</note> on *Hosea 4*: *It seems to me, therefore, that the people made for themselves the head of a calf to worship, and Jeroboam son of Nebat fashioned golden calves, so that what they had learned in Egypt—Apis and Mnevis—* <note>original: "Ἄπιν καὶ Μνεῦϊν" (Apin kai Mneuin)</note>; who under...

...they worshiped under the figure of oxen, as if they were Gods; this they maintained within their own superstition.

XVI. Once the place and manner of worship had been changed in this way, it followed that the Ministers were also changed. Because the Levitical priests refused to enslave themselves to this idolatrous worship, **Jeroboam** took for himself Priests <gloss>from the extremities of the people, who were not of the sons of Levi</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: miqtzot ha-am</note>, 1 Kings 12:31. In this way, the matter seemed to be reduced to its ancient simplicity and freedom: for indeed, before the times of Moses, no family was barred from the altar.

XVII. The most excellent man **Louis de Dieu** <note>A prominent 17th-century Dutch orientalist and theologian.</note>, in his learned observations on Ezekiel 33:1, noted that those who think "from the extremities of the people" is the same as "from the lowest of the people" are far mistaken. It is well known that the word *katzah* <note>Hebrew: קָצָה</note> properly denotes an *end* or *extremity*. However, because the extremity of a thing is its completion and its totality, it is used here to represent the "entirety" of a thing. From many examples, I shall bring forward only three, but those most evident. In Genesis 19:4, the **Sodomites** are said to have *surrounded the house of Lot, from the boy even to the old man*. Then it is added: <gloss>all the people from the extremity</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: kol-ha-am mi-katzeh</note>, that is, in its entirety. In Genesis 47:2, it is said of **Joseph**: <gloss>And from the totality of his brothers he took five, and presented them before Pharaoh</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: mi-ktzeh echaiv</note>. So also in Ezekiel 33:1: <gloss>And the people of the land shall take one man from their totality</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: mi-ktzehem</note>. In the same way, the passage concerning **Jeroboam** must be explained: He made Priests *from the extremities of the people*, that is, *from the whole of the people*. For he is not blamed because he neglected the nobles and created Priests from the common folk, but because, although the tribe of Levi alone had been destined by God for Priestly duties, he selected them *from the entire population*. Just as he also usurped the Priesthood himself, and offered sacrifices with his own hand to the Gods he had fashioned. 1 Kings 13:1.

XVIII. But neither did he leave the TIME of religious worship untouched. He instituted a new solemnity, to be celebrated not in the seventh month, as the law had commanded, but in the eighth: <italic>in that month which he had devised in his own heart</italic>. 1 Kings 12:32-33. All this was done with the plan that the Israelites might retain the substance and "body," as it were, of a religion held in common with the Jews—lest their minds be disturbed by too much innovation—yet in the circumstances there would be a notable diversity. This diversity would, as **Jeroboam** desired, alienate the peoples of the two kingdoms more and more from one another.

# THE TRIBES OF ISRAEL. CHAPTER I.

XIX. But however much these clever schemes were devised by a political man <note>Referring to Jeroboam I, the first king of the northern Kingdom of Israel</note>, they were nonetheless foul in the doing and unhappy in their outcome. For everything was profane: profane gods, profane priests, profane festivals, and profane sacrifices. For in matters of religion, whatever does not have God as its Author is profane. Therefore, these calves <note>The golden calves set up at Dan and Bethel</note> are called "Devils" instead of Gods in 2 Chronicles 11:15. And their initiates, instead of being Priests, are called <term>Chemarim</term> <note>original: כמרים; a term used in the Hebrew Bible for idolatrous priests</note> *sacrificing-menials* in Hosea 10:5. And the solemnities, instead of being God’s festivals, are called the *King’s days* in Hosea 7:5, because they were instituted by a King, not by God. And the place, instead of *Beth-El* <note>House of God</note>, is called *Beth-Aven* in Hosea 10:5—that is, instead of the House of God, it is the House of the Idol, or the *house of iniquity*. The scholar **Peter Martyr** <note>Pietro Martire Vermigli (1499–1562), a Reformed theologian</note> put it excellently:

> Certainly Jeroboam returned most unjust thanks to God. God raised him up all the way to the kingdom; but he, in turn, cast God Himself down all the way to the level of oxen.

XX. Thus we have seen the sorrowful beginnings of the defection, by which the ten tribes created for themselves a kingdom separate from the kingdom of David, and a congregation segregated from the Church of God. Nor should it be doubted that both **Jeroboam** and the people bound themselves in great wickedness in this matter. To be sure, God attributed this turning of events to Himself in 1 Kings 12:15, 24, and through the prophet **Ahijah** said to the king’s wife:

> Go, tell Jeroboam, thus says Jehovah the God of Israel: I raised you up from the midst of this people, and placed you as leader over my people Israel, and I handed over to you the kingdom torn away from the house of David. 1 Kings 14:7, 8.

But in the very matter where God acted most justly, **Jeroboam** acted with treachery toward the people. Here we must adore the providence of the most holy Divinity, which deservedly punished the sin of **Solomon**, but did so by means of another sin. For Jeroboam sinned because, unlike **David**, he preferred to seize the kingdom promised to him by God rather than wait for it; and having occupied it through rebellion, he administered it most wickedly. Likewise, the people sinned, who, being ignorant of God’s secret counsel, defected from the house of David against His express law and substituted a stranger for the legitimate successor. Accordingly, God rebukes them with these words in Hosea 8:3, 4: *Israel has deserted the good; the enemy shall pursue him.* <term>They made kings, but not by me</term> <note>original: הם המליכו ולא ממני</note> *They set up a king, but not from me: they established a Prince, and I did not acknowledge him: that is, without consulting me, and without my approval.*

XXI. For this reason, it turned out badly for both the kings and the people. For **Nadab**, the son who succeeded **Jeroboam** (the first author of the defection), reigned only two years; when those were finished, **Baasha** brought war against him,

XXII. Nor did the people congratulate themselves on that change of affairs. <note>2 Kings 17:20-21</note> *And the Lord rejected all the seed of Israel, and afflicted them, and delivered them into the hand of spoilers, until he had cast them out of his sight: because Israel was torn from the house of David, and they made Jeroboam the son of Nebat king.* For from this came the first stain of evil for the Israelites, both the defection in religion and almost internecine <note>term: internecinæ (deadly/mutually destructive)</note> disasters. Their ancient making of the calf <note>original Greek: μοσχοποιΐα (moschopoiia)</note> under Aaron was expiated by the slaughter of three thousand. <note>Exodus 32:28</note> This crime, however, resulted in five hundred thousand falling in a single battle. <note>2 Chronicles 13:17</note> You will not easily find a greater disaster than this. Thus *God deserts those who desert Him: nor do they merely fall shamefully, but they are utterly ruined.* This must be seriously considered by the people; it is rare that anyone carries out a rebellion with impunity. And let all learn by this example that *neglected religion has always dragged the state down with it, and will continue to do so.*

# ON THE TRIBES OF ISRAEL. CHAPTER II.

<margin>I.</margin> We now approach the second period. In this section, two points must be explained distinctly: 1. *The overthrow of the kingdom of the ten tribes.*
<margin>II.</margin> 2. *The status of the Israelites after the kingdom was overthrown.*

II. Regarding the OVERTHROW of the Kingdom, which is called the *Israelite* or *Samaritan* kingdom, observe three stages. The first is at the death of *Jeroboam II*, or his son *Zechariah*, the great-great-grandson of *Jehu*. After Zechariah had reigned for six months, he was killed by *Shallum* in a conspiracy carried out before all the people (2 Kings 15:10, 17). Thus, the truth of the Divine promise stood firm, by which God had pledged to *Jehu* that his descendants to the fourth generation would sit on the throne of *Israel* (2 Kings 10:30). However, the kingdom of the house of *Israel* was abolished when God "punished the house of Jehu for the bloodshed of Jezreel" (Hosea 1:4). *Jehu* had shed much blood in *Jezreel*, namely that of *Ahab* and *Jezebel*, and of *Ahaziah* and his kinsmen (2 Kings 9:25, 26, 27, 30, 36). He had indeed done this by God's command, but not with an upright heart, for he himself did not turn away from the sins of *Jeroboam*, by which he had led *Israel* into sin (2 Kings 10:31). Therefore, God imputed that blood as a guilt against the house of *Jehu*, demanding vengeance from his descendants. The consummation of this vengeance was in the slaughter of *Zechariah*, his great-great-grandson, who was stripped of both his kingdom and his life through conspiracy.

III. With this moment of judgment, the prophet *Hosea* connects the abolition of the kingdom of the ten tribes. This does not mean the people themselves immediately ceased to exist, but rather the King among the people. For the successors of *Zechariah* were not so much kings as they were thieves, robbers, and tyrants, unworthy of the venerable name of kings; they foully lost a tyranny that was ill-gotten and no better maintained. *Shallum* the conspirator was killed after only one month (2 Kings 15:14). *Menahem*, a murderer of his own kin, held the kingdom somewhat longer by purchasing the help of enemies with plunder taken from his own people (2 Kings 15:19, 20). *Pekahiah* his son, a king of only two years, was foully deposed and deprived of life by *Pekah* (ibid. verse 25). *Pekah's* fate was no different, as *Hoshea* killed him (ibid. verse 30). This *Hoshea*, by the favor of the *Assyrian* <note>The King of Assyria, Tiglath-Pileser III or Shalmaneser V</note>, finally obtained the royal title for a short while. Thus the throne fluctuated without a certain heir, becoming the prey of any plunderer prevailing by force or by ambush. Tyrants succeeded one another through mutual slaughters, invading kingdoms won by the sword with guilty hands. Just as with the *Diana of Aricia* <note>original: "Aricina Diana" — A reference to the Roman "King of the Woods" (Rex Nemorensis), a priest who obtained his position only by killing his predecessor</note>, no one obtained the priesthood [except by killing the previous holder].

...than he who, having been born to it, became a murderer and a priest before his time <note>original Greek: ὁ γεννηθεὶς αὐτόχειρ ϗ̄ ἱερεὺς πρότερον</note>, who had slaughtered the previous priest with his own hand. Or in the same way that among the Romans, *Julius Caesar* removed Pompey, *Brutus and Cassius* removed Caesar, and *Augustus* removed them. Or how *Otho* removed *Galba*, *Vitellius* removed *Otho*, *Vespasian* removed *Vitellius*, and *Domitian* removed *Titus*, the son of *Vespasian*. But these horrific turmoils and robberies were ominous omens of a republic verging toward its end.

IV. And such things were predicted by Isaiah. *Chapter 9, verse 11, etc.* For wickedness shall burn like a fire; the impiety of Israel shall spread far and wide, like a flame devastating whatever it touches: *it shall consume the briers and thorns; and it shall kindle the thickets of the forest*, so that they vanish into the finest dust as the smoke rises. The *briers and thorns* are the common and ignoble people, or even the unfruitful and scandalous who are obstacles to building up the nation. The *thickets of the forest* may signify the nobles and leaders bound together by mutual alliances and conspiracies. The *turning to dust by the rising of smoke* signifies the dissolution of the state. *Through the wrath of the Lord of hosts, the land shall be darkened.* As God’s indignation grows, all of Israel shall be enveloped in the smoke of error and handed over to a depraved mind. *And this people shall be as fuel for the fire:* they shall be worn down by continuous dissensions as if by a slow-burning fire. *No man shall spare his brother. And he shall snatch on the right hand and be hungry, and he shall eat on the left hand and they shall not be satisfied: every man shall eat the flesh of his own arm.* Such will be the madness, cruelty, and hunger of the Israelites that, just as a wild beast pressed by hunger rages among the herds and slaughters the cattle it meets now on the right and now on the left, so they shall rage among their brothers and neighbors. And just as we sometimes see madmen vent their rage upon their own hands and arms, so they shall attack those who are closest to them by blood, and from whom they would otherwise expect help and protection in times of adversity. *Manasseh shall devour Ephraim, and Ephraim Manasseh.* These tribes, otherwise most closely joined and descended from one father, Joseph, shall rush into mutual slaughter, burning with hatred. And they are so far from seeking protection for themselves in the kingdom of Judah that they shall instead be united against Judah. See 2 Kings 15:37. These are the evil omens of destruction. *For all this His anger is not turned away, but His hand is stretched out still.*

V. And indeed, under Menachem, *Pul*, the king of the Assyrians, invaded the land—

And having considered the years assigned to *Pul* by *Africanus* and *Eusebius*—whom the former calls *Acracarnes* and the latter *Ocrazapes*—and counting backward from the beginning of *Nabonassar* and the death of *Sardanapalus* (whom *Ussher* thinks was connected with him), this man might also seem to be the very one who was brought to repentance by the preaching of the Prophet *Jonah*.
