VI. Concerning this invasion, *Hosea* prophesies in *Chapter 7:1*: *When I would have healed Israel—by restoring the borders of Israel through Jeroboam II, 2 Kings 14:25, 27—the wickedness of Ephraim was revealed, which is the way of the house of Ahab; for they partly persisted in the way of Jeroboam, by burning incense (though in the name of the true God) outside the place God had chosen and not through the sons of Aaron; and they partly allied themselves with Ahab, worshipping Baal.* This wickedness was most clearly manifested when God had healed Israel. For then their devotion to falsehood shone forth, from which they allowed themselves to be moved neither by blessings nor by disasters. The punishment follows: *And the thief comes.* This is Shallum, the parricide, who stole the empire for himself with no right. *The army spreads itself out in the fields. This is the army of Pul the Assyrian, which, running down from the mountain like a river, flooded the land, and departed only after receiving silver.*

VII. The second stage of the kingdom's overthrow is in the victory of *Tiglath-Pileser the Assyrian*, who, turning his arms against *Pekah*, devastated all of *Gilead*, *Galilee*, and *Naphtali*, and led the inhabitants away into *Assyria*. *2 Kings 15:29; 1 Chronicles 5:25, 26: But when they had transgressed against the God of their fathers, and went whoring after the gods of the peoples of that region, whom God had destroyed before them: the God of Israel stirred up the spirit of Pul king of Assyria, and the spirit of Tiglath-Pileser king of Assyria, so that he deported the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh: and so he led them away into Halah, and Habor, and Hara, and the river Gozan, even unto this day.*

# CONCERNING THE TEN TRIBES

VIII. And this disaster was also foretold by *Hosea*. *Chapter 7:8. Ephraim mixes himself with the peoples.* <note>The Northern Kingdom is often called "Ephraim" after its dominant tribe.</note> *The Israelites joined with the Syrians in a plan to seize the Kingdom of Judah and to abolish the worship established by God. Isaiah 7:1-2.* This is the guilt. The punishment follows. *Ephraim has become like a cake not turned:* which, being placed upon the coals, must necessarily be scorched on one side and turned to charcoal. This hints at the deportation of half the kingdom into *Assyria* by *Tiglath-Pileser*. This is confirmed from the eleventh verse: *And Ephraim exists like a silly dove, without heart. They called to Egypt, they went to Assyria.* That is, when a great part of the Israelites had already gone into *Assyria*, and all had become subject to the Assyrian, they implored the help of the Egyptians with a foolish plan; this turned out very badly for them and was the cause of their final destruction. You have the history in *2 Kings 17:3-4.*

IX. The third step of the overthrow is in the expedition of *Shalmaneser*, who, having devastated the rest of the land, in the ninth year of King *Hoshea* and the sixth of *Hezekiah*, captured *Samaria* after a three-year siege, loaded the king with chains, deported all the remaining *Israel* into *Assyria*, and sent colonies of barbarian nations into the land of Israel. *2 Kings 17:4, etc.* And this was the end of the Commonwealth of the Ten Tribes, which under nineteen kings—the first of whom was *Jeroboam son of Nebat*, and the last *Hoshea son of Elah*—stood for 235 years, *seven months, and as many days*, according to the calculation of a learned man. <note>The "learned man" likely refers to a specific chronologist like Ussher or Scaliger, though opinions on the exact dates varied widely in the 17th century.</note> Others, however, attribute more years to it.

X. None of these things failed to be foretold to *Jeroboam* by that same *Ahijah the Shilonite*, who had first given him the hope of the kingdom. *1 Kings 14:14-15. Therefore the Lord will raise up for himself a king over Israel, who shall cut off the house of Jeroboam on that day. But what even now? Furthermore, the Lord will strike Israel, just as a reed is shaken in the water, and uprooting Israel from the excellent land which he had given to their ancestors, he will scatter them far away, beyond the River itself: because they had made their sacred groves, provoking the Lord.* <note>The "River" refers to the Euphrates.</note>

XI. There is a twin prophecy of *Amos*. *Chapter 5:27. And I will transport you <gloss>original Hebrew: "beyond Damascus"</gloss> beyond Damascus, said the Lord, whose name is the God of Hosts.* Stephen, quoting that prophecy in *Acts 7:43*, says *beyond Babylon* for the sake of explanation instead of *beyond Damascus*. In this sense: not only outside the borders of the fatherland and the sweet...

their borders, just as *Damascus* is the boundary of the Holy Land; but you shall also be transported beyond *Babylonia*, into more remote places, almost beyond the knowledge of your land and any hope of returning. *Amos* <note>The prophet Amos, writing in the 8th century BCE.</note> had a specific reason in his own time why he said "beyond *Damascus*." And *Stephen* <note>Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, whose speech is recorded in Acts 7.</note> had his own reason why he interpreted this as "beyond *Babylon*." Before the time of *Amos*, *Hazael* the King of *Damascus* had afflicted the land of the Ten Tribes with great slaughters, and having killed some, he had led others away as captives into *Syria*, as is credible. *2 Kings* 10:32-33. Therefore, the Prophet proceeds to announce a greater calamity to them: that they would shortly be deported further than *Damascus*. However, since he did not define how far, *Stephen* defined it: namely, beyond *Babylon*, into the borders of *Media*. And the event proved this true. It is not necessary, therefore, for us to think that *Stephen's* citation lies in error; for *Stephen*, saying nothing contrary to the truth but adding something to the prophecy of *Amos* for the sake of explanation, did not corrupt it—far be it!—but clearly illustrated it by the instinct of the same Spirit who had caused *Amos* to prophesy.

XII. Nor is this the only way the words of *Stephen* can be reconciled with the mind of *Amos*. *Samuel Petit* <note>A 17th-century French scholar known for his work on ancient law and biblical chronology.</note>, a most learned man, observed that the prophecy of *Amos* could be translated in this sense: *I will remove you further than Damascus was removed*. Truly, *Pekah* the King of the *Israelites* had conspired with *Rezin* the King of the *Syrians*, whose metropolis was *Damascus*, to destroy the kingdom of *Judah* and the family of *David*, from whom the *Messiah* was to be born. *Isaiah* 7:1-2; *2 Chronicles* 28:6-8. Neither bore such a great crime unpunished. Each felt the same avenger. For *Tiglath-Pileser* the King of *Assyria*, having killed *Rezin*, destroyed the kingdom of the *Syrians*, and overturned *Damascus*, deported the people of *Damascus*. *2 Kings* 16:9. Then, turning the force of the war against *Pekah*, he led away a part of the Ten Tribes as captives. But more grievous troubles are now predicted for the remaining *Israelites*. Namely, that they would be deported further than the *Damascenes* were deported. Now, the *Damascenes* were exported to *Kir*. *2 Kings* 16:9, according to the prophecy of *Amos* Chapter 1:5. Whether that be the *Coryna* of *Ptolemy* <note>The ancient geographer Claudius Ptolemy.</note>, interpreted as *Cyrna* by translators, an inland city of *Media*, as *Bochart* <note>Samuel Bochart, a famous 17th-century biblical geographer.</note> conjectures; or a part of *Albania* <note>Referring to Caucasian Albania, an ancient region in the east Caucasus.</note> where the river *Kyr* is, mentioned by the same *Ptolemy*, as *Grotius* <note>Hugo Grotius, the influential Dutch jurist and theologian.</note> opines; or a part of *Syria* called *Kyrrh* or *Cyrrhestica*, also recognized by *Ptolemy*,

# ON THE TEN TRIBES

...recognized, as Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a Dutch theologian known for his federal theology.</note> observes, or finally the city of Babylonia, which is called *Chiriphe* by Ptolemy, which Petitus prefers: it is at least certain, and in accordance with the mind of Amos, that Stephen said *Israel* was carried away beyond Babylon, since *Damascus* was carried away into it, or even beyond it: Amos prophesied that the deportation of this *Damascus* would occur earlier than that of Israel.

XIII. Isaiah did not only predict the destruction itself: but he also *predefined the time of it. Isaiah* 7:8. <note>original Hebrew: ועוד ששים וחמש שנה יחת אפרים מעם</note> *And within sixty-five years Ephraim shall be broken, so that it be not a people*: not that it should utterly cease to exist, but that it should not be a "people," meaning it should no longer have a commonwealth <term>rempublicam: the organized political body or state</term>. However, there is no small difficulty in finding a correct calculation of these years. It is certain that from the time Isaiah preached until the deportation of the Ten Tribes, no more than 23 years passed. This is demonstrated in this manner: This prophecy was issued in the times of *Ahaz (verse 1)*. The destruction of the Ten Tribes fell in the 6th year of *Hezekiah*: which is the 9th year of *Hoshea*, King of Israel. *2 Kings 17:6* compared with *18:1*. *Ahaz* reigned at most only 16 years: to which add the 6 years of Hezekiah, and you will have 23.

XIV. *Grotius* <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a famous Dutch jurist and scholar who often sought rationalistic explanations for biblical difficulties.</note> therefore, to remedy the difficulty, tampers with the text. *Altogether*, he says, *there seems to be an error in the Hebrew writing, by the addition of the letter "M" to the word "six" <note>Changing "sixty" (shishim) to "six" (shesh)</note>.* *He therefore orders it to be read as "six and five," that is, eleven. Of which two years, he says, pertain to the final times of King Pekah: and nine to the times of Hoshea, likewise king of the Ten Tribes.* See *2 Kings 15:27* and *16:1* and *18:10*; you will see that these things are most true. But truly, this is not a skillful way to heal a difficult passage, but rather to brand it with cruel marks and to mutilate it with a savage hand. For first, such a bold change is against the faith of all manuscripts and all ancient versions. Secondly, it is foreign to the Hebrew idiom to say *six and five* instead of eleven: of which phrasing, or anything similar to it, I believe he can provide no example from the Scriptures. Finally, there is nothing in the cited passages to support his rash assertion. For there is no certainty, indeed not even any probability, established from them that these words of Isaiah were spoken two years before the end of *Phacea*, or *Pekah*. Far be such bold divinations from us.

XV. It remains, therefore, that we must refer the beginning of this calculation to an earlier...

let us refer to the dates. But which ones exactly? Following the Hebrew scholars, many Christian interpreters guess that this refers back to the prophecy of *Amos*. It is as if the prophet had said: I, *Isaiah*, repeat, confirm, and illustrate the prophecy of *Amos*, who nearly 45 years ago already denounced the ruin and destruction of the Israelites of the Ten Tribes (*Amos 4:2-3, 5:27*) and even to Damascus itself (*Amos 1:3*). And I denounce—which *Amos* did not—that within 65 years, to be calculated from that prophecy of *Amos*, Israel is to be gradually weakened and finally crushed, so that it ceases to be a people. Moreover, those years are completed as follows: *Amos* prophesied in the 25th year of King *Uzziah*, two years before the earthquake (*Amos 1:1*), which fell in the 27th year of *Uzziah*. Now, if you calculate from the 25th year of *Uzziah* (who reigned 52 years), 27 years of *Uzziah's* reign remain. To these add the 15 years of *Jotham*, 16 of *Ahaz*, and finally 6 of *Hezekiah*, and you will find 65 years. So says *Cornelius a Lapide* <note>A prominent 17th-century Jesuit biblical exegete</note>, with whom most interpreters agree.

XVI. But not even in this way is everything brought to a clear and certain conclusion, such that no doubt remains. For, to pass over the fact that no mention of the *Amosian* prophecy exists in *Isaiah*: if some calculation of years must be started from a prophecy of the same event, what reason can be given why it should not rather start from that of *Ahijah the Shilonite*, which is no less eloquent, much older, and was made to the royal consort herself? (*1 Kings 14:15* <note>The original text cites 2 Kings, but the reference to Ahijah and the Queen is 1 Kings 14</note>). Furthermore, it is assumed without proof that the earthquake happened in the 27th year of *Uzziah*, and consequently that the prophecy of *Amos* falls in his 25th year. For the sacred scriptures nowhere say this; indeed, they rather suggest the contrary. *Amos* prophesied when *Uzziah* was King of Judah and *Jeroboam II* was King of Israel (*Amos 1:1*). However, *Jeroboam* did not reign concurrently with *Uzziah* except for 14 years. Let us suppose, therefore, that the word of the Lord came to *Amos* in the last year of *Jeroboam*; the earthquake would then have occurred in the 16th year of *Uzziah*. By this observation, it is clear that all those calculations of the Hebrews and those who follow them are utterly disturbed. See, if you please, the most celebrated *Cocceius* <note>Johannes Cocceius, a famous 17th-century Dutch theologian</note> on *Amos 1:1*.

XVII. What then? you will ask. Everything flows easily if, as the most renowned *Cocceius* contends, it is permitted to begin the calculation from the death of *Jeroboam II*, in which the legitimate kingdom of Israel was abolished. For *Zechariah* his son was admitted to the helm of government late, and possessed the empire for only six months; the rest were thieves and plunderers rather than kings,

# ON THE TEN [TRIBES]

They were [more numerous] than the kings, as we explained in the second paragraph. Therefore, *Isaiah* teaches that sixty-five years after the kingdom was abolished, the people would also be broken so that they would no longer be a nation. <note>Isaiah 7:8</note> It is not unusual in the Scriptures for an older era to be named from the point of its completion; various examples of this practice are brought forward from the Book of Judges. It is certainly clear that this number cannot be reconciled if you begin the calculation from the time when these things were prophesied by *Isaiah*. For in that case, the sixty-five years would end near the middle of the reign of *Manasseh*. If anyone should claim that the kingdom of *Israel* stood for that long, or that there was any appearance of a public state in it at that time, he will find himself destitute of—and indeed refuted by—the authority of sacred history. When *Esarhaddon*, the son of *Sennacherib*, led *Manasseh* captive to *Babylon* not long after the wicked beginnings of his reign, we do not read that he carried away any remnants of the *Israelite* kingdom with him. Therefore, one must not press too strictly the precise meaning of the particle <term>בעוד (be-od)</term> <note>original: "within yet" or "in still"</note> as if it had its beginning exactly in this present time. And if we must look back to an earlier point, as the evidence of the matter itself compels us, what era should we choose rather than that which was notably significant for that people, and from which the sought-after number of years is easily and certainly subtracted? Furthermore, that subtraction is performed in this manner: *Jeroboam* dies in the 41st year of his reign, which is the 15th year of *Uzziah*. Therefore, 37 years of *Uzziah* remain (for he ruled fifty-two years in total).

<margin>2 Kings 15:30.</margin>
In the twentieth year of *Jotham*—that is, the fourth year after his death—*Hoshea* the son of *Elah* becomes king of *Israel*. In the ninth year of *Hoshea*, Samaria was captured and *Israel* was carried away into exile.

Add them thus: 37 years of *Uzziah*.
->19 years of *Jotham*.<-
->9 years of *Hoshea*.<-
->Total: 65.<-

But perhaps we have been too diligent in these chronological numbers—if indeed any diligence should be considered "too much" when it sheds light upon the words of God, or when we certainly profit in the knowledge of those things in which nothing is trivial, and nothing is unworthy of our most expensive care. Nevertheless, turning now to more pleasant matters, let us follow the history we have begun.

XVIII. It is memorable what is narrated to have happened shortly before the final deportation of the Tribes: 2 Chronicles 30:11, etc. Not a few from *Asher*, *Manasseh*, and *Zebulun*, *Ephraim* and *Issachar*, having been invited...

...those from <note>original: "Hizkia"</note> Hezekiah had stood in Jerusalem and celebrated the Passover. When this was finished, they went out with the Jews through the cities of Judah, and even those of Ephraim and Manasseh, and they broke, cut down, and destroyed the instruments of idolatry and the places dedicated to it; afterward, they each returned to their own homes and their own cities. 2 Chronicles 31:1. It is gathered from this that all these events preceded the final deportation <note>The forced removal of the Israelites by the Assyrians</note>: because the reformation of Hezekiah—of which the celebration of that Passover was either a part or certainly an appendix—took place in the first year of his reign. 2 Chronicles 29:3. The deportation, however, occurred in the sixth year. 2 Kings 18:10.

XIX. <note>original: "Grotius"</note> Hugo Grotius <note>A famous 17th-century Dutch jurist and theologian</note> does not gain agreement here, as he restricts these towns to those which the Kings of Judah had acquired for themselves through wars: on the grounds that they would have no law for breaking idols outside the places of their own jurisdiction. For it is doubted, not without reason, whether at that time such cities of the ten Tribes were under the dominion of the Kings of Judah. For <note>original: "Joaz"</note> Jehoash, King of Israel, the victor over <note>original: "Amasiæ"</note> Amaziah, stripped Jerusalem itself of its walls and the temple of its gold and silver, taking hostages with him to Samaria. 2 Kings 14:12. Who would believe that he then left any cities of his jurisdiction to the Jews? Moreover, <note>original: "Achaz"</note> Ahaz, the father of Hezekiah, could not even protect Judah, let alone invade the borders of the Israelites. Isaiah 7:1. Furthermore, Hezekiah, at the beginning of whose reign these things occurred, had as yet done nothing by war. It would therefore be strange if any places of the Ten Tribes were under his empire. But the text also explicitly states that Hezekiah’s messengers, urging the restoration of sincere worship, traversed ALL OF ISRAEL FROM BEERSHEBA EVEN UNTO DAN. 2 Chronicles 30:5. So much so, that some gathered from almost every single city set their hands to that pious work, and having purged Judah, they did not rest until they had finished in *Ephraim and Manasseh*.

XX. The whole land of Israel was the land of Jehovah: which it was a sin to pollute with high places, altars, or sacred groves. Therefore, the Israelites did nothing contrary to the law when, encouraged by Hezekiah, they went to purge their own region also of those foul abominations. But, you will say, how could this be done in the jurisdiction of a foreign King, who wanted nothing in common with Hezekiah’s religious <term>precision <note>original Greek: ἀκριβείᾳ (akribeia) - strict adherence to religious law</note></term>? ## CHAPTER III.

->The State of the People after the Assyrian disaster, regarding those<-
->who remained in the land.<-

I. *The twofold status of the Israelites after the destruction of the kingdom.* II. *Some of the common people were left in the land by the Assyrians: as predicted by Isaiah, Chapter XVII:3 and following.* III. *In agreement with Amos, Chapter III:12.* IV. V. *As attested by History.* VI. *Those remnants were endowed neither with skill in Divine law, nor with much fear of the deity.* VII. *And many of them entangled themselves in marriages with the barbarian Cutheans <note>The Cutheans were people brought from Cutha in Persia by the Assyrians to repopulate Samaria; the term is often used synonymously with Samaritans</note>.* VIII. *Joiada’s son, who married the daughter of Sanballat the Horonite (Nehemiah XIII:28), is not Manasseh the brother of Jaddus the High Priest.* IX. *The mixture of marriages was followed by a mixture of religion.* X. *The ambition of Manasseh served greatly to strengthen this miscellaneous religion, as he built a temple and claimed the High Priesthood for himself on Mount Gerizim.* XI. *He became the head of the sect of the Samaritans.* XII. *Which at times wished to appear studious of the Mosaic law in part, but rejected the Prophets.* XIII. *Indeed, it was not sufficiently observant of the Law, especially in times of adversity.* XIV. *For in prosperous times, they approached closer to the sacred rites of the Jews.* XV. *Nevertheless, disputes over the temples always remained, often debated with futile arguments.* XVI. *Although the arguments on the part of the Jews were stronger.* XVII. *With a most wicked daring, the Samaritans corrupted the Divine law so that it might seem to favor their own institutions.* XVIII. *When these corruptions were made remains in obscurity.* XIX. *The Samaritans were greatly hated by the Israelites: especially those ancient idolaters.* XX. *For concerning the later ones, who had received the law, the judgment was a little more lenient.* XXI. *These things illustrate the Gospel history.* XXII. *The Lord Jesus condemns those thoughtless hatreds by his speech and example.* XXIII. *There were some among the Israelites left in their land by Shalmaneser <note>The Assyrian King who besieged Samaria</note> who constantly adhered to God.*

# THE TRIBES OF ISRAEL. CHAPTER III.

I. **After** the overthrow of the Kingdom by the Assyrians, the state of the people can be considered in two ways: partly regarding **THOSE WHO REMAINED IN THE LAND**, and partly regarding **THOSE DEPORTED INTO FOREIGN REGIONS.**

<margin>
Isaiah 17:
3, 4, 5, 6,
7, 8.
</margin>
II. For this deportation was not so total that some from the lower classes were not **LEFT BEHIND**. Isaiah had accurately foretold this in Chapter 17:3-6: *The fortress will disappear from Ephraim. And it shall come to pass in that time that the glory of Jacob will be diminished, and the fatness of his flesh will grow lean: it will be, I say, just as when a reaper gathers the standing grain, and his arm harvests the ears; finally, it will be like one who gathers ears of grain in the Valley of Rephaim.* <note>The Valley of Rephaim was a fertile plain near Jerusalem, used here as a metaphor for a thorough but not absolute harvest.</note> Thus the "harvest" of the people will happen so that they are indeed removed from their place, just as grain is separated from the ground and root by the sickle; yet they are not cast down to be trampled, or burned like thorns and briars, but by the arm of the reaper—God acting through the Assyrians—they are held like ears of grain during the cutting, transported to another place, and finally gathered into a bundle. This was commonly done by reapers in the fertile Valley of Rephaim near Jerusalem. Therefore, this parable explains partly the wrath and partly the mercy of God toward Israel: the former in the reaping and transporting of the people, the latter in the retaining and regrouping into a bundle. The prophet continues: *Only a gleaning will be left in it, as when an olive tree is beaten: two or three berries in the top of the uppermost branch, four or five in its fruitful branches, says Jehovah the God of Israel.* This pertains to the remnant of the people remaining in the land, which was to be small and despised, yet not entirely destitute of all life and vigor.

III. Amos 3:12 harmonizes with this: *Thus says Jehovah: Just as a shepherd rescues from the mouth of a lion two legs or a piece of an ear, so shall the Israelites be rescued who sit in Samaria on the corner of a couch and on the leg of a bed.* <note>original: "in crure spondæ"</note> Israel is compared to a torn sheep; the Assyrian enemy to a lion; and God to a shepherd who saves certain small parts of the plundered livestock. These are the remnants of the Israelites, but few in number (only "two"); humble in condition (not the head, nor the arms, nor the heart, but only the legs); and weak in strength, like those who lie sick and exhausted on the side of a bed or the support of a couch. Such was their land to be for them—no longer, as before, a seat of luxury and delights.

# ON THE TEN TRIBES

IV. History corresponds to prophecy. For it is recorded concerning the **Simeonites** that in the time of King **Hezekiah** <note>original: "Hizkiæ"</note>, they occupied new lands, devoted the inhabitants to destruction, took their pastures for their own flocks, and lived there *until the day the Books of Chronicles were written.* 1 Chronicles 4:24, 38, 41. Likewise, five hundred of them struck down the remnant of the **Amalekites** that had escaped, and lived there in the same manner until that same day. Now, the **Books of Chronicles** were written either by **Ezra** himself, as most believe, or certainly by someone who was his contemporary <note>original Greek: "σύγχρονος" (synchronos)</note>; after the **Jews** returned from **Babylon**. For they mention the return from the Babylonian captivity in 1 Chronicles 9:1-2 and 2 Chronicles 36:22, and the descendants of **Zerubbabel**, under whose leadership that liberation began, are listed in Chapter 3:19. Therefore, one of two things must be true: either these deeds occurred before the sixth year of **Hezekiah**, and thus these **Simeonites** escaped the **Assyrian** captivity; or they occurred after, and thus they reveal a certain number of people left behind by **Shalmaneser** <note>original: "Salmanaſſere"</note>.

V. Nor should we overlook what is mentioned in 2 Chronicles 34:6, 9: namely, that **Josiah**, the great-grandson of **Hezekiah**, many years after the principal families had been deported, purged the cities of **Manasseh**, **Simeon**, **Ephraim**, and the **Naphtalites**—which were for the most part devastated—of the instruments of idolatry, and collected and brought back a sacred tribute from the remnants of those tribes. He even consulted God on their behalf (verse 21). Therefore, some survivors remained.

VI. That these remnants were endowed neither with great skill in the Sacred Laws nor with much fear of the divine can be gathered from this: that the **Cuthites**, **Avvites**, **Hamathites**, and similar new colonists, moved by the **Assyrians** into the land of **Israel** <note>original: "Israëlitidem"</note>, were punished and treated very badly by lions sent by God because of their neglect of religion. They then requested a priest from the King of **Assyria** to teach them the rites of the God of that region. 2 Kings 17:24. These facts prove a deep-seated ignorance and negligence of religion among the surviving **Israelites**.

VII. It is probable that many of the remaining **Israelites** merged through marriage with this dregs of Barbarian nations, not only based on the character of those low-born common people, but especially from the fact that not even the **Jews** returning from **Babylon**—indeed, even those from the nobility itself—scorned affinity with the **Samaritans** or **Cuthites**. A shameful example of this matter was provided by one of the sons of **Joiada**, the son of **Eliashib** the high priest...

VIII. It is incorrectly asserted by certain very learned men that the individual whom *Nehemiah* identifies as the son of *Joiada* was actually *Manasseh*, the brother of the High Priest *Jaddua*, who betrothed himself to the daughter of *Sanballat*, the Prince of the *Cutheans* <note>The author uses "Cutheans" as a historical term for Samaritans, referring to their alleged origins in Cuthah.</note>: a story which *Josephus* records. For that *Manasseh* was not the son of *Joiada*, but rather of *Jonathan* (whom *Josephus* calls *John*), and thus the grandson of *Joiada*. Furthermore, his father-in-law *Sanballat* was not that *Horonite* who held the governorship under *Artaxerxes*; rather, he was a namesake of his, a certain *Cuthean* who succeeded *Bagoses*, and who was sent as a satrap <note>A provincial governor in the ancient Persian Empire.</note> into *Samaria* by *Darius*, the last king of the *Persians*, as *Josephus* expressly noted. See *Petavius*, *On the Doctrine of Times*, Book 12, Chapter 25; *Jacques Cappel*, *Sacred and Foreign History* at the year 3366; and *Huet’s Demonstration of the Gospel*, Proposition 4, "On the Books of Ezra," Paragraph 4, page 305 of the Octavo edition.

IX. This mixture of marriages was accompanied or followed by a mixture of Religion, which was a certain apostasy <note>A formal disavowal or abandonment of a religious belief.</note> and falling away from authentic and pure Judaism. For just as the Samaritans, having received the Law from a Priest, began in some measure to revere and worship God, so it is credible that they rubbed off some remnants of their ancient superstition onto the Israelites dwelling among them—especially those with whom they were joined by marriage. For we notice it has scarcely ever happened that these pagan and profane marriages did not bring about a notable corruption of morals and religion. See Nehemiah 13:26.

X. This mixed religion was most firmly established after the aforementioned *Manasseh*—having somewhat reformed the cruder superstition of the *Cutheans*—offered them many other things in turn with rash daring, which deviate greatly from the right rule of the Divine canon. An alliance of ambition drove him to these things. For when he saw that the path to honors in Jerusalem was closed to him because of his forbidden marriage, he went to his father-in-law *Sanballat* and told him that while he loved his daughter, he was unwilling to be deprived of the priesthood for her sake—an honor that was his by birthright and had always been held in the highest esteem among the Jews. *Sanballat* replied that he would not only preserve the *priesthood* for him, but would also provide him with the *High Priesthood* and make him the prince of his entire province, provided he kept his daughter as his wife:

# OF THE TEN

<margin>catchword: li.</margin>

...he maintained: that he would also build a temple equal to the one in Jerusalem on Mount Gerizim, which towers above the other mountains of *Samaria*. No sooner said than done. With *Alexander's* <note>Alexander the Great</note> permission, a sanctuary was built there. *Manasseh* was appointed High Priest. Many priests, who were entangled in marriages with foreigners, defected to *Manasseh*, while *Sanballat* provided them with money, land to cultivate, and homes, supporting his son-in-law’s ambition in every way. However, as the Hebrew History says, *that sanctuary became a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense* <note>A biblical metaphor for something that causes people to fall into sin or error</note>; for it was built out of rivalry and envy toward the Jerusalem temple, just as the golden calves had been long ago in *Dan* and *Bethel*. Indeed, one would not be wrong to call that Shechemite temple a *refuge* for wicked men. For, as *Josephus* noted, *if anyone among the Jerusalemites was accused of eating forbidden food, violating the Sabbath, or any similar crime, he would flee to the Shechemites*, claiming he was being falsely accused. That temple stood for nearly two hundred years, until it was destroyed by the fire and sword of *Hyrcanus* <note>John Hyrcanus, the Hasmonean leader</note>. *Josephus, Antiquities, Book 11, Chapter 8; Zemach David, page 26; Juchasin, folio 14, column 2.*

XI. In this way, *Manasseh* became the head of the sect of the **SAMARITANS**. This was a mixed crowd made up of barbarian settlers in Israel, ancient Israelites who had merged with them, and several Jews who had fled to join them. While their religion drew something from the truth, it was also defiled by many errors. I will remain silent regarding the Idolatry, the circumcision performed in the name of Mount *Gerizim*, and the image of a dove found on the mountain peak and placed upon their Temple to be religiously worshipped—charges we find constantly leveled against them by the Jewish teachers. For perhaps these things, which were wickedly committed by their ancestors, were ascribed to their descendants more out of hatred than truth. Surely, one might not inappropriately divide the eras of Samaria under the Second Temple into *Paganism* (though with some small mixture of *Judaism*) before the building of the Gerizim Temple; and from then on into *Samaritanism*, insofar as it was separate from *Judaism* yet largely imitated it, from the time *Manasseh* and many Jews with him joined the ancient Samaritans. For then the Samaritan religion began to be considered as a kind of *Jewish* sect: since it was neither purely pagan nor truly Israelite. The author of *Juchasin* put it well: *Then Israel was divided into factions.*

# THE TRIBES OF ISRAEL. CHAPTER III.

<margin>Folio 14. column 2.</margin>
One part followed Simeon the Just <note>A high priest during the Second Temple period, known for his piety</note>, and his disciple Antigonus, and their School; just as they had learned from Ezra and the Prophets. The other part followed Sanballat <note>A leader of the Samaritans who opposed Nehemiah</note> and his son-in-law; they offered sacrifices outside the temple of God, and instituted rites from their own hearts. The work *Zemach David* <note>A historical chronicle by David Gans, 1592</note> agrees, calling them a sect and attributing invented ceremonies to them: <margin>Part 1. page 26.</margin> <note>original Hebrew: הבית הזה חקקו חקים ומשפטים אשר מלבם ברו</note> *this sect established for itself statutes and judgments which it had devised from its own heart;* by no means receiving religion in its pure form, as God had delivered it to the Israelite people through Moses and the Prophets.

XII. They did indeed acknowledge the Mosaic Law, and according to the testimony of Maimonides <note>The influential medieval Sephardic Jewish philosopher</note>, they accepted it <note>original Hebrew: על פשוטו</note> *according to the literal sense*, and <margin>On Berachot chapter VIII. section VIII.</margin> they observed the precepts which they grasped most accurately, so much so that they were regarded as believers in the law, and as acknowledging *one God alone*. Obadiah of Bartenora <note>A 15th-century commentator on the Mishnah</note> adds: *every precept of the written law that they held, they observed more accurately and far more diligently than the Israelites themselves.* Yet in this they were the worst corrupters of religion, <margin>Chapter VII. section 1. of the same treatise.</margin> because *against* the express command of the Divine, they built a temple elsewhere than in that place which the Lord had chosen for Himself; and because they impudently and insultingly rejected the most sacred Oracles of the Divine prophets for the most vain reasons. For so it is commonly handed down concerning them: although <margin>On John 4:15.</margin> the most learned *Lightfoot* <note>John Lightfoot, a 17th-century English churchman and Hebraist</note> brings forward reasons for doubting this.

XIII. But they were not even sufficiently observant of the Mosaic Law, especially if dangers loomed. For when that madman *Antiochus Epimanes* <note>A play on "Epiphanes" (the Illustrious), changing it to "Epimanes" (the Madman)</note>—as he should rather be called than *Epiphanes*—raged quite cruelly against the Jews in the name of religion, the Samaritans protested in a letter given to Antiochus: *That their ancestors, compelled by frequent plagues in their region, and led by a certain ancient superstition, <margin>Josephus, Antiquities Book XII. Chapter VII.</margin> had made it a custom to observe that festival which among the Jews is called the Sabbath: and having built a temple on Mount Gerizim to an unnamed deity, they offered solemn victims in it. But now they asked the King to command Apollonius the Governor, and Nicanor the Royal procurator, not to trouble them hereafter as if they were involved in the same crime as the Jews, from whom they professed themselves to be different no less in customs than in origin: and that the temple, which hitherto had held the title of no God, should hereafter be called the temple of* GREEK JUPITER. This was an open renunciation of the Mosaic religion.

XIV. Later, however, when the persecution had ceased and the affairs of the Jews were more flourishing, they <note>the Samaritans</note> again drew closer to the Jewish rites. For, as has been observed elsewhere by Josephus, *the Samaritans are of such a disposition that when the affairs of the Jews are in distress, they deny they are related; but when they see fortune shining upon them, they immediately rush into fellowship, affirming that they belong to them, and tracing the line of their descent from Joseph and his sons, Manasseh and Ephraim*. Hence also in the Gospel, that Samaritan woman calls *Jacob her father*, and professes faith in the Messiah as one who also pertains to them, in *John 4:12, 25*.

<margin>Jacques Cappel on John 11:20. Lightfoot on the same place, Section 32. Elle Haddebarim Rabba, Folio 292, columns 2, 3.</margin>
XV. Meanwhile, perpetual quarrels remained concerning the Temple. It is a wonder to say, however, with what futile arguments both the Jews and the Samaritans pleaded their cause. Most learned men have brought to light certain specimens of these from Rabbinic writings. It is related in *Bereshit Rabbah, Section 81*, that Rabbi *Ishmael, son of Joseph*, when he was setting out for *Jerusalem* for the sake of praying, passed by Mount *Gerizim*. A certain Samaritan, seeing him, said, *Where are you going?* And he replied, *I go to pray at Jerusalem*. To whom the other said: *Would it not be better for you to pray on this blessed mountain, than on that cursed one?* But he replied: *I will tell you what you are like: a dog greedy for a carcass. You likewise, since you know that idols are hidden under this mountain—as it is said in Genesis 35:4, "and Jacob hid them"—are carried after them with all greediness*. Thus, of course, the *Jew* fought for his temple. But let us also hear the Samaritan, from the same commentary on Genesis. Rabbi *Yochanan*, setting out for *Jerusalem* to pray, passed by that mountain. A certain Samaritan seeing him said to him, *Where are you heading?* And he replied, *I go to pray at Jerusalem*. To whom the other said, *Would it not be better for you to pray on this blessed mountain, than in that cursed house?* "From where is this mountain *blessed*?" he asked. To which the Samaritan replied: <note>original Aramaic: דלא טף במוי דמבולא</note> *Because it was not inundated by the waters of the flood*. Almost the same was replied to *Rabban Jonathan*; when he asked why they held that mountain as holy, the Samaritan answered, *Because it was not punished by the waters of the flood*. And when an argument was demanded, he cited *Ezekiel 22:24: "Son of man, say to her: You are a land that is not cleansed, nor rained upon in the day of indignation."*

<margin>Josephus, *Antiquities*, Book 13, Chapter 6.</margin>

# THE TRIBES OF ISRAEL. CHAPTER III.

...a sedition between the *Jews* and the *Samaritans* concerning the sacred rites of each nation; while the *Jews* contended that, according to the prescriptions of *Moses*, the *Jerusalem* temple was the only legitimate one, the *Samaritans* truly argued for the temple on *Mount Gerizim*. The matter was brought before the King and an assembly of his nobles <note>The "purpurati" or those clad in purple, referring to high-ranking royal advisors</note>, under the condition that the advocates of whichever side lost the case would be punished by death. *Sabbaeus* and *Theodosius* acted as patrons for the *Samaritans*, while *Andronicus*, son of *Messalamus*, represented the *Jews* of *Jerusalem*. They swore by God and the King that they would bring forth proofs from the Law, and they asked the King to put to death whoever was found to have not kept his oath. Therefore the King, having called many of his friends into council, sat down to hear the case. And when *Sabbaeus* and *Theodosius* had agreed that *Andronicus* should speak first, he began to prove the sanctity of the *Jerusalem* temple from the Law, showing the propagation of the Priesthood through a continuous succession of High Priests down to his own times, and how the majesty of that place had been honored with gifts by all the Kings of *Asia*; whereas the temple of *Mount Gerizim* had never been held in any account by them, as if it did not exist at all. By these and similar arguments, he persuaded the King to decree that the *Jerusalem* temple was founded according to the judgment of *Moses*, and he sentenced *Sabbaeus* and *Theodosius* to execution.

XVII. But the matter did not remain within the bounds of debate. The *Samaritans* dared to lay sacrilegious hands upon the very Law of God, defiling it with a monstrous deed so that it might seem to patronize their own superstition. Although God said to the Israelites in *Deuteronomy 27:4*: *And it shall be when you have crossed the Jordan, that you shall set up these stones which I command you today* <note>original Hebrew: בהר עיבל</note> ON MOUNT EBAL: these most impudent of mortals endured to violate the sacrosanct words of the Lord, and substituted for them <note>original Hebrew: בהר גריזים</note> ON MOUNT GERIZIM. Nor did their audacity stop here. They attacked the very law of the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments</note>, than which no law since the birth of man has ever approved itself to the conscience of mortals with more arguments of Divinity and inviolable sanctity: and to its ten commandments they added an eleventh, namely, their own crime. In two places the Decalogue is set forth, evidently in *Exodus 20* where it was first given, and in *Deuteronomy 5* where it is solemnly repeated. In both places, they stitched that precept of theirs onto the commands of God. The words, as they appear in the *London Polyglot* <note>A famous 17th-century multi-language Bible edited by Brian Walton</note>, are as follows: *And when the Lord your God shall have brought you into the land of the Canaanites to which...*

XVIII. However, I would not rashly say exactly when they corrupted the sacred text with this wicked addition. XX. Furthermore, these things seem to be understood regarding those ancient *Samaritans* who were Gentiles and idolaters. For from the time they became entangled in marriages with the Israelites and grew closer to their religion, they were judged a little more mildly.

Truly, a Jew, following his ancestral customs, would not wish to give even cold water to a Samaritan, nor show him the way, nor point out a spring. Hence it seemed memorable to the Lord that a certain Samaritan understood the common duties of humanity better and performed them more promptly than a Priest or a Levite, proving himself a neighbor to the Jews, by whom his own race was treated with such great inhumanity. # THE TRIBES OF ISRAEL. CHAPTER IV.

...and in the cities of Media. <note>2 Kings 17:6</note> It was a custom of kings from ancient times to transfer nations here and there according to their whim, in the manner of cattle, which shepherds drive now into winter pastures, now into summer ones. For in this way the spirits of peoples are softened and changed; those who dare anything on their own soil become placid and quiet in a foreign land. Thus the Romans moved the *Ligures* <note>A people from the mountainous region of northwest Italy</note>—who frequently rebelled due to their confidence in the mountains—into the plains; and they banished the *Cilician* pirates to inland locations, removed from the sight of the sea. With the same intent, the Babylonians transported the *Jews*, and now the *Assyrians* have carried the *Israelites* as exiles from their fatherland, so that they might drink from the *Euphrates and Tigris* instead of the *Jordan*.

II. Furthermore, geographers dispute exactly in which tract of land the dwellings of the deported Israelites were located, and by what other names they are designated by secular writers; the lawsuit is still before the judge <note>original: "adhuc sub judice lis est" — a legal metaphor meaning the matter is undecided</note>. I do not care to go through every detail, as it would be as troublesome for us as it would be tedious for the reader. Above all others, the opinion of *Grotius* <note>Hugo Grotius, a famous Dutch jurist and theologian</note> and *Bochart* <note>Samuel Bochart, a French Protestant biblical scholar</note> pleases me,
<margin>Phaleg. book III. chapter XIV.</margin>
who rightly dislike the idea of them being banished to *Colchis* and *Iberia* <note>Regions in the Caucasus, modern Georgia</note>, or into *Lesser Armenia*, or into furthest *Scythia*, when the Scripture expressly says they migrated into *Assyria* and the *cities of the Medes*. This is especially true since in *Assyria*, or in the part of Media neighboring it, places are found with names very closely approaching those mentioned in sacred history: namely חלח *Chalach*, חבור *Chabor*, and גוזן *Gozan*. *Chalach* is the *Calachena* of *Ptolemy* <note>The famous Greco-Roman geographer</note> to the north of *Assyria*. The *Chabor* of the same *Ptolemy* is the *Mount Chabaras* <note>original: "ὁ Χαβώρας τὸ ὄρος"</note>, between *Media* and *Assyria*. For those traveling from that mountain toward the *Caspian* sea, the city of *Gauzania*—that is, *Gozan*—occurs at about the midpoint between two channels of the *Cyrus* river. It is likely that this city gave its name to the region and the nearby river before the *Persians* ruled those places, by whom that river began to be called the *Cyrus*, just as the other neighbor was called the *Cambyses*, in honor of *Cyrus* and *Cambyses* <note>Famous Persian kings</note>. In place of *Media* in 1 Chronicles 5:26, there is *Hara*. Indeed, *Media* is called by another name, *Aria*, even by the Greeks, and the Medes are called *Arii*, the aspiration being neglected. *Herodotus* <note>The Greek "Father of History"</note> says in *Polymnia*: *The Medes were formerly called Arii by everyone.* <note>original: "̔Οι Μῆδοι ἐκαλέοντο πάλαι πρὸς πάντων ῎Αριοι"</note>

> Ezekiel 36:19-20. I scattered them among the nations, and they were dispersed through the countries; according to their way and according to their deeds I judged them. Tobias laments that all his brothers and kinsmen in Assyria ate the food of the Gentiles. Tobit 1:11. <note>The Book of Tobit describes the life of a devout Israelite in Nineveh who struggled to maintain dietary laws.</note> And for that reason, they were deserted by God; we do not find that He sent prophets to them of the kind He sent to the Jews during the Babylonian captivity.

IV. Nevertheless, the captivity of Judah eventually benefited them so much that from 그 time they began to have some communion with the people of God and His Prophets. For since both were subject to the same masters, they were bound together by a mutual bond, as much of calamity as of brotherly charity and religion. Divine providence arranged it so that those who had been neighbors in their own land would also be neighbors in a foreign land: so that those whom God had united by the promise of His future calling might also be united in nearly the same settlements—or at least under the same masters—so that they might be called together. Jeremiah was commanded to invite them to repentance and to promise the mercy of God. Jeremiah 3:11-12. Ezekiel also prophesied concerning their restoration in Chapters 36 and 37. It is reasonable to believe that they were made participants in these prophecies through the pious Jews. There is no doubt that Daniel and his companions held their satrapies and governorships in those places of Assyria where the Israelites lived, at least in such a way that they could communicate to them those things which piety urged them to share.
<margin>Josephus, Antiquities, Book 10, last chapter.</margin> Certainly, Josephus records that Daniel lived in Ecbatana in Media, and built a Royal Palace—a most skillful and plainly stupendous work—the guardianship of which, for that reason, was entrusted to some Jewish priest even until later times, and even in the age of Josephus himself.

V. It could indeed have happened that some individuals, or even a few families of Israelites, gradually slipped away into more remote lands; however, the "body," so to speak, and the generality of the people remained in the settlements which their masters had assigned. 2 Kings 17:23. *So Israel was carried away from their own land to Assyria, unto this day.* Likewise 1 Chronicles 5:26. *And so he carried them away to Halah, and Habor, and Hara, and the river Gozan, unto this day.* That is, even after the books of Chronicles were written and the Babylonian captivity was ended.

# THE TRIBES OF ISRAEL. CHAPTER IV.

...account of the tribes. 4 Ezra 13:40 <note>A reference to the apocryphal book of 2 Esdras (often called 4 Ezra), which contains visions regarding the end of the world and the fate of the lost tribes.</note>. The sum of the matter comes to this: The Ten Tribes, having been deported by the Assyrians and seized by a new love for the religion which they had poorly observed in their own homeland, took counsel among themselves to leave the multitude of the nations and set out for a further region, never before inhabited by any men. The rapid Euphrates stood in the way of such a great endeavor. But He who presides over the waters of the sea and the rivers showed them favor. He stopped the channels of the river until the Israelites had crossed over. And so, having spent a year and a half on a long and troublesome journey, they finally arrived in the region they desired. That region, moreover, is called *Harfaret* <note>original: "Harfaret"; likely a corruption of the Hebrew "Arzareth" (Eretz Acheret), meaning "Another Land" as mentioned in 2 Esdras 13:45.</note>. And they shall dwell there until the final time, destined to return from there when the waters of the Euphrates flow back again as before.

VII. Many things have been observed by most learned men by which this foolish little fable is proved to be empty. We shall provide a summary of them. 1. Those things which the "False Ezra" <note>The author refers to the writer of the apocryphal 4 Ezra as "False Ezra" to distinguish him from the canonical prophet Ezra.</note> invents are clearly repugnant to the truth. For Ezra <insert>the true prophet</insert> expressly testifies, as we have just heard, that the Ten Tribes remained in the places of their first deportation even in his own times and after the return of the Jews from Babylon. Our storyteller, however, narrates that those revelations—in which he mentions that departure as having happened long ago—occurred in the 30th year of the Judean captivity (Chapter 3, verse 1).

VIII. II. It is also false that the region of *Harfaret* is a journey of a year and a half distant from *Assyria*. For *Ptolemy* <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian geographer.</note> locates the city of *Arsarata* in *Media*, on this side of the *Araxes* river, a little beyond the *Caspian* mountains. Nor is the conjecture of very learned men improbable, that this tract of land obtained its name from the Israelites themselves. Whether you wish it to be called, with *Fuller* <note>Nicholas Fuller (1557–1622), an English philologist.</note>, *the city of the remnant* <note>original Hebrew: עיר שארית (Ir She'arit)</note>, because a large enough band of Israelites lived there with the native *Medes*; or whether you prefer, with *Hottinger* <note>Johann Heinrich Hottinger (1620–1667), a Swiss philologist and theologian.</note>, *the mountain of service* <note>original Hebrew: הר שרת (Har Sharet)</note>, where a people of Israelites, otherwise free, were forced to serve.

IX. III. Nor does it have the appearance of truth that a nation recently expelled from its ancestral homes due to its ferocity, and stripped of all power, would have attempted and completed a journey to such distant shores by its own counsel, without consulting or against the will of the masters and fearsome tyrants who held them captive. Even the cause praised for that counsel—namely, the love of a purer religion—is utterly vain. For when did that new religious zeal come upon those who, as we just heard from Ezekiel, profaned the name of their God among the nations no less than they once did in their own land?

# ON THE TEN TRIBES

...did we [see]? If, however, they possessed such a great love of religion, what necessity was there to rush out into places never inhabited by any mortals, situated under another sun and other stars, and—to speak with the Tragedian <note>A reference to a classical poet, likely Euripides or Sophocles, often used to lend a grand tone to the description of remote wilderness.</note>—placed beyond winters and white snows, to avoid all traces of men through distances that are closed off, hidden, diverse, and pathless? What reason can be given why they did not prefer to return to the fatherland with their brothers from the tribes of Judah and Benjamin? That land was given by God to the Israelites as a pledge of heaven; outside of it, building a temple or an altar was a sin. It was there, finally, that the Messiah—the sole foundation of faith, the pillar of hope, and the center of religion—was to be awaited.

X. iv. The matter speaks for itself: such a journey is among those things that simply cannot happen. For how could these wretched, unarmed people, pressed under the harsh yoke of slavery and scattered in various ways through hostile lands, move a single foot? Return was impossible; moving forward was equally inexplicable. For either in returning, they would have had to break through the middle of impregnable enemy phalanxes, or in advancing, they would have had to stir up the vast and foul "Camarina" <note>A Greek proverbial expression (moving the Camarina) meaning to stir up a hornet's nest or provoke a great danger; here referring to the fierce tribes of Scythia.</note> of all *Scythia* <note>The ancient region of Central Eurasia, known for its nomadic and warlike inhabitants.</note>, and both provoke and defeat the innumerable forces of the most ferocious nations. Briefly, the journey was undertaken either with the *Assyrians* unwilling or willing. If the latter, why was that miraculous crossing of the Euphrates necessary when the ordinary road lay open? God is not accustomed to performing miracles without necessity. But if the former, how could they shake off a yoke that was then heavy upon the whole world? Or how could they, destitute of arms, courage, a leader, and every protection, claim for themselves a liberty which they had not been strong enough to defend behind their own paternal walls when they were equipped with all these things? Unless, perhaps, God acted as a *God from the machine* <note>original: "ἀπὸ μηχανῆς" (apo mechanes). A theatrical term referring to a god lowered by a crane to resolve a hopeless plot.</note>. But here, He threatened them with something far different: Leviticus 26:37-38. *You shall have no power to stand before your enemies; but you shall perish among the nations, and the land of your enemies shall consume you.*

XI. v. Furthermore, I would like this explained to me: if it were true that the receded waters of the Euphrates provided a path for the tribes as they crossed, how is it that neither sacred nor foreign histories mention a thing so wonderful and marvelous? For how could a thing so prodigious, done in such clear light, among such famous nations, and in the most cultivated region of the entire world—if it happened—remain hidden or be passed over in silence? Why did not even *Josephus* <note>Flavius Josephus, the 1st-century Jewish historian.</note>, such a great trumpeter of the affairs of his nation, mention it even with a little word...

reaches it? It is entirely credible that this whole scene was staged in imitation of the twin miracles, one performed at the *Red* Sea and the other at the Jordan, when the ancient Israel was marching toward the Canaanite land promised to them. But despite all his art, whoever authored this fabrication has played a losing game.

XII. vi. For the very layout of the places proves it a foul lie. Scripture teaches that the Israelites, having crossed the *Euphrates*, were led away not only into *Assyria*, but also into *Media* and neighboring places sufficiently remote from the *Euphrates* toward the east. Our storyteller says they set out for a further region where no human race had ever lived: that is, unless I am mistaken, a place situated further to the east; where they certainly would have had the Euphrates not in front of them, but behind their backs. For to retrace one's previous steps and return to the west is not to "proceed further." Once the Euphrates has been crossed, what new Euphrates remains to be crossed again by those advancing further? <margin>Dissertation on the Ten Tribes, Section IV, Paragraph IX.</margin> Please see the learned observations made by **Mr. WILHELM WILHELMIUS** <note>Wilhelm Wilhelmius (1671–1739) was a Dutch theologian known for his work on biblical geography and history.</note> in defense of this argument. We conclude that the entire story of the ten tribes' journey via a receding Euphrates is nothing but

XIII. Meanwhile, we do not deny that, with the passage of time, the descendants of the Israelites were carried into the most remote places of the East, namely *Hyrcania*, *Parthia*, *Persia*, *Carmania*, *India*, and *China* <note>original: "Sinas," referring to the Chinese people</note>; as well as into *Armenia*, *Colchis*, *Iberia* <note>This refers to Caucasian Iberia (modern-day Georgia), not the Spanish peninsula.</note>, *Egypt* and neighboring regions; then *Asia* Minor, *Greece*, *Macedonia*, and almost every corner of the globe. Nevertheless, at the time when the two Tribes returned from Babylon to their homeland, the greatest part of the nation still remained in those places, and neighboring ones, in which dwellings had been assigned to them by their victorious masters. As we have just demonstrated from sacred history.

# CONCERNING THE TEN

### CHAPTER V.

->The status of those from the Ten Tribes who returned to the fatherland together with the Jews after the Babylonian captivity was ended.<-

I. *When the Babylonian captivity was ended, some from the Ten Tribes returned with the Jews; but many others remained in the places of their exile.* II. — X. *That some returned is proved by many arguments.* XI. *That they would return was predicted in Isaiah 14:1.* XII. *Micah 2:12.* XIII. *Jeremiah 3:12.* XIV. *Jeremiah 30:3, 4, etc.; 33:7, etc.* XV. *Those from the ten tribes who lived in their own land with the returning Jews were of three different categories.* XVI. *Nor did they hold distinct possessions for each of their tribes and families as they once did.* XVII. *Those among them who knew their tribe and family held that knowledge from private records; for the public catalogs perished with the kingdom.* XVIII. *Others did not even know their genealogies in this way.* XIX. *Much less did those Israelites have a distinct Republic for themselves: but they merged with the tribe of Judah.* XX. *Which was also predicted in Isaiah 8:14.* XXI. *And Zechariah 9:9, 10.*

---

I. When the Babylonian captivity was ended, where the **THIRD** period begins, the condition of the Ten Tribes was not uniform. Some returned to their own land with the Jews, though they were few, whether compared with the whole body of their kinsmen or with those returning from Judah; nevertheless, by Divine blessing, they were afterwards immensely multiplied. *Others preferred their new fatherland to the old, remaining in the places of their exile.* These points must now be clarified and proved individually.

II. That some returned is shown as follows. The Edict of Cyrus gave the opportunity of returning to all who were of the people of God throughout his entire kingdom. 2 Chronicles 36:22, 23; Ezra 1:1, 2, 3, 4. *The Lord <note>original: "Jehova"</note> stirred up the spirit of Cyrus, king of Persia, so that he made a proclamation throughout all his kingdom, and also put it in writing, saying: .... Who is there among you* **OF ALL THE PEO-**

# THE TRIBES OF ISRAEL. CHAPTER V.

WHO IS HIS GOD? *May the Lord his God be with him, and let him go up.... And whoever remains in any place where he dwells, let the men of that place help him with silver and gold.* <note>original: "Jehova Deus ejus sit cum eo..." quoting the Decree of Cyrus from Ezra 1:3-4</note> However, by "all the people of God," we should not understand merely the two tribes of **Judah** and **Benjamin** with the **Levites** attached to them, or even those **Israelites** who had previously joined their government, but the whole of **Israel**. We gather this from the similar edict of **Artaxerxes**. *Ezra 7:13:* "I decree that anyone in my kingdom from the PEOPLE OF ISRAEL... who offers himself willingly to go to Jerusalem, shall go with you." If these are compared, we will easily perceive that "the people of God" and "the people of Israel" are of the same extent.

III. By the power granted to them, the men of the people of Israel went up. *Ezra 2:2.* and <gloss>the heads of the fathers' houses for Israel</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: ראש האבות לישראל (Rosh ha-avot l'Yisrael)</note> *chapter 4:3.* There is surely no reason to restrict this to the tribe of **Judah** alone. For the claim some make—that they are called **Israelites** merely to distinguish them from either the **Samaritans** or from the **Levites** and priests—is a weak and fragile argument <note>literally "leaden or glassy," meaning it lacks strength or clarity</note>. For what purpose was there in distinguishing **Israelites** from **Samaritans**, of whom no mention had been made at all, and who (even if **Ezra** were silent) the facts themselves showed had not come into the land with **Zerubbabel**? Furthermore, the rest are not so conveniently distinguished from the **Levites** by the name **Israel** (which is common to the whole people) as they would be by the names **Judah** or **Benjamin**, which are the specific names of the tribes.

<margin>In the additions to 1 Corinthians 14, chapter 11.</margin>
IV. This argument is strengthened by the observation of the most learned **Lightfoot** <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), an English churchman and rabbinical scholar</note>. The people returning from Babylon are numbered in *Ezra 2*, and the total sum is calculated in verse 64 as *forty-two thousand three hundred and sixty.* And yet, the number of families listed there individually does not rise above thirty thousand. From this, you may not improbably conclude that the remaining twelve thousand, who are included in the total sum but are not listed by family, were from the ten Tribes; their genealogy (as we will soon show) could not be assigned as accurately. The *Seder Olam Rabba* <note>The "Great Order of the World," a 2nd-century Hebrew language chronology</note> *chapter 29* held this view before **Lightfoot**.

V. Add to this that those who returned lived "each in his own city." *Ezra 2:1.* It is well known, however, that not only the cities of **Judah** (strictly so called) were occupied, but also the other cities of **Israel** which formerly belonged to the kingdom of **Samaria**...

# CONCERNING THE TEN

[The previous page argued that the land was] occupied and inhabited. Indeed, Samaria itself and several other cities were held by that collection of barbarian nations whom the *Assyrians* had brought in <note>referring to the resettlement of Samaria by non-Israelites after the fall of the Northern Kingdom in 722 BCE</note>: but the history of the New Testament abundantly teaches that *Galilee, the Decapolis* <note>The "Ten Cities," a group of ten cities on the eastern and southeastern frontiers of the Roman Empire in Judea and Syria</note>, and many tracts of the Israelite empire were inhabited by the people of God. But which inhabitants from the people of God did they have? Perhaps *Jews* <note>specifically members of the Tribe of Judah</note> and *Benjaminites*? But those, at least in the beginning, were too few in number to have been able to refill their own land. Furthermore, Ezra is the authority for the fact that *each person dwelt in his own city, and did not occupy those of others*. Now, the ancient inhabitants of *Galilee* were the *Issacharites, Zebulunites, Naphtalites, Asherites*, and partly also the *Danites*. Therefore, even in the time of Christ, that region is called the *land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali*. Matthew 4:15.

VI. Moreover, all doubt is removed in 1 Chronicles 9:2, where Ezra, about to begin the list of those who returned from the Babylonian captivity, begins thus: *And the first inhabitants who came into their possession, throughout their cities, were* ISRAELITES, *Priests, Levites, and Nethinim* <note>term for temple servants or assistants</note>. There is a clear reason why these first occupied their ancestral seats. Because, evidently, the possession of all these was certain, nor did they have the right of dwelling in the cities of the tribes of *Judah and Benjamin*: among the families of those tribes, a new distribution of possessions had to be made according to the genealogical tables.

VII. Afterward Ezra, having obtained a new permit from Artaxerxes, brought back other ISRAELITES to the fatherland in addition to the Priests, Levites, and Nethinim. Ezra 7:7. And when, having already left Babylon, he had come to the river that flows by Ahava, and having surveyed the people, he discovered that Levites were missing, he sent to Iddo, the chief man in the place called Casiphia, so that they might bring from there ministers for the house of God. Ezra 8:15, 17. Now *Casiphia* seems to be the land of the Caspians, where the seats of the Ten Tribes were located. For both the name fits perfectly, and the facts attest to it. For since in *Babylonia* or *Persia*, from where Ezra was coming and where the Jews had stayed, he did not find a sufficient number of ministers for the house of God; from what land could he seek them, if you exclude that where the Israelites were then living?

# THE TRIBES OF ISRAEL. CHAPTER V.

...they celebrated the dedication of the house of God with joy, and besides many other sacrifices for the dedication of the sacred Temple, they offered twelve young goats as a sin offering FOR ALL ISRAEL, ACCORDING TO THE NUMBER OF THE TRIBES OF ISRAEL. <note>original: "pro toto Israele, pro numero tribuum Israelis"</note> This is repeated in chapter VIII: 35: *Those who had come from the captivity, returning from the deportation, offered burnt offerings to the God of Israel: twelve bulls* FOR ALL ISRAEL. There is no doubt that these things were done following the example of the dedication of the Tabernacle by Moses, and of the first Temple by Solomon. Therefore, just as those sacrifices were offered for those who were to frequent the tabernacle and the temple, so it was here. From this it is established that all Israel, and all twelve tribes—that is, some individuals from each—were participants in the temple and had their share in its dedication.

IX. Finally, why should the Israelites of the Ten Tribes not have returned to their own land, when even the neighbors of the Jews—who were not even of the people of God, such as the *Moabites, Ammonites, Edomites, Philistines*, and others deported by Nebuchadnezzar—gradually migrated back to their homes when the opportunity of liberty was granted to the people of God? This is according to that passage of *Jeremiah* XII: 14-15: *Thus says Jehovah concerning all my evil neighbors, who touch the possession which I have given to my people Israel to possess: behold, I will pluck them up from their land, when I pluck up the house of Judah from the midst of them. And it shall come to pass, after I have plucked them out, that I will again have compassion on them, and will bring them back, every man to his possession, and every man to his land.*

# ON THE TEN TRIBES

toward the house of **ISRAEL**, and toward the house of **JUDAH**. Once again, the time preceding and accompanying the birth of Christ is designated, concerning which see verse 15.

XV. Whoever from the other tribes of Israel lived in the land with the Jews returning from Babylon seem to have been of three distinct orders. Either they were descended from those whom the **Assyrians** had left behind; or the offspring of those *who, out of love for their religion, had long desired to share common interests with the Jewish people*, and were led away and brought back with them; or finally, the descendants of those *whom we have often heard were deported into **Assyria** and **Media***. All of these, however, made up a small number, whether you compare them with the rest of their fellow tribesmen or with the returning people of Judah. This is what Jeremiah had predicted, and all history confirms it.

XVI. Therefore, they did not *possess cities, villages, and estates distinct for each of their tribes and families as they once did*. Under the Second Temple <note>The period from roughly 516 BCE to 70 CE</note>, there was indeed a common division of the land into **GALILEE** and **JUDEA**, which **SAMARIA** separated. And just as *this middle region was mostly occupied by the descendants of the **Cuthaeans** <note>A term often used in historical texts to refer to the Samaritans</note>, and the latter was inhabited by the Jews strictly so-called*, so it is likely true that Israelites of the other tribes held the former [Galilee]. It was even the case that those known to be **Zebulunites** lived in ancient *Zebulun*, and **Naphtalites** likewise lived in their own province; and so on for the rest. However, the distribution of possessions among them was by no means as accurate as it once was. Nor could it be: partly because of the small number of *those who returned*, partly because the **Cuthaeans** occupied a significant portion of the land of Israel; but most of all, because the **Israelites** had lost their <term>stemmatography</term> <note>The recording or drawing of family trees and genealogical lineages</note>, unlike the **Jews**, whose genealogical records, continued up to the return to the land and beyond, are extant in **Ezra**, **Nehemiah**, and the first book of Chronicles.

XVII. This observation requires some <term>persistence</term> <note>original Greek: ἐπιμονὴν (epimonēn); meaning a staying with the subject or detailed attention</note>. Many of the Israelites did indeed know from private records which tribe they belonged to. Thus it is established that **Anna the Prophetess** was of the tribe of **Asher**, and **Paul the Apostle** was of the tribe of **Benjamin**. They were unable, however, to produce an uninterrupted record of their clans from public catalogs. **Anna the prophetess**, for example, could not show by what direct line of sons and grandsons she had descended from **Asher**, the root of her tribe.

# THE TRIBES OF ISRAEL. CHAPTER V.

And the Hebrew interpreters believe this was hinted at by Ezra in 1 Chronicles 9:1:
*And all the Israelites <note>original: "התּיחש" (hityachesh)</note> were enrolled in genealogies, and behold, they were written in the book of the Kings of Israel: but the Jews were carried away to Babylon because of their transgression.* According to the thought of Solomon Jarchi <note>Rashi, the famous 11th-century French rabbi</note> and David Kimchi <note>Radak, a prominent medieval grammarian and commentator</note>, this is the paraphrase <note>original: "παράφρασις"</note> of those words: The Israelites of the ten tribes also had their own genealogical records, which, having been entered into the annals of the kings, were preserved in the Archives; but these were destroyed and perished with the overthrow of the kingdom. For this reason, I, Ezra, do not trace the succession of those tribes any further. But the Jews, deported to Babylon for their sins, carried their family records—part of which I present here—to that place, and brought them back from there.

XVIII. There were even those for whom not even the memory of their own tribe survived. Such were those mentioned in Nehemiah 7:61: *These are those who went up from Tel-melah, Tel-haresha, Cherub, Addon, and Immer* (which seem to be the names of regions or cities located in Assyria or Media) *but they could not show their ancestral family and their descent, whether they were of Israelite stock.* Yet these people, as Josephus and the facts themselves attest, claimed to be Israelites; but, having lost their genealogical tablets, they did not even retain the memory of the name that was specific to their own tribe. See, if you please, Jacob Alting’s *Shiloh*, Book 4, Chapter 12.

XIX. It is right and true that those who did not have distinct possessions according to the division of tribes in the new Republic had even less of a distinct leadership or kingdom for themselves. Instead, they merged into one body of the Republic with the tribe of Judah, were reckoned with it, and were called by the name of "Jews." This was partly because those returning were by no means equal to the tribe of Judah, "neither in reputation," as the author says, "nor in number" <note>original: "οὔτε ἐν λόγῳ... οὔτε ἐν ἀριθμῷ"</note>. It was also partly because, after the Babylonian captivity, the supreme power was in the hands of the Jews, or in the hands of the Levite priests, who had been joined to the tribe of Judah ever since the schism of Jeroboam. In this way—as the most learned Wilhelmius eruditely compares these events—the Romans did not wish to grant the Albans and Sabines the honor of having the people named after them as well, even though they had been admitted into the city.

# ON THE TEN

TRIBES OF ISRAEL, Isaiah 8:14 <note>original: "Jes. VIII : 14"</note> suggests that these two houses and two kingdoms must first be reunited, so that they become one people and one commonwealth, before Jehovah becomes a sanctuary and a stumbling block to both those houses—not at distinct times or turns, but simultaneously. And in Jeremiah, it is proclaimed to Israel: *I will take you, and I will bring you to Zion.* Jeremiah 3:14. You also shall have your part and lot in Zion, where the metropolis of the kingdom and the center of religion is, not separated from the sacred rites or the kingdom as in former times.

XXI. Nor should we omit that passage from Zechariah, Chapter 9:9-10, where it is clear that the kingdom of the Messiah is being described. It is added, moreover, as a mark of that time: *And I will cut off the chariot from* EPHRAIM *and the horse from* JERUSALEM. By these words, three things are signified: I. That EPHRAIM and JUDAH, which were formerly the two leading tribes, would be combined so that they fall under the government of a single senate. II. That they would at some time possess *the chariot and the horse*, in such a way that one contributes the chariot and the other the horse: that is, by joined forces, they would achieve military glory through great triumphs. This occurred in the wars of the *Hasmoneans* <note>The Maccabean dynasty that ruled Judea in the 2nd and 1st centuries BCE</note>, likewise against the Moabites and Edomites. III. That the power of waging war would be taken away from them around the advent of Christ: which was done through *Pompey and Augustus*, and later through *Vespasian* <note>Roman leaders and Emperors who gradually dismantled Jewish political autonomy</note>. The sum of the matter comes to this: all affairs, both prosperous and adverse, would be common to Ephraim and Judah, as they were joined in one Commonwealth.

And this was also according to the Prophecy in Genesis 49:21. XVIII. Those who were first called to the Apostleship were from the Ten Tribes. XIX. I. **T**he Israelites, who at first had returned to their land in small numbers, afterwards grew into an immense number through Divine blessing. And this was also according to the prophecies, which constantly promise the increase of the returning people. Isaiah 9:2: *You have multiplied the nation: all of Israel: and specifically that part of Israel to whom, while formerly walking in darkness, the great light of the Gospel first arose.* This took place in the seats of the ten tribes, as we shall soon see. *You have not increased the joy.* <note>The author is grappling with a difficult Hebrew translation where "not" (lo) and "to him" (lo) are often debated; he suggests the physical growth of the nation was not yet the fulfillment of the promised spiritual joy.</note> Nevertheless, that expansion of the people could not suffice for that great joy promised to the whole nation. They will still have to trust for a little while in darkness and the shadow of death. And whatever they have rejoiced in so far is nothing compared to this most exuberant joy which hangs over them. For *they shall one day rejoice before you; when you offer yourself to be seen face to face, exhibiting the true presence in place of the symbolic presence on the mercy seat.* This is that "great joy" <note>original Greek: χαρά μεγάλη (chara megalē)</note> of which the Angel speaks in Luke 2:10. It concerns, therefore, that time which precedes the "manifestation" <note>original Greek: ἐπιφάνειαν (epiphaneian)</note> of the Messiah. Just as also in Chapter 26:15: *You have increased the nation, O Lord, you have increased the nation: and you are glorified by the manifestation of the Messiah.*

II. Micah, in Chapter 2:12-13, is of the same opinion, unless I am mistaken. It is my intention now to explain this prophecy more at length (having briefly praised it above), so that we may remove, as much as possible, all doubts from the minds of the readers. *In gathering I will gather you, O Jacob, ALL OF YOU; I will surely gather the remnants of Israel; I will set them together as the sheep of Bozrah, as a flock in the midst of its fold; they shall make a noise by reason of the multitude of men.* <note>original Hebrew: אסף אאסוף יעקב כלך (Asoph aasoph Yaakov kulach)</note> *The breaker-through* <note>original Hebrew: הפורץ (ha-poretz); often interpreted as a title for the Messiah who breaks down barriers</note> *goes up before them; they break through and pass the gate, and go out by it: and their king passes before them, and the Lord at their head.* There is no lack of interpreters, both Jewish and Christian, who contend that God in this passage—
