...to pursue his threats against Israel, and to act regarding their violent confinement in fortified places for fear of the enemy: as if he had said: I will bring it about that, under pressure from the enemy, you will be gathered together in your fortified cities, which he is about to besiege: especially that you be besieged within *Samaria and Jerusalem*: for an equal fate is predicted for both peoples. By *Jacob* can be understood the *ten tribes*; by the *remnants of Israel*, the two remaining tribes <note>The Southern Kingdom of Judah</note>. Concerning *those*, God says, *I will gather you into one* to be carried away, *not in part*, as happened through *Tiglath-Pileser* <note>Assyrian King, c. 745–727 BCE</note>; but *all*, through *Shalmaneser*. Concerning *these* <note>Judah</note>, I will lead them together into one, and that through *Nebuchadnezzar*. And there they will likewise be placed like a *flock in Bozrah*, just as *the sheep of Bozrah are gathered within the enclosures*. Compare Isaiah 34:6: *Since the Lord has a sacrifice in Bozrah*. But the Greeks <note>The Septuagint translators</note> read different vowel points: and took the letter *Beth* for a preposition, and *Tzarah* for *distress* <note>original: "angustia"</note>. For they translated it as *like sheep in affliction* <note>original Greek: "ὡς πρόβατα ἐν θλίψει"</note>. And there they will be crowded together and will be in an uproar, giving forth a tumultuous noise in those straits because of the pressing multitude. And thus the *breaker* <note>term: Effractor - one who breaks through or breaches a wall</note> would denote the Assyrian and Babylonian soldier, attacking and capturing those cities. So nearly hold the *Father of David Kimchi*, *Theodoret*, *Vatablus*, *Junius*, *Drusius*, *Grotius*, and others, who, however much they go in different directions regarding the individual members of this prophecy, nevertheless all agree in this: they contend that a *denunciation of judgment* <note>original Hebrew: פורענות / pur'anut</note> is contained in this prophecy.

III. But we, along with the *Chaldean* <note>The Aramaic Targum</note> and the *Ancient Hebrews*, as well as *Rabbi Solomon* <note>Rashi</note>, and the *most excellent of the Christians*, willingly concede to an entirely different view, and interpret the words of God as a remarkable promise instead, by which the coming of the Messiah, and the characteristics of that time, are brightly described. Truly, God is accustomed to temper the most dire threats with the sweetest promises and consolations. Examples of this matter are so frequent among the sacred prophets that it can escape no one who has decided to apply his mind to the study of prophecies. Out of innumerable others, let the connection of the third chapter with the fourth in our Micah himself now be considered. Moreover, these words are such that we never find them used for threats. *To gather the remnants of Israel*, as far as it is given to us to know, is never placed in any sense other than that of blessing and grace. See Micah 4:6-7 and 5:6-7; Isaiah 10:20.

# THE TRIBES OF ISRAEL. CHAPTER VI.

To make them like sheep, and indeed like the sheep of Bozrah <note>Bozrah was a city in Edom/Moab famous for its livestock; the name itself implies a sheepfold or enclosure.</note>, which was a noble city of the cattle-rich land of Moab, where there are joyful pastures and fat sheep; and like a flock in a fold, which rests nowhere more safely or peacefully—this does not mean to hem them in within walls to be besieged or driven from their homeland. I shall not pursue the other interpretations for now.

IV. God therefore passes from sad matters to joyful ones. And here is the connection of the words, which *Castalio* <note>Sebastian Castellio (1515–1563), a French theologian and Bible translator known for his elegant Latin style.</note> acutely observed: if there were some windy and vain man who lied and promised much wine, you would believe him, however much he lied, rather than another speaking the truth, for this reason alone: that he predicted joyful things. But I too shall predict good things, and indeed concerning the greatest matter of all, which is of this sort: after I have banished you into exile, as I threatened above, I will gather you from there. It must be observed here to whom He makes the promise, and then what He promises. He promises something to the congregation of *Jacob*, and indeed to the whole of it—as much to the ten tribes as to *Judah*; as much to the people of *Samaria* as to *Jerusalem*. For the Prophet had seen the word of Jehovah concerning both; he had predicted destruction for both. Chapter 1, verses 1, 6, and 9. Now he consoles both.

V. Therefore, He promises to both: I. *Restoration* from their captivity into the land of Canaan, so that no tribe is missing. This is not as if every single individual were actually to be led back. For it is certain that most of the Israelites did not return, and a great part of the *Jews* remained in Babylon. But it means that for all of them, as we showed above, the gate was to be opened and the liberty of returning granted. II. *Union* of the remnants of the ten tribes with Judah into one Body Politic and a communion of religion in one temple; from which things they had formerly been separated by the schism of Jeroboam. This seems to be signified by those words: *gathering, I will gather the remnants of Israel, associating them among themselves and with Judah, so that together they may constitute the whole congregation of Jacob*. III. *Increase* of Israel, as much in number as in the abundance of all things. This is elegantly signified by the emblem of the *sheep of Bozrah*, and the *flock reclining in its fold, making a loud noise because of the multitude*. Compare *Zechariah 11:4*. IV. *Exaltation* of Israel out of all the hardships by which they were to be tried after the return from the Babylonian captivity, especially by the Kings of Syria. It is predicted, therefore, that it will come to pass that—by the power of God animating the Maccabees <note>The Maccabees were Jewish leaders who led a rebellion against the Seleucid Empire in the 2nd century BCE.</note> and other strenuous leaders of the people, who were to go before them like a *Breaker* <note>original: "Perfractoris"; a reference to Micah 2:13, describing one who breaks through barriers or gates.</note>—they shall break through all those hardships.

Since Naphtali is called a *doe let loose* <note>original: "cerva emissa"; a reference to Genesis 49:21</note> who gives beautiful words, what is more fitting than that we understand by those words that Christ would preach the Gospel of the kingdom and peace in the land of Naphtali? And that the people of Naphtali, having broken through the nets of worldly preoccupations, would run eagerly to the Lord Jesus? For the words are well-suited to signify that event, and the reality itself harmonizes with them. For Christ first taught in *Capernaum*, which is a city situated on the borders of Zebulun and *Naphtali*, that is, in that *Naphtalite* region which is adjacent to the territory of *Zebulun*. In those coasts, a very great multitude, stirred from their homes, flocked with the greatest eagerness to hear Christ. Matthew 4:25.

XVII. I do not hide the fact that there is something which seems to oppose our translation—namely, that the Hebrew words *Ayalah Shaluchah* <note>original: אילה שלוחה; "a doe let loose"</note> are placed in the absolute state. Therefore, according to the rules of grammar, they do not govern a genitive of a different thing (which would allow one to translate it as *the doe of the one giving*); rather, the word *doe*, as a noun, should be joined with the adjective *giving*, to be interpreted as *a giving doe*. However, that "something" is actually nothing at all. For however you construct the words, you cannot escape an irregularity. If you put together *Ayalah Noten* <note>original: אילה נותן</note> (*a giving doe*), the noun will be feminine and the adjective masculine; and besides the linguistic irregularity, you will fall into an absurdity of nature. For it is not the nature of a doe to speak. Furthermore, even schoolboys know from Buxtorf <note>Johannes Buxtorf (1564–1629), a famous Hebraist and grammarian</note> that in the Hebrew language the absolute state is frequently used for the construct. Yet, if another explanation is more pleasing to someone, they may enjoy it as far as I am concerned. It is not our place to wrangle over words.

XVIII. This at least is evident from Jeremiah 3:15: *That to the formerly turned-away Israel, shepherds are promised according to the heart of God, to feed them with knowledge and understanding.* Nor should it be overlooked that those who were first called to the Apostleship—Peter, *Andrew* his brother, and *Philip*—were from the land of Israel; for all were born in *Bethsaida*, a city of Galilee, in the tribe of Zebulun. John 1:45.

Jeremiah 31:6 agrees: *For there is a day to come in which the* NOTZERIM <note>original: נוצרים; "watchmen" or "keepers"</note>, *the guards or keepers, shall cry out on the mountain of* EPHRAIM: *Arise, and let us go up to Zion, to Jehovah our God.* Whom can we better understand here by the *Notzerim* than the Disciples and Apostles of Christ the Lord? They were the keepers of the covenant, and they strove to preserve their brothers, and so that faith—

VII. These were, of course, the laws they learned from *Moses*, which were handed down to the entire people.

Furthermore, it is likely that the settlements of the dispersed Israelites were located in *Media* <note>An ancient region in northwestern Iran</note> and the neighboring regions. Nor would I wish it to be objected to me again that this entire multitude is designated by the name of *Jews*. For all the circumstances cry out that not a *tribe*, but a *religion* is signified by that term: just as *Jews* are frequently opposed to *Greeks* in this sense, as worshippers of the true God opposed to idol-worshippers. For those who are called *Jews* in verse 5 <note>Referring to Acts 2:5</note> are the same ones divided in verse 11 into *Jews*, who were such by both race and religion, and *Proselytes*, who were Jews by religion but not by race. By this, it is implied that some from all the tribes were present at that time.

X. Add to this *Acts 26:7*, where Paul testifies that the *TWELVE TRIBES OF ISRAEL assiduously worship God day and night, and hope to attain the promise made by God to the fathers.* To restrict this only to the inhabitants of the land of Israel, and not allow it to be extended to the many God-fearing people from all the posterity of Israel wherever they might live, is the mark of a man permitting himself too much in limiting Paul's narrow speech. This we certainly do not dare to do. For since Paul had been falsely accused of stirring up sedition among *all the Jews throughout the world (Acts 24:5)*, he wisely appeals to the common faith of the entire nation, in whatever part of the world they might spend their lives.

XI. And indeed, James and Peter compel us to think of the dispersed tribes even against our will. For the former writes to the *TWELVE TRIBES IN THE DISPERSION* <note>original: "διασπορᾷ" (diaspora)</note>, the men of which tribes he calls his brothers, and offers excellent testimony of their faith (*James 1:1, 2, 3*). The latter, however, addressed his epistles to the *strangers of the dispersion throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia:* who had been carried away into those regions far from the land of Israel by more than one *dispersion* <note>original: "διασπορᾷ"</note>, namely by the *Assyrians*, the *Babylonians*, *Antiochus Epiphanes*, and others; and there, worshipping God and acknowledging His Christ, they were partakers of sanctification through the Spirit and of *a faith of equal standing with ours* <note>original: "ἰσοτίμῳ ἡμῖν πίσεως" (isotimō hēmin pisteōs)</note>. (*1 Peter 1:1, 2; 2 Peter 1:1*).

The Jews are divided again into HEBREWS and HELLENISTS <note>Hellenists refers to Greek-speaking Jews living outside of Judea</note>: and the Hebrews, finally, into those who dwelt WITHIN THE LAND OF ISRAEL, and those who dwelt WITHOUT. From that time, the Gospel was preached to them also by the Apostles in the lands of their dispersion.

II. *Titus*, coming from *Alexandria* with two legions, to which all the forces were joined with the auxiliary troops of the Kings, pervades *Galilee*; he captures the city of the *Gadarenes* <note>The people of Gadara, famous for the miracle of the swine</note>—who had preferred their pigs to the Gospel—at the first assault, overthrows it, and sets it on fire. Then he comes to *Jotapata*: which, having been bravely defended by *Josephus* <note>Flavius Josephus, the Jewish historian who commanded the forces in Galilee</note>, who was there in command, he finally occupies by force after a 40-day siege and reduces it to ashes. Once *Jotapata* was cut off, *Vespasian* prepares himself for the siege of *Tiberias* and *Tarichaea*; and indeed, since the *Tiberians* surrendered themselves immediately, the city was granted to the prayers of King *Agrippa* <note>Herod Agrippa II</note> so that it would not be destroyed. *Tarichaea*, however, since it had allowed itself to be besieged, was destroyed. In a naval battle on Lake *Gennesaret*, six thousand five hundred *Israelites* fell. After the city was captured, *Vespasian* ordered the elders with the non-combatants, who numbered about one thousand two hundred, to be killed; moreover, he sent six thousand of the strongest young men, chosen out, to *Nero* at the *Isthmus* <note>The Isthmus of Corinth, where Nero was attempting to dig a canal</note>. The rest of the multitude, thirty thousand four hundred, he sold into slavery. And thus gradually all of *Galilee*, which was in the territory of the Ten Tribes, yielded to the victorious *Roman* forces before they equipped themselves for the destruction of *Jerusalem*.

III. Moreover, once the *Jewish* polity was deleted, and those who survived the nefarious slaughter were miserably scattered, and the genealogies were burned along with the temple and the city, and the entire body of the *Israelite* nation was struck by a Divine curse <note>original: "anathemate"</note> and hated by all peoples, all the *Tribes* were gradually confused and mingled in the lands of their dispersion; having set out on long journeys, some to one place and others to another, as necessity compelled or the hope of a more convenient habitation invited: so much so that they filled almost the entire world to its furthest corners with exiles.

### ON THE TRIBES OF ISRAEL. CHAPTER VIII. 371

IV. Those of the Israelites who had remained until then in *Assyria, Media*, and neighboring places, were confused and mixed with the *Jews* <note>The author distinguishes between the "Israelites" of the northern kingdom and the "Jews" of the southern kingdom of Judah.</note> dwelling in those same locations; for they had no cause to quarrel over the temple or the kingdom. Driven by the same circumstances, they all wander together without distinction among the nations. Nor can it be demonstrated from any trustworthy history that the ten tribes are now a people distinct from the rest of the Jews, much less that they possess any Republic or organized Government. Although I would not wish to deny that perhaps some remnants of them may be found here and there, they are of no great reputation, but are instead poor and afflicted, and such that you could not easily distinguish them from the other Jews.

V. And this also happened to them according to the Prophecies. Hosea 9:17: *My God will cast them away, because they did not obey him; and they shall be* **WANDERERS AMONG THE NATIONS.** These words contain the final part of the Divine sentence against rebellious *Ephraim* <note>Ephraim is often used by the prophets as a name for the entire Northern Kingdom of Israel.</note>, which the Prophet, like a court clerk for God, read to the people from His own mouth. VI. And so we have now followed the history of the ten Tribes, from the beginning of their separation from Judah, through the distinct intervals of the centuries, up to that time when the memory of them ceases among men; they have partly either wasted away among the nations, or, being confused among themselves by various misfortunes, have ceased to be distinguished both from one another and from their brothers, the Jews.

# ON THE TEN TRIBES

...places which were afterwards under the dominion of Nebuchadnezzar, and then of Cyrus. After the Babylonian captivity of *Judah*, both the *Israelites* <note>Referring here to the members of the northern Ten Tribes</note> and the *Jews*, acknowledging the same Lords and being neighbors to one another in the land of exile—just as they had formerly been in their homeland—were united by many bonds. By the edict of Cyrus and Artaxerxes, the opportunity was granted to all without distinction who were of the People of God and of Israel to return to the Fatherland. Using this liberty, a great part from all the tribes returned to the land of *Canaan*, partly under the leaders Zerubbabel and Ezra, and partly by private initiative, seizing the opportunity. There, *they dwelt each in their own cities*, under one Senate, all frequenting the same temple, and united into the same republic; which, on account of the many pre-eminences of the tribe of *Judah*, was called *Jewish*. Many also from all the tribes, especially those ten, remained in the lands under the dominion of the *Persians*, *Greeks*, and later the *Romans* and *Parthians*. As many of these as adhered to the law of Moses were considered *one people*, and all were named *Jews*. And since they remained freely in those foreign lands, they traveled to Jerusalem for sacred rites whenever they pleased. Those from the ten tribes who had returned to the fatherland were the first in their own land to hear the Gospel from the mouth of Christ and his disciples. To those who remained in Babylonia and Assyria, Peter and his companions traveled. Once the City and the State were overthrown, and the genealogical books burned or certainly lost, the tribes became more and more confused: *and all those who did not receive Christianity wander without distinction among the nations*, exiles from their own sky and soil, *one people*, now subject to the same calamity, and by a wonderful providence of the Deity reserved for the same hope until now, and to be reserved hereafter.

# ON THE TEN TRIBES

They belong. Not all of them, certainly: for God himself restricted the promise first to Isaac and his seed, excluding Ishmael (Genesis 21:18-21); then to Jacob and his sons, excluding Esau (Genesis 25:23; 26:24). Here the exclusion ends, and all twelve Patriarchs with their posterity are called heirs of the promise. *O seed of Israel his servant: children of Jacob his chosen ones. He is the Lord our God: his judgments are in all the earth. Remember* **FOREVER HIS COVENANT**; *unto* **A THOUSAND AGES** <note>original: "mille aetates"</note> *the word which he commanded: Which he pledged with Abraham, and of his* **OATH** *with Isaac: Which he established also to Jacob as a statute, and to Israel as an* **EVERLASTING COVENANT** (1 Chronicles 16:13-17). Here we see enumerated in accurate order: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the sons of Jacob—the seed of Israel—through a thousand generations. Under this universality, the **Ten Tribes** are no less included than those of **Judah and Benjamin**.

IV. *The promise is twofold: one spiritual, the other more earthly.* The spiritual promise is this: *I will be your God, and the God of your seed after you.* By this, He signifies that He would everywhere have some among that posterity of Abraham and all the tribes of Israel who would be a people for Himself, and whom He would bless with the intimate and mystical communion of Himself. Many of them, indeed, were to be unbelieving and worldly; it was also to happen that a great part of the people would be separated from their brothers and from the communion of the temple and religion; and finally, that the entire body of the people would be rejected by God. However, that was not to prevent God from having some here and there within that nation in whom He might fulfill the truth of this promise. *Has God therefore cast away His people? Far from it. God has not cast away His people whom He foreknew. Therefore at this time also a remnant* **ACCORDING TO THE ELECTION OF GRACE** <note>original: "secundum electionem gratuitam"</note> *has been made. The elect have obtained it; but the rest were hardened* (Romans 11:1, 2, 5, 7). *For I would not have you ignorant, brothers, of this mystery, that blindness* **IN PART HAS HAPPENED TO ISRAEL** (verse 25). Nor is it right to confine that promise within the limits of any specific time, as if it were thought to cease with that terrible rejection of the people which was accompanied by the destruction of the temple and the land. For God Himself calls this an eternal covenant, and extends it, as we have just heard, to the thousandth generation.

# THE TRIBES OF ISRAEL. CHAPTER IX.

V. But the preservation of such a <term>remnant</term> <note>original: "λείμμα & reliquiarum" — referring to the small portion of the Jewish people who remained faithful</note> from all of Israel does not fully equal the entire magnitude of this promise. For God also said to Abraham: *I will make you exceedingly fruitful, and I will make many nations of you.* *Genesis 17:6.* If this is to be extended to the nations that are to be reckoned to Abraham—as indeed it is—it certainly includes the multiplication of the spiritual seed within the natural posterity of Abraham. For to that seed was promised the inheritance of the nations and of the world. *Romans 4:13.*

VI. The Israelite Church holds the position of a mother: those who are from the nations <note>Gentiles</note> are like *sons and daughters*, as the Scripture speaks in various places. Therefore, the Israelite Church cannot rejoice in the *inheritance of the nations* if she herself remains excluded from the goods of the testament, or bereaved of her natural children so that adopted ones fill their place. *In the beginning, the wealth of the nations resulted from her diminishing; but it will not be so when the fullness of the nations enters; then all Israel shall be saved. Romans 11:12, 25, 26.* All Israel, I say—both the *natural* and the *mystical*. Both the faithful descendants of Abraham and the faithful from the nations will see themselves remarkably multiplied. And this is that promised *inheritance of the nations* in which the Israelite Church will one day rejoice, when she herself, the nourishing mother of innumerable children, shall delight in the God of her salvation together with the nations added to her. *For you shall break forth on the right hand and on the left; and your seed shall possess the nations by hereditary right. Isaiah 54:3.* All glory will be common to the nations and to Israel: and in such a way that even the remnants of the Ten Tribes shall come into that communion. It is said no less to the *House of Israel* than to the *House of Judah*: *How shall I place you among the children? and give you a pleasant land, a beautiful heritage of the hosts of nations? Jeremiah 3:19.* There is none of these things which is not founded in the covenant of Abraham, and which ought not to be derived from it.

VII. To this spiritual promise another of an *earthly* matter was added, which was nevertheless to be a *type, symbol*, and pledge of a *spiritual* and *heavenly* reality: namely, the possession of the entire land of Canaan, *as an everlasting possession*: so that as long as any of the seed of Abraham remained, they would have a right to that land by the gift of God. To be sure, the possession was *not immediately* to be entered by Abraham or his seed, and once entered, it was to be *interrupted* several times; yet the *right* founded in God’s gift remains secure and protected for Israel

# ON THE TEN

It remains; so much so that even in the longest exile, one may cherish the hope of returning to it by the right of recovery <note>Latin: *postliminio*, a legal term referring to the restoration of rights to a person returning from captivity</note>. I say, even in the longest exile: for God has bound himself to the *thousandth generation*. Psalm 105:8, 11: **HE IS MINDFUL FOREVER OF HIS COVENANT**, *of the word which he commanded* **TO A THOUSAND GENERATIONS**: *Saying, to you I will give the land of Canaan: the portion of your inheritance*. He speaks not only of obtaining, but also of preserving the possession of that land. Lest anyone should say the promise is now exhausted and the covenant satisfied, God pledges his faith to the *thousandth generation*, that is, to those at the greatest distance of time from Abraham. And since not even the *five-hundredth* generation has yet passed, the descendants and late-born grandsons of today's Israelites still have reason to console themselves: for God will no more prove himself a liar to those yet to be born than he did to their ancestors.

VIII. Finally, the firmness of this covenant must be considered, by reason of which it is called an **ETERNAL COVENANT**. For it is not some promise suspended upon an uncertain condition, but it has the character of a most firm and irrevocable *testament*. Hence in Psalm 105:8 and following, it is marked by various names which are all intended to emphasize its immovable stability. It is called a *Covenant, a Word of command, a statute, an oath, an eternal covenant*, which God *remembers forever*. What could be said more powerfully to express the unchangeableness of his counsel? <note>original Greek: *τὸ ἀμετάθετον τῆς βουλῆς αὐτοῦ* (Hebrews 6:17)</note>

IX. Nor shall the unworthiness of Israel place any barrier here. For that unworthiness is to be graciously removed, the guilt pardoned, and the depravity purged away. I do not even except the *rejection of the Messiah* and his most shameful murder: which otherwise leaves all other most atrocious crimes far behind. *There shall come out of Zion the deliverer, and shall turn away ungodliness from Jacob. And this is my covenant unto them, when I shall take away their sins*. Romans 11:26, 27. And again: *For what if some were unfaithful? shall their unfaithfulness make the faith of God without effect? God forbid: yea, let God be true, but every man a liar*. Romans 3:3, 4.

These threats are predictions: for although *they are proposed here under the condition of disobedience, Moses nevertheless testifies elsewhere that the people would not walk in the commandments of God, and would make the covenant void*. <note>original: "sub conditione inobedientiæ hic proponantur, alibi tamen testatur Moses, non ambulaturum esse populum in præceptis Dei, & fœdus irritum facturum."</note> Deuteronomy 31:27, 29. Therefore, once that condition is met, they pass into absolute prophecies: and they are arranged with such skill that history corresponds to each one in order.

XI. It would be tedious to go through every detail. It is sufficient for our purpose to observe that not only one expulsion from the land into a wasteland is predicted, nor only one return to the land. In verse 31 and those following, he deals with the devastation of the land, the desolation of the sanctuaries, the scattering of the people among the nations, the Sabbaths of the land in which it shall rest, and all those evils and calamities to which they were to be exposed in that grievous exile. This is also what the outcome taught. *For they were restored to their land*.

XII. From then on, God threatens in verse 41 that *he also would walk haphazardly with them*: so that he might not seem to care for them or hold them in regard. *And he would lead them into the land of their enemies*. This is a new calamity, following the return. And it seems to signify that they were to be reduced to the power of the nations, to whom they, along with their land, were to be tributary. This was completed at various times and stages: while first they were forced to serve the successors of *Alexander the Great*, then the *Romans*, having been subjugated by *Pompey*; as we are soon to explain more fully. God adds *that then their uncircumcised heart would be humbled, and that they would accept the punishment of their iniquity: and then he would remember his covenant with Jacob, Isaac, and Abraham, and would remember the land itself*. Surely this was by presenting the promised seed, the *Messiah*, in whom is the blessing of the nations; and by presenting him in the land, while the Sanctuary was standing, and all the tribes of Israel were gathered together. This took place at that time when, through the ministry of *John* <note>Referring to John the Baptist</note>, many of the children of Israel were turned to the Lord.

# CONCERNING THE TEN

It must be understood that such a magnificent promise is not fulfilled by certain benefits conferred upon a few selected individuals from an immense multitude; but just as those things said concerning the gathering and enlargement look toward the public *affairs* of the people, so also the remaining promises must be referred to the multitude and, as it were, the body of the *entire* nation. Of the *entire* nation, I say: whose public assembly Moses was then addressing, and to whose descendants—without any distinction of families—this entire inheritance is assigned.

III. *The promises themselves are of two kinds. Some are spiritual, concerning the conversion to Jehovah their God, which does not occur without faith in the Messiah; concerning the obedience to be shown to his voice, especially the Gospel <note>original: "Euangelio"</note>, and that with the whole heart and the whole soul; concerning the circumcision of the heart to love God with all one's strength, and the propagation of this as a heritage to their offspring; and other such things of this kind. Others are more physical, concerning the gathering of the exiles from all the lands of their dispersion; concerning the return into the land possessed by their fathers by hereditary right; and concerning the increase in number, wealth, and glory beyond that of their ancestors.* All these things are brought forth in such grand language that it would be a sin to imagine anything meager or mediocre.

IV. Moses partly designates the epoch of time, and the matter itself partly indicates it: for if so great a thing, which fulfills all the grandeur of the words, has not yet been seen in Israel, it is necessary that we wait for it in the future.

V. *Moses* speaks concerning the time in these words. Verse 1. *And it shall be* WHEN ALL THESE THINGS HAVE COME UPON YOU, THIS BLESSING AND CURSE WHICH I HAVE SET BEFORE YOU, *then you shall call them to mind among all the nations where Jehovah your God has driven you.* We must see, therefore, what is the most recent curse proposed by Moses, to which this so remarkable a blessing is subjoined. It is mentioned in the 23rd verse and following of the preceding chapter. Namely, that the whole land would be burned with sulfur and salt, so that it would neither be sown, nor sprout, nor would any herb grow in it, after the likeness of Sodom and the neighboring cities, which Jehovah overthrew in his anger and glowing heat. So much so that the nations, utterly stunned, would inquire into the cause of such a horrific judgment; and, having weighed the matter well, would acknowledge that this happened to Israel because they deserted the covenant <note>term: "foedus" - the formal treaty or contract between God and the Israelites</note> of Jehovah the God of their fa—

IX. Immediately after the captivity was ended, the Republic was tributary to the *Persians*: and in such a meager condition that they were exposed to the harassments and mocks of their most contemptible neighbors, as *Nehemiah* and *Ezra* testify. <margin>History, Book 5.</margin> *Tacitus* writes: *While the East was under the power of the Assyrians, Medes, and Persians, the Jews were the most despised part of those subjected.* They were very nearly treated most terribly by *Alexander* the Great, and it would have been all over for them, had not the spirited *Macedonian* been appeased by the high priest *Jaddus* through the remarkable favor of the Divine Will. Yet they were forced to pay tribute to him, as they had to the *Persians* before, with an exemption granted only for the seventh year. After the death of *Alexander*, *Judea* first obeyed *Ptolemy* son of *Lagus*, King of *Egypt*, who occupied it by force of arms; then *Ptolemy Philadelphus*; then *Ptolemy Euergetes*; and finally his son *Ptolemy Eupator*. *Antiochus*, surnamed *the Great*, snatched *Syria* from him. When *Ptolemy Epiphanes*, the successor of *Eupator*, could not endure this, he sent his general *Scopas* and wrested it from *Antiochus*. But *Antiochus*, renewing the battle near the springs of the *Jordan*, put *Scopas* to flight, took *Sidon*, besieged the citadel of *Zion* for a long time and captured it. He added all of *Judea*—which had long been suffering miserably from wars, whether *Antiochus* won or was defeated—to his own dominion. He later granted it as a dowry to his daughter *Cleopatra* upon her marriage to *Ptolemy*, along with *Coele-Syria*, *Phoenicia, and Samaria*.

X. How, in the intervening time, *Antiochus Epiphanes* devastated *Judea*, occupied *Jerusalem*, entered and plundered the temple, killed many, and sold very many into slavery—as if wishing that no people of the true God should exist—is clear to anyone from the books of the *Maccabees*. This hostile fury did not cease with *Antiochus Epiphanes*: new expeditions were undertaken by *Antiochus Eupator*, *Demetrius*, *Alexander*, *Demetrius II* (son of the former), and *Antiochus* son of *Alexander*, who was called *Sidetes*. These aforementioned attempts seem to be predicted in *Zechariah 12:3*. # ON THE TEN

<note>The header "DE DECEM" likely refers to the Ten Tribes or a specific division of the historical narrative.</note>

...not only from violence and plunder, but also from the yoke and servitude of the nations; indeed, they even extended their own empire into neighboring regions: yet they remained far from that splendor of empire which the ancients had seen under Solomon.

XI. **Judas Aristobulus**, the son of Hyrcanus, called **Philellen** <note>original: "Philellen," meaning "Lover of the Greeks"</note>, was the first of the **Hasmoneans** to place the royal crown upon his head: but with little prosperous success. For there were continuous and bloody contentions over the empire and the priesthood between him and his brothers, and the other successors from then on: until, while the brothers **Aristobulus** and **Hyrcanus** were disputing before **Pompey at Damascus** concerning the priesthood and the kingdom, **Pompey** cast Aristobulus into chains. Having been received at **Jerusalem** by the faction of **Hyrcanus**, Pompey took the Temple—which had been occupied by the faction of **Aristobulus**—by force after a three-month siege. He slew twelve thousand Jews and entered the temple during the consulship of **Antony and Cicero** <note>63 BCE</note>. He restored a precarious kingdom and the priesthood to **Hyrcanus**, but took away from the **Jews** those cities which they had previously occupied in neighboring areas, ordering that they contain themselves within their old and proper boundaries.

XII. Moreover, since **Hyrcanus** could scarcely protect himself from **Aristobulus** and his son **Alexander**, **Gabinius**—whose help he needed against his brother—settled the affairs of the Jews almost according to his own will. **Crassus** then, preparing an expedition against the **Parthians**, arrived in **Judea** and carried off the sacred money which **Pompey** had not touched, amounting to two thousand talents; he despoiled the temple of all the remaining gold, the sum of which approached eight thousand talents. He also took a beam of solid gold weighing three hundred **minas**. Now, a **mina** <term>A unit of weight or currency; the author specifies its value here</term> consists of two and a half pounds. After **Crassus**, **Cassius** visited **Judea**: he took **Taricheae** in his first assault and led away nearly thirty thousand captives. This same **Cassius**, after the murder of **Julius Caesar**, again afflicted **Judea**, demanding more than seven hundred talents of silver: these were exacted with such severity that four principal cities were sold at auction along with their inhabitants. Not long after, **Herod the Great**, the son of **Antipater the Idumaean**, invaded the kingdom; he was declared King of the Jews at **Rome** by a **Decree of the Senate** through the procurement of **Antony**, and from then on he was always a servant of Roman greatness. After his death, **Judea** was reduced to a province and was annexed to **Syria**.

Did God, while the Second Temple was still standing, increase and adorn the Jews—not only in number, but also in wealth, honor, the majesty of the kingdom, and similar benefits—beyond their ancestors, such as under **David** and **Solomon**? Was it perhaps during the times of **Alexander Jannaeus** <note>A Hasmonean king of Judea, 103–76 BCE, known for his military conquests</note>? Regarding these times, **Josephus** writes: *During these times the Jews already held the cities of the Syrians, Idumeans, and Phoenicians: by the sea, Strato’s Tower, Apollonia, Joppa, Jamnia, Azotus, Gaza, Anthedon, Raphia, and Rhinocolura. In the interior, throughout the region of Idumea, they held Adora and Marisa, and all of Samaria, and Mounts Carmel and Tabor. In addition to these, Scythopolis, Gadara, Gaulanitis, Seleucia, Gabala, and the Moabite cities of Heshbon, Medaba, Lemba, Oronas, Telithon, Zara, Cilician Aulon, and Pella.* This last city they destroyed because the inhabitants refused to adopt Jewish rites. They also possessed other notable towns of Syria which they had recently added to their empire.

XIV. These things are indeed narrated magnificently by **Josephus**, as he is not usually sparing in proclaiming the glory of his own nation; yet we see nothing here that surpasses the affairs of the ancestors when they were at their most flourishing. XV. Add to this that the prosperous affairs of the Jews under **Alexander Jannaeus** <note>A Hasmonean King and High Priest, 103–76 BCE, known for his military expansion and cruelty.</note> were stained by many calamities. **Ptolemy Lathyrus** killed thirty thousand—or according to **Timagenes**, fifty thousand—Jews in battle: he ordered women and children to be slaughtered indiscriminately and cut into pieces, and their limbs thrown into boiling cauldrons, so that the survivors would believe the enemy fed on human flesh. **Alexander** himself acted more like a cruel tyrant than a legitimate king. For, having been offended by the Jews, he besieged the most powerful among them in **Bethoma**, and ordered eight hundred to be nailed to crosses; while they were still alive, he slaughtered their wives and children before their eyes. Furthermore, he was forced by his own people to restore to the **Arabs** the places he had conquered in the regions of **Moab** and **Gilead**. After the death of this **Alexander** and his wife **Alexandra**, there occurred the dispute over the kingdom between his sons **Hyrcanus** and **Aristobulus** before **Pompey** <note>The Roman general Pompey the Great, who intervened in Judea in 63 BCE.</note>, which we have just mentioned. From that time on, the **Romans** claimed much authority for themselves over Judea. Are these things equal to the most flourishing empire of David and Solomon?

XVI. Perhaps you will say the Jews of that later time were superior in this: that they brought subjugated nations into the communion of the covenant, forcing them to adopt Jewish rites. Such was the case with the **Moabites** (in part) and the **Idumeans**, a truly powerful nation; nothing similar was ever done in the past. However, if ever it were true, certainly here that Jewish proverb was fulfilled: <note>original Hebrew: קשים להם גרים לישראל כנגע צרעת</note> *Proselytes are as difficult for Israel as a plague of leprosy.* For by the proselytism of those nations—which was forced rather than sincere—it resulted that the Jews adopted their customs no less than they adopted those of the Jews. Indeed, if it is permitted to believe the Most Celebrated Interpreter <note>Likely a reference to a contemporary scholar like Cocceius or Voetius.</note>, who holds a different view from us here, it was because of that communion of customs and religion (certainly not a good one) that the Israelites are referred to by the Prophets under the names of **Moabites** and **Idumeans**.

For circumcision was not to them a sign of the covenant, a <note>original: "σφραγὶς δικαιοσύνης πίσεως"</note> **seal of the righteousness of faith**, as it was for Abraham; but rather an accusation of a broken covenant. Therefore, when the Levites offered sacrifices on their behalf, and did not themselves teach them to keep the covenant of God, to what did they burn incense, if not to their own dung—that is, to demons? Thus these peoples became a stumbling block to Israel, and brought it about for the greatest part of them that they themselves were called Edom and Moab, and were judged alongside those foreigners.

XVIII. And indeed, the bringing of the Idumaeans <note>The people of Edom, traditional rivals of Israel</note> into the communion of the covenant resulted in the Israelites being forced to acknowledge the Idumaean Herod as their King. Who is ignorant of how great a loss of religion and liberty that entailed? We conclude, therefore, that the Divine promise concerning the enlargement of the affairs of the returning Israelites—beyond how the affairs of their ancestors were enlarged—has not yet been fully satisfied; and therefore, it must be expected in the future.

XIX. I am not unaware that certain words of this prophecy we are discussing are cited by Nehemiah and applied, as it seems, to the restoration from the Babylonian captivity (Nehemiah 1:8-9). But this was not with the intent that said return should complete everything predicted by Moses, but rather that by the citation of the greater promises he might urge God, and create for himself a hope for the fulfillment of the lesser ones. For in truth, in that return there is a certain type <note>A "type" is a historical person or event that foreshadows a future reality</note> and, as it were, a down-payment of the other. We have been a little more prolix <note>wordy or detailed</note> in inquiring into the sense of this prophecy because we saw that a most celebrated interpreter went in an entirely different direction; whose observations, otherwise, we gratefully and willingly admit have greatly aided us in this very exercise.

And the bear shared a single pasture. The world, which until recently was bristling and raging against Christians under Diocletian, Maximinian, Galerius, Maxentius, and Licinius <note>These were Roman Emperors known for the "Great Persecution" of Christians in the early 4th century AD.</note>, marveled to see itself so completely transformed into something else. Those who just a moment ago could not tolerate the Church living as a pilgrim among them, now rejoiced to dwell alongside the Church; having deserted the superstitions of their fathers, they wished to be called Christians themselves. 

It is also suggested, according to the interpretation of some—which I have no intention of either confirming or refuting at this time—that the rise of the Antichrist is symbolized by the Asp and the Basilisk <note>The basilisk was a mythical serpent king said to cause death with a single glance.</note>. Certainly, those final times are being sketched for us, in which the Christian Church takes the form of a Holy Mountain, and *the earth is full of the knowledge of Jehovah:* times in which *the Root of Jesse shall stand as a sign for the peoples,* <note>The "Root of Jesse" is a traditional title for the Messiah, Jesse being the father of King David.</note> that is, the Messiah, demonstrated by the most evident proofs, will be received by all peoples as a lighthouse and a tower. In those times, finally, *his rest shall be glorious,* while he reigns peacefully in the most vast territory of the Church. On that day at last, the events predicted in the passage we have cited will come to pass. The entire sequence of the prophecy leads us toward future times.

III. But what will God do then? *He will again set forth his hand* <note>original Hebrew: יוסיף ידו (Yosif yado)</note> *to acquire his people for himself.* That is, he will demonstrate his immense power in the vindication of his redeemed people. And he will do this *a second time.* This can be compared with more than one previous act of vindication. Specifically, it may refer either to the liberation from *Egypt,* which involved the *entire people,* and to which this second liberation will be very similar in signs and wonders, as Abravanel <note>Isaac Abravanel (1437–1508), a prominent Jewish statesman and biblical commentator.</note> maintains; or to the return from *Babylon,* with the intent that the Lord here promises the gathering of those who had remained dispersed at that time—but primarily a *Spiritual* gathering. Or finally, it refers to the vindication of the *elect from the Gentiles,* which was discussed in the preceding verses, so that just as God once extended his hand to claim the *Gentiles* for himself, he will now again extend that same hand to claim the *Israelites.* Namely, the *remnant* of those who remain from those deported or fled into *Assyria, Egypt, Pathros*—which Bochart <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a French Protestant scholar of biblical geography.</note> proves to be the Thebaid region—and *Cush,* which is *Arabia and Ethiopia.*

IV. This, however, is what must be most especially observed: that this promise was made to the whole universality of the *Israelite* nation. Indeed, it dictates that the driven-out of *Israel* are to be gathered no less than the scattered members of *Judah*; and that so distinctly, that it is added that the ancient rivalry which came between *Judah* and *Ephraim* <note>Ephraim often represents the Northern Kingdom of Israel, while Judah represents the Southern Kingdom.</note> will be plainly abolished. Namely, all contention concerning the kingdom or other privileges will be removed, with the remnants of the tribes being mingled and blended together, with no earthly Sanctuary over which they might wrangle, and with the minds of all securely resting in the one kingdom of the Messiah—which is spiritual and heavenly—through the same faith and communion of love.

V. I do not see what compels us to transfer into *allegories* those words which of themselves produce such a plain and easy sense. It is pleasing to attach the discourse of *Musculus* <note>Wolfgang Musculus (1497–1563), a prominent Protestant reformer and biblical commentator.</note> commenting on this passage as follows: *In the preceding verse, the Prophet prophesied concerning the calling of the Gentiles: now in the following verses until the end of the chapter, he specifically adds concerning the gathering together of the remnants of Israel from everywhere. However, those things which are enigmatically proposed concerning the manner of this great work in verse 15 and following, lie hidden in the secrets of the fates; it is better to wait for these to reveal themselves by the event itself with faith and hope, than to violate them with a bold mind and speech.

**VII.** This entire discourse is directed toward the Israelites, and if not primarily to those who were of the ten tribes, at least to the whole people in such a way that these tribes can by no means be excluded. *Jonathan the Chaldean* <note>The Targum of Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation and interpretation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> paraphrases the first section of this prophecy, with which the third chapter begins, in this way: *Go, prophesy a prophecy over the house of Israel, who are like a woman who is beloved by her husband, yet she commits adultery against him; and nevertheless he loves her, and does not wish to dismiss her.* Please see and weigh the arguments with which *Rivet* <note>André Rivet (1572–1651), a prominent French Huguenot theologian.</note> contends that this prophecy must be understood chiefly concerning the ten tribes. For the following words lead us there (verse 11): *And the children of Judah and the children of Israel shall be gathered together, and shall appoint for themselves one head, and shall come up out of the land.*

## XII.

my [prayer] comes to you. *You shall be dear to me for the sake of the Fathers.* <note>original: "Cara mihi eris propter Patres." A reference to Romans 11:28, suggesting God's enduring love for the Jewish people due to their ancestors.</note> Nor will I abolish my covenant with you.

X. II. More distinctly: I. **The Removal of the Kingdom and Civil Government.** *Without King, without Prince.* <note>Quoting Hosea 3:4.</note> However, the Lawgiver could not utterly depart from the people of God with his scepter before the coming of Shiloh <note>A Messianic title from Genesis 49:10; the author argues that the loss of self-governance proves the Messiah has already appeared.</note>: from which it is argued that these times being discussed are those which followed the *manifestation* <note>original Greek: ἐπιφάνειαν (epiphaneian)</note> of the Messiah. What Benjamin and others hold regarding the "Leader of the Captivity" <note>original: "Aichmalotarcha," referring to the Exilarchs or Jewish communal leaders in Babylon.</note> from the family of David is of no account, and reeks more of a schoolmaster’s pomp than the majesty of a princedom. The *Ephod* is the garment of the High Priest, to which belonged the breastplate of judgment, with the *Urim and Thummim* <note>term: Urim and Thummim (Lights and Perfections). Sacred lots used by ancient Israelite priests to determine God's will.</note>, by which God was consulted. And thus it was a symbol as much of the judicial power in the priest as of prophecy. These things, failing little by little under the second temple, have now plainly ceased. III. **The Removal of Idolatry.** *Matzebah* <note>Hebrew: מצבה</note>, which word signifies either a statue (2 Kings 3:2) or a pillar—a stone which is a *monument* or *tomb* <note>original Greek: μνῆμα ac σῆμα (mnēma ac sēma)</note>. Genesis 31:25. It was an instrument of idolatry (Leviticus 26:1). Just as were the *Teraphim* <note>term: Teraphim. Household idols or figurines used for divination in the ancient Near East.</note>. See our *Aegyptiaca, Book I, chapter x.* What is clearer than that such a condition of Israel is described here as exists today? Whence the force of truth has extorted this confession even from the more recent Hebrew interpreters: that those times in which they now live are being delineated by Hosea.

XI. The **Re-assumption** follows. Afterward, many centuries having slipped away, *the children of Israel shall return from their wicked ways which they have pursued until now:* just as Paul also speaks in 2 Corinthians 3:16. *But when it shall have turned to the Lord, that veil shall be taken away.* <note>Referring to the "veil" over the heart that prevents understanding the scriptures.</note> *And they shall seek Jehovah, striving to know him, to do things pleasing to him, and to enjoy him. Their God,* according to the covenant of grace, for whose communion they shall then most greatly long: *and David, the Messiah, David’s Son and antitype.* <note>term: Antitype. The reality or person that fulfills a prophetic "type" or symbol from the Old Testament.</note> Compare Jeremiah 23:5, 33:15; Ezekiel 34:23. *Their King,* of whom in their blindness and hardening they once said, *we do not want this man to be King over us*, but to whom they shall then acclaim, *Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.* *And they shall approach Jehovah trembling;* that is, they shall run in haste, and with holy reverence and confession of their unworthiness. *And to his goodness,* the grace preached in the Gospel. *In the end of days:* in the time of the New Testament, and indeed in its final period.

# THE TRIBES OF ISRAEL. CHAPTER XI.

XII. SIXTH. Does not the following also point to the same conclusion? JEREMIAH 31:1: *At that time, says the Lord, I will be the GOD OF ALL THE FAMILIES OF ISRAEL, and they shall be my people.* <note>original: "Tempore eo, dictum Jehova, ero DEUS OMNIBUS FAMILIIS ISRAELIS, & ipsi erunt mihi populus."</note> Here, above all else, we must pay attention to which period of time the Prophet is designating. Unless we do violence to our own judgment, it must be admitted that the Prophet is discussing that time which he described in the preceding verses. In the penultimate and final verses of the previous chapter, he had described *a whirlwind of the Lord's wrath that would dwell indefinitely upon the head of the wicked, and would not be turned away until the Lord has performed and fulfilled all the thoughts of his heart.* <note>Jeremiah 30:23-24</note> It is difficult for us to understand this in any other way than as the most just vengeance of the Divine Power <note>term: numinis (Divine Power/Will)</note> brooding over the rebellious Jewish people because they despised the Messiah. For he had made mention a little earlier of that Messiah, and of the grace to be conferred through him upon the faithful Israelites. Now he explains what punishment awaits the stubborn; which Paul also follows up in 1 Thessalonians 2:16: *For wrath has come upon them to the very end.* Yet, if we look at the whole body of the people, there will eventually be an end to this wrath. For *when the Lord has performed and fulfilled all the thoughts of his heart*—both those decreed concerning the exercise of wrath and those concerning the pouring out of grace—namely, *until the fullness of the Gentiles comes in* (Romans 11:25), then the blindness and hardening shall cease. *In the end of days, in the final time,* after all those things have been done; then, says the Lord, you will finally notice it, considering and understanding those things at which your fathers were stunned. *In these very times,* the Lord now continues, *I will be God to all the families of Israel.* The entire sequence of the context teaches that this refers to Israel according to the flesh <note>The physical descendants of Jacob/Israel, rather than a purely spiritual interpretation of the church.</note>; who, after wrath has been exercised upon them, are to be received back into favor by right of return <note>term: postliminio (a legal term referring to the restoration of rights to one returning from exile or captivity)</note>. And this is not granted to just one or two, but is promised to all the families of Israel; just as we heard the Apostle prophesying in Romans 11:26: *and so all Israel shall be saved.*

XIII. And in my judgment, one would be in error if they denied that the things predicted in the same chapter, verse 31 and following, pertain to this. *Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, in which I will strike a NEW COVENANT WITH THE HOUSE OF ISRAEL and with the HOUSE OF JUDAH etc.* <note>Jeremiah 31:31</note> Here indeed those blessings of the New Testament are described which are common to all the faithful alike; but it is also predicted that there will come a time when *the house of Israel and the house of Judah shall be a participant in that covenant and its blessings.*

There are many things that persuade us that these words cannot be understood as referring to that rebuilding of Jerusalem which was carried out by Zerubbabel and Nehemiah <note>Leaders who led the Jews back from Babylonian exile in the 6th and 5th centuries BCE</note>. For:

I. From the entire series of the prophecy, it is clear that it deals with those times which follow the coming of the Messiah in the flesh.

II. Jeremiah says that not only the temple, but also the entire city, the valley, and the nearby fields—even the most impure Valley of the Sons of Hinnom <note>original: "vallem filiorum Hinnom"; a site associated with illicit sacrifices, later known as Gehenna</note>, which he names from the corpses and ashes—shall be holy to Jehovah. That is, those places shall be no less holy than the ground of the temple had once been. This is exactly as Ezekiel (Chapter 43:12) predicts this law for the building of the house in the times of the New Testament: *that the entire limit of the whole mountain all around shall be the most holy place.* This cannot be understood as the rebuilding of Jerusalem done by Zerubbabel. For in that city, one part was *holy* and another was *profane*. Although, eventually, through the coming of the Messiah, the whole city became a *throne of glory* (Jeremiah 3:17). Here, however, it is signified that as soon as it has been rebuilt, the whole shall be holy to the Lord.

III. Finally, he denies that this city will be either plucked up or destroyed until the last day. This again is proof that it does not concern that Jerusalem whose destruction Daniel predicted and the Romans executed.

XVIII. What then? Nothing remains except that we understand a new Jerusalem is promised, to be inhabited by the house of Israel after they have been called <term>universally</term> <note>original Greek: "πανδημεὶ" (pandēmei), meaning the whole people or the entire population</note> to the communion of the New Covenant. Whether, however, this refers to a material city or a spiritual one—such as was prefigured to Ezekiel and to John in his Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note>—it is not a sin to be ignorant until the fates themselves explain it by the outcome of events. In the meantime, it is pleasing to add the commentary of a most celebrated interpreter:

*He promises,* he says, *the rebuilding of Jerusalem, and indeed that it may be for Jehovah. For he says: it shall be built for the Lord. Now, in the New Testament, there cannot be a city of Jehovah unless it belongs to Christ and is held by Christians. This is not a private benefit for that city alone, but pertains to the promise regarding the restoration of the losses of Jacob. It implies that the losses of the Church are to be so restored that even the city of Jerusalem is restored, and indeed to the Lord. It is easily understood how great a moment this is, and how great a change of things in the world is needed for this to happen. Moreover, all these...*

All those things which must necessarily occur so that Jerusalem may be inhabited by Christians—and indeed by the Christians of Israel—and so that the nations may serve them, are to be understood as implied here. **I. SEVENTH.** Remarkable prophecies of this matter also exist in EZEKIEL; of which I am pleased to mention at least some here. <term>Chapter 16</term>: 53. Thus he speaks: <note>original Hebrew: ושבתי את שבותהן את שבית סדם ובנותיה ואת שבית שמרון ובנותיה ושבית שביתיך בתוכהנה</note> "And I will bring back their captive multitude, the captive multitude of Sodom and her daughters, and the captive multitude of Samaria and her daughters: even the captive multitude of your captives among them." <note>The "daughters" of a city refer to the surrounding smaller towns or dependent villages.</note> And again, verse 55, according to the Hebrew truth <note>A common scholarly phrase for the original Hebrew text</note> holds thus: *And your sister Sodom and her daughters shall return to their former state, and Samaria and her daughters shall return to their former state: and you also and your daughters shall return to your former state.*

**II.** It can hardly be said how much these prophecies have tormented the interpreters. Since they could not conceive how Sodom could be restored with her children, and held nothing determined regarding the restoration of Samaria, they have devised I know not what fictions so that the unexpected words of the Prophet might result in some tolerable sense. Please see those things which Cornelius a Lapide <note>A prominent 17th-century Jesuit biblical exegete known for his encyclopedic commentaries.</note> has collected. Those of the interpreters whose faith, diligence, and judgment we value most highly, think these pronouncements are conditional, such that the latter parts of the passages are to be connected with the first parts by a hypothetical particle; in this sense: *If I bring back Sodom and Samaria, I will also bring you back.* Furthermore, they think it must be inferred: but I will not bring back Sodom and Samaria. Therefore, I will not bring you back either. And thus the meaning would be plainly contrary to that which the Hebrew words seem to show the reader at first glance. Nor would we have here any promise of good, but an irrevocable denial.

# THE TRIBES OF ISRAEL. CHAPTER XII.

III. Truly, I do not think we are forbidden from weighing those reasons for which other most learned men have declared themselves unable to agree with that opinion. 1. Because the prophetic phrasing and speech portends no such thing, but plainly the opposite. 2. Because it is certain that God will at some time lead back that people whom He addresses through the Prophet. This is stated in this very chapter, verse 60:

> *And I will remember my covenant entered into with you in the days of your youth, and I will establish for you an everlasting covenant.* <note>original Latin: "Et recordabor fœderis mei tecum initi temporibus pueritiæ tuæ, & præstabo tibi fœdus perpetuum."</note>

3. Because God explains Himself in such a way that He says He will restore to *Jerusalem* her sisters, *Sodom* and *Samaria*, in verse 61:

> *For remembering your ways, you shall be filled with shame, when you receive your sisters, those older than you with those younger than you. AND I WILL GIVE THEM TO YOU AS DAUGHTERS, though not by your covenant.* <note>original Latin: "Nam recordata viarum tuarum, pudore suffunderis, assumendo sorores tuas majores te cum minoribus te. ET DABO TIBI EAS IN FILIAS, quamvis non ex fœdere tuo."</note>

Could it be said more clearly?

IV. One thing, however, seems to stand in the way: that elsewhere God has sworn the devastation of *Gomorrah* would be eternal, just like that of the *Moabites* and *Ammonites*. *Zephaniah 2:9*:

> *Therefore, as I live, says Jehovah of hosts, the God of Israel, Moab shall be like Sodom, and the Ammonites like Gomorrah, a place abandoned to nettles and salt pits,* <term>and a desolation forever</term> <note>original Hebrew: "ושממה עד עולם" (v’shimamah ad olam); Latin: "ET DESOLATIO IN ÆTERNUM."</note>.

Nevertheless, this very prophecy, rightly weighed, sufficiently proves that an absolute eternity—one which never at any time results in a happier end—is not to be understood here. For the same kind of eternity is attributed to the devastation of *Sodom* and *Gomorrah* as is attributed to the devastation of the *Moabites* and *Ammonites*. And yet, their devastation is to have an end at some point. For so *Jeremiah*, who lived at the same time as *Zephaniah*, explained the shorter prophecies of the latter with his own more lengthy ones. *Jeremiah 48:47*:

> *Yet I will bring back the captive multitude of Moab in the latter days, says Jehovah.*

And *49:6*:

> *but afterward I will bring back the captive multitude of the Ammonites.*

Therefore, a devastation is designated that will indeed last for many centuries, yet is to be ended at some time.

V. Furthermore, when it is promised that *Samaria* and *Sodom*, her sisters, are to be restored with *Jerusalem*; we should not think so much of the cities themselves as of the remnants and posterity of those nations. And that by *Samaria* the *Israelites* of the ten tribes can be understood—who had the capital of their kingdom at *Samaria*—is a matter in itself plain

The matter is clear. Regarding the *Sodomites*, the question is more troublesome. This much is certain: not all inhabitants of the Pentapolis <note>The "Five Cities" of the plain, including Sodom and Gomorrah.</note> perished. Zoar was preserved, and perhaps some from the other cities who were traveling abroad. Others understand this to mean the *Ammonites* and *Moabites*, for they arose from an incestuous union—similar to the foulness of Sodom—between Lot and his daughters in the region of Sodom. There are those who prefer to suspect that other nations are designated emblematically, sharing some similarity with *Sodom*. But *Castalio* <note>Sebastian Castellio (1515–1563), a French theologian and proponent of religious toleration.</note> did not speak poorly when he said: *the nature of that future restoration will be known in its own time*. For our part, we do not wish to be anxious about Sodom now; the fates will explain themselves. It is enough for our purpose what is said concerning *Samaria*—that is, the ten tribes—which is to be restored together with Jerusalem.

VI. But into what state? Into their *former* state. But that state, you might say, was the worst, not only if you look at Sodom, but also at Samaria, whose beginning and progress were both evil. Thus it would happen that, if they are returned to their former state, there would be a perpetual cycle of sinning and being punished. However, it must be known that both *Sodom* and *Samaria* once had flourishing and very prosperous affairs. God now promises a similar prosperity to their descendants—though not similar in every way—so that they may see the earthly happiness of their ancestors (which they abused for luxury and crimes by the worst example) exchanged for the spiritual happiness to be granted to them through the grace of Christ. And as far as *Samaria* is concerned, its inhabitants were Israelites, once bound to the friendship of the Divine by a sacred covenant. When they had basely violated that covenant, they were rejected and cast away by God for a time, called by the shameful names *Lo-Ammi* and *Lo-Ruhamah*; God declaring, *you are not my people, nor have you obtained mercy*. But now, says God, they shall be restored to their former state, taken back into the covenant, and it shall be said to them *Ammi* and *Ruhamah*: *O my people, and O she who has obtained mercy*.

*“For I did not give them to Abraham your father in the covenant between the pieces.”* <note>original: "non enim dedi eos Abrahamo Patri tuo in foedere inter segmenta." This refers to the "Covenant of the Pieces" in Genesis 15, where God passed between divided animals to seal his promise.</note> So records *Abarbanel* <note>Don Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508), a celebrated Jewish statesman and biblical commentator.</note> *from the Midrash* <note>original: "ex Derasch." Midrash refers to the ancient Jewish tradition of biblical interpretation and legal commentary.</note>. But whoever that Jewish author may be, he is mistaken. For in *Genesis 15:18–21*, God promises Abraham that he would give to his offspring that land from the river of Egypt *even unto* the Euphrates. In that patrimony, *Samaria* and *Sodom* are included. Regarding *Samaria*, indeed, there can be no doubt. Regarding *Sodom*, however, it is proven thus: when a contention arose between their shepherds, *Lot* and *Abraham* divided the land between themselves. *Lot*, looking out toward the region of *Sodom* and seeing its pleasantness, chose it for himself (*Genesis 13:10*). After his departure, God promises *Abraham* that He would give him all that land, in whatever direction he could look (*verses 14, 15*): *“And Jehovah said to Abraham, after Lot had separated himself from him: Lift up now your eyes, and look around from that place where you are: toward the North and toward the South, and toward the East and the West. For all this region which you see, I am going to give to you and to your offspring forever.”* From this it is inferred that even the region of *Sodom* was given to *Abraham*; for he was able to take it in with his eyes from the place where he stood, no less than *Lot* could.

VIII. It is necessary, therefore, to understand another covenant when we hear God saying to *Jerusalem*: *“but not by your covenant.”* <note>A reference to Ezekiel 16:61, where God promises to give Jerusalem her "sisters" (Sodom and Samaria) as daughters, but not by the old legal covenant.</note> To be sure, God had struck a ceremonial and symbolic <note>original: "typicum." In theology, a "type" is an Old Testament person or event that foreshadows a New Testament reality.</note> covenant with *Jerusalem*. By that covenant, *Jerusalem* was established as the Metropolis of the people whom God had made heirs of the land of Canaan, so that the Temple might be there, along with the Aaronic Priesthood, and the Senate of the people, holding the leadership and the power. But it is not by this covenant—which is specific to the earthly *Jerusalem*—that *Samaria* and *Sodom* are given to her as daughters, as if they were to approach some material temple there, having a communion of symbolic sacred rites and depending on the Senate of leaders residing there. It is another and much more excellent covenant, by the participation of which both *Sodom* and *Samaria* must grow together into one body with *Jerusalem*. Namely, the covenant of peace, by which those who were far removed are moved closer; by which both are made one, the barrier of the dividing wall is dissolved, and the enmities—that is, the law of commandments in rituals—are abolished through the flesh of Christ. In one word: the New Testament <note>original: "Testamentum novum." This refers to the New Covenant established by Jesus.</note>. By its power, and in its communion, this beautiful inheritance is to be assigned to *Jerusalem*. By its force, she herself will one day...

<margin>IX.</margin> And thus we understand that the time is simultaneously assigned when these things will reach their fulfillment. Indeed, all these things look toward the future. It will be at that time when the Eternal Testament shall flourish, distinguished from that other shadowy one <note>The "shadowy" testament refers to the Old Mosaic Law, which was seen by theologians as a foreshadowing of the New Covenant</note>: when Jerusalem—that is, the Jews—rejoicing in the blessings of that Testament, shall remember their ways, suffused with holy shame, and shall know that God is Jehovah. He is the one who has fulfilled His faith by the performance of the greatest promises, and—what is the heart of the matter—by the presentation of the Messiah. Indeed, they shall know that the Messiah himself is Jehovah, whom their ancestors had accused of blasphemy for claiming this very name for himself. They shall know this, however, not by mental speculation alone, but by experience and a sense of the Divine truth, goodness, and all-encompassing sufficiency for salvation found in the Messiah. For they shall be cleansed from all that they have done, their sins being forgiven on account of the <term>ransom-price</term> <note>original Greek: ἀντίλυτρον (antilytron). This refers to the "substitutionary ransom" paid by Christ for humanity.</note> of the Surety, laid hold of by faith. *As it is written: The Deliverer will come out of Zion, and He will turn away ungodliness from Jacob. And this is my covenant with them, when I shall take away their sins. Romans 11:26-27.*

<margin>X.</margin> **EIGHTHLY**. Does not that passage of **EZEKIEL** found in **CHAPTER 20, verses 40, 41, 42, 43, 44** also pertain to this same matter? To be sure, God explains almost the entire history of Israel in a brief discourse. Beginning from Egypt, He relates in order what had been done wickedly by them in the desert, and what had been done justly and holily by Himself; then He follows what had occurred in the land of Canaan, up to those times in which this prophecy was given to Israel. From there, He prepares Himself to predict future events in verse 32. Very many of the Jews were harboring desperate thoughts, believing that in the future no worship of God would remain in the world, thus renouncing that most noble promise concerning the coming of the Messiah and the perpetual covenant which God had struck with their ancestors. "And we," they were saying, "shall eventually be like those Gentiles, serving wood and stone." God bore this with indignation. He swears, therefore, on this occasion, that He will hold kingship over them with a mighty hand, an outstretched arm, and with wrath poured out, and thus He will lead them back from the peoples among whom they were scattered. Which indeed He has performed: having asserted His dominion over the Israelites,

XI. But even then, they had to be introduced into the *wilderness of the peoples*. By this phrase—as I believe was acutely observed by a most celebrated interpreter—it seems to be designated that *Judea* would become part of the *Roman* jurisdiction, or a *province of the Roman Empire*, which happened after the exile of Archelaus <note>Archelaus was the son of Herod the Great; his removal in 6 AD led to Judea becoming a Roman province under a prefect.</note>. Thus, from that time, the Jews lived partly in their own land and partly outside the land, in the midst of the Gentiles. For in symbolic language, the *wilderness* is called a world that has no cultivation for bearing fruit to God. To this is opposed the *inhabited world* <note>original: "ἡ οἰκουμένη" (he oikoumene)</note>, signifying a people in which there is worship and fruit. Therefore, the *wilderness of the peoples* is that part of the world which, occupied by profane nations, is destitute of true piety. Into such a *wilderness* the Jews were led when their land itself became part of the *wilderness*—that is, of the *gentile empire*.

XII. *And there*, God continues, *I will plead with you face to face*; that is, I will come to you, so that you may see me present and hear me speaking, pleading with you concerning justice and faith. *Just as I pleaded with your fathers in the wilderness of Egypt*; there seen in a cloud and heard from the thunder; here to be seen in the flesh and heard in the proclamation of the Gospel. He adds in verse 37: *And I will make you pass under the rod*; using a metaphor taken from a shepherd, who is accustomed to count and review his sheep in this manner. This can be understood as the separation of the elect from the non-elect through an effective calling, and the care of Christ for each of his sheep so that none of them may perish. *And I will bring you into the bond of the covenant*: uniting you to me through faith, for the participation in the blessings of the covenant of grace, and binding you to one another through charity, with the indissoluble bond of brotherly friendship. XIII. Thus far, God's discourse through the Prophet is clear enough. What follows in verse 38 is more enigmatic; however, it must be explained so that we may see the sequence of the prophecy. *And I will pick out*, says God, *the rebels and those falling away from me, separating them for evil from the tribes of Israel*, excluding them from the prerogatives of the covenant, and exposing them to my most just vengeance. Compare Deuteronomy 29:21 and Matthew 25:31. *I will lead them out from the land of their pilgrimage*, power having been given indiscriminately to both the rebellious and the reprobate, as well as to the elect and the obedient, to leave the lands of their exile and to dwell among themselves in the same place, in the same temple, and in the same Synagogues.

XIV. *And into the land of Israel they shall not enter.* It does not seem possible to explain this otherwise than in a mystical sense. For if by the *land of Israel* you understand the land of *Canaan* according to the letter, it is certain that the wicked prevailed immensely in that land during the time of Christ. We must therefore think of a more secret meaning. This, however, is not to be fashioned by our own judgment, but gathered from a comparison of prophecies. From these we learn that the *land of Israel* sometimes denotes that beautiful *inheritance of the nations*, which, having been promised long ago, the pious Israelites enjoyed after the Messiah was revealed. We have God himself as the interpreter of this matter in **Jeremiah 3:16: And I said, how shall I place you among the children? and I will give to you the DESIRED LAND, the BEAUTIFUL INHERITANCE OF THE HOSTS OF THE NATIONS.** Nor does that passage of Isaiah wander far from this, *Chapter 14:1-2: For Jehovah will have mercy on Jacob, and will again choose the Israelites whom he will replace in their own land—this is the land of Canaan—and the stranger, the proselyte, will join himself to them, and they will associate themselves with the house of Jacob. For the peoples will take them and lead them into their own place—namely, the place of the peoples in which the church shall find its seat—and the house of Israel will claim them for themselves as an inheritance in the* **LAND OF JEHOVAH.** Therefore the *land of the nations* shall become the *land of the Lord* and of the *house of Israel*. Furthermore, those rebels and the disobedient shall be excluded from the possession of such a great thing, destined to perish for the most part in a land loved too carnally, when God shall strike it with a curse. <note>original: "anathemate"</note> We acknowledge these observations as received from the most celebrated Cocceius; <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669) was a famous Dutch theologian known for "Covenant Theology," which interprets the Bible through the lens of various covenants between God and humanity.</note> to wish to deprive him of his due praise is mere spite, the motives for which we keep far from ourselves.

XX. If anyone should object, noting from the Acts of the Apostles how great the peace was in the land of Israel during that time when the Gospel was first preached—and how the Churches grew in all places and enjoyed peace—I respond: neither were the waste places rebuilt then, nor was the abundance of that peace so great that it could strike the nations with astonishment. For that was only a brief respite from evils, which was followed by even heavier troubles after the lapse of a "week" of years <note>A reference to the "seventy weeks" in the prophecy of Daniel</note>. Furthermore, to turn toward allegories and apply what is said here concerning Israel inhabiting its ancient mountains to the Christian Church gathered from the nations—or to that Reformation of the Church which occurred in the age of our fathers—is problematic. For that Reformation could not happen without persecutions, wars, and the overturning of cities and lands, even if peace and the rebuilding of wasted places followed afterward. To turn to such allegories, I say, is—to put it most mildly—to turn a <term>riddle</term> <note>original Hebrew: חידה (chidah)</note> into a <term>proverb or figure of speech</term> <note>original Hebrew: מליצה (melitzah)</note>, and to make an obscure enigma out of a clear and plain discourse without any necessity. Since, therefore, it cannot be shown that these things promised to Israel have been fulfilled for them, and yet the promise of God never fails, we must not be forbidden from expecting this in future times, so that the glory of God's goodness and truth may remain undiminished.
