XXIII. Unless we allow ourselves to be carried away by prejudices, shall we not clearly see the following? 
I. That the discourse continues concerning the same Israel whose history was described in the preceding passages. 
II. That it predicts the closest union of the ten tribes with the tribe of *Judah*, in the unity of both the *Commonwealth* and *Religion*. 
III. That all Israelites, thus united, will acknowledge the *Messiah* as their King, not with the tongue alone, but also with the soul; so that, having abandoned their filth and abominations, they may walk constantly in the ways of the Lord. 
IV. That it will then come to pass that they, with their remote descendants, shall dwell in their own land, and shall have the Divine Goodness present with them, not merely in a symbol, but in actual reality, forever. 
V. That this prophecy has not yet been fulfilled. For although the Israelites lived in their land after the Babylonian captivity under the same senate without a separation of tribes; and although several thousands of them acknowledged the Messiah; nevertheless, the Israelite people did not, with a *national* piety (if I may speak thus), leave behind their filth and acknowledge the Messiah. Instead, *when he came to his own, his own received him not* (John 1:11). And He Himself, when already near death and departing from the temple with a dire warning, said: *you shall by no means see me from this time until you say, "Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord"* (Matthew 23:39). We all agree, unless I am mistaken, that they have not yet said this. Add to this, that not even those of the Israelites who did receive the Messiah remained in the land given to Jacob with their children and grandchildren, nor were they multiplied there; since it is well established that approximately thirty-seven years after the death of Christ, the entire commonwealth of Israel was destroyed by slaughter. 
VI. That there exists no indication in the entire context of the discourse by which we are compelled to abandon the literal sense and flee to allegorical interpretations. 
VII. Consequently, lest anything be taken away from the authority of the sacred discourse, it is a matter of our piety that we should, in silence and hope, await the interpretation of this prophecy through the actual events themselves.

# THE TRIBES OF ISRAEL. CHAPTER XIII.

## C H A P T E R  XIII.

The restoration of Israel is a matter that should not be investigated with excessive curiosity regarding its specific circumstances, nor defined rashly; likewise, it must not be conceived in such a way that it prejudices the Spirituality, Universality, or Liberty of the Kingdom of Christ.

->*I. Regarding the restoration of Israel, we must wait in silence and hope to see what the fates bring forth. II. Let there be neither a curiosity for inquiring nor a rashness in defining. III. Paul places a fastening pin <note>Latin: fibulam; a metaphor for a restraint or closure</note> upon both tendencies when he calls it a Mystery. IV. This restoration of Israel does not prejudice the Spirituality of Christ’s Kingdom. V. Nor its Universality. VI. Nor its Liberty. VII. For in place of a ceremonial constitution <note>original Greek: πολιτείας (politeias); referring to the civil and religious administration of a state</note>, the Kingdom of Heaven shall prevail. VIII. And the Commonwealth of Israel shall be governed by the same or similar laws as the other nations that are subject to Christ’s kingdom. IX. The son of David whom Jeremiah (Chapter 33:17, 21) promises will rule on the throne of Israel is the Messiah. X. The Priests to whom the power of pronouncing judgment in the New Jerusalem is promised by Ezekiel denote the Teachers of the Church; the Prince with his sons denotes godly Magistrates. XI. Ceremonies cannot be restored to the converted Israelites without a denial of the Gospel. XII. XIII. XIV. XV. XVI. The Temple described by Ezekiel is not material, but Mystical. XVII. Likewise, the circumcision is mystical. XVIII. The Priests are mystical. XIX. Why, according to Ezekiel, they are said to be only from the sons of Zadok, while according to Isaiah, they are from all the brothers. XX. The Sacrifices are mystical. XXI. An Epilogue, in which all things are submitted to the judgment of the Church.*<-

AND these are the things which, out of many other prophecies of the most Holy Scriptures—of which there are very many extant in the books of both the Old and New Testaments—it has now been pleasing to give to the Reader for consideration. Indeed, I do so with no other feeling than that I judge it to be in the interest of Divine glory, our own consolation, and the joy of all the godly, that we should not be entirely ignorant of those things which God’s Goodness has predicted He will one day bring to pass. Nevertheless, just as these things are less clear...

# ON THE TEN

...some may seem to be; it is not our place to command faith, which the Spirit of God alone engenders in souls through the humble and gentle meditation on His word. Let us at least wait modestly for what the fates may bring forth; nor should we, by our prejudices or hasty determinations, place any limits on divine destiny. *Neither because this thing is marvelous in our eyes, should we therefore suppose it to be marvelous also in the eyes of God.* <note>original Latin: "Neque quia ea res mirabilis est in oculis nostris, idcirco eam mirabilem quoque esse opinemur in oculis Dei."</note> Zechariah 8:6.

II. Let there be no excessive curiosity in inquiring, nor rashness in defining. Neither let us weary ourselves with questions of this kind: *Whether the conversion of the Israelites, who will then exist in the whole world, will proceed at the same moment in time, or successively? Whether through the ordinary ministers of the Church, or through extraordinary ones, sent immediately for that purpose by God? Whether that multitude of Jews is to be converted before they are led back to Palestine, or led back there before they are converted? Under what leader, under what guidance, is both that conversion and return to be carried out? By which nations, and by what reasoning induced, will passage be granted?* and many more things of this kind which are very easy for anyone to devise. We do not think these questions are proposed with sufficient piety. For what do we believe the Prophets would have answered to the Israelites if they had raised the same difficulties regarding the return from the Assyrian and Babylonian captivity? Would they have allowed that passion for inquiring to pass without indignation and rebuke? Would they not have ordered them to cling to the words of God, to expect the effects of the promise with certain faith, and meanwhile to commit the manner, the means, and other <term>circumstances<note>original Greek: περιστατικὰ (peristatika) – the specific details or surrounding conditions of an event.</note></term> to the Divine Providence to be unfolded? God does not love the overly curious.

III. It is credible that in this final liberation of the Israelite people, it will happen as the sacred songs record happened in the return from Babylon: namely, that it will come upon them as if they were dreaming. Psalm 126:1. And indeed, Paul, as if by a deliberate plan, placed a fastening <note>a "fibula" or clasp, used here metaphorically to restrain curiosity</note> upon our curiosity when he marked the prediction of these things with the name of a *mystery*. Romans 11:25. On which passage there exists a beautiful observation by Calvin, which ought to be sufficient to strike down all those petty questions. *As often*, he says, *as a longer delay casts us into despair, let the name of MYSTERY occur to us: by which Paul clearly warns that the manner of conversion will not be common or usual; and therefore, those who attempt to measure it by their own sense act wrongly.* For what...

# THE TRIBES OF ISRAEL. CHAPTER XIII. 415

For what is more perverse than to consider incredible that which is removed from our own senses? Especially since it is called a "mystery" precisely because it is incomprehensible until the time of its revelation. Furthermore, it has been made open to us, just as it was to the Romans <note>A reference to the Epistle to the Romans, particularly chapters 9-11, where Paul discusses the mystery of Israel's future.</note>, so that our faith, being satisfied with the Word, may sustain us in expectation until the actual result comes forth into the light. This is spoken piously and with gravity.

IV. Nor does this restoration of the Israelite people which we believe in any way prejudice the *Spirituality*, the *Universality*, or the *Freedom* of the Kingdom of Christ. We do not intend to diminish its *Spirituality*. Indeed, we detest with our whole soul those crude imaginations of the carnal Jews and the Millenarians <note>original: "Chiliastarum." Chiliasts or Millenarians believed in a literal 1,000-year earthly reign of Christ, often interpreted with physical or material excess.</note>, who dream of a happiness for themselves similar to a *Muhammadan Paradise* <note>A common 17th-century polemical comparison, likening literalist earthly interpretations of heaven to Islamic descriptions of paradise.</note>, and a Jerusalem made of gold and jewels. We place all the happiness of the true Israel in knowledge, in faith, in Holiness, in communion with God and Christ, and in justice, peace, and joy through the Holy Spirit. To these things may be added that prosperity of this civil life which the Goodness of the Divine power has assigned to the godly, not only in the Old Testament, but also in the New. *Matthew 6:33; 1 Timothy 4:8.*

V. Nor do we take anything away from the *Universality* of the Messiah’s kingdom. For we do not imagine some specific people or land to which the Messiah binds himself by a special covenant, or where he presents himself physically present; but rather, we believe that what John heard being said by great voices in heaven will one day come to pass: *Revelation 11:15.*

> *The kingdoms of the world have become the kingdoms of our Lord and of his Christ, who shall reign forever and ever;*

We do not think the Israelite people should be excluded, as if they too should not be subject to the kingdom of Christ. And just as the whole earth with all its fullness belongs to the Lord, so too that portion of the earth which gave the Lord his birth, which he honored with the Gospel, with Miracles, with his Death and Resurrection, and which he himself walked upon with his own feet—not only in the days of his flesh, but even after he had been raised to heavenly life; and which for so many centuries now, on account of the wickedness of its inhabitants, has been trampled down by enemies and has not belonged to the Lord’s gracious kingdom; that portion of the earth, I say, we expect will one day belong to the Lord no less than the others. Do we do an injustice to the Lord by hoping that where fury and impiety conspired against him, there he might triumph over treachery, so that he might erect the eternal trophies of his victory in the midst of the people and the land of Israel?

Regarding this matter, *I will hear what God, that mighty Lord <note>original: "Jehova"</note>, will speak: for he will speak peace to his people, and to those whom he follows with kindness: but let them not return to folly. VI. Finally, our opinion is not opposed to the Liberty which is right to flourish in the kingdom of Christ. For what prevents that land from being possessed as freely by the free people of God as any other? I do not believe that any natural servitude <note>A legal term for a burden or restriction on property</note> weighs upon that land more than other parts of the world; or that an arbitrary one has been imposed by an eternal and immutable decree. It is memorable that in Ezekiel Chapter 48, the Land is assigned to be distributed to the 12 tribes in a far different manner than it was once distributed to the fathers. *By which we are taught*, as has been learnedly observed by a most celebrated Interpreter, *that those ancient things have passed away, and the land has ceased to be a pledge of future things and of heavenly glory, as it once had been; and therefore the Israelites will not require the boundaries by which the inheritance and field were once given to their fathers.*

VII. And indeed, that servitude which belonged to that land in ancient times consisted chiefly in this: that under that Economy <note>The "Old Covenant" system of religious law</note> it was given to Israel as the seat of a ceremonial polity <note>original: "πολιτείας" (politeias) - meaning a system of civil and religious government</note>. Therefore, when that ceremonial polity ceases, the servitude also ceases. Moreover, we certainly have no doubt that this Polity will cease, and will not be restored forever. In place of that earthly apparatus, by which God once formed a republic for himself—which, because he willed to be its King and Lord in a singular way, was rightly called a Theocracy <note>A government ruled by God</note> by Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, the 1st-century Jewish historian</note>—in place, I say, of that *earthly empire*, by which that nation was distinguished from the other nations of the world, and which, being accommodated to a typical economy, itself also held the character of a type <note>A "type" is a historical person or event that foreshadows a future spiritual reality</note>, there is created by the Messiah a heavenly

VIII. It is neither necessary nor appropriate that, because the Israelite people will one day have a Republic in Palestine, it must be arranged according to the ancient form. Different times demand different customs and different laws. Whatever in the ancient Polity <note>The Greek term *Politeia* refers to the civil administration or form of government.</note> of the Israelites was derived from the principles of natural law remains binding as an eternal necessity. However, whatever was adapted to that specific time at the Legislator's discretion—whether it served the ceremonies or was some part of them—having now fulfilled its role, it will give way in the "time of reformation" <note>A reference to Hebrews 9:10, suggesting a transition from old rituals to spiritual truths.</note> to better statutes worthy of a more joyful liberty. And finally, what is to stop the Israelite people from being governed by the same or similar laws as the other nations who venerate the scepter of Christ?

IX. Jeremiah indeed prophesies concerning this state of affairs in chapter 33:17, 21: *At that time, David shall never lack a man to sit on the throne of the house of Israel, nor shall he lack a son reigning on his throne.* But that son of David is the King Messiah, whose throne and governance are not earthly, but heavenly. Concerning whom Zechariah says in 6:13: *He shall bear the glory, and shall sit and rule on his throne.* And the Angel in Luke 1:32-33: *He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High; and the Lord God will give him the throne of his father David. And he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end.* The Throne of Israel is also the Throne of all nations that are to be gathered to Israel, so that they may complete one mystical Israel. *Ascribe to the Lord, O families of the peoples, ascribe to the Lord glory and praise. Say among the nations, "The Lord reigns."* Psalm 96:7, 10. *Behold, I have appointed him as a witness to the nations,* <note>original Hebrew: נגיד ומצוה לאמים</note> *a Leader and Commander for the nations.* Isaiah 55:4. Besides this King and this Throne, no other is promised to Israel on earth.

Israel is the Church, of which the descendants of the Patriarchs <note>The "Patriarchs" refers to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; the author suggests the Jewish people will eventually become a significant part of the Christian Church.</note> will one day be a part not to be despised. The Priests of Israel are the *Teachers* of the Church, who manage the affairs of God before the Church, and the affairs of the Church before God. To them is committed the judgment over disputes, certainly in matters of *religion and faith*, so that they may instruct the unlearned toward all wisdom and discernment, and demonstrate to the conscience what must be embraced or rejected according to the will of God. This must be done by them according to the *laws*, or *judgments of God*, that is, according to the *Canon of His word*: lest the reason for believing, speaking, or acting be anything other than the declaration of the Divine will through the Scriptures. Moreover, that *Prince* with his *sons* signifies the pious *Magistrates* of the Christian people—such as the converted Israelites shall also have—under whom they shall live not as if under rigid masters, but as if under fathers or brothers, who have their own portion in the common inheritance, and who protect and assist the Church.

XI. Much less do we believe that the old *ceremonies* will be restored to the Israelites when they have been converted and returned to their land. For, as has been demonstrated more extensively by us elsewhere, there is in the ceremonies a *yoke*, which in the time of liberty ought to be broken. There is a *pedagogy* <note>original: "paedagogia"; referring to the Galatians 3:24 concept of the Law acting as a schoolmaster or tutor until Christ arrived.</note>, and a reproach of childhood, which can have no place in an adult age. There is a *partition wall* <note>original: "septum parietis intergerini"; a reference to Ephesians 2:14, the barrier between Jews and Gentiles.</note>, to be broken down when, all distinction of nations having been removed, the Messiah is to be all in all. There is an enmity, to be abolished at that time when the Messiah is to announce *peace* to the nations, as much with Israel as with God. Finally, there is a *Handwritten Bond* <note>original: "Chirographum"; a legal document or debt-record, here referring to the Mosaic Law's requirements.</note>, convicting one of a guilt not yet expiated and a payment not yet performed; which, all things having been fulfilled by the Messiah, and a *receipt* <note>original: "apocha"; a formal discharge of debt.</note> having been granted to Him in the resurrection, must be taken out of the way, lest any institution of God be found to testify against the truth and the Son of God.

But all the circumstances cry out that this is not to be understood as a material Temple, such as was the house built by Solomon. For a material temple must be in the tribe of *Judah*, in the city of *Jerusalem*, and on Mount *Zion*. There exist the words of God by which He declares

XIV. Furthermore, Ezekiel saw the *glory of God* entering into this temple in a far different manner than it had previously come into the temple of Solomon. In the former case, *God descended into the Sanctuary in the appearance of a cloud, which filled the temple as the priests were departing from the holy place. 1 Kings 8:10-11.* <note>original: "1 Reg. VIII: 10. 11."</note> Here, however, the glory of the God of Israel came *by the eastern way, by the way of the gate that looks toward the east: its sound was like the sound of many waters, and the earth shone with His glory. The appearance of the vision was exactly like that vision which he had seen when prophesying about the city being destroyed, and like those visions which he had seen at the river Chebar. Ezekiel 43:2-5.* <note>original: "Ezech. XLIII: 2. 3. 4. 5."</note> Moreover, the form which he had seen at the river Chebar was the appearance of a man sitting upon a Throne, above the Cherubim. Chapters 1:26; 10:1, 18-20. Clearly, the glory of the mystical temple is not a symbolic cloud, but *God manifested in the flesh*. He enters through the eastern gate, just as John saw the *Angel ascending from the rising of the sun, and having the seal of the living God. Revelation 7:2.* <note>original: "Apoc. VII: 2."</note> This is because the kingdom was first founded in the East, and from there, by the power of the Most Holy Spirit, it spread itself to the West and to the islands of the sea. *The voice of the one coming was like the sound of many waters.* For He comes with the preaching of the Gospel, and with the speech of many men concerning it, frequented throughout the whole world. Compare Revelation 1:15. *The light of glory from which the whole earth shone* is contrasted with the darkness of the cloud in which God formerly dwelt; it denotes the splendor of Evangelical wisdom, and the joy and consolation of the Church spread most widely. Compare Luke 2:32; Isaiah 49:6.

XV. Add to this what has been noticed by the Jews themselves: that Ezekiel gives *new ordinances concerning the feasts*, and as it were, a new law different from the Mosaic one. Chapters 45:17–25; 46:4–7. Hence, those who cling to the literal letter torment themselves miserably, since it is well known to be a sacrilege for anything to be added to or taken away from the Mosaic Law. But whatever they may devise, they are in vain unless they think of the new year of grace, whose sacrifices and exercises of piety are different from those of the old: they are all spiritual. Of these things, those ancient rites were indeed shadows; nevertheless, lest the reality itself be confused with the shadows, different emblems were represented to Ezekiel for that purpose.

It tells of *waters issuing from the lower part of the threshold of the house toward the East, and descending from the right side of the house from the Southern part of the altar,* and how the further *they proceeded toward the East, the deeper they became, until they grew into a torrent that could not be crossed on foot,* and other things that follow on this matter. In the meantime, while we wait for more certain interpretations, let it be permitted that through those waters the *doctrine of the Gospel* is designated, teeming with the Divine Spirit, and indeed the Spirit himself especially, with his various <term>charismata<note>original Greek: χαρίσμασι; spiritual gifts or graces bestowed by God.</note></term>. Moreover, that they proceed *from the threshold of the house*—the function of which is to steady the posts and provide passage for those entering—signifies they come from God himself, from whom all the firmness of the Church is derived, and who gives us entrance to his house in Christ. Furthermore, that these waters *flow toward the Rising Sun <note>The East</note>*, is different than in the past, and follows a backward flow. At the beginning of the Gospel, the word proceeded with the Spirit from the East toward the West, as we just observed. But in the process of time, it was to be otherwise, so that from the *West the word of God is poured back into the East. So that they may fear the name of Jehovah from the West, and his glory from the rising of the sun.* Isaiah 59:19. Truly, the Church of the New Testament, having been led from the *East to the West*, just as it received with its whole soul the word which came from the East; so also it will open the door to those who are in the East, that is, the *Jews*, whose conversion it desires and strives for with earnest prayers to God. As for what is added concerning the *Southern part of the Altar*, let it be permitted to remain unknown for now; unless one wishes to suspect, along with a most skillful interpreter, that it refers to *Africa*, where through *Augustine* and his disciples a vein of salutary words was opened, namely the doctrine of grace. *The increase of the waters into a torrent that could not be crossed;* what else does it denote but the exuberance of the sacred word, until *the earth is filled with the knowledge of Jehovah, just as the waters cover the channels of the sea.* Isaiah 11:9. The rest I commend to the meditations of the pious and diligent reader. Surely, of whatever nature these waters are, such must the Temple be. Nothing material. *All things are mystical.*

This will be made clear to the attentive reader. I find that circumcision—not only of the heart, but also of the flesh—is required of him who shall be permitted to enter into the Sanctuary. Ezekiel 44:9:
> *No foreigner, uncircumcised in heart and uncircumcised in flesh, shall enter my sanctuary.* <note>original: "Ullus alienigena, præputiatus carne, non venito in Sanctuarium meum."</note>

Furthermore, since this discourse is not concerning Israelites converted to the Messiah, but concerning foreigners, for whom there will also be a place in this New Temple (Isaiah 56:6-7), and since no necessity of circumcision can be imposed upon them <note>The author argues that since New Testament believers are not bound by the ritual law of circumcision, the "fleshly" requirement must be symbolic.</note>; it follows that a different circumcision must be understood here than that which God once gave to Abraham as a seal of his covenant. But, you say, he desires the foreskin to be absent not only from the heart but also from the flesh. Correct, I say. *Foreskin* <term>præputium: literally the foreskin, but used here as a metaphor for spiritual blockage or impurity</term> denotes any moral impurity and the depraved disposition of man. Moreover, that impurity is either of the flesh or of the *spirit*, according to Paul’s distinction in 2 Corinthians 7:1; that is, either of *external actions* which are carried out by the members of the body, or of the *mind* and interior affections. Hence we also read of the *uncircumcised lips* in Exodus 6:11 and *ears* in Jeremiah 6:10 and Acts 7:51. Ezekiel teaches that both types of impurity must be laid aside by him who shall be counted among the communion of the people of God. It is exactly as the Psalmist says in Psalm 24:3-4:
> *Who shall ascend the mountain of Jehovah, and who shall stand in his Holy place? He who is innocent in hands, and pure in soul.*

XVIII. I find mention of the Levitical Priests. Jeremiah 33:18: *Neither shall the priests, the Levites, lack a man before me to offer burnt offerings.* v. 21: *My covenant with David my servant shall not be broken, nor with the Levites, the priests, my ministers.* v. 22: *So will I multiply the seed of David my servant, and the Levites who minister to me.* But that which is predicted concerning the Priests is sometimes so narrowed, and sometimes so expanded, that neither can be consistent with the Levitical Priesthood as it was instituted by Moses. In Ezekiel’s temple, the priesthood is given only to the sons of Zadok <note>Zadok was a high priest during the reigns of David and Solomon; his descendants were seen as the only "legitimate" priestly line in certain prophetic visions.</note>, Ezekiel 40:45, 43:19, 44:15. If this is to be understood literally, the remaining families of the descendants of Aaron, however religious they might be, would be excluded from the right given to them by the law of Moses. On the other hand, Isaiah 66:21 predicts that God will take even from those who are neither Priests nor Levites and appoint them as Priests and Levites. These things cannot be reconciled at all if the letter of the Law is to be held. What then? Priests denote the *Leaders* <term>Antecessores: those who go before or lead the way</term> of the Church, going before their brothers in the public ministry of the word and of prayers.

XX. From such imaginations, we recoil with our whole soul.

## SUMMARY.

I. *Jesus asserted Divine Truth through the stupendous wonders of his teaching.* II. *And he imbued his followers with the power of performing similar, or even greater, deeds.* III. IV. *Which power flourished in the Church throughout the course of several centuries.* V. *The history of the miracle by which, during the reign of Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, the Roman army is said to have been saved at the prayers of Christian soldiers.* VI. *Many points are brought forward to establish the credibility of this history. And first, indeed, the name of "Thundering" bestowed upon that Legion.* VII. *Then, the letters of the Emperor to the Senate regarding that matter.* VIII. *Of which a copy is displayed.* IX. *Furthermore, the Edict of the Emperor in favor of the Christians.* X. *Which is believed to have still been in force under the reign of Commodus.* XI. *Added to this is a fragment of Ulpian <note>Domitius Ulpianus, a famous Roman jurist</note>, which Alciatus <note>Andrea Alciato, a Renaissance legal scholar</note> argues pertains to the Christians.* XII. *Gentile <note>Pagan or non-Christian</note> historians do not indeed conceal that the event took place: but they attribute it neither to the Christians, nor to the God of the Christians.* XIII. *And it deserves to be investigated whether the arguments just praised are sufficiently firm. For in the age of Augustus, the Twelfth Legion was already called "Thunder-bearing."* XIV. *Moreover, men of the greatest learning have proved that the letter attributed to the Emperor is a forgery <note>original: "νοθείας" (notheias) - meaning spurious or illegitimate</note>.* XV. *Nor was it long after the German thirst was quenched that there was cruel raging against the Christians.* XVI. *To this point—*

# DISCOURSE ON THE LEGION

*The column of* Marcus <note>The Column of Marcus Aurelius in Rome</note> *stands carved with victories, representing the image of* Jupiter the Rain-maker, *not the God of the Christians.* XVII. *That which* Eusebius <note>An early Christian historian</note> *narrates to have happened under* Commodus *does not seem to pertain to any edict of* Marcus. XVIII. *Less so that which is brought forward from* Ulpian <note>A famous Roman jurist</note>. XIX. *Our* Judgment <note>original: "Ἐπίκρισις" (Epikrisis) - a critical assessment or determination</note>: *The history is true, but the arguments brought forward are not equally valid.* XX. XXI. XXII. *It is everywhere confessed that* Marcus *was saved with his army by a prodigious force of rain falling upon his own men and lightning hurled against the enemy; all historians of those times agree on this.* XXIII. *The* Pagans <note>original: "Gentiles"</note> *claim this for* Jupiter the Rain-maker. XXIV. *But we know it is owed to* Jehovah. XXV. *He sends not only raining showers to refresh friends, but also those which destroy enemies.* XXVI. *He likewise moderates the fates of both wars and Empires.* XXVII. *And he has more than once routed enemies with wind and lightning.* XXVIII. *Finally, what was wickedly imputed to* Jupiter the Rain-maker *on the column of* Marcus, *He openly claimed for Himself by His admirable providence.* XXIX. *The trifles that* Claudian, Dio, *and* Lampridius <note>Ancient Roman authors</note> *babble regarding* Magic *arts in this business are ridiculous.* XXX. *For* Magic *is not an art, but the mockery of every vain person.* XXXI. *At least, that it has no power over storms and lightning is argued with false witticisms by* Seneca. XXXII. *And the matter speaks for itself: for if* Magic *is worth anything, why did so many adversities befall those Kings and Emperors who were themselves* Initiates <note>original: "Epoptae" - those who have seen the secret rites</note> *of the art and led around the most celebrated practitioners?* XXXIII. *Why did* Magic *not also destroy the* Christian *name, which was so hostile to it?* XXXIV. *Why was it forced to yield to* Christianity? XXXV. *As shown by* eyewitness evidence <note>original: "αὐτοψίᾳ" (autopsia)</note>. XXXVI. *And with the* Christians *surrendering themselves to punishment, unless the evidence of the fact proved this testimony of theirs.* XXXVII. *Therefore, away with those follies concerning magic incantations.* XXXVIII. *Especially since* Marcus *himself protested that he detested that race of men, in that book which he wrote during this very expedition among the* Quadi <note>A Germanic tribe</note> *at the* Granua <note>The Hron river in modern Slovakia</note>. XXXIX. *It is more true that this rain and these lightning bolts were obtained by the holy prayers of pious men.* XL. *But who are they? Not* Marcus, *whatever* Claudian *may flatter, or* Marcus *may boast elsewhere of his own piety.* XLI. *But the* Christian *soldiers.* XLII. XLIII. XLIV. XLV. *That the* Ancient Christians *also served as soldiers...*

# THE THUNDERING LEGION OF THE CHRISTIANS.

*The presence of Christians in the army before the Emperors embraced Christianity is confirmed by many arguments. XLVI. XLVII. Nor is it far from the truth to suggest that some Legion was composed entirely, or for the most part, of Christians. XLVIII. The Theban Legion <note>A famous legion of Christian soldiers said to have been martyred under Diocletian for refusing to sacrifice to Roman gods.</note>, under Diocletian, was entirely Christian. XLIX. Christian soldiers fought with weapons as soldiers, and with prayers as Christians. L. Nor did they cease to pray for their persecutors. LI. This is a point that Athenagoras <note>A 2nd-century Christian apologist who wrote to Marcus Aurelius.</note> also impressed upon our Marcus. LII. There is, moreover, a certain omnipotence in such prayers. LIII. LIV. LV. This is proven by three histories which have a great affinity with our own. LVI. But a fourth example is added, somewhat more marvelous than all the others. LVII. II. The Lord Jesus granted the power to perform similar, or even greater miracles—though in his name—to those whom he had designated as witnesses of his deeds and teachers of heavenly discipline after his ascension into heaven. And so that this miraculous power might spread more widely, he promised the same to those who would put their faith in the Apostolic instruction. For he himself said: *Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do; and greater works than these will he do.* John 14:12. See also Mark 16:15-18 and 1 Corinthians 12:9-11.

III. Nor was this power active for only a few years, or restricted to certain geographical boundaries; rather, wherever the world lies open and the doctrine of faith was published, it exerted itself firmly for several centuries. This continued until God willed us to be content with the secret sealing of the Spirit and the Gospel having been sufficiently confirmed by so many proofs of Divinity. For among the ancient leaders of the Christian cause, <note>original Greek: ὁ κηρύσσων τοῖς λόγοις ἐλευθερίαν ἐπιστοῖ τοῖς πράγμασι τὴν ἐπαγγελίαν</note> "the one who proclaims freedom with words confirms the promise with deeds." *There were, as Augustine rightly judged, miracles necessary before the world believed, for the purpose of making the world believe:* <note>original Greek: ἵνα, οὓς οὐκ ἔπεισε κηρύττουσα γλῶσσα, τούτους ὀφθαλμοὶ ἐλέγξωσι μαρτυροῦντες</note> *so that those whom the proclamation of the tongue had not persuaded might be convinced by the testimony of their eyes;* as Basil of Seleucia <note>A 5th-century bishop and ecclesiastical writer</note> elegantly stated. The testimonies of Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, Tertullian, Origen, Cyprian, Lactantius, and others—who frequently appeal to the miracles still common in their own times—are famous and well-known to the learned. See, if you please, Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius, the influential Dutch jurist and theologian</note> on Mark 16:17-18.

IV. Let one testimony of Irenaeus now suffice for us, which Eusebius presents in his *Church History, Book 5, Chapter 7.* "Wherefore his true disciples, in his name, through the grace received from him, perform such things for the benefit of the rest of men, according as each of them has received the gift from him. *For some certainly and truly drive out demons, so that not infrequently those who have been cleansed of evil and wicked spirits then receive the faith and persevere constantly in the Church and the society of faithful men. Some [possess] foreknowledge of divine matters, by divine vision...*"

# THE THUNDERING LEGION OF THE CHRISTIANS

...and are imbued with prophetic foresight. Others cure those afflicted by heavy diseases through the laying on of hands, and restore them to their former health. Indeed, even the dead have been raised, and remained among us for many years afterward. In another place, the same Irenaeus <note>Irenaeus (c. 130–202 AD) was a Greek bishop known for his writings against heresy.</note>, as cited there by Eusebius: We ourselves have heard many brothers in the Church who possess the gifts of Prophecy, and who speak in various languages through the grace of the Holy Spirit, and bring the hidden things of men into the open for the benefit of others, and explain the mysteries of God clearly and evidently. In the Council of Nicaea <note>The first ecumenical council of the Christian Church, held in 325 AD.</note>, many Bishops renowned for miracles appeared. Paphnutius, Bishop of the Thebaid <note>A region in Upper Egypt.</note>, who is said to have been scarcely inferior to the Apostles. *Rufinus, Book 1, chapter 4. Jacob of Nisibis, Theodoret, Book 1, chapter 7. Spiridion, Rufinus, Book 1, chapter 5.* Regarding the age of *Augustine* and *Chrysostom*, see *Montagu, preface to the Historical Collections, page b. 3. v.*

V. Among the other miracles by which the truth of Christianity has been asserted, that one is especially memorable which is said to have occurred at the prayers of Christian soldiers under the Emperor MARCUS AURELIUS ANTONINUS. The history of this matter is reported as follows. The Emperor *Antoninus*, entangled in a fierce war with the *Quadi* (these were a people of Germany), was so hemmed in by the difficulties of the terrain that he and his entire army were in extreme danger. He and his men suffered from a severe lack of water under a burning sun and on parched soil, laboring under a cruel thirst, while the enemy meanwhile offered no opportunity for battle. Stripped of all his plans, he expected the very worst. At this critical turning point, the prefect of the Praetorian Guard approached him, reminding him that there was in the army the MELITENE LEGION <note>Also known as Legio XII Fulminata (the Thundering 12th Legion).</note> consisting of Christian soldiers; and that there was nothing which those called Christians could not obtain by their prayers. Having learned this, they say Marcus requested of them that they should supplicate their God. Therefore, when they had placed their knees upon the ground and turned themselves entirely to prayer, suddenly a rush of lightning fell from heaven, along with hail in the form and likeness of fire, which turned the enemy to flight and killed a great part of them; meanwhile, an entirely unexpected abundance of very cold rain refreshed the Romans who were exhausted by thirst. This is mentioned by *Tertullian in the Apology, Chapter 5, and To Scapula, chapter 4. From the same author, and from Apollinaris, Eusebius in the Church History, Book 5, chapter 5, and the Chronicle, Book 1. Nicephorus Callistus, Book 4, chapter 12. Zonaras, Annals, Volume 2. Xiphilinus's Epitome of Dio.*

*Dio in his account of Marcus. Orosius, History, Book VII, chapter 15, and others.*

**VI.** Since this history is not undeservedly seen as being of the greatest importance to Christian affairs, many arguments have been gathered by various authors to establish its credibility. Great emphasis is placed on the name <term>Keraunobolos</term> <note>Greek: ΚΕΡΑΥΝΟΒΟΛΟΥ</note>, or **THUNDERING** <note>Latin: Fulminatrix</note>, bestowed upon that legion from that time onward in memory of this miracle. Apollinarius, quoted in *Eusebius*, states: *From that time, the legion which had performed the miracle through prayer received from the Emperor a title appropriate to the event, being called the "Thundering" in the Roman tongue.* <note>original Greek: Ἐξ ἐκείνου τὴν δι’ εὐχῆς τὸ παράδοξον πεποιηκυῖαν λεγεῶνα... ΚΕΡΑΥΝΟΒΟΛΟΝ</note> From that time, the legion by whose prayers the miracle was produced was called the **THUNDERING** in the Latin language by the Emperor, a name which skillfully expresses the outcome of the event. Xiphilinus likewise writes: *The unit of soldiers specifically called the THUNDERING... for no other cause (for no other is mentioned) than from what happened during this war was it so named.* <note>original Greek: τὸ τάγμα τῶν στρατιωτῶν τὸ ΚΕΡΑΥΝΟΒΟΛΟΝ ἰδίως καλούμενον</note> Zonaras writes in a similar fashion.

**VII.** Appeal is also made to the **LETTERS** of the Emperor, by which he informed the Senate and the Roman people of such a great matter, not without notable praise for the Christians. *Tertullian, in his Apology: But we, on the contrary, produce a protector: if the LETTERS of Marcus Aurelius, that most grave Emperor, be sought, in which he bears witness that the Germanic thirst was dispelled by rain obtained through the prayers of Christian soldiers.* *Orosius* adds: *There exist even now among many people the letters of the Emperor Antoninus, where he confesses that by the invocation of the name of Christ by Christians, both that thirst was driven away and victory was granted.* Indeed, a transcript or copy of those letters exists at the end of the *Second Apology* of *Justin Martyr*. Lest the reader lack it, I shall present it here.

**VIII.** *The Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Antoninus (the Philosopher), Germanicus, Parthicus, Sarmaticus, sends greetings to the Roman people and the sacred Senate. I have informed you of the magnitude of my plan and undertaking. Beyond measure, heavy hardships followed in Germany; we were in danger and struggling at the border, and were hemmed in at the ninth milestone by seventy-four <term>dracones</term> <note>Standard-bearers or military units named after the dragon standards</note> in the territory of the Cotini. -># THE THUNDERING LEGION OF THE CHRISTIANS<-

The scouts indicated to us that the enemy were not far off; and likewise Pompeianus <note>Tiberius Claudius Pompeianus, a high-ranking general and son-in-law to Marcus Aurelius</note>, the prefect of our military forces, signaled those things which were already known to us. I was being overwhelmed by a vast multitude, though I had with me the chosen forces of the First, Tenth, and Twin <note>original: "Geminæ"</note> legions, as well as the Light-Armed <note>original: "Ferentariorum"</note> and Mixed troops. When it was reported that an army from a gathered mob of nine hundred and seventy-seven thousand was present, I began to examine my own strength and calculate the number of my troops. Comparing them with the multitude of Barbarians and enemies, I turned to making prayers to my ancestral gods through divine ritual. However, being neglected by them and seeing my strength reduced to a narrow strait, I summoned those among us called CHRISTIANS. Upon inquiry, I found a great number of them, and I raged against them quite sharply. This was something I should not have done at all, because of the virtue I later discovered to be in them. For they begin the fight not by the preparation of weapons and armor, nor by the blast of trumpets—for such things are displeasing to them because of the God whom they carry in their conscience. Therefore, it is only fair that those whom we suspected to be atheists <note>original: "αθεος" (atheos) - those without gods</note> and estranged from God, we should now recognize as having a God who has entered their conscience of His own accord and remains there. For casting themselves upon the ground, they prayed not only for me, but for the entire army then present, so that they might be a comfort to us in our current hunger and thirst; for we had not taken water for five days, as it had failed us. For we were in the heart of Germany and within the borders of the enemy. As soon as they had prostrated themselves on the earth and invoked a God whom I did not know, water immediately followed from heaven—for us it was most cool, but upon the Romans' looming enemies, it was a fiery hail. Indeed, with that prayer, the presence of God was immediately there, as one insurmountable and invincible. Starting from that point, therefore, we shall permit these people to be Christians, lest they seek that same kind of weapon against us and obtain their wish.

If anyone is found to report a Christian simply because they are a Christian, and that Christian who has confessed is found to be accused of no other crime than being a Christian, I desire that the Christian be allowed to conduct themselves openly; however, I will that the informer himself be burned alive. Furthermore, the official to whom the prefecture of the province is entrusted shall not force a self-confessed Christian—who is therefore safe and secure under that name—to repent of such a profession or reduce them to an ignoble status. Verasius Pollio, the Prefect, shall also see to it that it is sent to other provinces. Anyone who wishes to use this edict and have a copy of it shall not be prohibited from receiving it from that which has been posted by us.

X. That this edict remained in force during the times of Commodus, his son and successor, seems to be shown by the punishment of a certain servant. This servant, because he had accused the Senator Apollonius of the crime of Christianity without charging him with any other offense, had his legs broken in Rome by the sentence of the judge Perennius: as reported by Eusebius in *History*, Book 5, chapter 21.

XI. To the same effect is a reference by Ulpian the Jurist <note>Ulpian was a famous Roman legal authority whose writings make up a large part of the Digest of Justinian</note>, who was otherwise a bitter enemy of the Christians. In Book 3, at the end of the section *On Decurions*: *To those who follow the Jewish superstition, the Divine* VERUS AND ANTONINUS *permitted the attainment of honors; but they also imposed duties upon them which would not offend their superstitions.* The celebrated interpreter of law, Alciatus, argues that these words should be understood as referring to Christians, asserting that this sanction was published after the victory over the Marcomanni <note>A Germanic tribal confederation</note> received through the benefit of the Christians. *Dispunct: Book 3, chapter 8.* And reason favors this view. For it is better known to the learned than needs to be proven that Christians often passed under the name of *Jews* among the gentiles, since they originated from the Jews. Furthermore, Tacitus, Pliny, and Suetonius frequently called the Christian religion a *Superstition*. An inscribed stone is seen in Rome, dedicated to Nero: FOR PURGING THE PROVINCE OF ROBBERS AND OF THOSE WHO WERE INCULCATING A NEW SUPERSTITION UPON THE HUMAN RACE. There is little doubt that these words refer to Christianity. Nor does it seem possible to reconcile this sanction in any more convenient way with other laws by which all access to honors is closed to Jews properly so-called.

# THE THUNDERING LEGION OF THE CHRISTIANS

XII. Nevertheless, the Gentile *Historians* <note>Non-Christian or "Pagan" writers of antiquity.</note> take an entirely different view. Although they neither deny the event took place nor entirely conceal it, they do not attribute it to the *God of the Christians*. Instead, they credit their own *Jupiter Pluvius* <note>Jupiter the Rain-bringer.</note>. They claim the relief came not through the prayers of the *Melitene Legion*, but either through the incantations of *Arnuphis*, an *Egyptian Magician* who was present with *Marcus* <note>Emperor Marcus Aurelius.</note>—as *Dio* <note>Dio Cassius, a Roman historian.</note> would have us believe—or, as others cited in *Suidas* <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia.</note> claim, by the tricks of a certain *Julian*. Others still, such as *Julius Capitolinus* and *Claudianus*, ascribe it to the prayers and merits of *Marcus* himself.

XIII. Nor do the arguments we just brought forward in favor of the *Christians* seem so strong that they leave no room for more skeptical minds to argue or doubt. Experts will not easily grant that no *Thundering Legion* was known to the *Romans* before that time, or that this specific miracle gave rise to that nickname. It is well-established from *Dio* and ancient inscriptions that as far back as the age of *Augustus*, the *Twelfth Legion* was already called by that same title. On this matter, one may consult *Scaliger* in his *Notes on Eusebius* (at number 2188), *Lipsius* in his *Gleanings on the Roman Military* (Book II, Dialogue 5), and *Baronius* (for the year 176, sections 18 and 19). By this observation, the edge of our first argument is considerably dulled.

XIV. Furthermore, regarding that *Letter* <note>A famous letter purportedly written by Marcus Aurelius to the Senate praising the Christians.</note> which is read at the end of the second *Apology* of *Justin*: in the judgment of *Scaliger*, supported by *Salmasius* and not denied by *Huetius*—and what great men these are!—it is so far from being dictated in Greek by the Emperor himself, or translated from his Latin into Greek, that it clearly appears to have been forged by some "Greekling" <note>original: "Græculo" - a diminutive, often derogatory term for a Greek person, implying a lack of Roman gravitas.</note> utterly ignorant of Roman affairs, sometime after the reign of the Emperor *Justinian*.

<margin>*Eusebius, Church History, Book 5, Chapter 1.*</margin>
XV. Moreover, who can believe that such an *Edict* in favor of the *Christians* was sanctioned on that occasion (in the 14th year of *Marcus*, to which the *Quadic War* <note>A conflict between Rome and the Germanic Quadi tribe.</note> is dated)? Anyone would doubt this who knows that not only before, but also shortly after that "Germanic thirst" was so miraculously quenched—specifically in the 17th year of *Marcus*—a countless multitude of *Christians* were subjected to dreadful interrogations, and *Christians* everywhere were most bitterly harassed by a massive persecution.

# DISCOURSE ON THE LEGION

It can be gathered that a column still stands today, carved with the victories of Marcus <note>Emperor Marcus Aurelius, reigned 161–180 AD</note>, upon which is seen a depicted image of this most remarkably accomplished deed. However, it is shown with such symbols that it represents the likeness of Jupiter sending down rain and mixing lightning bolts with them; Baronius <note>Cesare Baronius, a 16th-century Cardinal and church historian</note> provides a graphic engraving of this from the column. But in my opinion, Casalius presents it more accurately. Compare the *Vatican Library of Angelo Rocca, page 288*. Now, if the Emperor publicly declared with such a notable monument that he owed that victory to "Jupiter the Rain-Giver," how could he have ordered an Edict to be posted in the Forum in which Christians—the sworn enemies of Jupiter—were honored for that very reason?

XVII. Furthermore, the punishment of that slave—who suffered the breaking of his legs during the time of Commodus <note>Son and successor of Marcus Aurelius</note> for accusing his master, Apollonius, of being a Christian—does not sufficiently confirm this edict. For the type of punishment does not match (since the edict, at least if we are to believe that alleged letter, mandates burning alive, whereas this history speaks of leg-breaking); moreover, Apollonius himself, being guilty of Christianity, was condemned to death by a decree of the Senate. Of what use, then, was the Edict of Marcus to that Christian?

XVIII. Finally, one might rightly doubt whether the passage cited from *Ulpian* <note>A famous Roman jurist</note> pertains to this matter at all. For it is a <term>very great leap of logic<note>original Greek: μέγα λίαν αἴτημα</note></term> to interpret "Jewish superstition" as the Christian religion; and it is doubtful whether the "Antoninus" mentioned there is our specific Emperor. Even if all these things were certain, it remains uncertain whether this rescript <note>A formal imperial response to a legal query</note>, such as it was, emanated from the Emperors on the occasion of this miracle. Indeed, as observed by Baronius, the chronological evidence is entirely contradictory. For this reason, the interpretation by Alciatus, though rashly seized upon by others, is rejected by Antonio Agustín in his singular book on Modestinus.

XIX. Since these matters are argued with some probability on both sides, I believe I shall perform a service not unwelcome to scholars if I set forth what should be determined as the truth, and support it with firm arguments as far as the nature of the task allows. And this indeed is my opinion: this history contributes too much to the glory of Jesus Christ, our Lord and God, and too much to the honor of the Christian people, for a pious man knowledgeable in these affairs not to labor in its defense. It rests upon supports too firm for the fabrications of the pagans to be equal to tearing it down.

# THE THUNDERING LEGION OF THE CHRISTIANS

[The previous arguments] may be true: nevertheless, we must not seize upon everything without examination <note>original: "ἀβασανίστως" (without testing/trial)</note> and without discrimination, even those things produced by men who are otherwise most learned, perhaps out of an unconsidered zeal for the truth. It is now my intention to pursue these individual points more extensively.

XX. And first, I take it as certain and confessed that *Marcus* [Aurelius], along with his army, was rescued from imminent destruction by a sudden abundance of falling rain upon his own men, and by the force of lightning bolts routing the enemies. For, as *Eusebius* well observed, even to those "historians from the outside, being strangers to our faith, this marvel has been recorded" <note>original Greek: "τοῖς ἔξωθεν ἱστορικοῖς, ἅτε τῆς πίστεως ἀνοικείοις, τέθειται τοῦτο τὸ παράδοξον"</note>; this miracle was mentioned by historians of that age, although they were alienated from our faith: though they were ignorant of its true cause, or wickedly disguised it, they interpreted it in another direction.

XXI. *Julius Capitolinus* <note>A writer of the Augustan History</note> hints at this rather than fully explaining it: *He drew down lightning from heaven by his prayers against the engine of the enemy, while rain was obtained for his own men when they were suffering from thirst.* *Claudianus*, a Pagan Poet, in his poem on the sixth consulship of *Honorius* (Book I), sang of it elegantly and poetically, yet truly:

# THE THUNDERING POWER OF THE CHRISTIANS.

Macrobius says that the force of this oracle—the interpretation of the deity and the name by which Father Liber <note>A Roman name for Bacchus/Dionysus</note> and the Sun are signified as *IAO* <note>original: "IAΩ"; a Greek transliteration of the Hebrew Divine Name</note>—was followed by Cornelius Labeo in the book titled *On the Oracle of the Clarian Apollo*. Nor is it only over wars, upon which the fates of empires depend, that Jehovah presides; He often routs the enemy with those very weapons <note>Referring to the elements/weather as weapons</note> which we are now discussing. He did this in ancient times. When the five Kings of the Philistines <note>The Amorite coalition</note> had conspired against Joshua, He cast down great stones of hail from heaven, by which more were slain than by the weapons of the pursuing Israelites. *Joshua 10:11.* This is what the Psalmist sings: *Psalm 11:6. Jehovah shall rain down upon the wicked coals, fire and sulfur: and a most stormy wind shall be the portion of their cup.* And again, *Psalm 18:13-14. With Jehovah thundering in the heavens, and the Most High uttering His voice, hail and fiery coals come forth: Thus sending out His arrows He scatters them: and hurling lightnings He puts them to flight.* He threatens to do the same against the forces of Gog: *Ezekiel 38:22-23. I will contend with him by pestilence and slaughter; and an overflowing rain, and stones of immense hail, fire and sulfur will I rain upon him, and upon his troops, and upon the many peoples who shall be with him. Thus will I magnify myself, and sanctify myself, and make myself known in the eyes of many nations, so that it may be known that I am Jehovah.*

XXVIII. And lest we wander too far from our purpose, our God has reclaimed for Himself the glory of this very miracle <note>The miracle of the rain for the Melitene Legion</note>, which by a wicked and sacrilegious daring was attributed to "Jupiter the Rain-Maker" <note>Latin: Jovi Pluvio</note>. He acted through His adorable providence so that such a famous monument to the Christian faith, which we mentioned in Section 16, might survive after so many centuries for the conviction of others. Yet, because it had been obscured and defiled by pagan superstition, He formerly saw to it that it was burned from its lowest parts by barbarian fury, while He Himself struck it from above with a lightning bolt: justly avenging that sacrilege by which insane Heathendom had attempted to attribute a victory given by lightning to their own Jupiter. See *Baronius <note>Cesare Baronius, the 16th-century ecclesiastical historian</note> at the Year 176, Section 28.* Therefore, the glory of so great a miracle remains entirely with Jehovah our God.

Clement of Alexandria <note>A prominent Christian theologian of the 2nd century</note> also touches upon the laws of the Twelve Tables <note>The ancient foundation of Roman law</note>, which provide a warning *that no one should enchant another’s crops* <note>original Latin: "ne quis alienos fructus excantassit"</note>. XXXII. But let us grant that magi do not always deceive with their illusions; let us grant that they have some power in summoning rain, hail, and lightning. No one, I think, will demand such a senseless mind from us that we should believe the outcomes of wars, or the fates of Emperors and empires—which are the subjects at hand—depend upon the songs of sorcerers. If that were the case, what probable reason can be given why all things did not turn out favorably and prosperously in empire and war for the Kings of Egypt and the rest of the East, or for Tiberius, Nero, Hadrian, Caracalla, Julian, and other Roman Emperors? For these men were either themselves initiates <term>Epoptae: those fully initiated into secret mysteries</term> of the secret arts, or at least kept with them the most skilled masters of that craft, who were obedient to every duty both because of the Emperors' authority and the hope of vast rewards.

XXXIII. Why did magic not primarily ensure that the name of the Christians—so hostile to its own honor and efficacy—should utterly perish? Why do these "divine" men not at least procure for themselves those riches and dignities which they are proven to pant after with breathless greed, even while they serve others in such great matters?

# DISCOURSE ON THE LEGION

XXXVII. Since, therefore, all Magic consists of the *tricks* of traveling performers and the mockeries of empty minds; since the wisest of the Philosophers have denied it any power over *rain, hail, and lightning*; since even when it was most highly cultivated, it could never control the uncertain dice of war nor the fortunes of empires; and since, finally, whatever power it might have possessed *in the past*, it has lost most of its efficacy through the Gospel of Christ: who would believe that the magical incantations of some unknown Chaldean <note>The author refers to Julianus the Chaldean, to whom pagan sources attributed the miracle.</note> could have caused a cold rain to fall on the Romans and a fiery one on their enemies at the same moment, unless that person were lacking not only in wisdom, but in sanity?

XXXVIII. But I also add this: history does not testify that the Emperor Marcus <note>Marcus Aurelius, reigned 161–180 AD.</note> was devoted to Mages, or that he held them in high regard or in his retinue. *Xiphilinus* <note>A 11th-century epitomizer of Cassius Dio's Roman History.</note> says: *For it is not recorded that Marcus took pleasure in the company or the sorcery of magicians.* <note>original Greek: οὐδὲ γὰρ μάγων συνεσίαις καὶ γοητείᾳ ὁ Μάρκος χαίρειν ἱσόρηται.</note> On the contrary, Marcus himself testifies

<margin>Book 1, Section 6.</margin>
that he detested that class of men. For he says: *From Diognetus, I learned not to busy myself with vain things, and to be incredulous toward the stories told by miracle-mongers and sorcerers about incantations, the driving away of demons, and such things.* <note>The author provides both the original Greek and a Latin translation of Marcus Aurelius's "Meditations."</note> Nor should it be overlooked that this book was written, as he himself notes at the end, AMONG THE QUADI AT THE GRANUA <note>The Hron river in modern Slovakia.</note>, during that very same expedition of which we are now speaking. Rightly, therefore, did Scaliger <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger, a famous 16th-century scholar.</note> say: to pierce through the empty talk of Dio and Claudian, no weapon more effective than this testimony could be found, even if one were to exert all the force of their industry.

XXXIX. Since, therefore, it is not credible that Magic incantations were used, nor would they have been capable of achieving such a great thing if they had been used: it remains for us to conclude that the salvation of the Roman army was procured by the holy prayers of pious men. This, the Pagans do not deny, and our people <note>The Christians.</note> hold as certain. For both secular and sacred history provide evidence that rains were obtained by prayers in the past.

<margin>Stromata, Book VI, page 529 in my edition.</margin>
It is pleasing to explain this in the words of Clement of Alexandria, whose discourse on the subject follows: *When a long-lasting drought once afflicted Greece, and there was a great barrenness of crops, those who remained, it is said, coming as suppliants to Delphi because of the famine, asked the Pythia how—*

Whatever the Gentiles called religion was vain superstition; whatever they called piety and holiness was an artificial affectation; whatever they called virtue was a splendid and gilded vice. All of it was a corpse devoid of spirit. There is no piety without the knowledge and worship of God in Christ. No prayers are pleasing to God without faith in the Son of God. None are worthy of that name except those which the Spirit of grace and prayer has dictated to the faithful. Desist, as many of you as [deny] Christ...

XLI. It seems to remain, therefore, that we must confess this grace [the miracle] was owed to the *prayers of the Christian soldiers*. For whichever historians have narrated this miracle, they propose one of these three things: that it be attributed either to *Magic art*, to the *Emperor’s piety*, or to the *supplications of the Christians*. Since the first and second have been refuted, only this last one remains. This is what we must now derive and confirm.

<margin>
Baronius <note>Cesare Baronius (1538–1607), a cardinal and historian known for his "Annales Ecclesiastici."</note> on the year 108.

XLII. It is certainly established that *Christians* frequently *served as soldiers* around those times. Regarding *Trajan*, they report that when he was purifying the army according to the custom of the ancestors during the Eastern expedition, *ten thousand Christians* were found in it who refused to perform sacrifices to the gods. He separated them from the rest and banished them to *Armenia*, so that, marked by that ignominy, they might cease to be Christians. Likewise, we read of forty-six Christian soldiers beheaded at Rome under *Flavius Claudius* (who succeeded *Gallienus*) around the year of our Lord 269. Another sixty-five soldiers, reported for their Christianity, were ordered to be led outside the Salarian Gate under *Aurelian*; similarly, another fifty soldiers underwent a noble martyrdom in the *Roman Port* <note>Portus, the ancient harbor of Rome.</note> under the same *Aurelian*. And it is certain that *Maximian*, when he discovered to his surprise that his army was filled with Christian soldiers, burned with such hatred against them that, after countless numbers were slaughtered, he determined the army must be purged of them entirely, calling them enemies of the Gods. For he believed that Hercules—whom he worshipped above all others and from whom he took his surname so as to be called *Herculeus*—would be favorable to him only if the soldiers who spurned his divinity...

XLIII. Boldly, as is his custom, **Tertullian** <note>An influential early Christian author from Carthage, c. 155–220 AD</note> writes: *We are but of yesterday, and yet we have filled all the places you hold—cities, islands, forts, towns, marketplaces, THE CAMPS THEMSELVES.* When he says the camps were filled with Christians, he is certainly not speaking of camp-followers and servants, as some have liked to argue in jest, but of soldiers. To set aside countless other proofs, that single book which he titled *The Soldier’s Crown* <note>Latin: "De Corona Militis," a treatise discussing whether a Christian could serve in the army and wear a laurel wreath</note> proves this. The history he narrates at the beginning provided the occasion. Recently, he says, *the bounty of the most excellent Emperors was distributed.* These were *Lucius Septimius Severus the father, and Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Caracalla the son.* <note>Joint emperors from 198–211 AD</note> *The soldiers, wearing laurel wreaths, were being officially recorded in the camps. There was presented a certain* SOLDIER OF GOD, MORE STEADFAST THAN THE REST OF HIS BROTHERS, *who had presumed that he could serve two masters; he alone had his head bare, holding the wreath idly in his hand. After other details which would be tedious to relate:* HE ALONE WAS BRAVE AMONG SO MANY BROTHERS AND FELLOW SOLDIERS. Clearly, this soldier, about to receive his bonus, refused to wear the laurel on his head—something which other Christian soldiers had done before him, and were still doing even then. This act by the soldier, which became the occasion for a new persecution, was actually disapproved of by his fellow Christian soldiers. Tertullian defends it. Certainly, it appears from this that Christians were serving in the military at that time. And why is there a need for ambiguity? Let us hear the eloquent words of Tertullian: <margin>Apology, chapter 42</margin> *We sail with you, and* WE SERVE IN THE ARMY, *and we farm, and we trade; likewise, we join our arts and make our works public for your use.*

XLIV. I do not hide the fact that there is something in **Origen** <note>An early Christian scholar and theologian from Alexandria, c. 184–253 AD</note> from which you might conclude that Christians did not serve in the military in those times. For when *Celsus* <note>A 2nd-century Greek philosopher and opponent of Christianity</note> urged them to bring help to the Emperor with all their strength, and to wage just and pious wars under his leadership, and not to refuse military service if the situation demanded it; Origen responds in such a way that he openly admits his people refuse war, saying they fight not with arms, but with prayers. <margin>Book VIII, page 426 and following</margin> <note>original Greek: Ἡμεῖς καὶ μᾶλλον ὑπερμαχοῦμεν τοῦ Βασιλέως... κ.τ.λ.</note> *Thus we, more than others, fight for the Emperor: with him,* ALTHOUGH HE MAY URGE US, WE DO NOT SERVE AS SOLDIERS; *but for his sake we are drawn up—*

...we establish our own camps under the auspices of piety, conducting our affairs through prayers.

XLV. But the response is not at all difficult. The ancient Christians did not all hold the same view regarding military service. There were those who condemned or avoided it due to the circumstances of the times, which scarcely allowed military service to be practiced without certain acts that conflicted with Christian law. *Origen* <note>A prominent early Christian theologian (c. 185–253 AD) known for his pacifist leanings.</note> now aligns himself with their opinion. But this was not the universal consensus of the Church. In the *Constitutions* which bear the name of *Clement of Rome*, *Book VIII, chapter XXXII*, the text discusses those who were anciently accustomed to be admitted to baptism or rejected from it; and among other things, these words appear: <note>original Greek: Στρατιώτης προσιὼν διδασκέσθω... translated below</note> *A soldier requesting baptism should be taught to abstain from injuries and harassment, and to be content with his wages. If he obeys these things, let him be admitted.* <margin>Book IV, page 217.</margin> *Cyprian* <note>Bishop of Carthage, died 258 AD.</note> *writes of Laurentius and Ignatius of Africa: they themselves once served in secular camps, but as true and spiritual soldiers of God, while they overthrew the Devil by the confession of Christ, they earned the palms of the Lord and illustrious crowns through their suffering.* But even *Origen* is not entirely consistent with himself; elsewhere, while discussing the "government" of bees, he says: <note>original Greek: τάχα δὲ, inquit, καὶ οἱ οἱονεὶ πόλεμοι... translated below</note> **PERHAPS EVEN THE WARS OF BEES TEACH US TO WAGE WAR JUSTLY IF THE SITUATION SO REQUIRES.** It is clear enough from all these examples that Christians frequently served as soldiers, even at a time when the Emperors were not yet Christian.

XLVI. But if it seems too incredible to anyone that an entire *Legion* existed consisting solely of Christian soldiers, I do not wish to stubbornly oppose him, yet neither can I entirely agree. Nor does the total certainty of this narrative depend on the reliability of that single point. For the most ancient of the Elders who mention Christian soldiers do not praise a specifically *Christian Legion*. Not even the purported letters of the *Emperor* <note>Referring to the letter attributed to Marcus Aurelius regarding the miracle.</note> suggest this. Rather, they suggest the opposite. For if he ordered the Christians to be summoned, and only through an inquiry found a great number of them, they certainly were not all gathered into one single legion. Furthermore, by what fate did it happen that either all those of whom that legion was composed were touched by the spirit of Christianity, or that those who were Christians were all received under the same standard?

# THE THUNDERING LEGION OF THE CHRISTIANS.

### XLVII.

These things are not said without some appearance of truth; yet they are not of such a nature that nothing can be offered in reply. As for those letters <note>Referring to the purported correspondence of Emperor Marcus Aurelius regarding the "Thundering Legion."</note>, we shall soon indicate how much weight they should carry. When the most ancient Christian writers praise those soldiers, they do not explicitly say they belonged to a single Legion; however, they do not deny it either. Indeed, the fervor of the Christian Spirit at that time was so great that, like a sacred fire, it seized everything nearby. The faith of the Gospel, first conceived in the minds of a few, was like a leaven that in a short time permeated the entire mass. Suppose the *Primicerius* <note>The "First-on-the-List," a high-ranking administrative officer in a Roman legion.</note> of a Legion had given his faith to Christ and found many soldiers of the same sect; is it not credible that he sought out others like them, and that others who followed the same sacred rites flocked to him whenever the opportunity arose? Thus, little by little, if not entirely all, at least most became Christians.

### XLVIII.

In this manner, I believe, that famous *Theban Legion* was assembled, which served under the Emperors Diocletian and Maximian. As the *Acts* <note>The "Acts of the Martyrs," historical records of the trials and executions of early Christians.</note> teach us, it consisted of six thousand, six hundred and sixty-six soldiers, all Christians, who met their end through glorious martyrdom at the village of *Agaunum* <note>Modern-day Saint-Maurice, Switzerland.</note> because they refused to perform sacrifices to the Pagan Gods. *Eucherius* <note>Saint Eucherius of Lyon (c. 380–449 AD), who recorded the history of the Theban Legion.</note> wrote the history of this event copiously and eloquently. For our purpose, we shall extract these few details. When *Maximian* had ordered every tenth man to be killed by the officers—who easily executed the command as no one resisted—and after that punishment was carried out, he issued the same orders as before to the survivors; they all replied thus:

> We are indeed your soldiers, Caesar, and we have taken up arms for the defense of the *Roman* Republic. Never have we been deserters of wars, nor traitors to military service, nor have we deserved to undergo the punishment of cowardly fear. We would also obey your precepts, were we not instructed by Christian laws to avoid the worship of demons and altars polluted with blood.

By this speech, they protest that, however much they are Christians, they have refused no duties of military discipline.

### XLIX.

Furthermore, it is the duty of all Christians to apply themselves to Prayer. Who would doubt that this was the most frequent and sweetest exercise for soldiers also professing that name? Especially when they were about to go into battle, or when the atrocity of the danger inflamed their fervor. Nor did they pray for themselves and their own alone, but specifically for...

Do this, good Governors, wring out the soul that is supplicating God for the Emperor. This will be the "crime" where there is truth and devotion to God.*

This shall also be beneficial for us, so that leading a quiet and tranquil life, we may meanwhile promptly serve you in whatever is commanded.*

# THE THUNDERING LEGION OF CHRISTIANS

### LII.
Furthermore, it cannot be expressed how pleasing to Jehovah <note>The Latin text uses the Hebrew name for God</note> is that worship offered by his servants, who observe him alone, who are slain for the sake of his discipline, and who offer to him *not grains of incense worth a single penny, nor the tears of an Arabian tree <note>referring to myrrh or frankincense</note>, nor two drops of unmixed wine, nor the blood of a rejected ox wishing for death: but a rich and greater sacrifice, which he himself commanded—a prayer proceeding from a chaste body, from an innocent soul, and from the Holy Spirit.* I borrow these words again from the writings of Tertullian <note>An early Christian author (c. 155 – c. 220 AD) known for his defense of the faith</note>. There is a certain omnipotence in such prayers. There is nothing they are not able to obtain from God. They close and reopen heaven itself almost at their pleasure, and they draw the power of heaven to their side. No phalanx is more formidable to enemies than a troop of the faithful in prayer. *The effective prayer of a righteous man avails much: Elijah was a man subject to the same passions as we are, and he prayed most earnestly that it might not rain: and it did not rain on the earth for three years and six months. And he prayed again, and the heaven gave rain, and the earth produced its fruit.* James 5:16–18. At his prayers, fire descended from heaven more than once to consume his enemies. 2 Kings 1:10, 12. With these same weapons, Moses overcame the Amalekites. Exodus 17:11. With these, David obtained not only victory, but also earthquakes, smoke, fire, burning coals, whirlwinds, thunder, and lightning, by which—as if by the arrows of God—the King's enemies were laid low. Psalm 18:7–11. To speak briefly, the Lord of Heaven has granted this to his praying servants: *that if anyone wants to harm them, fire proceeds from their mouth and devours their enemies; for if anyone wants to harm them, he must be killed in this way. These have the power to shut heaven, so that it does not rain... and they have power over the waters, to turn them into blood, and to strike the earth with every plague, as often as they wish.* Revelation 11:5–6. While I do not believe these sayings should be understood entirely according to the literal sound of the words, I contend that it is clear from these metaphors how the elements themselves stand ready to aid the faithful whenever their necessity and the glory of God require it. Since, therefore, similar things were performed in the past at the prayers of the pious, and God promises no less for the future, why is it wrong to believe that praying Christians obtained both cold and fiery rains for the preservation of the Roman Emperor and his army?

### LIII.
And this is all the more likely because, after those times, not dissimilar events occurred elsewhere. From many such instances, I now produce three examples—
