In the city of Sebaste <note>modern Sivas, Turkey</note> in Armenia, forty soldiers obtained the crown of martyrdom. After the time of *Basil the Great*, *Gregory of Nyssa* celebrated their praises extensively in three orations. Among the other noble deeds performed by them, he relates one in his *Second Oration* which, although somewhat lengthy, I will not hesitate to transcribe word-for-word because of its great similarity to our own subject. Thus he writes:

*There was an ancient band of soldiers stationed near a neighboring city, serving as a defense for the entire nation against the attacks of the Barbarians. Because of a certain divine vision previously granted to them, their faith was held with greater zeal than even their military affairs and discipline. And perhaps it would not be untimely to mention in passing one particular outstanding deed of faith by those men. For when a war against the Barbarians broke out at one time, and all the advantageous positions had been seized by the enemy army—including the water supplies which were in their power—our men were reduced to extreme danger. This happened either through the lack of skill of our leaders, or by a better and more Divine plan and arrangement, so that it might clearly appear what a difference there is between Christians and those who are outsiders and strangers to the faith. When they could find no way to remedy their current situation, and there was great trembling and despair—since no spring appeared in that place, nor any means of obtaining water from elsewhere—there was a danger that, overcome by thirst, they would be subdued by their adversaries. Then those famous and excellent men, setting aside the protection of their weapons, turned their attention to an invincible aid that cannot be resisted in times of hardship. Leaving behind in the camp those who had not yet received the faith, and separating themselves, they imitated the miracle that took place in the time of the Prophet Elijah: with a common and joined voice, they sought through prayers to be rescued from the desperate circumstances into which they had fallen. And indeed, as they prayed, their prayers were immediately transformed into action. For while they were still persevering in prayer, a cloud gathered from elsewhere by a violent wind hung high in the air over the enemy camp. Then, thundering above with massive crashes and casting the fires of lightning down upon those below, it sent down water more violent than rivers; so much so that for the adversaries, both the continuous lightning and the force of the unceasing rain were the cause of utter destruction. But for these men, who had deployed the battle-line of prayer, the storm sufficed for both needs: for conquering the enemy and for the relief of their thirst, as the flowing torrents supplied them with drink in abundance.*

Thus far *Gregory*. Can one egg be more like another <note>a Latin idiom meaning "perfectly identical"</note> than this history is to our own?

54. LVI. He then understood what that vision signified, and said that **GOD FIGHTS FOR THE ROMANS.** Then indeed the admirable Ephrem <note>Saint Ephrem the Syrian (c. 306–373 AD), a prolific hymnodist and theologian</note>, who was the most eminent writer among the Syrians, asked the Divine Jacob <note>Saint Jacob of Nisibis, a leader at the Council of Nicaea</note> to climb onto the wall, look upon the Barbarians, and hurl the weapons of a curse against them. That wonderful man, complying with him, climbed a certain tower; and seeing the innumerable multitude of men, he prayed for no other evil upon them, but only that gnats and mosquitoes might be sent against them, so that from these tiny creatures they might recognize the power of Him who was helping [the Romans]. A cloud of gnats and mosquitoes immediately followed Jacob’s prayer. They filled the trunks of the elephants, which are hollow like tubes, as well as the ears and nostrils of the horses and the other beasts of burden. Since they could not endure the attack of such small creatures, they snapped their reins and began to throw off their riders; they threw the ranks into confusion, and abandoning the army, they fled at full speed. Since, therefore, in subsequent times the prayers of Christians have been like keys by which the barriers of lightning, winds, and rain have been unlocked, and unusual weapons twisted against the enemy, what reason can be given why we should deny that this happened in the time of Marcus Antoninus? <note>Emperor Marcus Aurelius (reigned 161–180 AD)</note>

# DISCOURSE ON THE LEGION

...he should remember the "Thundering" <note>original: *fulminatricis*</note>: namely, that *Twelfth* Legion which already existed under *Augustus*. For it is possible either that *Dio* <note>Dio Cassius, a Roman historian</note> retained the ancient surnames of the legions while disregarding this newer one; or even, as is the conjecture of *Baronius* <note>Cardinal Caesar Baronius, known for his ecclesiastical history</note>, that one legion was composed out of two "Thundering" Legions during the time of *Alexander Severus*, and the one recently honored with this name was added to the former. For the same *Dio* testifies in that same passage that legions exhausted of soldiers were sometimes mixed with others, and two were fused into one. Added to this is the observation of *Scaliger* <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger, a leading Renaissance scholar</note> that there is another Thundering Legion, distinct from both of these, mentioned by *Constantine Porphyrogenitus* <note>A 10th-century Byzantine Emperor and author</note>: *as the legion of the Martyrs was called the THUNDER-STRIKING, and another was the Pisidian.* <note>original Greek: ὡς ἡ λεγεὼν ἡ μ Μαρτύρων ἐλέγετο ΚΕΡΑΥΝΟΒΟΛΟΣ, καὶ ἄλλη Πισιδική.</note> Indeed, it is evident from the coins of *Goltzius* <note>Hubert Goltzius, a 16th-century numismatist</note> that there were six *Thundering* Legions, each distinguished by its own specific surnames.

LVIII. Furthermore, that which our writers have handed down concerning the letters of the Emperor Marcus to the Senate can hardly be considered a fable. Could such innate madness have existed in *Tertullian* <note>An early Christian author (c. 155–220 AD)</note>—a man of insight, seriousness, and gravity, well-versed in public life—that he would lie so magnificently about such a memorable event? Especially when witnesses were still living who could refute the lies, and in the presence of those who were otherwise accustomed to mocking and attacking Christians with insults for the slightest reason? He was, after all, pleading a most serious case, arguing for the truth of the Christian faith and the innocent lives of Christians. He would have known his cause was lost if he could be convicted of even a minor lie. He would have incurred the greatest charge of fraud if he had credited to his Christians a victory that had been won by the Emperor's own merits. Finally, he would have made himself a victim of public hatred, either as a defiler of divine and human trust or as a madman and a lunatic, by falsely appealing to those letters of the Emperor which the entire Senate and the Roman people knew had never existed in the nature of things.

LIX. However, because we believe such letters once existed, it is not necessary for us to think that those commonly seen today in the works of Blessed *Justin* <note>Justin Martyr, an early Christian apologist</note> are the genuine ones. For *Scaliger*, *Salmasius*, and *Huetius* easily gain our assent when they assert that those were forged by someone unlearned—not a Greek, but a semi-barbarian man. Evidently, since the true letters (which everyone believed existed or had existed) were not available to the public, someone decided to mock the credulity of others with this unfortunate substitution.

<meta>The catchword "LX." indicates the start of the next section on the following page.</meta>

# THE THUNDERING LEGION OF THE CHRISTIANS

LX. We conclude the same regarding the Emperor’s *Edict* in favor of the Christians. We certainly do not dare to apply it here, nor that history of *Eusebius* <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, a 4th-century historian often called the "Father of Church History."</note> which we discussed in *Thesis IX* for the reasons alleged above; nor that statement of *Ulpian* <note>Domitius Ulpianus, a celebrated Roman jurist.</note> concerning the *Jews*. It is as easy to demonstrate that this does not pertain to the matter at hand as it is to see that rain falls when it storms. For even if it were true that *Christians* were sometimes categorized alongside *Jews*, and that their religion was called a "superstition" or atheism <note>original: ἀθεϊσμὸν (atheism/godlessness)</note> by ethnic writers: it is nevertheless incredible that the Emperors, newly indebted to the *Christians* for a great benefit, would have wished to confuse them with the *Jews*, or that they would have failed to abstain from insults while recommending the Christians' cause to others. For under what pretense would they have traduced that Christian religion—which they had found so powerful for the preservation of themselves and the entire Roman army—with the hateful reproach of *Jewish superstition*?

LXI. But, what is the heart of the matter, it is not established that the authors of this rescript <note>A formal imperial response to a legal query.</note> were the "Divine Brothers" *Marcus Aurelius Antoninus* and *Lucius Verus*: for the best manuscripts read, *Severus* and *Antoninus*. This *Antoninus* is *Caracalla*, the son of *Severus*, who is entirely different from our subject. Logic also supports this: for in the rescripts of the Divine Brothers, we see *Antoninus* everywhere placed before Verus; whereas here, it is believed to be done otherwise without any cause. And even if it were established that our *Antoninus* was praised here with his brother *Verus*, it would still offer no protection to this cause. For whatever was ordered simultaneously by the *Divine Brothers* (as they are usually called in Roman Law), occurred at least five or four years before the miraculous storm-cloud, and consequently cannot have that miracle as its foundation. Indeed, the *Quadic War* <note>A conflict between the Roman Empire and the Germanic Quadi tribe.</note> fell in the 14th year of *Marcus*, as we warned above. However, *Verus* died of a stroke while sitting in a carriage with his brother in the 9th or at the latest the 10th year of *Marcus*. From this we conclude that the citation of that rescript is entirely irrelevant <note>original: ἀπροσδιόνυσον (unrelated/beside the point)</note>: and we agree with *Gothofredus* <note>Jacques Gothofredus, a prominent 17th-century jurist and editor of the Theodosian Code.</note>, who teaches that it should be understood as referring to *Jews* properly so called: since it is known elsewhere that men of any superstition could be promoted to the *Decurionate* <note>The rank or office of a city councilman (decurio) in the Roman Empire.</note>, and that the colleges of the *Jews* were sometimes approved and sometimes disapproved by the Emperors.

LXII. This interpretation is strengthened by the observation of *François Baudouin* <note>A 16th-century French jurist and historian.</note> in his learned book *On the Edicts of the Roman Princes concerning the Christians*, a copy of which was provided to me by that most kind and highly literate man—

ANSELMUS BENTHEM, *a friend of mine, and one of a rare sort. This*
*Baldwin <note>François Baudouin (1520–1573), a famous French jurist and historian.</note> therefore observes that the jurist Ulpian was of a mind quite hostile toward the Christians; according to the testimony of Lactantius <note>An early Christian author (c. 250 – c. 325) who became an advisor to Constantine I.</note>, Ulpian collected the wicked decrees of the emperors in seven books regarding the "Office of the Proconsul," so that he might teach what punishments ought to be inflicted upon those who confessed themselves to be worshipers of God.*
*It is believable that the occasion for this collection was as follows: Ulpian guided Alexander Severus <note>Roman Emperor from 222 to 235 AD.</note>, and in his name gave mandates to the proconsuls about to depart for the provinces. But when he saw that the Emperor was not estranged from the Christians—or was certainly shrinking back from their blood—and could scarcely be impelled to issue any edict concerning their extermination, Ulpian seems to have presented the old decrees of impious tyrants to the Proconsuls, so that they might judge their own duty in this matter by those precedents. These books of Domitius [Ulpian] regarding the office of the Proconsul no longer survive. Many fragments of them remain, however, in the Pandects <note>The Digest or Pandects, a compendium of juristic writings compiled by order of Justinian I.</note>; but in these, there is not a single word concerning the Christians. One passage exists from the third book, where this decree of Severus and Antoninus <note>Septimius Severus and his son Caracalla.</note>—which we are discussing—is praised, by which Jews are permitted to attain honors <note>Public offices or magistracies.</note>. When Baldwin had reported these things, he began thus: "Did Ulpian record this specifically to further gall the Christians? Just as the Emperor Julian is said to have favored the Jews out of hatred for the Christians." Since Ulpian was entirely devoted to collecting those things which were adverse to the Christians in order to harass them, while spitefully suppressing those things that were favorable, it is not probable that this which he wished to reveal concerning the Jews pertained to the Christians.*

LXIII. However, it is certain that the favor of the Emperors Severus and
<margin>On Daniel 11.</margin>
Antoninus toward the Jews was great: so much so that, according to the testimony of Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, the translator of the Vulgate Bible.</note>, certain of the Hebrews understood those words of Daniel which appear in Chapter 11:34—*And when they shall fall, they shall be helped with a small help*—as referring to the Princes Severus and Antoninus, who loved the Jews very much. Yet this was not always the case. It is clear from Spartianus <note>One of the authors of the Augustan History.</note> that the Palestinians were punished by Severus because they had stood in arms for a long time on the side of Niger <note>Pescennius Niger, a rival claimant to the throne.</note>; but the same author also testifies that *Severus remitted the punishment to the Palestinians which they had deserved on account of Niger's cause.* Furthermore, since a punishment had been inflicted upon them, they had fallen from the right of Roman citizenship; the remission of the punishment is the restoration of that right.

Petitus <note>Samuel Petit (1594–1643), a French scholar.</note> indeed doubts whether the Jews are understood by the name "Palestinians," nor does it please us to contend the point. This much is established: in the ninth year of Severus, the Jews were harassed by war; for which reason the Senate decreed a Jewish triumph for Antoninus. And when he returned to Rome, in the tenth year of his reign—

# THE THUNDERER OF THE CHRISTIANS. 461.

In the tenth year <note>10th year of the reign of Septimius Severus, approx. 202 AD</note>, under the consulship of Severus himself (for the third time) and Antoninus Augustus, he forbade anyone from becoming a Jew or a Christian under heavy penalty while on his journey. However, Severus seems to have changed his mind regarding the Jews, and as much as he previously hated them, he later loved them: to the extent that he permitted Jews to obtain honors by a public edict. But perhaps we have discussed these matters regarding that fragment of Ulpian <note>Domitius Ulpianus, a famous Roman jurist</note> a bit too extensively. It is time for us to return to our intended subject.

LXIV. Nevertheless, simply because these points do not strongly prove the Emperor's Edict was in favor of the Christians, it does not mean the entire story of the Edict is a fiction. For Tertullian <note>An early Christian author from Carthage</note> would not have dared to falsely claim its existence just a few years later, at the very beginning of the persecution that occurred under Severus's rule—especially in public writings, some of which were given to be read by the Roman *Overseers* <note>original: "Antistites", referring to Bishops</note>, and others to *Scapula*, the proconsul of *Asia*.

LXV. But, you will say, the very light of history refutes an Edict of that kind: since in the seventeenth year of Marcus <note>Marcus Aurelius</note>, a more violent persecution was stirred up against the Christians, which, according to the testimony of Eusebius, *Book 5, Chapter 1*, produced almost innumerable martyrs throughout the whole world. However, this difficulty can be resolved in more than one way. First, there is a significant suspicion that Eusebius's numbers are in error, and that instead of the seventeenth year, he either wrote, or at least should have written, the seventh year. *Ado of Vienne, Chronicle: Book 6, Chapter 15*, says those heavy persecutions in *Asia* and *Gaul* occurred *in the days of the Parthian War*. Regarding the Parthians, a triumph was celebrated at Rome in the Year of our Lord 166, which is the 6th year of Marcus according to the calculation of *Blondel, in "Defense of the opinion of Jerome on Bishops and Presbyters" Section 2, Chapter 9*. Whatever the case may be, it is certain that the German war is more recent than the Parthian one. For *Capitolinus* <note>One of the authors of the Augustan History</note> says: *While the Parthian war was being waged, the Marcomannic war was born, which was delayed for a long time by the skill of those present, so that the Marcomannic war could be conducted once the Eastern war was finished.* Add to this, from the *Roman Martyrology for June 2nd*, regarding the Holy Martyrs of Lyon, Bishop Pothinus and others: *that there were brave and repeated struggles in the time of Marcus Aurelius Antoninus and Lucius Verus.* However, we just noted that Verus died in the 9th or 10th year of Marcus. From this it is inferred that the persecution which took away Pothinus, and which Eusebius narrates in the mentioned place, did not finally break out in the 17th year of Marcus, but before the 9th year—five years before the German victory: consequently, it cannot be used as an argument against the edict of Marcus <note>The author is arguing that the persecution happened earlier than usually cited, thus not contradicting a later edict of tolerance</note>.

# DISCOURSE ON THE LEGION

<margin>Page 86.</margin>
LXVI. But let us be generous. Let us grant to *Valois* <note>original: "Vallesio"; Henri Valois, a 17th-century scholar known for editing ecclesiastical histories</note> that the chronological numbers in *Eusebius* <note>The "Father of Church History"</note> have not been corrupted, and that the persecution was indeed renewed in the *seventeenth year of Marcus Aurelius*. Nevertheless, I deny that it follows that no Edict was issued by *Marcus* on behalf of the Christians. For the fact that the Christians did not gather the hoped-for fruits from this rescript <note>A formal imperial response to a legal query</note> must be attributed to the cruelty of the Proconsuls, Governors, Procurators, and Judges, and to the madness of the impious common people. These groups, having sought out other pretexts—or rather, mere colors of legality—raged against the innocent and well-deserving: *Like unto wild boars* <note>original Greek: Ἀγροτέροισι σύεσσιν ἐοικότες</note>. Let *Balduinus* <note>François Baudouin, a renowned 16th-century jurist</note> speak for me again: *No edicts of the Roman princes,* he says, *were more despised than those which seemed to favor the Christians.* And elsewhere: *The Christians usually found the Emperors themselves to be more fair-minded, but they had the Senate, the Magistrates, and the Jurists as harsher adversaries. For even if the execution and protection of imperial mandates intended to defend the Christian community were entrusted to them, they nevertheless evaded such mandates as much as they could.* *Eusebius* himself teaches in so many words that that persecution arose *from the attacks of the populaces in individual cities* <note>original Greek: ἐξ ἐπιθέσεως τῶν κατὰ τὰς πόλεις δήμων</note>.

<margin>Page 16.</margin>
LXVII. Nor are examples lacking where the common people and lesser magistrates raged against the Christians despite the edicts of Emperors prohibiting it in vain. It is well established from *Melito* <note>Bishop of Sardis</note> in *Eusebius's Church History, Book IV, Chapter XXVI*, and from the records of *Justin* <note>Justin Martyr</note> which still survive, that *Hadrian* (the grandfather of our *Marcus*) wrote letters in favor of the Christians to many others and specifically to *Fundanus*, the Proconsul and Governor of *Asia*. Furthermore, *Antoninus Pius* (the Father), during the time when *Marcus* was administering all affairs together with him, forbade any innovations <note>legal changes or new persecutions</note> regarding them. Yet, the persecution of Christians did not cease because of this. This is proved by that invective of *Justin* against malignant judges: *Apology II, p. 55. You do not conduct trials with a legitimate examination, but driven headlong by irrational passion, and incited by the whips of malignant spirits as if by furies, you inflict punishments without the case being judged, having no regard for justice.* And there is the complaint of *Melito*, in the place cited above: *For,* he says, *that which had never happened before, the race of godly men now suffers persecution, harassed throughout Asia by new decrees. For the most impudent informers and those greedy for the wealth of others, having snatched an opportunity from the imperial edicts (those ancient ones, which were adverse to the Christians—*

(they were involved) they roam openly day and night, plundering innocent men. If these things are done by your command, let them be considered rightly and properly done. <note>The author suggests that the writer of this petition did not believe the Emperor actually authorized such cruelty.</note> He did not think, therefore, that such unjust and bitter things were happening by the will or command of the Emperor.

LXVIII. The primary cause of this savagery was that the Christians were already condemned by the hatred of the human race, viewed as enemies of the Gods and the authors of all the evils pressing upon the Republic. Furthermore, the monstrous acts of the Gnostics <note>A diverse group of early religious thinkers often deemed heretical by the mainstream Church.</note> and the shameful deeds of other heretics were falsely attributed to all Christians through slander. The report of these things had spread so widely that, setting aside the more merciful decrees of the Emperors, provincial judges considered the mere name of "Christian" sufficient grounds for punishment. But why do I hesitate to relate the very words of the people of Lyon and Vienne, in which they clearly explain the cause of the cruelty exercised against them? They say:

<margin>Eusebius, Book 5, Chapter 1</margin>
> Certain of our servants who were Gentiles <note>Non-Christians</note> were also captured, since the Governor had openly ordered all of us to be sought out. These servants, driven by a demon and fearing the tortures they saw the saints enduring—and with the soldiers inciting them to this very end—falsely invented accusations against us. They claimed we held "Thyestean feasts" <note>A reference to Greek mythology where a father is fed his own children; here it implies ritual cannibalism.</note> and "Oedipal incests" <note>A reference to the myth of Oedipus; here it implies incestuous relations during secret meetings.</note>, and other things which it is not lawful for us to speak or think of, and which we cannot even believe were ever committed among men. Once these rumors were spread among the common people, everyone immediately became so enraged against us that even those who had previously been moderate toward us due to kinship now roared with the most bitter indignation.

<margin>Book 9, Chapter 5</margin>
LXIX. Eusebius recorded that the same things occurred during the reign of Maximinus. For a certain commander in Damascus, a city of Phoenicia, after seizing some disreputable women from the marketplace, threatened them with torture. He drove the wretched women to testify publicly in the official records that they had once been Christians and were privy to the crimes committed by Christians. They asserted that Christians perpetrated obscene acts in their very sacred buildings, along with whatever else the commander wanted them to babble to defame our religion. The testimony of these women was inserted into the Acts <note>Official government records.</note> and sent to the Emperor; by the Prince's command, they were published in every city and public place. From this, the flight of Christians and the most bitter persecutions began anew, as the governors of the provinces rose up sharply against them.

# DISCOURSE ON THE LEGION

### 70.
But what, finally, shall we say concerning that famous column <note>The Column of Marcus Aurelius in Rome, which depicts the "Miracle of the Rain."</note>? How could the Emperor have attributed the victory to the prayers of the Christians when, on a public and lasting monument, he credited *Jupiter the Rain-maker* <note>original: "Jovi Pluvio"</note>? This argument is difficult, I confess, yet I do not believe it is unsolvable. However much *Marcus* <note>Emperor Marcus Aurelius</note> professed himself indebted to the Christians, he did not, for all that, become a Christian himself. He remained in ignorance of the true God and in the worship of false deities. He was exactly like *Nebuchadnezzar*, *Cyrus*, *Darius* (more than one of that name), and *Artaxerxes* in the books of Daniel and Ezra; although these kings issued magnificent decrees in favor of the God of Israel elsewhere, they remained immersed in their own superstitions and repeatedly fell back into the worship and praise of gods who are no gods at all.

In the same manner, our Emperor, wishing a monument to exist for such a memorable event, had never seen any other image of the God who commands the rains within the Roman Empire except that of *Jupiter the Rain-maker*. Since the God of the Christians—who forbade all such images of Himself—possesses no specific image of His own, it is not surprising that the rain-bringing God, whoever He truly was, was expressed by a Gentile Emperor under the sign of Jupiter the Rain-maker.

Since the Emperor was a Philosopher, he himself likely regarded this carving as nothing more than an emblem of the Divinity insofar as He presides over rains and lightning. For he had learned from the Stoic discipline <note>A school of Hellenistic philosophy that taught that God and nature were closely linked.</note> that there is one God, to whom (as *Seneca* says in *On Benefits*, Book 4, Chapter 7) *you may properly apply whatever names you wish, provided they contain some force or effect of heavenly things: He may have as many titles as He has functions.*

But it is better to hear *Antoninus* <note>Marcus Aurelius Antoninus</note> himself in Book 7, Section 9 <note>of his *Meditations*</note>: *For there is both one world through all things, AND THERE IS ONE GOD THROUGH ALL THINGS.* <note>original Greek: "κόσμοϚ τε γὰρ εἷς διὰ ἁπάντων, ΚΑΙ ΘΕΟΣ ΕΙΣ ΔΙΑ ΠΑΝΤΩΝ."</note> Yet, because he was an Emperor and a politician seeking popular favor, he did not wish to offend a people enslaved to superstitions with unfamiliar images of a foreign and hated God. You might rightly apply here the words of *Lactantius* <note>An early Christian author (c. 250 – c. 325 AD) often called the "Christian Cicero."</note> from Book 1, Chapter 11: *When they are convicted of the existence of one God and cannot deny it, they claim that they themselves worship Him; but they say it pleases them that He be named Jupiter.*

Let these things now be said for the vindication of our God and His people.

The Priesthood belonged to Aaron alone and to his sons. 138
Who was *Abenephius*? <note>Likely referring to the Arab author Ibn Wahshiyya, often cited in 17th-century works on Egyptian antiquities.</note> His testimony concerning *Thammuz* <note>A Mesopotamian deity associated with fertility and mourning.</note>. 67. 68. and concerning the *Teraphim* <note>Household idols or cult images mentioned in the Bible.</note>. 72. Likewise on the rites of the *Hebrews*. 285

The Abomination of the *Egyptians*. 62. 63.

His readiness in offering his son is not obscured by any previous example among the *Egyptians*. 229. etc. The opinion of *Philo the Jew* <note>A Hellenistic Jewish philosopher from Alexandria.</note> regarding that deed. 230.
*Abraham* is the same as *Saturn* to *Sanchuniathon* <note>A Phoenician author whose works survive in fragments; the text here links biblical patriarchs to pagan mythology.</note>. 231. The objections of *Marsham* <note>Sir John Marsham, a contemporary chronicler of Egyptian history.</note> are answered. 232. He was to be venerated by the *Canaanite* and *Egyptian* Kings and Sages. 264. 265.
The opinion of the *Kabbalists* <note>Followers of Jewish mysticism.</note> is that the soul of *Adam* migrated into *David*, and from there would migrate into the *Messiah*. 15. The immortality of the soul was known to him. 178. 179. That his name was known in *Asia*

is gathered by *Vossius* <note>Gerardus Vossius, a noted Dutch scholar and humanist.</note> from the city of *Adana*. 463
*Adonis* is the same as *Osiris* and *Thammuz*. The ceremonies in his worship. 66. He was also taken to represent the *Sun*. 67
